This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the <term>public domain: Creative works that are no longer protected by intellectual property laws, allowing the public to use them freely.</term> A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other <term>marginalia: Notes, sketches, or comments written in the margins of a book by its previous owners or readers.</term> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

### Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on <term>automated querying: The use of software scripts or "bots" to automatically download or search large amounts of data without human intervention.</term>

We also ask that you:

+ **Make non-commercial use of the files** We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ **Refrain from automated querying** Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition <note>original: "OCR," the process of converting images of typed or handwritten text into machine-encoded text.</note> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ **Maintain attribution** The Google “watermark” <note>A faint, identifying image or text overlaid on the digital page to show its source.</note> you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ **Keep it legal** Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

I will not delay those about to embark on this long journey by recounting how many rough patches <note>original: "salebrae"</note> I had to overcome, how many gaps and pits had to be filled, or how many obstacles had to be removed. However, I cannot help but warn readers not to assume that my labor has made the path too easy or entirely clear for them. 

Besides the Basel edition <note>original: "exemplar Basileense"</note>—which was the only one available and was most poorly printed—published by Simon Grynaeus <note>A German scholar (1493–1541) known for publishing Greek texts</note> from a British manuscript in 1534 along with the works of Plato, I had access to only one manuscript. This volume was formerly held in the Augsburg library <note>original: "Augustanae bibliothecae"</note>. The scholar Eschenbach, who lacked a printed copy, noted that this manuscript was shared with him for his work on *Epigenes* (pages 72 and 104). It is now held in Munich as No. 382 <note>original: "Monacensis numero 382"</note>. It is a paper <term>codex</term> <note>A "codex" is a manuscript in book form rather than a scroll</note> of the largest format, written <note>original: "exaratus"</note> in the fifteenth century, as Ignaz von Hardt writes in his *Aretini Symbolis* (Vol. 8, Page 206). It consists of 479 leaves <note>original: "foliis"</note> with full pages of thirty lines each, containing about fifty letters per line. This manuscript is somewhat more accurate than the Basel edition, though it appears to be derived from a similar source.

Furthermore, I made use of a Latin translation supplied by the Rehdiger Library in Wroclaw <note>original: "Vratislaviensi Rehdigerana"</note> covering the section from page 416 to 557 of this edition. This translation was made from a manuscript with more words than necessary <note>original: "iusto verbosius"</note> but not at all unskillfully by Niccolò Leonico Tomeo <note>An Italian scholar (1456–1531) who was among the first to teach the original Greek text of Aristotle in Padua</note>, of whom I spoke in the preface to my winter lectures of 1841. It was first published in a book with the following title: 

*The Minor Works of Niccolò Leonico Tomeo, recently brought to light, the names of which are held on the following page. With privilege. <note>A "privilege" was an early form of copyright granted by a sovereign or the Church</note> These names are: Paraphrase of Aristotle's short commentary on the motion of animals. Paraphrase of the same philosopher’s booklet on the gait of animals. Certain natural questions, with twenty amatory problems. A translation of the Mechanical Questions of Aristotle, with figures and certain annotations.* <note>original titles: "Paraphrasis in commentariolum Aristotelis de animalium motione. Paraphrasis in eiusdem philosophi libellum de animalium incessu. Quaestiones quaedam naturales, cum amatoriis problematibus .xx. Conversio Mechanicarum quaestionum Aristotelis..."</note>

# **Proclus of Lycia’s** explanation of Plato’s *Timaeus* where it treats the generation of souls, translated into Latin, with a complex figure of numbers and harmonies. 

->The title of the translation itself is: *A translation of Plato from the Timaeus on the generation of souls, with the explanation and digression of Proclus the Lycian.*<- 

At the end, however, is the following subscription: *This small work was reproduced from print by Bernardinus Vitalis of Venice in the Year of our Lord 1525, on the 23rd day of February. From Venice.* The format of the book is square; the total number of leaves is 139, of which 63 contain the passage from Proclus. 

Finally, for the interpretation of the entire Commentary, I have made use of the English translation published by Thomas Taylor in London in the year 1820, in two large volumes under this title: *The commentaries of Proclus on the Timaeus of Plato, in five books; containing a treasury of Pythagoric and Platonic physiology. Translated from the Greek, by Thomas Taylor.* If he achieved this by his own efforts <note>original: "Marte suo rem gessit" — a Latin idiom meaning to do something by one's own skill or strength</note> (for after reading the entire work, I began to greatly doubt those things which I had partially conjectured in the preface to the winter lectures of 1842 regarding Taylor’s admirable sagacity or his harmony of thought and feeling with Proclus), it is a miracle how successfully he sometimes attained the hidden meaning of Proclus—and even corrected corrupted words—despite such ignorance of the Greek language. 

With these aids, I confess that I have been unable to fulfill that which is demanded of an editor: either to present the very hand of the writer, or, having perceived his mind, to demonstrate what he seems to have written. Indeed, I do not know if I could have provided much more even if I had been supplied with many more resources. Certainly, neither the four Parisian manuscripts <note>original: "codices"</note>, of which Simon the Swiss <note>original: "Simo Helvetius," likely referring to Simon Grynaeus, the scholar mentioned on the previous page</note> spoke in the introduction of the booklet (cited on page 156 of this edition), nor those which were at hand for Leonico Thomaeo <note>Niccolò Leonico Tomeo (1456–1531), an Italian scholar who taught Greek at Padua</note>, if there were more than one...

---

*) Along with Thomaeus and many others, we have also named him **Proclus**, not unmindful of those whom Lobeck <note>Christian August Lobeck (1781–1871), a German classical scholar</note> in *Aglaophamus* (Page 115) teaches that he should be named **Proculus**, just as Lobeck himself does. However, we believe that the persona of the man—who was undoubtedly Greek, being both born among Greeks and conducting himself as a Greek throughout his whole life, and never held for anything but a Greek—should be considered more than his Latin lineage. Therefore, we preferred that form of the name by which you would recognize a Greek, especially since we saw it approved by the analogy of the name *Patroclus* and by the usage of writers such as Tertullian (whose passage Fabricius recorded in the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, Vol. 8, Page 461) and by the common custom of philologists.

<meta>This page continues the editor’s critical evaluation of the primary sources used for this edition. After discussing Thomas Taylor’s 19th-century English translation on the preceding page, the editor now compares the physical manuscripts—specifically those from Munich and Vienna—and the 1534 Basel printed edition, explaining his methodology for correcting errors and handling variations in the text.</meta>

...were more intact than our Munich manuscript <note>original: "Monacensis"</note> seems to be; the Vienna manuscript <note>original: "Vindobonensis"</note>, however, which I mentioned in the note on page 644, suffers from both the same disorder in that passage as the Basel copy and from interpolation <note>the unauthorized insertion of foreign material into a text</note>. But nevertheless, the work of correction had to be begun at some point, so that these most useful matters would not be absent from literature forever; and it seemed possible to begin with the resources I have indicated, in such a way that foundations were laid upon which others might later build what was necessary to complete the work. 

Those who approve of this plan will not look down upon my diligence in recording the readings of the Munich manuscript and the Basel edition as useless—though I knowingly omitted several errors and instances of the "movable nu" <note>original: "ν ἐφελκυστικοῦ" — a Greek grammatical feature where the letter 'n' is added to the end of a word to avoid a clash of vowels</note> placed before a consonant in the second part of the book, as well as infinite faults of punctuation. Nor will they take it badly that space was granted to nearly all the variant readings of Thomaeus <note>referring to Nicolaus Leonicus Thomaeus, the 1525 translator</note> and the commentaries of Taylor, if they consider that otherwise future critics could not be provided for, nor the burden of comparing those books removed. 

But perhaps some will accuse me of inconsistency <term>levitatis: literally "lightness," referring here to a lack of uniform editorial rigor</term> when they see some errors corrected within the text itself, while others equally obvious are only noted with an indication of a conjecture—and that varied in different places. The reason for this inequality is that some errors could be corrected with certainty, while others could not be corrected without greater or lesser hesitation. 

In the <term>lemmata: the snippets of Plato’s original text that Proclus is commenting upon</term>, however, I corrected nothing based on conjecture, however obvious it was. This is because most of these existing excerpts seemed not to have been placed there by the author of the commentary himself [Proclus], but were instead supplied by some later reader from a manuscript of Plato. The text of such a manuscript, which was perhaps corrupt, should not be restored to the "truth"—that is, to the exact words of Plato that Proclus would have originally used—unless supported by one of the source books. Moreover, in cases of discrepancy between them, it was right to prefer that which came closer to the truth. 

By a similar reasoning, in the words of Proclus himself, where it seemed he might have written a phrase in either of two ways, I did not simply follow the Munich manuscript (which, though better, was not of such supreme excellence). Instead, I wrote in such a way that each choice was more probable in itself and more consistent with Platonic usage, which Proclus generally follows. Nevertheless, regarding the infinitive ending in *-an* [ᾶν] <note>a Greek verb ending</note>, I have added the iota <note>the "iota subscript," a small mark under a vowel</note> which Plato and his contemporaries seem to have used, just as in the age of Proclus...

<meta>This page continues the editor’s explanation of his editorial choices, specifically addressing orthography (spelling) and the correction of Greek accents. ...of inconsistency <term>levitas</term> <note>original: "levitati"</note> for having removed the iota subscript <term>iota subscript</term> <note>A small Greek letter 'iota' written under a vowel (ᾳ, ῃ, ῳ) to indicate an ancient sound that had become silent by the medieval period.</note>, which has for a long time now been customarily omitted. I was not particularly moved by the authority of the manuscript, which usually adds it, because it was added not only to dative-like forms <note>original: "δοτικοφανῆ"</note>—which do not seem to have possessed it even in Plato’s own age—but also to other words that never could have had it. For example, it was written with the letter *eta* <note>the Greek long 'e'</note> in "examined" <note>original: "ἐξητασμένας"</note> (1, 41), "unmoved" <note>original: "ἀτρεμῇ"</note> (92, 32), "unmixed" <note>original: "ἀμιγῇ"</note> (131, 7), and "sympathetic" <note>original: "συμπαθῇ"</note> (245, 28); and with the letter *omega* <note>the Greek long 'o'</note> in "further" <note>original: "πόῤῥῳ"</note> (17, 7) and "nearer" <note>original: "ἐγγυτέρῳ"</note> (55, 21 and 244, 49). 

I did not hesitate to correct the accents that were often placed incorrectly in both books. I now see there was not enough reason why I should not have corrected—rather than merely noted—the words "cooling" <note>original: "ψύξις"</note> (146, 51) and "mixing" <note>original: "μίξις"</note> (218, 23) and elsewhere, especially since I had written "mixing" <note>original: "μῖxis"</note> (49, 9) correctly myself, and "mixture" <note>original: "μῖγμα"</note> (204, 10 and 213, 3) was even written correctly in the manuscript. Therefore, let these things be corrected. Furthermore, in the annotation for page 83, line 22, let it be added that C. E. A. Schmidt—a professor at the Stettin gymnasium—in his dissertation on the restoration of Plato’s *Timaeus* from the commentaries of Proclus (published in 1842, page 26), judged that the word "something" <note>original: "τι"</note>, which the Munich manuscript omits, should indeed be omitted, and that the word "wherefore" <note>original: "διὸ"</note>, in which both books agree, should be changed to "because" <note>original: "διότι"</note>; he did not, however, demonstrate in what sense those obscure words were spoken.

In the index, which I have called an "index of matters"—not using the term "matters" <note>original: "res"</note> as Proclus is accustomed to do (for the studious reader must seek a view of those matters from the book itself), but as we commonly use the term for concrete things—I have recorded everything that pertains to history, and especially to the history of literature. This was done so that it might be of interest even to those who care less for the philosophical doctrines of Proclus. In these entries, I have given primary consideration to Plato and his sayings. I have intentionally omitted many mentions of the gods which serve more to explain Proclus's own theology than to help one understand the mythology of the Greeks. The numbers and letters that I have used in the index, as well as in the margins of the book, refer to the pages and the tens of lines in the Basel edition <note>the influential 1534 printed edition</note>.

Finally, if there are any who shall be grateful for this work of ours, let them share that gratitude with Eichhorn <note>Johann Albrecht Friedrich von Eichhorn (1779–1856), a high-ranking Prussian official and supporter of the arts</note>, an excellent man and a friend of our King, by whose kindness and support this book has come forth into the public.

He concludes the preface by thanking his patron, the Prussian official von Eichhorn.</summary>

# PROCLUS THE SUCCESSOR ON PLATO’S TIMAEUS
## BOOK 1.

---

<margin>1</margin> It is clear to me—at least to those who are not entirely blinded to reason—that the purpose <note>original: "πρόθεσις"</note> of Plato’s *Timaeus* encompasses the whole of natural philosophy <term>physiologia</term> <note>In the Neoplatonic tradition, this refers to the study of the physical world as an expression of divine principles.</note>, and that it pertains to the theory of the universe, treating this subject from beginning to end. Indeed, the very writing of the Pythagorean Timaeus <note>Proclus refers to a work attributed to Timaeus of Locri, which Neoplatonists believed was the Pythagorean source Plato used for his dialogue.</note> is organized according to the Pythagorean method regarding nature. Starting from that basis, Plato attempted to "write his Timaeus," as the satirist <note>original: "σιλλογράφον"</note> <note>This refers to Timon of Philius, a skeptical poet who joked that Plato bought a Pythagorean book to use as his source material.</note> says. We have established this at the very start of these commentaries so that we might be able to recognize which parts of Plato's *Timaeus* say the same things as that work, which parts he added, and which parts are in disagreement, so that we may investigate the cause of such disagreement with proper care. 

<margin>B</margin> This entire dialogue has as its goal the study of nature throughout its whole, observing the same principles in images <note>original: "εἰκόσι"</note> and in models <note>original: "παραδείγμασιν"</note>, and in both wholes and parts. For it has been filled with all the most beautiful definitions of natural philosophy, taking up simple things for the sake of the complex, parts for the sake of the whole, and images for the sake of their models, leaving nothing unexamined among the primary causes of nature. 

That the dialogue addresses such a purpose worthily, and that Plato alone—having preserved the Pythagorean character of the theory of nature—finely crafted the teaching before us, is something that the more sharp-witted readers must now consider. For natural philosophy is divided into three parts, to speak concisely: one part is occupied with matter <note>original: "ὕλη"</note> and material causes; the second adds the investigation of form <note>original: "εἶδος"</note> and declares this to be the more primary cause; <margin>C</margin> while the third part demonstrates that these former two do not possess the status of "causes" but rather "co-causes" <note>original: "συναιτίων"</note>, and it posits other factors as the primary causes of things that come to be by nature: the efficient <note>original: "ποιητικόν"</note>, the exemplary <note>original: "παραδειγματικόν"</note>, and the final <note>original: "τελικόν"</note> causes. Most of the natural philosophers before Plato spent their time on matter...

---

<note>1, 1: The goal of the dialogue; note from the margin of Manuscript A.</note> 
<note>1, 3: "Into" (εἰς); the Basel edition uses the form "ἐς".</note> 
<note>1, 7: "The satirist"; Manuscript A specifies "Timon".</note> 
<note>1, 17: "Teaching" (διδασκαλίαν); Manuscript B uses a variant spelling.</note> 
<note>1, 18: "Threefold" (τριχῇ); Manuscript A uses a variant accent.</note> 
<note>1, 19: "Declaring" (ἀποφαινομένης); Manuscript A uses a different case ending.</note>

<summary>Proclus introduces his commentary by arguing that Plato’s Timaeus is a complete study of the natural world based on Pythagorean principles. He outlines three levels of natural philosophy, moving from basic matter to the "primary causes" (Efficient, Exemplary, and Final) that Plato focuses on.</summary>

<keywords>Proclus, Plato, Timaeus, natural philosophy, Pythagoreanism, efficient cause, exemplary cause, final cause, matter, form</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’ introduction to his commentary on the *Timaeus*. Here, he begins to contrast Plato’s comprehensive approach to causality with the more limited views of his predecessors and successors.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...one thing, while others say the subject matter <note>original: "ὑποκείμενον"; referring to the underlying substance or "substrate" of the world</note> is another. For indeed, even Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who famously introduced the concept of Mind (Nous) as the ordering force of the cosmos.</note>, who seems—while the others were sleeping—to have been the first to see Mind as the primary cause of things that come to be, makes no use of Mind in his actual explanations. Instead, he blames certain "airs" and "ethers" for what happens, just as Socrates says in the *Phaedo* <note>original: "Φαίδωνι"; referencing Plato's *Phaedo* 98c, where Socrates expresses disappointment that Anaxagoras didn't explain *how* Mind acts for the best.</note>. 

Those who led the school <term>hairesis</term> <note>Referring here to the Peripatetics or followers of Aristotle.</note> after Plato—not all of them, but at least the more accurate ones—also deemed it worthy for the natural philosopher to contemplate the Form <term>eidos</term> along with the Matter <term>hyle</term>, reducing the principles of bodies to matter and form. For even if they happen to mention the "efficient cause" <note>The "maker" or "producer" of a thing.</note>, such as when they call "nature" <term>physis</term> a principle of motion, they rather strip it of its active and truly creative character. They do not allow for there to be rational plans <note>original: "λόγους" (logoi)</note> in nature for the things it produces, but instead allow many things <margin>D</margin> to happen spontaneously. Furthermore, they do not simply admit that an efficient cause exists for all natural things, but only for those caught in the flow of "generation" <note>Things that are born and die in the physical world.</note>. Regarding eternal things, they explicitly say there is no efficient cause. In this, they fail to notice that they are either constructing the whole heaven from chance <note>original: "ταὐτομάτου"</note> or declaring that the "spontaneous" is what produces itself.

But Plato alone, following the Pythagoreans, provides the "co-causes" <note>Supporting factors that aren't the primary cause.</note> of natural things—namely, that which is "all-receiving" <note>Matter, or the Receptacle.</note> and the "material form"—which serve the primary causes in the process of birth. Before these, however, he investigates the primary, creative causes: the Maker, the Model <term>paradeigma</term>, and the End <term>telos</term> <note>The "End" is the goal or purpose (The Good).</note>. Because of this, he sets over the whole a creative Mind <note>The Demiurge or Divine Craftsman.</note> and an Intelligible Cause <note>The World of Ideas.</note> in which the "Whole" primarily exists, as well as The Good, which is established before the Maker in the rank of the "desired object." 

Since that which is moved by another depends on the power of the mover, it is clearly not of a nature to produce itself, nor to perfect itself, nor to preserve itself. In all these things, it needs the efficient cause and is brought together by it. Therefore, the co-causes of <margin>E</margin> natural things must also be suspended from the true causes, from which they were sent forth and toward which they were crafted by the Father of all, for whose sake they came to be. 

It is reasonable, then, that all these things have been handed down by Plato, having been examined with precision, and that the remaining two—Form and the Substrate—are hung from them. For this world is not the same as the Intelligible or Intellectual worlds, which subsist in pure forms; rather, in this world, one part is like "reason and form" and the other is like the "substrate." But we shall be able to look at these things again later. 

From this, it is clear that Plato reasonably handed down all these causes of the world-making: the Good, the Intelligible Model, the Maker, the Form, and the underlying Nature. If he were speaking about the Intelligible Gods, he would have shown only The Good to be their cause; for the Intelligible number <note>The first order of divine beings.</note> comes from this cause alone. But if he were speaking about the Intellectual Gods, he would have hypothesized both the Good and the Intelligible in their place; for the intellectual multitude proceeds from the Intelligible Unities <note>original: "ἑνάδων" (henads)</note> and the one fountain of all beings. But if...

<summary>Proclus critiques Anaxagoras and later philosophers for failing to recognize the primary efficient cause of the universe. He argues that Plato correctly identifies five causes (the Good, the Model, the Maker, Form, and Matter) to explain how the physical world is crafted and maintained by divine principles.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’ introduction to the *Timaeus*. Having previously critiqued earlier philosophers like Anaxagoras and the later Peripatetics for their limited view of nature, Proclus now begins to explain Plato’s specific approach: how the physical world is linked to the divine realm and how the structure of the dialogue reflects the structure of the cosmos itself.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK I

...concerning the gods who exist above the world <note>original: "ὑπερκοσμίων" (hyperkosmiōn); these are the transcendent deities in the Neoplatonic hierarchy who exist beyond the physical universe</note>, he would have derived them both from the intellectual <margin>2</margin> craftsmanship <note>original: "δημιουργίας" (dēmiourgias); the work of the Demiurge or 'Craftsman' god</note> and the universal craftsmanship, as well as from the intelligible gods <note>The highest level of reality in Proclus's system, representing pure Being</note> and the Cause of all things. For indeed, those things of which secondary beings are generative exist primarily, ineffably, and beyond our comprehension in that higher realm. But since he is going to discuss things within the world <note>original: "ἐγκοσμίων" (enkosmiōn)</note> and the universe as a whole, he will provide it with matter <term>hyle</term> and form <term>eidos</term> sent down into it from the gods who are above the world. He will also link it to the entirety of craftsmanship, make it a likeness of the "Intelligible Living Being," <note>The divine blueprint or "animal-itself" that contains the forms of all living things</note> and show it to be a god by its participation in the Good. Thus, he will complete the whole world as a living being, possessed of intellect and soul.

This, then, is the goal <term>skopos</term> which we say Timaeus aims for, and it is of such a kind as we have described. Since this is the case, it is fitting that at the beginning the order of the whole is shown through images; in the middle, the entire creation of the world <note>original: "κοσμοποιΐα" (kosmopoiia)</note> is handed down; and toward the end, the particular parts and the final results of the craftsmanship are woven together with the wholes. For the summary of the *Republic* <note>original: "Πολιτείας"</note> and the <margin>B</margin> myth concerning Atlantis reveal the theory of the world through images. For whether we look at the unity and the multiplicity of things within the world, we shall say that the Republic—which Socrates summarizes—is an image of unity, having set forth as its goal the community that extends through all things. But of the division and especially the opposition according to the two "columns" <note>original: "συστοιχίας" (systoichias); a Pythagorean concept of pairs of opposites, like light/dark or limit/unlimited</note>, we shall say the image is the war of the Atlanteans against the Athenians, which Critias relates. Or if we look at the heavenly realm and the realm below the moon <note>The "sublunary" realm of change and decay</note>, we shall say that the Republic is likened to the heavenly arrangement—for Socrates says its "paradigm" <note>original: "παράδειγμα"; a model or blueprint</note> is established in heaven <note>original: "ἐν οὐρανῷ"; referencing Plato's *Republic* Book IX, 592b</note>—while the war of the Atlanteans is likened to the realm of "generation" <note>The physical world of birth and death</note> which exists through opposition and change. These things, therefore, precede the entire study of nature <term>physiologia</term> for these reasons.

Following these, the creative cause of the universe is handed down, as well as the exemplary <note>The "model" cause</note> and the final cause <note>The "purpose" or "end" cause</note>. Once these are pre-established, the whole is crafted both in its entirety and in its parts. Indeed, the bodily nature of the world is fashioned by being cut into its forms, its creative divisions, and its divine numbers; <margin>C</margin> and the Soul is produced by the Craftsman and filled with harmonic ratios <note>original: "λόγων ἁρμονικῶν" (logōn harmonikōn)</note> and divine, creative symbols. Then, the "Living Being as a whole" is woven together according to the unified encompassment found in the Intelligible World, and the parts within it are appropriately arranged within the whole, both those that are bodily and those that belong to the life-force. For indeed, even the particular souls that are settled within...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’ introduction to the *Timaeus*. The previous page established that the physical world is a divine "living being" modeled on the Intelligible Realm. Here, Proclus begins to explain why human nature is central to the study of the universe, introducing the famous concept of the human being as a "microcosm."</meta>

# PROCLUS

...are arranged around the leading gods <note>The *hēgemones*, or "ruling gods," who govern the various spheres of the universe in the Neoplatonic hierarchy</note> and become worldly beings <note>original: "ἐγκόσμιαι" (enkosmiat); those residing within the physical cosmos</note> according to their own vehicles <term>ochēmata</term>, imitating their own leaders. Furthermore, mortal living things are crafted and given life by the celestial gods. It is in this context that we examine how humanity was composed and for what reasons. This study is prioritized over all others because the theory of man is especially appropriate for us, as we are the ones proposing this discourse and living according to it. This is also because man is a **microcosm** <note>original: "μικρὸς κόσμος" (mikros kosmos); the idea that the human being contains the same structures and elements as the entire universe</note>, and there exists in him in a partial way everything that exists in the world in a divine and universal way. 

For we possess an active **intellect** <term>nous</term> and a **rational soul** <term>psychē logikē</term> that has proceeded from the same Father <note>The Demiurge, or Divine Craftsman</note> and the same life-giving Goddess <margin>D</margin> <gloss>The whole soul and the partial soul proceed from the same life-giving source and the same craftsman</gloss> as the physical world. We also possess an ethereal vehicle <term>ochēma</term> analogous to the heavens, and a terrestrial body kneaded from the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>, to which it is corresponding. 

If, therefore, it is necessary to contemplate the Whole in many ways—in the intelligible and the sensible realms, through paradigms and images, and both universally and partially—then the discourse concerning human nature would be a worthy and perfectly completed part of the theory of the Whole. One might also add the argument that, according to the **Pythagorean custom**, it is necessary to join the discourse about the observer to the discourse about the thing observed. Since we now understand what the world is, I believe it is necessary to add: what is it exactly that examines these things and understands them rationally? 

That Plato also looked toward this goal is clear when he says explicitly at the end of the work that the one who intends to attain the **blessed life** must liken the observer to the thing observed. For while the Whole will always be blessed, our own nature will also become blessed by being made like the Whole. In this way, the human is led back to his Cause. For just as the man here on earth is to the Whole, so the **Intelligible Man** <margin>E</margin> is to the "Living-Being-Itself" <note>original: "αὐτοζῶον" (autozōon); the divine blueprint of life</note>. Just as in that higher realm the secondary things always depend upon the primary, and the parts remain within the wholes and are established in them, so too when the man here is made like the Whole, he will imitate his own paradigm. He becomes a "world" in the proper manner through his likeness to the world, and becomes blessed through his resemblance to the blessed God. 

Following these points, the final products of the craftsmanship are detailed according to their kinds and species: those that consist in the celestial heights, those on the earth, and those within living creatures—both those that are contrary to nature and those according to nature. It is here that the principles of **medicine** <term>iatrikē</term> come to light. For the natural philosopher ends his study with these things, since he is a student of nature...

<summary>Proclus explains the "microcosm" theory, arguing that human nature contains all elements of the universe (intellect, soul, and body) and that by studying ourselves and likening our minds to the cosmos, we achieve a blessed, divine life.</summary>
<keywords>microcosm, intellect, rational soul, vehicle, Demiurge, Pythagorean custom, blessed life, Intelligible Man, medicine, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’ introduction to Plato’s *Timaeus*. Having established the human being as a microcosm on the previous page, Proclus now compares Plato’s approach to natural science with that of Aristotle and other earlier philosophers, arguing that Plato provides the foundational "primary causes" while others focus on material details.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 1

...nature. For along with nature <term>physis</term> comes that which is according to nature, and the departure from this is that which is contrary to nature. To understand in how many ways this deviation occurs, and how it is brought back to measure and nature, is the task of the natural philosopher; however, the consequences of these deviations are the threads from which the art of medicine is woven. In these matters, Plato especially shares common ground with other natural philosophers. <margin>F</margin> For those others spent their time on the most material things <note>original: "ἐνυλότατα" (enylotata); things deeply embedded in matter</note> and the final works of nature, neglecting the whole of heaven and the ranks of the worldly gods, as if they were seeing only the matter, while letting go of the forms <term>eide</term> and the primary causes. 

It seems to me that even the "divine" Aristotle, zealously following Plato’s teaching as much as he could, arranged his entire treatise on nature in this way: he looked at the things common to all things constituted by nature—form <term>eidos</term>, the substratum <term>hypokeimenon</term>, the source from which motion begins, motion itself, time, and space. <margin>3</margin> These are the very things Plato handed down here: space, and time which is an "image of eternity" <note>original: "εἰκόνα αἰῶνος" (eikona aiōnos); a famous Platonic definition of time as a moving reflection of the eternal realm</note> and which exists alongside the heavens, as well as the diverse forms of motion and the auxiliary causes of natural things. 

Furthermore, Aristotle treated the specific properties of things divided by essence—first, those belonging to the heavens, in harmony with Plato, insofar as he calls the heaven ungenerated and a "fifth essence" <term>pempte ousia</term>. (For what difference does it make to call it a "fifth element" or a "fifth world" and a "fifth shape," as Plato called it? <note>Referring to the dodecahedron, the fifth Platonic solid, which Plato associates with the shape of the universe as a whole</note>). Second, he treated those things common to the whole of generated composition. Here, one might marvel at Plato, who contemplated their essences and powers with great accuracy and rightly preserved their harmony and their oppositions. Again, among those things concerning generation, some belong to the celestial phenomena, of which Plato handed down the principles while Aristotle extended the teaching beyond what was necessary. <margin>B</margin> Others extend to the study of living beings, which in Plato are articulated according to all causes—both final and auxiliary—but in Aristotle are contemplated with difficulty and in only a few cases according to form. For for the most part, Aristotle stops at the matter, and in making his explanations of natural things from this starting point, he shows us how much he falls short of the guidance of his master <note>Proclus refers to Plato as Aristotle's "leader" or "guide" (kathēgemōn)</note>.

So much for these matters. Next, let us discuss the form of the dialogue and its character <note>original: "χαρακτήρ" (charaktēr); the literary style and persona</note>. It is agreed by everyone that Plato, having received the book of the Pythagorean Timaeus <note>Timaeus of Locri, a semi-legendary Pythagorean philosopher to whom a treatise "On the Nature of the World and the Soul" was attributed</note>—which was composed by him concerning the universe in the Pythagorean manner—undertook to "write a Timaeus" himself. Moreover, this is also agreed upon by those who have had even a small acquaintance with Plato: that his own character remains Socratic, philanthropic, and demonstrative. If, therefore, he blended the Pythagorean and Socratic identity anywhere else, he has certainly done so in this dialogue...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’ introduction to the Timaeus, moving from a comparison with Aristotle to an analysis of the specific "character" or style of the dialogue. It explains how Plato blends different philosophical traditions to create a work that is both scientific and theological.</meta>

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 1

...he appears to be doing this. For in this dialogue, from the Pythagorean tradition, there is a <margin>C</margin> high-mindedness—the intellectual <term>noeron</term>, the divinely inspired, the way of suspending all things from the intelligible realms <note>original: "νοητῶν" (noētōn); the world of pure ideas or forms</note>, the defining of the whole of reality through numbers, the revealing of things through mysteries and symbols, the way of elevating the mind above partial concerns, and the declarative style. Yet, from the Socratic tradition of "philanthropy" <note>Socratic philanthropy refers to Socrates’ love of humanity and his habit of engaging in dialogue for the benefit of others’ souls</note> comes the conversational quality, the gentleness, the use of logical demonstrations, the practice of viewing true beings through images, the focus on ethics, and all such things. Because of this, the dialogue is majestic; it makes its approach from above, starting with the very first principles. It mixes the logical demonstration with the declarative statement, and it prepares us to understand physical things not only as nature <term>physikos</term> but also as theology. For nature itself, which guides the universe, is suspended from the gods and inspired by them. It directs the physical world of bodies; it is neither a god itself, nor is it outside the divine character <margin>note: "that nature is neither god nor outside the divine character": m. A.</margin> because it is illuminated by the truly existing gods. If, then, it is necessary for words to be Likened to the things they explain—as Timaeus himself will say <note>A reference to Timaeus 29b, where Plato argues that accounts of the world must be as stable and enduring as the world itself</note>—it would be fitting for this dialogue to possess both a physical and a theological character, mimicking the very nature it observes.

Furthermore, according to the Pythagorean view, things are divided into three levels: the intelligibles, the physical things, and the "intermediates" between them, which they usually call <margin>D</margin> mathematicals. One can see all of these levels within each other in a way appropriate to each. In the intelligible realm, the middle and the lowest levels exist in a primary, causal way. In the mathematical realm, both are present: the first things appear as "images," and the third things appear as "models" <term>paradeigmata</term>. In the physical realm, there are traces of those things that came before them. It is reasonable, then, that Timaeus establishes the nature of the Soul through mathematical names to show its powers, its ratios, and its elements. Plato, meanwhile, defines the properties of these elements through geometric shapes, while leaving the ultimate causes of all these things to pre-exist as principles within the intelligible and "demiurgic" <term>demiourgikos</term> or "craftsman-like" intellect.

Regarding these matters, let this suffice; a more detailed investigation of each part will better help us understand the character of the dialogue. The setting <term>hypothesis</term> is something like this: Socrates, having gone down to the Piraeus <note>The port city of Athens</note> for the festival of the Bendideia <margin>E</margin> and its procession, held a discussion there regarding the Republic with Polemarchus (the son of Cephalus), Glaucon, Adeimantus, and Thrasymachus the sophist. On the day following that event, while in the city, he recounts that gathering in the Piraeus to Timaeus, Hermocrates, Critias, and a fourth person who remains anonymous, just as it is set down in the *Republic*. After finishing his narration, he invited the others to "feast" him in return with their own appropriate discourses on the following day.

<summary>Proclus explains that the Timaeus blends Pythagorean "high-minded" theology with Socratic "human" ethics and logic, reflecting the three-fold structure of reality (intelligible, mathematical, and physical). He then transitions to the narrative setting, linking the dialogue to the events of Plato's Republic.</summary>

<keywords>Pythagoreanism, Socratic method, Intelligible realm, Mathematicals, Nature, Theology, Republic, Socrates, Timaeus, Demiurge</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s introduction to Plato’s Timaeus. Having discussed the dialogue's style and its blending of Pythagorean and Socratic elements, Proclus now turns to the dramatic setting—specifically the timing of the conversation and the number of participants—before transitioning into a technical definition of "Nature" (physis).</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 1

They have therefore come together to listen and to speak on this very day, which is the third since the gathering in the Piraeus. For in the *Republic*, the words "I went down yesterday" <note>original: "Κατέβην χθὲς" (Katebēn chthes); the opening words of Plato's Republic</note> are spoken, and here we find the phrase, "Of yesterday’s guests, today’s hosts" <note>original: "Τῶν χθὲς μὲν δαιτυμόνων, τὰ δὲ νῦν ἑστιατόρων" (Tōn chthes men daitymonōn, ta de nyn hestiatorōn); see Timaeus 17a</note>. However, not everyone is present for this lecture; rather, the fourth guest is absent due to illness. One might ask: why are there only three listeners in a discussion concerning the entire universe? It is because, I would say, it is fitting for the "father of the words" <note>the main speaker, Timaeus</note> to stand in analogy to the Father of the works <note>the Demiurge, or Creator of the universe</note>. For the <margin>F</margin> creation of the world through words is an image of the creation of the world through Intellect. To the | one and universal production of the Father, there corresponds a creative triad <note>a grouping of three divine forces in Neoplatonic theology</note> which receives it; likewise, there is a triad of those who receive these words, the summit of whom is Socrates. Because of a kinship of life, Socrates immediately connects himself to Timaeus, just as the first member of the "exemplary" triad is united with the one who stands before the three.

We shall examine these matters more clearly through what follows, if it is pleasing to the gods. Since we have already spoken about the scope of the work—what and how great it is—and about the "economy" <note>the structural arrangement</note> of the dialogue and the <margin>4</margin> admirable blend of its character, | as well as the whole hypothesis and the suitability of the persons to the present discourse, it would be appropriate to proceed to the text itself and examine each part to the best of our ability. But since the name of "Nature" <term>physis</term> is used in different ways by different people and confuses those who love to contemplate Plato’s thought—as to what he thinks it is and what he wishes the essence of Nature to be—come, let us first discuss this. For it is surely fitting for a study that takes "physical" <note>relating to the study of nature</note> theory as its subject to know what Nature is, where it proceeds from, and how far its productions extend. For among the ancients, some called matter "nature," such as Antiphon; others called it "form," as Aristotle does in many places; and others called it the "whole," as did some before Plato, whom he recorded in the *Laws* <note>Laws, Book X, 892b</note> because they addressed "natural things" as "nature." Others used the term for physical powers—heaviness, lightness, rarefaction, and condensation—as did some of the <margin>B</margin> Peripatetics | and even older natural philosophers. Some called nature the "art of God," others called it "soul," and others called it something else of this sort. But Plato does not think that the "whole," or the "form-in-matter," or the "body," or "physical powers" should primarily be named "nature," and he even hesitates to call it "soul" directly.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the introduction to Plato’s Timaeus. Having discussed the participants of the dialogue, Proclus now moves into a deep philosophical definition of Nature (Physis). He establishes its position in the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being, placing it below the Soul but above physical matter, and explains its role as the governing force of the visible world.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...and placing its essence in the middle of both—I mean between the Soul and bodily powers—he <note>Proclus refers to Plato or the figure of Timaeus</note> has handed down to us the most accurate theory concerning it. He describes Nature as being lower than the Soul <gloss>¹)</gloss> <note>original: "ὑφειμένην μὲν ἐκείνης" (hypheimenēn men ekeinēs)</note> because it is divided among bodies and does not turn back upon itself, yet superior to those things that come after it because it possesses the "reasons" <term>logoi: the formative rational principles</term> of all things, and it generates and gives life to everything. According to our common notions, "nature" is one thing, "that which is according to nature" is another, and "that which is by nature" is yet another. Just as a craft is distinct from the object made by that craft, so too the intellectual Soul is distinct from Nature. For Nature belongs to bodies, being powerful over them and inseparable from them, whereas the Soul is separable, established within itself; it belongs simultaneously to itself and to another, because while it is participated in <gloss>⁴)</gloss> by an-

<margin>C</margin> other, it does not incline toward that which participates in it. | Just as the "father of the soul" <note>likely the Demiurge or the higher Intellect</note> belongs to himself while being unparticipated—or, if you prefer, consider the Intelligible Model of the entire world itself before him. For these things follow one another in a sequence: *The Same*, *That of Itself*, *That of Itself and Another*, *That of Another*, and *The Other* <gloss>⁶)</gloss>. It is clear that "The Other" refers to the entire sensible world, in which there is every kind of distance and division. Of those others: "That of Another" is Nature, which is inseparable from bodies; "That of Itself and Another" is the Soul, which exists in itself but also illuminates a secondary life into another; "That of Itself" <gloss>⁹)</gloss> is the Demiurgic <term>Demiurge: the divine Craftsman of the universe</term> Intellect, which "abides in its own accustomed character" <gloss>¹⁰)</gloss> <note>original: "ἐν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ μένων κατὰ τρόπον ἤθει" (en tō heautou menōn kata tropon ēthei); a quote from Plato’s Timaeus 42e</note>; and "The Same" <gloss>¹¹)</gloss> is the Intelligible Cause of all things and the Model for everything created by the Demiurge, which for this reason Plato saw fit to call "The Living-Being-Itself" <gloss>¹²)</gloss> <note>original: "αὐτοζῶον" (autozoon); the archetypal form of all life</note>. Nature, therefore, is the last of the causes that create this bodily <gloss>¹³)</gloss> and sensible world and is the limit of the extent of incorporeal essences. It is full of rational principles and powers through which it directs all worldly things. It is called a "god" by the fact of it being deified <gloss>¹⁴)</gloss>, and <gloss>¹⁵)</gloss> not by having its being as a god from itself (for we also call the divine bodies "gods," as they are images of the true gods).

<margin>D</margin> Nature guides the whole | world by its own powers: holding the heavens together by its highest peak, governing the realm of change and generation through the heavens, and everywhere weaving together particular things with the wholes. Being such as it is, it has proceeded forth from the life-generating Goddess <note>Proclus here refers to the goddess Rhea or Hecate, who in Neoplatonism represents the source of vital power</note>:

> Around the back of the Goddess, boundless Nature
> Is suspended;

From her, all life proceeds—both the intellectual life and the life that is inseparable from the things it manages. Dependent upon her and suspended from her, Nature travels through all things without hindrance and breathes life into everything. Because of Nature, even the most soulless things participate in a kind of soul, and things that perish remain eternally in the world, held together by the causes of the Forms within it. And again, as it is said:

> Untiring Nature rules both worlds and works.

In Manuscript A, the second "the other" is written above the line. — ⁷) 4, 23: "one is [Nature]" — in Manuscript A, "that of another" is written above this. — ⁸) 4, 23: "another is [Soul]" — in Manuscript A, "that of itself and another" is written above this. — ⁹) 4, 24: "another is [Intellect]" — in Manuscript A, "that of itself" is written above this. — ¹⁰) 4, 24: "abiding in its own accustomed character" — these are the words of Timaeus from Page 42 E of Plato’s dialogue. — ¹¹) 4, 24: "another is [the Model]" — in Manuscript A, "The Same" is written above this. — ¹²) 4, 25: "Living-Being-Itself" — written as two words in Manuscript B. — ¹³) 4, 26: "bodily" — written as "bodily-wise" in Manuscript A. — ¹⁴) 4, 28: "by the [fact]" — written as "the" in Manuscript A. — ¹⁵) 4, 28: "and" — Manuscript A adds "and the." — ¹⁶) 4, 30: "by its" — the gender of the article differs between Manuscripts A and B.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s investigation into the definition of Nature (Physis). Having established that Nature is an incorporeal power inseparable from bodies, Proclus now addresses various philosophical opinions on the "Three Creators" and the relationship between the two great Platonic dialogues, the Timaeus and the Parmenides.</meta>

### ON THE TIMAEUS I.

...the oracle says, **"That the Heaven may run an eternal course, drawing along [its path] and so forth."** <note>This is likely a reference to the Chaldean Oracles, a collection of hexameter verses often cited by Neoplatonists</note>. So, if someone who speaks of the "three creators" <term>demiurges: the divine craftsmen or creative powers of the universe</term> wants to trace them back to these principles—the creative Mind, the Soul, and Nature as a whole—they would be speaking correctly for the reasons stated. But if they suppose there are three other creators of the universe beyond the Soul, they would not be correct. For there is one Creator of all things; but his total creative work is divided among more particular powers. Whether Amelius <note>A student of Plotinus who proposed a triad of creators</note> wants to arrange it this way, or Theodore <note>Theodore of Asine, a later Neoplatonist</note>, we do not accept that argument ¹); rather, we shall strive to remain within the Platonist and Orphic ²) <margin>E</margin> frameworks. Furthermore, those who have called Nature a "creative art" ³)—if they mean the nature that remains within the Creator himself, they are incorrect; but if they mean the nature proceeding from him, they are correct. For we must conceive of "art" <term>techne: craft, skill, or systematic production</term> as being threefold: one that never leaves the craftsman; one that proceeds but turns back toward him; and one that has already proceeded and come to be in another. The art in the Creator remains in him and is the Creator himself—by which he is also ⁴) named by the oracles "the work of the craftsman" and "the craftsman of the fiery world" <note>original: "κόσμου τεχνίτου πυρείου" (kosmou technitou pyreiou)</note>. The intellectual Soul is also an art, but one that remains and proceeds at the same time; Nature, however, has only proceeded. Therefore, it is called the "instrument of the gods," not as something lifeless or moved only by another, but as possessing a kind of self-motion by acting from its own resources. For the instruments of the gods are substantialized in active "reasons" <term>logoi: the formative rational principles or "seeds" of reality</term> and are full of life, running along with | their activities. <margin>F</margin>

Since it has been stated what Nature is according to Plato ⁶)—that it is an incorporeal essence, inseparable from bodies, containing their "reasons," yet unable to look into itself—and since it is clear from this why the dialogue is "physical" (dealing with nature), as it teaches about the entire creation of the world, it would be appropriate to connect what follows to these points. For all philosophy is divided into the study of "intelligible" things <term>noeta: things grasped by the mind, like divine forms</term> and "cosmic" things (the world around us) ⁸). This is reasonable because the world itself is twofold: one part is intelligible and the other is sensible (perceived by the senses), as Plato himself will say further on. Thus, the *Parmenides* | covers the <margin>5</margin> treatment of the intelligible, while the *Timaeus* covers that of cosmic things. For the former hands down all the divine ranks, while the latter hands down all the progressions of the cosmic realm. Yet neither does the former completely leave out the study of things in the universe, nor does the latter omit the intelligible, because sensible things exist in the intelligibles as "models" <term>paradigms: original blueprints</term>, and the intelligibles exist in the sensible as "images." However, the one focuses more on the physical and the other on the theological, which is fitting for the men after whom the dialogues are named ¹¹) <note>original: "ὀνομάζονται" (onomazontai)</note>. For Timaeus wrote a book of this kind about the [nature] of the universe...

He also explains the thematic division between Plato’s dialogues, noting that the Timaeus focuses on the physical world while the Parmenides focuses on the divine realm.</summary>

# PROCLUS

...it happens in this way also for Basilides, arising from the substances of matter insofar as God gazes upon the matter of Plato, as he [Basilides] says in his [treatises] on the generative <margin>B</margin> powers resulting from these. But for Iamblichus <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized theurgy and divine hierarchy</note> and Porphyry, the whole state of invocation from above and of illumination has as its goal that each thing among them—even the final ranks of beings—unfolds 7) to be a kind of generative force within the reflections of the school. And the manner of multiplicity of Jacob <note>Likely Jacob of Corycus, a student of Iamblichus</note> against Praxiphanes was prepared 8); for just as Jacob attaches the tension of these things in the world to the primary creators, so Praxiphanes blames the whole bulk on the prayer of the man and on the ways of ancient storytelling which he held. He understood the things that exist through his [Jacob’s] confused way of thinking. And also 9), just as Jacob [understood] the stage-setting <term>skenopoieia: the dramatic arrangement or "set design" of the dialogue</term> and the others understood the creation of images, so Praxiphanes, before the annual inquiry into the forms of the arguments, made a search for the divinity, and he transfers the forms that are always coming into being—those concerning the best **Republic**—by means of discourse into the hypothesis of the universe. For it is necessary that, having flourished with the 6) images from the Forms, one falls upon the natural theory of beings. In this stated manner, one might grasp the phrasing of Plato and examine each point as far as possible. 1)

->One, two, three; but where, indeed, 8) is the fourth, my dear Timaeus, of those who yesterday were the <margin>C</margin> guests, but are now the hosts? (Page 17 A, Stephanus edition)<-

Along with the grace and the beauty of the words, he raised and elevated the entire phrase through this trope <term>trope: a figurative use of language</term>. But Praxiphanes, the companion of Theophrastus <note>A Peripatetic philosopher and student of Aristotle</note>, accuses Plato: first, because he attributed the "one, two, three" to Socrates 10) according to his own judgment. For why did Socrates need to count in order to know the number of those who had come to the gathering? Second, because he changed the 11) word "fourth" and it does not agree with what was said before; for it would be consistent with "one, two, three" to say "four," or with 12) "fourth" to say "first, second, third." These things, then, are his [Praxiphanes'] fable; but the philosopher Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus (c. 234–305 AD) who defended Plato against Peripatetic criticisms</note> answers him step by step: regarding the second point, he says that this is the Greek custom 13), which works to produce beauty in interpretation. For example, Homer has said many such things; for he says 14) that the unwearied bronze went through the folds 15) and was held in the seventh, and he speaks in this way 16) with that word and in many other 17) places. Indeed 18), there is a reason even here...

<meta>The previous page concluded with Proclus explaining the dramatic setting of the dialogue and the transition from the political themes of the Republic to the natural philosophy of the Timaeus. This page focuses on the opening line of the dialogue where Socrates counts his guests: "One, two, three—but where, my dear Timaeus, is the fourth?"</meta>

### ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK 1. 11

<margin>D</margin>
...the variation: for he was able to count those present by pointing at them; for "one, two, three" is a demonstrative <note>original: deiktikon—a term in logic and grammar referring to words that point directly to something in the immediate context</note> way of counting. But the one who was absent (since it was impossible to point to him) he signaled through the word "fourth." Indeed, we use the term "fourth" even for someone who is absent. In relation to what came before, since as many were present as were expected to arrive, counting them would be redundant; however, when someone is missing—someone whose name we do not know—the enumeration of those present highlights the absence, as if longing for the remainder and showing that the total number is incomplete. Plato, indicating this very thing, has Socrates both counting those who have arrived and demanding the one left behind. For if he had known that person and were able to identify him by name, he would perhaps have said, "I see Critias and Timaeus and Hermocrates, but I do not see so-and-so." But since the absent person was a stranger and unknown to him, he only knows that he is missing through the number, and he makes this clear to us who have come so much later. All these points, and any others one might think of regarding the interpretation of the passage before us, are elegant. However, one must also remember that the dialogue is Pythagorean in character, and one must make the explanations in a manner appropriate to those men <note>The Pythagoreans, followers of the 6th-century BC philosopher Pythagoras, who emphasized mathematics, harmony, and a communal lifestyle</note>.

<margin>E</margin>
Therefore, you might derive the following ethical Pythagorean doctrines from this: those men made friendship <note>original: philia</note> the goal of all their philosophy, along with a life lived in harmony. Socrates places this before everything else by calling Timaeus his "friend." They believed that the agreements they made with one another should remain firm; Socrates demands this as well, longing for the "fourth" member. They embraced a communal spirit in the discovery of doctrines, and the writings of one were common to all; Socrates confirms this by calling upon them to be the same "fellow-banqueters" and "hosts," <term>hestiatoras: hosts or feast-givers; here used metaphorically for those providing intellectual discourse</term> both filling others and being filled themselves, both teaching and learning. Now, others have written technical manuals on instruction through which they claim to make the characters of their pupils better; but Plato, through the very imitation <term>mimesis: the representation or "acting out" of character in literature</term> of excellent men, outlines for us the models of our duties. These models are much more effective than those laid down in bare rules, for imitation shapes the lives of the listeners according to its own particular quality.

<margin>F</margin>
Regarding what subject the philosopher will most abound in, he makes it clear through these words: that it is regarding the listening to discourses <note>original: logoi</note>. And what will he consider to be a true feast? Not the one the masses believe in (for that is animal-like), but the one that feasts the "human within us." <note>A Platonic concept where the rational soul is considered the "true human," while the body is more akin to a beast or a shell</note> Therefore, for him, "feasting" is frequently used in reference to discourses. As he says elsewhere: "Or is it clear that Lysias feasted you on discourses?" and "You two will feast together, but you do not share it with us." <note>Proclus is quoting from Plato's *Phaedrus* (227b) and *Lysis* (211d) to show that Plato consistently uses the metaphor of a banquet for intellectual conversation.</note> These points then, and others like them, are ethical; the physical <note>original: physika—referring to the study of nature (physics)</note> points are as follows:

<summary>Proclus interprets Socrates’s opening count of his guests as an ethical lesson in Pythagorean friendship and intellectual community, arguing that true "feasting" consists of philosophical dialogue rather than food.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the opening of Plato's Timaeus. Having discussed the literal counting of the guests, Proclus now moves into the metaphysical and Pythagorean significance of number as the foundation of the natural world.</meta>

# PROCLUS

### ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK 1. 12

...they used to say that the entirety of natural creation is held together by numbers, and that all the works of nature were composed¹⁾ according to numbers. They held that these numbers are "participated" <note>original: metechomenous—meaning these numbers are present within physical things, though their source is higher</note>, just as all forms within the world are things in which matter participates. It is reasonable, then, that as the discourse begins, it proceeds through numbers and employs numbers as "things counted"²⁾, but not those primary Numbers themselves, in which even these counted things participate. For the **Monad**, **Dyad**, and **Triad** are one thing; whereas "one, two, and three" are quite another. The former are simple and the "things-themselves"³⁾, while the latter are merely participants in those higher realities. Therefore, Aristotle is not correct when he says that those men [the Pythagoreans] placed numbers within sensible objects. For how could they, since they hymned Number as the "father of the blessed and of men" and the **Tetractys** <note>The Tetractys is a triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows (1, 2, 3, 4), which the Pythagoreans revered as a symbol of the organization of the universe</note> as the "spring of ever-flowing⁴⁾ nature"? Since⁵⁾ this dialogue concerns nature, the opening has been crafted from participated numbers, of the sort⁶⁾ that all⁷⁾ natural things are. Furthermore, those men championed "natural communion"—both the communion found in the realm of "becoming" [the physical world], according to which all things are brought to completion as rational and symmetrical to one another, and the communion found in the heavens; for there too, the celestial bodies share their own powers with one another. 

<margin>B</margin>

Rightly, then, does Socrates—and in a manner fitting the subject at hand—expect the same individuals to become⁸⁾ both guests and hosts of the feast. You might also contemplate theological thoughts of the following kind from these words: those men generated all things through the first and leading numbers, and from the three gods they gave existence to all things within the world. The **Monad**, the **Dyad**, and the **Triad** provide an indication of these, so that it is necessary for the one who would become⁹⁾ a spectator of nature to begin from them and look toward them. Furthermore, while the "co-causes" of natural things had been observed by others¹⁰⁾, the **Final**, **Paradigmatic**, and **Paternal**¹¹⁾ causes were investigated specifically by Plato himself. 

<margin>C</margin>

These causes, then, are revealed through the numbers set forth: the **Final** cause [the goal or purpose] through the Monad, for it stands at the head of the numbers in the rank of "The Good"; the **Paradigmatic** cause [the model or blueprint] through the Dyad, for the "otherness" of beings distinguished the primary causes of the whole. Moreover, the Dyad is the principle of the Tetractys of the intelligible models. The **Efficient** (or Creative) cause is signaled through the Triad, for the **Intellect** <note>original: nous</note> is appropriate to the Triad, being third from Being by way of the middle of Life, or from the¹³⁾ Father by way of Power, or from the Intelligible by way of Intellection. For there is an analogy: as the Monad is to the Dyad, so¹⁴⁾ is **Being** to **Life**, the **Father** to **Power**, and the **Intelligible** to **Intellection**; and as the Dyad is to the Triad, so is...

These are the "participated" numbers. — ³⁾ 6, 7 *the things-themselves*: [Manuscript] B reads "the thing-itself." In A, *ou* is written over *a*. — ⁴⁾ 6, 9 *ever-flowing*: [Manuscript] B and A (with a second *n* written above) read "ever-flowing." — ⁵⁾ 6, 9 *since*: [Manuscript] B reads "since indeed." — ⁶⁾ 6, 10 *of the sort*: [Manuscript] B reads "of a sort." — ⁷⁾ 6, 10 *all*: omitted in A. — ⁸⁾ 6, 13 *to become*: [Manuscript] A uses a different spelling for "to become." — ⁹⁾ 6, 17 *one who would become*: [Manuscript] B has a spelling error. — ¹⁰⁾ 6, 18 *others*: To this, a note in the margin of A adds "such as Anaxagoras and Zeno"; and [Manuscript] B has "such as Anaxagoras and Zeno" in the main text after "observed." — ¹¹⁾ 6, 19 *paternal*: [Manuscript] B reads "paternal [variant spelling]." Thomas Taylor conjectured "creative/efficient," which indeed is read a little later (v. 22). But "paternal" means almost the same thing. — ¹²⁾ 6, 19 *these*: [Manuscript] A uses the fuller form of the word. — ¹³⁾ 6, 24 *the*: omitted in A. — ¹⁴⁾ 6, 25 *so*: [Manuscript] B uses the alternative form of "so."

<meta>This page continues Proclus's metaphysical exploration of the opening scene of Plato’s *Timaeus*. Proclus is moving from the significance of the number of guests to the spiritual "communion" or "banquet" of ideas that they share, drawing parallels between human philosophical discussion and the eternal life of the gods.</meta>

# PROCLUS

### ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK 1. 13

...life [is directed] toward the Intellect, as are power and thought. Furthermore, all divine things exist in all others and are united with one another, so that <note>original: hōste</note> all are in one and each is in all, held together through divine friendship. Even the **Sphere** <note>The "Sphaeros" is a concept from Empedocles and the Pythagoreans representing the universe in a state of perfect, harmonious unity</note> there contains the single union of the gods. It is reasonable, then, that Socrates, who looks toward the divine, initiates this communion and harmony, and invites the others into it. Moreover, "feasting" and "banquet" are names appropriate to the gods, especially <margin>D</margin> those within the cosmos. For they go up to join the absolute gods for feasts and banquets, as Socrates says in the *Phaedrus* <note>Phaedrus 247A</note>, and the "feast at the birth of Aphrodite" <note>Symposium 203B</note> takes place at the house of the great Zeus. Socrates considers it worthy that these things happen by analogy among those sharing divine thoughts with one another; it is no wonder, then, if Timaeus feasts the others and is feasted by them in turn. 

Furthermore, among the theologians, "distributions" of powers and "participations" are celebrated in hymns, where divine beings fill one another and are filled by one another. For we have heard from the poets inspired by Apollo <note>meaning poets like Homer who were thought to be divinely inspired</note> that the gods greet one another with intellectual activities or with providential actions for the creation of the whole: *“They pledged one another with golden cups, looking toward the city of the Trojans.”* <note>Homer, Iliad 4.3</note> And if they indeed know and think of one another: *“For gods are not unknown to one another.”* <note>Homer, Odyssey 5.79</note> Since, according to the Oracle <note>The Chaldean Oracles, a sacred Neoplatonist text</note>, "the intelligible is food for the thinker," it is clear that "reciprocal feasting" exists primarily among the gods. The wiser among men, by imitating the gods even in this way, <margin>E</margin> share their own private thoughts with one another without stinting.

**"A certain illness befell him, Socrates; for he would not willingly have missed this gathering."** (Plato, *Timaeus* 17A)

The philosopher Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century scholar and student of Plotinus</note> says that in these words, Plato outlines a duty: that for sensible people, there is only one reason to miss such gatherings—bodily illness. He suggests we should regard any such event as an accidental circumstance <note>original: peristatikon</note> and involuntary. Additionally, he notes that friends ought to make whatever excuses are possible for their friends when they seem to act against the common expectation. At any rate, this speech encompasses both points, demonstrating the character of Timaeus and the necessity of the one who is absent; it shows the former as gentle and a lover of truth, and the latter as a hindrance to the life of a lover of learning. But the divine Iamblichus <note>A later Neoplatonist who emphasized theurgy and more mystical interpretations</note>, taking a loftier...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the opening lines of Plato’s Timaeus, specifically addressing the mystery of the "missing fourth guest." Proclus explores both the symbolic meaning of this absence and the historical debates among ancient scholars regarding the identity of this individual.</meta>

# PROCLUS

<margin>F</margin> One being discussed in this passage, those practiced in the vision of the <term>intelligibles<note>The "intelligibles" refer to the realm of perfect, eternal Ideas or Forms, which can only be grasped by the mind, as opposed to the "sensible" world we see and touch.</note></term>, are said to be "out of proportion" when it comes to dealing with <term>sensible things<note>The physical, material world perceived by the senses.</note></term>. It is just as Socrates himself said in the *Republic* <note>original: "Politeia"; reference to Republic VII, 516A–E</note>: those raised in the pure dawn of light have dimmed vision when they descend into the cave because of the darkness there, just as those who have ascended from the cave cannot yet look directly at the light. For this reason, the fourth guest is left behind, as he belongs to another kind of vision—that of the intelligibles. Indeed, this "weakness" of his is actually an "excess of power," by which he surpasses the present contemplation. For just as the "power" of evil is rather a form of "powerlessness," so too is a "weakness" regarding secondary things actually a superiority of power.

<margin>7</margin> Thus, the argument says that the one left behind is absent because he is disproportionate to <term>physical accounts<note>Discussions regarding nature (physics) and the material world.</note></term>, though he would wish to be present if they were about to occupy themselves with the intelligibles. Almost all the parts of the text preceding the discussion on nature are explained in a more "political" way by Porphyry <note>A famous Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>, who relates them to the virtues and so-called duties, whereas others explain them more "physically." For everything ought to be in harmony with the proposed goal; and this dialogue is "physical," not "ethical."

These, then, are the interpretations the philosophers set out regarding these matters. I will pass over those who cause us much trouble by trying to prove that this fourth person was Theaetetus <note>A brilliant young mathematician and character in Plato’s dialogue of the same name</note>. They argue this because he had become a student of the Eleatic school <note>original: "Eleatikou"; a school of philosophy focused on the nature of being</note> and because it is recorded that he was ill <note>referring to the opening of Plato's Theaetetus, 142B</note>; therefore, they say he is absent now due to illness. This is how Aristocles <note>A Peripatetic philosopher</note> tries to establish that the absent one is Theaetetus.

<margin>B</margin> And yet, Theaetetus became an acquaintance of Socrates and the Eleatic Stranger only a short time before Socrates's death. Even if he had been known to that Eleatic man long before, what would Timaeus have in common with him? 

Ptolemy the Platonist thinks the guest is Cleitophon; for in the dialogue named after him, he was not even deemed worthy of a response from Socrates. Dercyllides thinks it is Plato himself, for Plato was also absent from Socrates's death due to illness. These people, as I said, I will pass over, as they have been rightly rejected by those before us for seeking things not worth seeking and for saying nothing certain. 

All of them attempt their proofs clumsily, and it contributes nothing to the argument even if we were to find what they are looking for. To say it was Theaetetus or Plato because of illness does not even harmonize with the dates. One of them [Plato] is said to be ill when Socrates was being judged, and the other, Theaetetus, when he was dying. As for it being Cleitophon, that is completely absurd; for he was not even present on the previous day when Socrates was recounting what Cleitophon had said on the day before that during the gathering in the Piraeus <note>referring to the Republic, Book I, 340A</note>. 

<margin>C</margin> Only this much does Atticus <note>A 2nd-century Platonist</note> correctly point out: this missing person seems to be one of the foreign guests staying with Timaeus. This is why Socrates [refers to him in this way]...

<summary>Proclus discusses the symbolic meaning of the "missing fourth guest" in the Timaeus, arguing that his absence represents a soul focused on higher spiritual truths rather than physical science. He also critiques various historical theories that identify the guest as Plato, Theaetetus, or Cleitophon, dismissing them as chronologically flawed.</summary>
