<meta>This page continues Proclus's allegorical interpretation of Plato's Republic as summarized in the Timaeus. Having discussed the "guardians" as cosmic forces, Proclus now interprets their "wages" and "communal life" as symbols of the continuous cycle of creation and the shared activity of the divine powers.</meta>

# PROCLUS

<margin>F</margin>
...if we were to interpret this as a return of gratitude and a thanksgiving of favors, how would it still follow for us that the gods "dwell together in common" and "consume" such a wage? It is better, therefore, to understand this "wage" in a more natural sense. For since **emanations** <note>original: "aporrhoias" — divine energy flowing downward from the gods into the material world.</note> come from that divine realm into this mortal place, while **exhalations** <note>original: "anathymiaseis" — the upward movement of refined matter or energy from the earth back toward the heavens.</note> are moved from here <note>original: "ekeithen" — the note indicates this refers to the mortal realm.</note>, and through these the **demiurgy** <note>original: "dēmiourgia" — the act of "crafting" or "building" the universe.</note> of the gods concerning mortal things is completed, he [Plato] called such transformations and transitions of earthly things a "wage" paid by the **material earth** <note>original: "hylēs gēs" — the physical, underlying substance of the world.</note> to the heavens, so that the process of **generation** <note>original: "genesis" — the constant cycle of birth, growth, and change in the physical world.</note> might be unceasing. Furthermore, he calls the "communal life" the single harmony of divine creation and the unified providence of the celestial gods. It is because of this providence that everything changing from the earth is "consumed" <note>This refers to the idea that nothing in the universe is wasted; the "decay" of one thing is the "food" or "fuel" for another.</note>, and generation is varied and transformed through the "dance" of the heavenly bodies. Looking toward these very things, Timaeus will say that the **whole cosmos** is a friend and acquaintance to itself because of **virtue**, and that its own nature provides it with food, doing all things within itself and being acted upon by itself. What then is the end <note>The "telos" or ultimate purpose.</note> of this one and common life of the citizens? "Virtue," he says, "virtue"—divine virtue, clearly. For virtue exists first among the gods, and then from them it descends both into the higher ranks of beings <note>Such as angels, daemons, and heroes in the Neoplatonic hierarchy.</note> and into us, as a certain portion of it. Living according to this virtue, <margin>15</margin> the guardians of the world keep themselves at leisure from all other pursuits (for they do not look toward needs, nor do they look outside of themselves, for all things are within them); they preserve all things and fill them with the beautiful and the good, serving and cooperating with the one Father and Creator <note>original: "dēmiourgō"</note> of the whole. Since they themselves also define the measure for the transformations of the earth without departing from themselves, but remaining turned toward themselves and being within themselves, for this reason he called the "wage" moderate and for the **temperate** <note>original: "sōphrosi" — those possessing "sophrosyne," the virtue of self-control and sound-mindedness.</note>. For by being temperate—staying within their own being—they also measure the secondary things, containing the various transformations of the world within the simplicity of their own life. This, then, is the interpretation according to this path. But according to the other path, we shall say that **holiness** and the return toward the gods possesses the greatest measure and is held fast by the Good; and this is defined by the gods themselves according to divine wisdom, as they are able to preserve both themselves and all other things.

And indeed, we also mentioned women: how their natures ought to be joined as being similar to those of men, and how all <margin>B</margin> occupations should be given in common to all of them, both in war and in the rest of their lifestyle. (Page 18 C.)

It was reasonable that the idea of virtues being common to both men and women should please Plato, since he declares that there is one "form" <note>original: "eidos" — the essential blueprint or species.</note> that is human, and not one that is male and another...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the Timaeus, transitioning from a discussion of the "wages" and "communal life" of the guardians to a defense of the equality of the male and female principles in both the human and divine realms. It builds on the idea that the "guardians" (the celestial powers) work in pairs.</meta>

-># ON THE TIMAEUS A. 33<-

...to one who posits that the female is something different. For things that possess a different **perfection** <note>original: "teleiotēta" — the state of being complete or reaching one's full potential.</note> according to **form** <term>Form: "eidos," the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing that makes it what it is.</term> are different in form; but those things that are the same in form also possess one and the same perfection. Although some have rejected this, <margin>15, 13: This means the same perfection of the male and the female (from manuscript A).</margin> they do admit there is a difference according to form in these matters, even though Plato has demonstrated that this is both possible and beneficial. 

It is possible because history confirms it; for it appears that women who are well-reared are by far **better than men** <margin>15, 15: Such as Telesilla of Argos (from manuscript A). <note>Telesilla was a 5th-century BCE poet who famously led the women of Argos to defend their city against the Spartans.</note></margin>. And it is beneficial because it is better to have twice as many people—rather than just half—demonstrating virtue through their actions. Just as we produced male guardians through such upbringing and such studies, so also shall we produce female guardians from the same, and just as we have those men who fight in the front lines, so too shall we have women who fight in the front lines. 

But so that we may more greatly admire Plato’s **intelligence** <note>original: "anoian" — literally "lack of mind" or "folly," but here likely a scribe's error for "dianoian" (intelligence) or a reference to a "divine madness" that transcends ordinary logic.</note>, he refers us to the <margin>C</margin> whole and to the arrangement of the universe, where we shall see a wonderful harmony of the male and the female. For among the gods, these are so naturally joined to one another that the same deity is even called **male-female** <note>original: "arrenothēlyn" — androgynous or hermaphroditic.</note>, just like Helios <note>the Sun</note> and Hermes and certain other gods. <margin>15, 21: That the Sun and Hermes are male-female (from manuscript A).</margin> Even where they are divided, the works of the male and female within the same rank are common, coming primarily from the male and in a **subordinate** <note>original: "hypheimenos" — a lowered or secondary manner.</note> way from the female. <margin>15, 23: The word for subordinate is written as "hyphemenos" in manuscript A.</margin>

For this reason, even among mortals, nature has shown the female to be weaker than the male in all things. Therefore, those very things which the male generates, the female also generates, while the subordinate status is preserved. Thus, Hera proceeds together with Zeus, bringing forth all things alongside the Father; for this reason, she is also addressed as his **equal in rank** <note>original: "isotelēs" — literally "paying equal tax/tribute," meaning she shares his status and authority.</note>. <margin>15, 26: That Hera is addressed as equal in rank to Zeus (from manuscript A).</margin> And Rhea proceeds with Cronus; for this goddess is the "womb" of all the Cronian power. And Earth proceeds with Heaven; for Earth is the mother of all things of which Heaven is the father. 

And if we take the **Limit** and the **Infinite** <note>original: "peras kai apeiron" — the two fundamental principles in Pythagorean and Platonic philosophy that combine to create all reality.</note> prior to these elements—which indeed take the rank of principles and causes—we shall find that all things that enter into being in any way whatsoever are generated from both. You have, therefore, the fitting together of the male and the female among the **intelligible** gods, the **intellectual** gods, and the <margin>D</margin> **super-cosmic** gods. <note>Proclus is describing a hierarchy of reality: Intelligible (pure being), Intellectual (pure thought), and Super-cosmic (the powers ruling the world from above).</note>

See these same things in the heaven as well. For the entirety of **generation** <term>Generation: "genesis," the world of change, birth, and decay.</term> is governed by both the Sun and the Moon; more greatly and in a fatherly way by the former, and in a secondary way by the latter. For this reason, she has been named "a lesser Sun" by some. <margin>15, 31-32: Manuscript A omits "but" and spells "named" differently; it also notes the Moon is named a "lesser Sun" by anonymous authors.</margin> And there are lunar ranks analogous to the male gods in the Sun. And if you should observe the **spirits** <note>original: "daimosin" — daimons or intermediary spirits.</note>, you will everywhere see the providence of these two kinds yoked together. For with the divine male spirits, there are divine female spirits...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato's Timaeus. Having argued that women are capable of the same virtues and "front-line" duties as men, Proclus now moves into the metaphysical justification for this equality, linking the social structure of Plato’s ideal city to the fundamental laws of the cosmos and the nature of the gods.</meta>

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK I, PAGE 34

...female monads <note>original: "monides" — female units or principles.</note> unitedly accomplish all things in a secondary way, just as the male principles do primarily. Souls do this for the psychic realms, nature-spirits for the physical, and bodily powers for the corporeal. These female principles stand in the relation of **mothers** to the males, and as **dyads** <term>Dyad: The principle of "twoness" or "otherness," which in Neoplatonism represents the power of expansion and generation that proceeds from the "Monad" or unity.</term> to the monads. For they generate all things in a subordinate manner, whereas the male principles produce them in a paternal and pre-eminent way. 

If, therefore, we were right to compare the **guardians** <term>Guardians: The ruling class in Plato's Republic, characterized by wisdom and the protection of the state.</term> to the celestial gods, and the **auxiliaries** to the daemons <note>original: "daimosi" — intermediate spirits, not "demons" in the modern sense, but divine messengers and attendants.</note> who follow and serve their providential plans, then Plato quite reasonably embraces the similar fitting together of the male and the female in these classes of beings. <margin>E</margin> He grants to both a common virtue and common pursuits, just as the creator bound these classes together and made them exist with one another. He did not divide one from the other, for he considered that if they were separated, they would be **barren** in those realms where generation arises from both. 

And yet, there is a greater difference in their physical organs than there is in their lives; nevertheless, nature assigned them a common work. Much more, then, is it worthy to honor their community in terms of their pursuits and their entire way of life.

->But what then of the matter of procreation? Is this easy to remember because<-
->of the truth <note>original: "alētheian"</note> of what was said, to the point that even these things<-
->are easy to remember, as you say? (Plato, Timaeus 18D)<-

If anyone asks why the **unusual** is "easy to remember," it is not difficult to explain: it moves our imagination more because it is paradoxical, and thus it implants its imprint within us more strongly. Furthermore, it is easy to explain the "community of women" <note>This refers to the controversial proposal in Plato's Republic that the guardians should share wives and children to ensure total social unity.</note> in a way that follows Plato's intent. He wishes for unions to be celebrated at appointed times with sacrifices <margin>F</margin> and prayers, and that no woman should be the private possession of any one man. Instead, they should separate after the union and live apart, only to be joined again at other times as the guardians see fit. 

The argument demonstrates these things in this way. But let us discuss the **contemplative theory** <note>original: "theōrian" — a deep, philosophical observation of the underlying reality.</note> of these matters as it pertains to the nature of the universe. For these arrangements exist much earlier among the gods because of their perfect union. Indeed, all things are the offspring of all, even if certain things are characterized by a specific identity; for all are in all, and all are united before the others with the **unmixed purity** befitting the gods. <margin>16</margin> It was by looking toward this divine state that Socrates embraced this community of life and the distribution of pursuits to each individual according to their nature. For even the fact that one does **not know one's own offspring** privately exists among the gods, which is why their offspring are common to them all...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s metaphysical defense of Plato’s social reforms. Having previously discussed the shared virtues of men and women, Proclus now explains how the familial structure of the ideal state—where citizens view one another as universal kin rather than private relatives—is modeled on the eternal relationships between the gods and the laws of the cosmos.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS A. 35

Their productions are common, and each thing born is nurtured and preserved by every person as something belonging to all in common. Furthermore, the practice of regarding all those of the same rank as **brothers**, those who are superior as **fathers and ancestors**, and those who are subordinate as **offspring and children**, has been transferred to this constitution from the gods themselves. For among the divine, the similarity of essence derived from the same cause constitutes "brotherhood"; the fertile cause constitutes the "ancestral" rank; and the "outflow" of essence proceeding into a second or third series manifests the category of "offspring." <note>original: "homoiotes... gone... aporrhoia" — Proclus is mapping human family terms onto the Neoplatonic process of "emanation," where reality flows down from a single source.</note> <margin>B</margin> Indeed, you might grasp the principle of one person being joined to another, or one to many, from the mystical teachings and the "Sacred Marriages" spoken of in the secret rites. Plato, to the best of his ability, followed these divine models by designating the marriages among the citizens as **sacred marriages**. <note>original: "hierous gamous" — In Greek religion, this refers to the marriage of gods (like Zeus and Hera); Plato uses the term in *Republic* 458e to elevate the state-sanctioned unions of the guardians to a divine status.</note>

Furthermore, in the study of nature, one can observe that a single and identical **receptacle** <term>Receptacle: In Plato's philosophy, the underlying "space" or "matter" that receives the imprint of divine Forms.</term> can receive various rational principles, and a single principle can be reflected in a multitude of receptacles and extend through many underlying subjects. By analogy, the **Forms** <term>Forms: The eternal, perfect blueprints of reality.</term> correspond to the male, while the **receptacles** correspond to the female. 

Why, then, is this principle observed in the universe as a whole, yet seen as a paradox in human lives? It is because, I would say, the whole of the human soul has been **fragmented** and partitioned off from the "Wholes." <note>original: "apotetemachistai" — cut off or butchered into pieces. Proclus suggests that because we identify as individual "parts," we find it hard to understand the "whole" perspective of the state.</note> Because of this, the doctrines concerning this communal way of life appear to the soul as utterly difficult to accept. If, therefore, someone were to set aside their specific station and lead themselves back to the "Whole," they would embrace such a communion, looking down upon the divided sympathies found among the masses. But to the extent that each of us exerts ourselves over a "part" and is broken into small change <note>original: "katakermatizetai" — a metaphor for being divided into tiny coins, i.e., trivialities.</note>, falling away from the Whole and the One, <margin>C</margin> to that same extent one is coiled back toward a life of "unheld" relationships—a station that is un-stationed, and a division that cannot be divided.

### "How they might immediately become as excellent as possible in their natures... [up to the point of] considering chance as the cause of conception." (Republic 18 E.)

Plato introduced **similarity**, **identity**, and **geometric equality** along with arithmetic equality into this same constitution in a distinctive way. He did this so that he might perfectly preserve the state's likeness to the Heavens (as it exists in sensible things) or to the **Intelligible Realm** (as it exists in heavenly lives). For this reason, even in marriages, he joins the best man with the best woman and the lesser man with the subordinate woman. For among the gods as well, the primary beings are more closely joined to the primary, and the secondary to the secondary; and along with this union, there is a pure and unmixed...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the social and metaphysical structures of Plato's ideal state. Proclus is explaining how the "lottery" system for marriages and the distribution of ranks in the Republic is not merely a political tool, but a reflection of the hierarchical "distribution according to merit" found in the divine and natural cosmos.</meta>

-># PROCLUS<-

...flow, so that even in the secondary generations following the gods, such a **distribution according to merit** is carried out in accordance with the Intellect of the gods. For this reason, divine female spirits are ranked with divine male spirits <term>Daimones: In Neoplatonism, these are not "demons" but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans</term>, the psychic with the psychic, and the material with the material. <margin>D</margin> And everywhere the **proportion** proceeds in order down to the very last things. Since the fact that the rulers "engineer" the lottery in secret sufficiently mirrors the cause of such a gathering of races, which exists invisibly among the gods. This gathering arises primarily from that divine source, and secondarily from the rank of each individual, which the **lot** <note>original: "kleros" — a lot or portion assigned by fate or ritual</note> indicates. This lot possesses its binding power from the **similarity of life**, according to which each thing is ranked with its like: the divine with the divine, the material with the material, and the middle with the middle. 

Because of this, all stability and even discord is suspended from the divine, as each being loves what is its own according to its own rank, seeing this as natural and not as something incidental or engineered. The practice of assigning citizens their pairings by lot bears an image of all these truths, even though the citizens themselves do not see the sophisticated design behind it. For even in natural things, the "receptacles" are distributed appropriately to the "forms," and each of the forms might attribute its own arrangement to the variation found in matter; yet, this too is carried out according to the **governing effects** <note>original: "aitiata" — the results or effects of a higher cause</note> that stand over the whole of creation, being analogous to the Guardians.

<margin>E</margin> Let these things be said for the sake of contemplating the whole. However, **Longinus** <note>A famous 3rd-century literary critic and philosopher who often disagreed with the Neoplatonists</note> raises a difficulty here: he wonders whether Plato thinks that souls are cast down along with the **seeds** <note>procreative seeds/sperm</note>. For in order that the children may become "the best," Plato joins like with like. And **Porphyry** <note>The student of Plotinus</note> meets this objection, though not quite sufficiently. But our **Teacher** <note>Syrianus, Proclus’s beloved predecessor as head of the Academy</note> deemed it right to first observe that Plato himself added the phrase "so that they may become the best **in their natures**." For children receive a physical similarity from their fathers, and by their noble birth, they participate in something of their parents' character regarding natural virtues. 

Secondly, one must consider that even if it is not true that souls are "cast down with the seeds," the distribution of the "organs" <note>the physical bodies</note> is nonetheless according to merit. For not all souls are housed in just any chance organ, but each enters into the one that is suitable for it. As **Homer** says: *"The good man put on good armor, and the worse man he gave to the worse."* <note>Homer, Iliad 14.382</note> Furthermore, just as the **ritualist** <term>Telestes: A priest or initiator who performs the rites to animate a divine statue</term> places certain symbols around the statues to make them more suitable...

***

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on how the social structure of Plato's ideal city reflects the metaphysical laws of the universe. Having discussed the "marriage lotteries," Proclus now addresses how nature prepares different bodies for different types of souls and how the "secret" distribution of children mirrors divine providence.</meta>

-># ON THE TIMAEUS I.<-

...into a participation of higher powers, so also whole Nature, molding bodies by natural principles <note>original: "logois" — here meaning the formative blueprints or ratios in nature</note> as statues of souls, sows a different suitability in different bodies for the reception of different souls, both better and worse. The statesman, understanding this correctly, takes great account of the "seeds" <note>referring to genetic or biological heritage</note> and of every natural suitability, so that the best souls might be joined to the best natures. This must also be said in response to the difficulty raised by Longinus <note>Cassius Longinus, a 3rd-century philosopher and critic who often questioned Plato’s literal meanings</note>. For what reason did Plato think it better for the citizens to consider "chance" <note>original: "tyche"</note> as the cause of such a distribution? Is it because, for those things we consider good, it is beneficial to also know the cause—for we will admire it more—but for those things we perceive as bad, it is better to think their presence is without a specific cause, rather than blaming the cause that distributes these things for a good purpose? For such blame rouses contempt <margin>17</margin> towards the giver, or rather hatred, because everyone naturally avoids what is harmful.

> And indeed, that the children of the good must be reared, but those of the bad must be secretly distributed to the other city. 
> (Page 19 A.)

These things are defined there <note>in the *Republic*</note>, but they occur much earlier in the universe. Of the things produced by gods and spirits <note>original: "daimones"</note>, some remain within themselves, being pure kinds and far from the realm of generation <note>original: "genesis" — the world of change and physical birth</note>; these are called "unpolluted" <note>original: "achranta"</note> for this reason. Others descend into generation, unable to remain fixed in heaven. Some are from the good, and some from the lesser. For "bad" here indicates the "lesser." Indeed, "the horses and charioteers of the gods are all good," but those of individual souls <margin>B</margin> are mixed. Because of this, there is a downward pull, a leaning, and a "shedding of wings" <note>a reference to the soul's loss of divine power in Plato's *Phaedrus*</note> in these souls, which the celestial beings and the spirits presiding over the soul's descent send into generation. Thus, the heavenly kinds of souls, being unpolluted, are nourished following the gods to "the banquet and the feast," as is said in the *Phaedrus* <note>original: "Phaidro" — Plato's dialogue on the soul and love</note>; but those that produce generation share in that generation, being sent from there "secretly," as the text says. This indicates the unseen and hidden cause among the gods for the descent of souls, showing that the souls descending from there come under a different providence and different overseers who preside over the world of birth.

> As they grow up, we must always keep watch and bring back those who are worthy, while transferring the unworthy among them to the place of those moving up. (Page 19 A.)

In the *Republic*, he makes this transfer not only from those given from above...

# PROCLUS

<margin>C</margin>...distributed into the lower city, but also of those born there recently; however, in this case, he effects the "leading upward" <note>original: "anagogas" — the process of raising the soul from the material world to the divine</note> of those who have descended. How then might these accounts agree with one another? Perhaps it is possible to reconcile this passage with what was defined there <note>in the *Republic*</note>, if you do not understand the phrase "being increased" as applying only to those sent down from above, but to all those being nourished below. For as those born below simply grow—or more accurately, as those from above come to be below—we must examine their natures, what kind they are, and thus lead back those who are worthy.

But if someone wishes to understand it as we said from the beginning, it must be stated that Socrates has now adopted what is in harmony <note>original: "synadon" — sounding together or concordant</note> with the matters at hand. For the souls that have descended go back up again—at least those that did not have their primary existence <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> from the start within the realm of generation <note>the world of change and matter</note> and around matter, such as the souls of many irrational animals. So much for the literal text.

Observe, however, how these same principles apply to the Whole <note>the Universe</note> just as Socrates ordains them in his own Republic. Some things always hold the same rank in heaven, remaining divine and unchangeable; others have always sunk into the realm of generation; <margin>D</margin> while the middle things are somehow between both—sometimes suspended from those divine beings, and sometimes mingling with those who embrace the world of change.

It is not, therefore, the race of <term>daimons</term> <note>spiritual intermediaries between gods and humans</note> that is reassigned up or down, nor are the various forms of life or deaths found among the daimons themselves. Rather, these changes concern **particular souls**, which at one time associate with generation, and at another time are transferred to a divine, daimonic lot. Socrates, knowing this, established the analogy in the *Republic*. For even Heavenly Zeus has set gods in heaven and daimons who lead particular souls upward, while others lead them down into generation, so that the descents and ascents of souls may never fail the Universe. Even if you see *this* specific soul restored to its place, the Father <note>the Creator or Demiurge</note> sends another in to be counted among the number, according to the inspired indication concerning these matters.

For within the Universe, generated things are distinguished, and each one, participating with the others according to its own unique character, is active. The primary things are exempt from the secondary, yet they use the activities of the secondary as necessary for the completion of the Whole. The secondary things are ordered by the primary, and the best of the things within the cosmos are naturally joined to the best; the middle to the middle, and the last to the last. # ON THE TIMAEUS I.

...while many subjects are present, the same entities and the same receptacles participate in multiple rational principles <note>original: "logoi" — here referring to the formative principles that shape matter</note>; and lives exchange different lots at different times according to their own worth. All these things, then, have sufficiently directed us toward the ordering of the whole universe. For Socrates duly summarized the entire form of the commonwealth into an intellectual indivisibility <note>original: "noeran amereian" — a state of pure thought that is not divided into parts</note> by ascending to the heights, in order to imitate the God who ordered the heavenly commonwealth in an intellectual and paternal manner. 

Since, in every case, the measures and perfection of secondary things are defined by their causes, for this reason Socrates himself asks Timaeus to say whether he has included the entire form of the commonwealth. For every mind <note>original: "nous" — the higher intellect</note>, by resting itself upon the God prior to it, defines itself by looking toward that One. Since even the act of speaking "in headings" <note>summarizing main points</note> is a symbol <margin>F</margin> of the fact that the primary parts of the universe and the "head" <note>the highest level of reality</note> have been ordered by the Creator; and now the Creator of the universe will order things more perfectly by looking toward the whole and the single life of the cosmos. 

These things concern the analogy of the parts to the wholes. But as to whether the text means that the commonwealth he went through yesterday is what he has now gone through in headings, or whether he encompassed it in headings both yesterday and again today—this is not a matter worth much trouble to seek out. <margin>18</margin> For whether he spoke in a more varied way yesterday and now in headings, or in headings on both occasions, the divine Iamblichus <note>A 3rd-4th century Neoplatonist philosopher whom Proclus held in high regard</note> is satisfied, and it makes no difference to us. 

Perhaps, however, this latter view is more harmonious. For to "return again as if in headings" indicates that it was also spoken in headings yesterday. And it is not surprising if the summary that took place is not found in the text of the *Republic* <note>Proclus notes that the written dialogue "The Republic" and the conversation Socrates is recalling here do not perfectly match</note>. For many other things mentioned here as having been said the day before are not found in that work. Unless, of course, the word "again" here should not be applied to "in headings," but to the act of "returning." For a person who recounts previously spoken words at length "returns" to them, but a person who shortens the narration "returns again" by summarizing in headings. Whichever way it may be, it is of no great consequence.

> You might hear now, following these things, how I happen to feel toward the commonwealth which we described. (Page 19 B.)

These are five points, to speak in headings, which the subsequent speech of Socrates has encompassed. First, what it is that he yearns <margin>B</margin> to happen to the things already said after the tradition of the commonwealth; second, that he himself is not capable of providing this; third, that none of the poets is capable of this; fourth, that one must not entrust such a task even to the sophists; fifth, that only the listeners <note>Timaeus, Critias, and Hermocrates</note> could worthily perform what is being earnestly sought by

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the transition from the summary of the Republic to the main narrative of the Timaeus. It explores why Socrates wishes to see his ideal city "in motion"—specifically in the context of war—and how this mirrors the Creator’s joy in the living movement of the universe.</meta>

# PROCLUS

Socrates. What then is this thing (for we must first necessarily speak about it) which Socrates desires after this commonwealth? It is to see, as he says, such a city set in motion in contests and prizes and the acts of war, so that after the peaceful life which he himself has handed down, he might observe its activities in difficult circumstances. This, then, is what is sought by him; but one might ask <note>original: "aporessie" — to raise a philosophical difficulty</note> where this longing of Socrates is looking, and for what reason he desires this to happen. 

Now, Porphyry <note>A famous Neoplatonist philosopher and scholar</note> solves the difficulty by saying that activities bring habits to completion, not only the activities that come before the habits, but also those that proceed from them. For perfection in a habit <note>original: "hexis" — a stable disposition or character trait</note> exists alongside the act of doing; otherwise, the habit is in a sense "at rest" and potentially failing in its activity. Therefore, in order that Socrates might behold the commonwealth as truly perfect, he demands to see it in his mind's eye set in motion in the acts of war and struggling against others. Through these things, Porphyry says, Socrates seems to show that it is not the habit of virtue by itself, but virtue in action that is self-sufficient for happiness. 

<margin>C</margin>

But if the "end goal" <note>original: "telos"</note> were war, someone might say to him that he ought to say war perfects the commonwealth; but if the goal is peace, why is it necessary to introduce Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle, who emphasized active virtue</note> solutions to solve Platonic difficulties? Or is it that even if the goal is not war, war nonetheless demonstrates the greatness of virtue more than peace does? Just as the "triple-waves" and the surging sea demonstrate the skill of the pilot, so too do difficult circumstances reveal virtue. As the <term>Stoics</term> <note>Philosophers who taught that virtue is the only good and that one must endure trials</note> are accustomed to say: "Give me a circumstance and take the man" <note>original: "dos peristasin kai labe ton andra" — meaning: give me a challenge and you will see the true character of the person</note>. For to be undefeated by those who would enslave others reveals the total worth of a life. 

Perhaps, however, it is absurd to attribute the cause to these things alone, even if they have a political logic, and not look toward the whole purpose of Plato. Just as the 

<margin>D</margin>

God who ordered the heavenly commonwealth <note>the cosmos</note> also wills that the realm of <term>becoming</term> <note>original: "genesis" — the physical world of change and growth</note> be governed by the heavenly gods, and that the "war of forms" within matter always be maintained so that the cycle of becoming might mirror the heavenly cycle. And this is what it means "to see the city set in motion in wars": it is to see the realm of becoming coordinated with the heavenly realm and guided by it in every way. 

And this seems to be analogous to what will be said a little later <note>Referring to Timaeus 37C</note> regarding the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator of the world in Plato's philosophy</note> of this universe. For when the Father who generated the world beheld it moving and living, having become an image of the eternal gods, he marveled and was gladdened. For in a similar way, Socrates also wants to see his own city moving and acting, just as the one who holds together the heavenly commonwealth sees the things there acting and ordering the opposition that generates the world. Let this much be said now regarding the analogy in these matters. And if previously we assigned the "lower city" to the realm of becoming, but now we assign it to "war," do not be surprised. For it is safe to assign the same things to different matters according to different analogies, since even the realm of becom...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s analysis of the characters in the Timaeus. Having discussed Socrates’ desire to see the ideal city in action, Proclus now moves to a systematic "harmonization" of the dialogue's characters with the cosmic powers they represent. He argues that Socrates, Timaeus, Critias, and Hermocrates are not merely historical figures but symbols of the divine hierarchy that governs the universe.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS I.

<warning>The bottom left corner of the page is faded and damaged, making some text in the footnotes difficult to read.</warning>

...the soul, in accordance with its inseparable lives <note>original: "achōristous zōas" — lives or vital functions that cannot exist apart from a physical body</note>, resembles the lower city; but in its oppositions <margin>E</margin> and material turmoil, it resembles war and military divisions. But indeed, in order that we may harmonize everything with the contemplation of the cosmic wholes before our specific inspection of each part, consider the second point, and how it is in accord with this: since Socrates is analogous to the first of the three fathers <note>The "three fathers" refer to the triad of Demiurgic or creative deities in Neoplatonic theology</note> who ordered the primary things, he says he is not sufficient to fashion the things that follow. For the sustainer of the whole is one, while the sustainer of the middle or the third things is another. 

And the third point is that the poets are not sufficient; the fourth is that neither are the sophists. The poets are insufficient because they merely imitate the things they were raised with; the sophists because they are wanderers <note>original: "planētes" — referring to the fact that sophists traveled from city to city, unlike settled citizens</note> and not at once both philosophers and statesmen. Again, consider how these points follow from what has been said: for the powers that are to preside over "generation" <note>original: "genesis" — the realm of physical change and becoming</note> must neither be inseparable from it nor turned toward it. Such powers are analogous to the poets who fashion myths and to imitators; for these powers dwell only around images, praising only those things they know—the material and the divisible—and being unable to look upward away from matter. 

<margin>F</margin> Nor, indeed, should they be separable but highly changeable, ascending or descending at different times to different ranks—such as are partial souls <note>original: "merikai psychai" — individual souls, like those of humans, as opposed to the World Soul</note>, which are likened to the sophists. This is because these souls also possess most beautiful reason-principles <note>original: "logous"</note>, yet they wander at different times to different parts of the cosmos. It is necessary, therefore, that the powers which hold together the generation governed by the heavens be both philosophers and statesmen at once. This is so that through the "philosophical" aspect, they remain separate from the things they govern, and through the "political" <note>or "statesman-like"</note> aspect, they exercise providence <margin>19</margin> and govern their own allotted domains according to Intellect. For the "natural" aspect, being productive, is inseparable from matter, while the form of partial souls, being "sophistic," is prone to much wandering. But before the things that are moved, there must be the gods’ providences, which always stand in the same way; and before the changing allotments, there must be those that are unchanging. 

Fifth, then, following these points, he hands down who those are who are able to do this (for these things must be transferred from words to deeds): namely, the Creator <note>original: "demiourgos"</note> of the whole in a total and transcendent way, and the other fathers—one being the sustainer of the middle things, the other of the final things—to whom Timaeus, Critias, and Hermocrates are analogous. Of these men, the first <note>Timaeus</note> is wonderfully praised, with Socrates adding his own opinion, as it seems to me; the second <note>Critias</note> is praised moderately according to his own rank; and the third <note>Hermocrates</note> is praised last according to the testimony of others.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the opening of Plato’s Timaeus. On the previous page, Proclus discussed the symbolic roles of the characters and Socrates’ request to see his ideal city "in motion," like a living organism. Here, he examines the specific analogy Socrates uses to describe his desire and records the interpretations of earlier scholars like Longinus and Origen.</meta>

# PROCLUS

"My feeling seems to me to be something like this: it is as if a person, having seen beautiful animals—whether produced by the art of painting or truly living but remaining at rest—should then feel a desire to behold them in motion and struggling in some contest that seemed to belong to their bodies." ¹) (Page 19 B.) <note>original: "Proseioike de dē tini moi toiōde to pathos..." — This is a direct quote from Plato's Timaeus (19b), where Socrates uses a famous analogy to explain why he wants to hear an account of his ideal city engaged in war and diplomacy.</note>

<margin>B</margin> **Longinus** ²) says that in these lines **Plato** is "beautifying" his style; he suggests that by embellishing the discourse through parables and the grace of his vocabulary, ³) Plato is demonstrating to certain Platonists that this mode of expression is natural to the philosopher and not merely a product of artificial craft. For these Platonists argue that while Plato’s choice of words is carefully considered—and he does not pick them at random—one might say this skill came to him from the common and habitual language of his time, and that he took great care even with everyday speech. ⁴) Indeed, they say that the atoms of **Epicurus** <note>Epicurus (341–270 BCE) was a philosopher who taught that the universe was formed by the random collision of indivisible particles called atoms. Neoplatonists like Proclus often mocked this idea.</note> coming together would sooner create a world than words and verbs put together by chance could produce a successful speech. While some have criticized Plato for his use of language, specifically his frequent use of metaphors, everyone admires his composition ⁵); nevertheless, one should not judge his care for expression from composition alone, but also from the specific literary devices he displays here. For Socrates does not simply state what he wishes from **Timaeus** and his circle; rather, he seems to be "beautifying" himself 
<margin>C</margin> and "charming" <term>psychagōgounti</term> <note>From 'psyche' (soul) and 'agōgos' (leading); literally "leading the soul." It refers to the persuasive or enchanting power of beautiful speech.</note> the listener. "My feeling," he says, "seems to me to be something like this: as if someone had seen beautiful animals produced by painting," and so forth. Such are the views of Longinus. 

**Origen**, ⁶) <note>This likely refers to Origen the Platonist, a contemporary of Plotinus, rather than the famous Christian Church Father of the same name.</note> however, conceded that Plato took care to provide literary grace, yet argued he did so not merely to aim at what is pleasant, but rather to use this image to represent his own internal state <term>pathos</term>. 

And we <note>Proclus often uses "we" to refer to the consensus of his school or his own developed Neoplatonic view.</note> would say that this parable was written to imitate divine things. The "grace of words" is an image of the grace bestowed upon heavenly things by the **Demiurge** <note>The "Craftsman" or creator-god in Plato's philosophy who fashions the physical world after eternal models.</note>. The way his technical skill in expression is blended with a natural quality mirrors the divine act of creation; for divine creation possesses both its own internal limit and a progression that stems from its very Being and Essence. If you were to examine the image itself: the "beautiful animals" signify those things that shine forth with beauty; those "produced by painting" or "truly living" refer to things that display physical images and true lives 
<margin>D</margin> prior to these imitations. For the figures of the gods are statues of the animals within them. Those "remaining at rest" ⁷) are full of intellectual order and a smooth, continuous life, while those "in motion" ⁸) and proceeding into another state...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Socrates’s request in Plato’s Timaeus (19b-c). On the previous page, Proclus introduced the analogy of the "living animals" and began exploring why Socrates wishes to see his ideal city in action. This page explores the metaphysical parallels between the city in motion and the universe in motion, while also providing a historical defense for the political actions of Socrates and Plato.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK 1. 43

...decoration and a second demiurgic creation; while those things which perform some of the feats that seem to belong to bodies, imparting their own emanations and powers to more imperfect things and acting upon others through their own powers. This is what is meant concerning the image. As for the phrase "whether produced by the art of painting or truly living," both are correctly said regarding divine bodies; for the universe is "drawn" <note>original: *diezōgraphētai*</note> in the shape of a dodecahedron <note>In the Timaeus, the dodecahedron is the geometric shape associated with the element of the Heavens or the universe as a whole.</note> and it possesses active and demiurgic lives. 

But if these terms were understood separately, they would signify that the aforementioned polity [the ideal city] was worked out in speech and made similar to the heavens, and that it exists, if not among men, then among truly living or daemonic <note>In Neoplatonism, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> lives. Furthermore, the desire to see the city "in motion" is analogous to the passage: "When the Father saw it moving, he was delighted and wished to make it even more like its paradigm." <note>A reference to Timaeus 37c, describing the Demiurge's joy at seeing the world come to life.</note> For in this way, the decorator of the heavens also wishes to see it moving and, through this motion, governing the "war" that is generation. <margin>E</margin> The phrase "some of the feats that seem to belong to bodies" is used because some contests belong to souls and others to bodies—for example, racing, wrestling, and gymnastics are called contests of the body.

**I feel the same way toward the city we have described, as far as the interpretations in these words concerning each of the cities.** (Page 19 C.)

In these words, you have a brief defense <note>original: *apologia*</note> of why **Socrates** associated with **Alcibiades**, and why **Plato** traveled to **Dionysius** [of Syracuse]; for both expected to be creators of a good polity and to see the "political art" in motion. Since this is also the case here—namely, what Socrates desires to be added to it: that praise be spoken of such a city as it contends in wars—the reason why this is said and what sort of paradigm it looks toward has been explained. 

And because cities use both deeds and words against their enemies—words in embassies, in treaties, and in battle-exhortations, and in all such things; <margin>F</margin> deeds in encampments, ambushes, and skirmishes—for this reason, he wishes such a city to be praised in both respects: in words as being prudent, secure, high-minded, and vigorous, and in deeds...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus. On the previous page, Proclus discussed the "image" of the city and compared the desire to see it in motion to the Demiurge’s joy in seeing the universe move. Here, he addresses Socrates's claim that he is unable to properly praise the ideal city and its citizens.</meta>

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK 1. 14

...as courageous, as intense, and as well-trained; for in this way, it would imitate its own paradigm <note>original: *paradeigma*; the ideal blueprint or "Form" in Platonic thought</note> in both respects—that paradigm which, by shining through both natural and intellectual creations, adorns the entire war of generation <note>The "war of generation" refers to the constant flux, conflict, and change inherent in the physical world of "becoming" as opposed to the eternal world of "being."</note>.

"Therefore, O Critias and Hermocrates, I have judged this of myself: that I would never be able to sufficiently praise these men and the city." (**Plato, Timaeus 19 D**)

<margin>20</margin> This is the second of the proposed chapters, for which we previously stated the cause, and now it must be examined again according to another method. For already some of the elder commentators have said that the "encomiastic" <note>praising or celebratory</note> style of speech is bold, haughty, and magnificent, whereas the Socratic character of speech is slender, precise, and dialectical <note>Logical and focused on question-and-answer</note>. Thus, his style is the opposite of the former. This is why Socrates avoids giving a formal praise-speech, knowing his own power is suited to what it was naturally made for. 

However, those who say this seem to me to flatly reject the *Menexenus* <note>A Platonic dialogue where Socrates actually does deliver a long funeral oration</note>, and they do not even consider the inspiration and grand eloquence of Socrates in the *Phaedrus*. 

There are others who say that a person who crafts such praises should be experienced in military matters; therefore, many historians fail in their descriptions due to a lack of tactical experience. But Socrates, having served in the campaigns at Delium and Potidaea <note>Actual battles in the Peloponnesian War where the historical Socrates served as a hoplite</note>, was certainly not inexperienced in all such things. 

Others, then, say that he is being ironic—just as he says he knows nothing about other matters, so here too he says he is unable to praise the city worthily. But the irony of Socrates is usually directed toward sophists <note>Professional teachers of rhetoric whom Socrates often challenged</note> and young men, not toward men as prudent and knowledgeable as these. 

It is better, then, to say instead that he is guarding himself against becoming "third from the truth" <note>original: *tritos apo tēs alētheias*; a reference to Republic Book X, where an imitation (like a poem or painting) is three steps removed from the ideal Form</note>. For the actual deeds of a correctly governed city are "third" from the paradigm of the state. Because he wishes to remain at the second level <note>The level of the "ideal city in speech" or the mathematical/intellectual model</note>, he says it is not possible for him to endure the descent of life into the third kind. 

And such an "inability" is actually an abundance of power; for remaining within the paradigms belongs to those with surpassing power. You see how this is also in harmony with what we said before regarding the analogy of these things to the whole of reality. For the "secondary creation" <note>original: *demiurgia*</note> is modeled after the primary one and is therefore close to it. Indeed, the entire creative chain is one, possessing union along with its distinctions. It is reasonable, then, that Socrates should primarily [aim] for something...

<margin>B</margin>

Here, Proclus explains why Socrates turns to the other characters—Timaeus, Critias, and Hermocrates—and addresses the critique of poets as "imitators" who cannot capture the philosophical life.</meta>

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK 1. 15

<margin>C</margin> He extends his address to Critias and Hermocrates and asks them <note>The editor notes: specifically, to those things said by him concerning the Republic</note> to weave together what follows. For Timaeus was going to deliver these things in a more universal and loftier manner, not through images, but directly preserving the <term>analogy</term> <note>The mathematical and metaphysical correspondence between the physical world and the divine realm</note> to the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "Divine Craftsman" or creator of the universe in Plato's philosophy</note> of the whole—depicting the heaven by means of the **dodecahedron** <note>In the Timaeus, the universe as a whole is associated with the 12-sided platonic solid</note>, and generation by its proper shapes.

> As for my own case, it is nothing surprising. But I have the same opinion about the poets of old and those now living, not because I dishonor the poetic race, but because it is clear to all that the mimetic tribe will most easily and best imitate those things in which they were raised. But as for that which happens to each person outside of their upbringing, it is difficult to imitate well in deeds, and even more difficult in words. (**Plato, Timaeus 19 E**)

This is the third of the previously noted chapters, in which he shows that poetry is in no way able, by itself, to achieve the praise of such men who have been stationed by fortune in warlike actions. However, this argument is questioned by **Longinus** and **Origen** <note>These are 3rd-century philosophers; Origen here is likely the Platonist, a contemporary of Plotinus, rather than the famous Christian theologian</note>, wondering if perhaps he has included **Homer** among the poets when he said he held the same opinion not only about those now living (for that is nothing new) <margin>D</margin> but also about the poets who existed of old. 

Indeed, **Porphyry** says that **Origen** spent three whole days shouting, blushing, and dripping with much sweat, saying that the hypothesis and the problem were great. Origen was eager to show that the imitation in Homer is sufficient for deeds according to virtue. For who is more "grand-voiced" than Homer? Having set even the gods into strife and battle, he does not fail in his imitation, but speaks with a loftiness that is sufficient for the nature of reality. Such was the argument of the objector.

But Porphyry, responding, says that while Homer is capable of bestowing magnitude and height upon the passions, and of raising actions into a grand imaginative bulk, it is not possible for him to transmit **intellectual impassivity** <note>original: *apatheia*; a state of being unmoved by irrational emotions or physical disturbances</note> and the active philosophical life. 

But for my part, I wonder: if Homer is not sufficient for these things, is Critias sufficient? Or Hermocrates? And are they worthy to speak of such things? It seems to me, therefore, that Plato divides poetry into the **inspired** and the **technical**. Having made this division, he attributes the "grand-voice" and the <margin>E</margin> height that comes from **divine inspiration** <note>original: *enthousiasmos*</note> to the gods—for the oracles possess the robust and magnificent quality of interpretation to an extraordinary degree. But regarding the poetry that comes from human art, he declares that it is not sufficient to praise the excellence of this city and the greatness of the men raised within it. For even if something is technical...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus. On the previous page, Proclus discussed Socrates’s claim that he is unable to properly praise the citizens of his ideal city in action. He argued that Socrates does not dismiss the "poetic race" entirely, but specifically the "mimetic" poets who lack the proper upbringing to represent high philosophical virtue. This page explores the distinction between natural and contrived style and why it is harder to imitate someone’s words than their deeds.</meta>

# PROCLUS

The loftiness found in some poets possesses much that is contrived and pompous, employing metaphors for the most part, just like the style of **Antimachus** <note>Antimachus of Colophon, an epic and elegiac poet whom Plato reportedly admired, though others found his style difficult and obscure</note>. But Socrates requires a praiser who displays a natural loftiness and possesses a "grand voice" without force and with purity, just as great deeds possess their grandeur not by chance, but as something proper to the nurture and education of the men performing them. That Socrates does not reject the inspired poet <note>original: "ton enthoun... poiētēn"</note>, nor the whole of poetry, but only the "technical" kind, he has made clear, I believe, by saying himself that he does not "dishonor the poetic race." For the poetic race is indeed "divine," as he himself says elsewhere <note>original: "en allois," referring to Plato's Laws, Book III, 682 A</note>. Rather, he rejects the mimetic kind, and even this not simply, but that which is 
<margin>F</margin> reared in base | habits and laws. For this kind, being prone toward the worse, is not suited by nature to be an imitator of the loftier characters. Regarding the difficulty raised, then, these things must be said. But since the end of the speech is somewhat difficult, come, let us grant it some clarity. It is this: "But as for that which happens to each person outside of their upbringing, it is difficult to imitate well in deeds, and even more difficult in words." For it seems to be easier to imitate words than deeds. At any rate, 
<margin>21</margin> not a few | play the **sophist** <note>Here used in the sense of a "clever talker" or "pretender"</note> by displaying virtue in their words, while in deed they are entirely far removed from it. Perhaps, then, it is better to explain these words in this way: understanding "that which is outside of upbringing" as the "best" thing; taking "in deeds and words" as equal to "according to both deeds and words"; and taking "to imitate well" as "to be well imitated." Thus, collecting the sense from all these points, it means that the "best" thing is difficult to imitate well in deeds, but even more difficult to imitate in word through speech. For this <note>The Latin editor notes: specifically, the act of imitating through speech. Since this kind of imitation is necessarily proposed to everyone discussing the poetic art and mentioning imitation, Proclus teaches this here truly, but perhaps too briefly; there is a suspicion that something has been lost from the text after "proposed."</note> was the subject at hand: poetic art. And you see how this is consistent with the facts. For one who recounts the deeds of the best men through speech composes a **history** <note>original: "historian," meaning a factual record or inquiry</note>; but one who arranges their words, if he is to preserve the character <note>original: "ēthos"</note> of the speaker, will adopt an internal disposition <note>original: "diathesin"</note> similar to the speaker. For words appear different according to one's inner dispositions. This is why we laugh at most of those who have written "Defenses of Socrates" for failing to preserve the 
<margin>B</margin> Socratic character | in his words—with the exception of Plato. And yet, in simply recording the facts—that Socrates was accused, that he made a defense, and that he received such-and-such a verdict—they would not be worthy of laughter; rather, it is the lack of resemblance in the imitation of the words that reveals the imitators as ridiculous. Even regarding **Achilles**, to say that he went out armed in such a way and did such things is not difficult; but to teach further what kind of words he would say while being hemmed in by the river <note>A reference to the battle with the river-god Scamander in Book 21 of the Iliad</note> is not easy, but belongs to one capable of assuming that character.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus. Following the previous discussion on why Socrates—despite his mastery of the "inspired" poetic mode—claims he cannot properly praise the ideal city in action, Proclus now addresses the limitations of both poets and sophists. He evaluates the arguments of the rhetorician Longinus and the philosopher Porphyry regarding why imitation (mimesis) requires more than just technical skill; it requires a life lived in accordance with virtue.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK I, 47

...hero and, once established in that state, to bring forth the words. Socrates in the *Republic* makes this clear, for the most part rebuking **Homer** regarding the imitation of words. But regarding the gods, they say, it is easier to imitate the words of the gods in speech than their deeds. For who could sketch out their "making" <note>original: "poiēsin" — Proclus uses this to mean both poetic creation and the divine act of creation</note> worthily? Or rather, in the case of the gods, is it the same thing to imitate their deeds and their words? For since words are thoughts, and these thoughts are "makings" (creations), the imitator of words is also an imitator of creations; thus, insofar as he falls short in the one, he is equally in need of imitation for the rest.
<margin>C</margin>
**Longinus** <note>Cassius Longinus, a 3rd-century rhetorician and philosopher</note> raised a difficulty regarding this specific statement. For if poets are not worthy imitators of the deeds belonging to such a city because they were not "reared in its habits," then neither would **Critias** and his associates be able to represent what was done; for these men did not live as citizens under such a government either. But if it is because they lack knowledge <term>epistēmē: certain, scientific knowledge as opposed to mere opinion</term> and are only imitators, why—having received the "patterns" from us—can they not imitate them, since they possess the power of imitation? 

To these difficulties one must say that the imitation of such a state proceeds through a life that is in harmony with the paradigms. For he who does not live according to virtue cannot render the words that befit serious men. Therefore, it is not enough merely to hear what kind of life the state possesses in order to imitate it, as the argument of Longinus's questioning claimed. **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> adds that just as not everything is imitable for painters—such as the light of midday—so too the life of the best state is not imitable for poets, as it transcends their power.
<margin>D</margin>

->The race of sophists, on the other hand, I have always considered to be well-versed in many and fine words, but I fear that, being wanderers from city to city and never having inhabited dwellings of their own, they might miss the mark of what philosophers and statesmen would do and say. (Timaeus Page 19 E.)<-

The **sophists** often laid claim to many subjects—some to astronomy, others to geometry, others to politics, and others to the art of division <note>original: "diairetikēs"; a footnote suggests "diaitētikēs" or the art of lifestyle/diet</note>—and for this reason they are now said to possess "many and fine words." But since they did not possess *scientific* words, they were called "experienced" <term>empeiroi: those with practical experience or a 'knack' but lacking the theoretical 'why'</term>. For "experience" indicates a mindless practice <note>original: "tribēn alogon"</note> carried out in empty words without an intelligent cause. 

Because they did not merely graze upon different cities at different times, but were also full of deceit, "opinion-wisdom" <note>original: "doxosophia" — the illusion of being wise when one is not</note>, and unscientific wandering, they are rightly called "wanderers." And since they led an unordered and uneducated life, acting according to passion, they are reasonably said not to have "managed their own dwellings," for it is necessary for each person to order himself before all others. For all things that exist in a household and in a city also exist in one’s character, and these take precedence over external things...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus (20A). Following the previous discussion on why poets and sophists are unsuitable to describe the ideal city, Proclus now identifies the specific qualities of those who can: the philosopher-statesmen. This page includes a famous philological debate between the rhetorician Longinus and the philosopher Origen concerning Plato's sophisticated prose style.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...must be directed. Who, then, are the fitting imitators of the deeds and words of the best form of government, if neither the poets nor the sophists are? These are surely the statesmen and the philosophers. For there is a need for both: through the political capacity, they are able to perceive the deeds, and through the philosophical capacity, the words. This is because they have already embraced this life within themselves; through the former, they grasp the practical wisdom <term>phronēsis: practical wisdom or prudence in action</term> of the rulers, and through the latter, they grasp their intellectual activity. From these images, we must also transition to the demiurgic <note>original: "dēmiourgikas" — referring to the Divine Creator or 'Craftsman' of the universe</note> causes, noting that these too must be both intellectual and universal, if the "All" is to be filled and if the realm of generation <note>the physical world of change</note> is to possess as images everything that the heavens possess primarily.

**"There remains then the class of your own disposition, sharing by nature and upbringing in both." (Timaeus, Page 20 A.)**

**Longinus** <note>Cassius Longinus, a 3rd-century rhetorician and critic known as a 'living library'</note>, not disdaining to examine the literal phrasing, remarks on the beauty of the passage. He says: **"I fear that of the sophists, because it is a wandering tribe,"** and suggests that it changes the phrasing out of a desire for majesty at the very start. He considers the subsequent phrase, **"whatever such things as men might do in war and battles,"** and what follows, to be a distortion of natural phrasing. Thirdly, he claims the phrase 
<margin>F</margin>
**"there remains then | the class of your own disposition"** is altogether strange; for he says it is no different from Homeric expressions like "the mighty strength of Hercules" or "the sacred power of Telemachus" <note>Homer often used "the strength of X" as a poetic way to simply say "X"</note> and other such things. **Origen** <note>This is Origen the Neoplatonist, a student of Ammonius Saccas, not the Christian Father</note>, however, accepts the style of interpretation of the words laid out here as being "writerly" <note>original: "syngraphikon" — appropriate for a historian or prose author</note>; for he argues that such circumlocutions <note>lengthy, indirect ways of speaking</note> are as appropriate for such a writer as they are for a poet. But we <note>Proclus speaking for himself</note> say that **Plato** appropriately varies his delivery everywhere to suit the underlying subject matter, and pursues variations in interpretation even for unusual things. We do not say that the current phrasing is a mere circumlocution; for it does not mean the same thing as simply saying "you," just as "the strength of Hercules" does not. From this [disposition] alone would they be able 
<margin>22</margin>
to | render what is fitting in the imitation of the best government. For they will do this by acting according to the "disposition" <term>hexis: a stable internal state or character trait</term> which they possess—a state that differs from the poetic and <note>original: "politikēs" — some manuscripts say 'political', others say 'poetic'</note>...

---

<note>Translator's note on the critical apparatus: The footnotes indicate various manuscript corrections. In line 42, manuscript A reads "of this" instead of "this." In line 45, manuscript A originally had "our" but corrected it to "your." In line 51, manuscript A suggests "Origen" is the speaker. Regarding line 22,1, there is a noted gap (lacuna) in the manuscript B. The scholar Thomas Taylor attempted to resolve this by suggesting the text means: "For they do not manifest the same thing as the expression 'you,' like 'the strength of Hercules'; from which there would only be an ability of giving that which is adapted to the imitation of the best polity." Fabricius also suggests "of Hercules" should be written instead of "Heracleitus."</note>

<summary>Proclus argues that only those who combine political experience with philosophical insight can truly describe the ideal state. He defends Plato's complex prose style against critics like Longinus, arguing that Plato’s language reflects the internal character (hexis) of the speakers.</summary>

# ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK I, 49

...sophistical <note>original: "sophistikēs" — referring to the deceptive or superficial rhetoric of the Sophists</note>. So much for the phrasing itself. Now, looking toward the meanings of these words, we shall say that Socrates rouses Critias and Hermocrates toward the remaining tasks of the Republic, and he also exhorts Timaeus to take hold of the investigations. This is the fifth chapter of those proposed for our explanation. And see how, from the very introduction, he has bestowed dignity upon these men. He called them a "disposition" <note>original: "hexin" — a stable state of character or habit</note> in order to exclude the sophistical "wandering" <note>Socrates previously called sophists a 'wandering tribe'</note>. He said they participate in the life of citizens by "nature and upbringing," so that you might distinguish them from the poetic imitation that is nourished by inferior laws. He defined their perfection as arising from both nature and upbringing so that you would not make nature "lame" <gloss>1)</gloss> by depriving it of upbringing, or think that upbringing <margin>B</margin> had been cast into an unsuitable and unharmonious reception. These things are said of the men in common; but if you wish to speak of them in relation to the Divine Paradigms, there remains the demiurgic class <note>the 'demiurge' is the divine Craftsman or Creator</note>, which, being both universal and intellectual, is appointed to the providence of the whole. We must also observe what is said about each of them individually.

> For here is Timaeus, who belongs to the best-governed city of Locris in Italy, and is second to none there in property and birth; he has held the greatest offices and honors in the city, and, in my opinion, has reached the very summit of all philosophy. (Plato, Timaeus 20 A.)

What testimony could be more wonderful than this, or what praise greater? Has he not first testified to Timaeus’s political standing <gloss>4)</gloss>, and then to his intellectual knowledge, by saying he has reached the summit of all philosophy? And by adding "in my opinion," he has placed the crowning touch <note>original: "kolophon" — the final stroke or summit of a work</note> upon all the encomiums. What other image among men could be more closely assimilated to the one Demiurge? First, | in being both a statesman and a philosopher, <margin>C</margin> he belongs to the rank of Zeus. Second, by belonging to a "well-governed city," he imitates the God <note>Zeus</note> who was nourished by Adrasteia <note>Adrasteia is the goddess of Divine Law and Necessity; in Orphic myth, she helped raise the infant Zeus</note> in the intelligible realm. By his excellence in "birth," he is a portrait of the Creator’s universal, intellectual, and unified nature <gloss>5)</gloss>—for he possesses all these things by participating in the Fathers who preceded him <gloss>6)</gloss>. By having "held the greatest offices," he mirrors that kingly and governing power over the whole, whose scepter, according to the theologians <note>Proclus often refers to the Orphic poets as 'theologians'</note>, is "four and twenty measures" <gloss>7)</gloss> long. By enjoying the "greatest honors," <gloss>8)</gloss> he represents that transcendent <gloss>9)</gloss> superiority in seniority and power over all things—for is it not the Creator himself who distributes honors to the others? <gloss>10)</gloss> And as for "philosophy"...

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK I, 50

...from the highest point to come toward the one who contains all knowledge within himself at once, they would say <note>original: "phaien" — The editor notes that this should perhaps read "phaimen" (we would say)</note> that he is entirely modeled after him. Thus, from all that has been said, you might grasp who the Creator of the universe is as if from images: he is a Mind encompassing many minds, stationed among the intellectual gods and full of the primary intelligibles, holding royal dignity as he is established above the other creative gods by seniority <note>original: "presbeia" — rank or privilege due to age</note>. 

<margin>D</margin> If Plato calls the city of Timaeus "Locris"—even though the Greeks do not usually call it that, but only "the Locrians"—it is for the sake of distinguishing it from the Locris across from Euboea; this is not surprising, for he changes many terms to signify the subject more clearly. It is clear that the Locrians were well-governed, for Zaleucus <note>A legendary 7th-century BCE lawgiver of the Locrians, famous for his strict but fair legal code</note> was their lawgiver.

->Critias, as I suppose everyone here knows, is no amateur in any of the things we are discussing.<-
->(Page 20 A.)<-

Critias was of a noble and robust nature; he also took part in philosophical circles and was called "an amateur among philosophers, but a philosopher among amateurs," as history says. He even became a tyrant himself, being one of the Thirty <note>The Thirty Tyrants were a pro-Spartan oligarchy installed in Athens after the Peloponnesian War; Critias was their most violent leader</note>; but it is not just to blame Socrates for this because he now deems him worthy of some praise. First, one must pay attention to *how* he praised him: that he is "no amateur" in the things we speak of due to both his nature and his time spent in philosophical circles. 

Secondly, even the tyrannical character itself is a sign of natural talent, as the myth in the <margin>E</margin> *Republic* <note>Referring to the Myth of Er in Book X, 618 B-C</note> teaches that souls descending from heaven are led particularly toward the tyrannical life. For having been accustomed there to revolve with the gods and help govern the whole, they run toward the apparent powers here as well, just as those who remember intelligible beauty embrace apparent beauty. 

That Critias belongs by analogy to the "middle demiurgy" <note>Proclus links the three speakers to the three levels of divine creation: Timaeus is the highest, Critias the middle, and Hermocrates the lowest</note> you might grasp first from his taking up the discourse from Socrates, then from his narrating the Atlantean story (since the Atlanteans were descendants of Poseidon), and thirdly from his own life. For the quality of leadership, that which extends over many things, and power in general, belongs to the middle entities. Therefore, he also holds the middle position in the praises. To be called "not an amateur" but a participant <note>original: "metochos"</note> in Timaeus's advantages shows his subordination compared to the first [Timaeus], but also that he does not entirely lack a kinship with him.

->As for Hermocrates, again, we must believe the many witnesses who testify that his nature and upbringing are sufficient for all these tasks.<-
->(Page 20 B.)<-
