# PROCLUS

...assigning a creative form that orders the whole, holding together the oppositions within it and its manifold movements in a single, uniform way. Just as in Homer, Zeus sits on the peak of Olympus "in a fold" <note>original: "ptychi" — the OCR incorrectly reads "pnyki" (the Pnyx), but the Homeric reference in Iliad 20.22 is to a fold or cleft of the mountain</note> and, remaining in his own proper unity <gloss>manuscript B reads "youthfulness"</gloss>, sends the gods to the Greek war <gloss>manuscript B reads "of the Greeks"</gloss>—those who preside over <margin>C</margin> | cosmic opposition—so too does Socrates stand purely in the **intelligible form** <term>intelligible form: the perfect, non-physical blueprint of a thing</term> of the Republic. He prepares those who come after him to be able to celebrate the movement and power of this Republic: calling upon the science of Timaeus for a universal contemplation of all things, while preparing the others for a universal yet concise embrace of particular things. For just as he went through the Republic in a universal way, so he wishes its power to be celebrated by the others. Since all these words are images of the **demiurgic** <term>demiurgic: related to the Creator or the act of world-making</term> works, and this entire gathering is an image of the creation of the world, Socrates appropriately says that he is "ordered" <note>The Greek word "kekosmēmenos" means both "adorned/ordered" and is related to "Kosmos" (the world-order)</note> and ready to receive their speeches, having clothed his speech in "orderliness," which is the fitting form of virtue.

**"And indeed, just as Timaeus here said, O Socrates, [we are ready]; for... even on the way here we were considering these very things." (Page 20 C)**

It was necessary for Hermocrates also to say something, rather than being present in silence like the "mute characters" in a comedy who stand by idly; for this reason, he is depicted saying <margin>D</margin> | something to Socrates. While this serves a literary purpose, it is also appropriate to the subject matter. It shows that even the lowest parts of creation follow the one Father of all things and, through their likeness to him <gloss>perhaps "to that one"</gloss>, they incline toward the single providence of the world <gloss>it seems the phrase "you might see" or something similar has fallen out of the text here</gloss>, as can be seen from the images being discussed now. For Hermocrates, following Timaeus, says that nothing is lacking in terms of either eagerness or power for the speeches requested by Socrates. For these two things especially hinder us from acting upon one another: our own laziness and any external obstacle. He removes both of these by saying that "eagerness is not lacking," and that there is no "pretext" preventing them from fulfilling Socrates's command. Appropriately, then, he also called upon Critias to provide the narration of the ancient deeds of the city of Athens—in which Socrates's command reached its fulfillment—just as Socrates called upon Timaeus; in this way, he makes himself a sort of partner in those speeches. For he says that they <gloss>rather, "he himself"</gloss> had considered these things with him on the previous day, just as the **third creator** <note>Plato. <meta>This page continues Proclus's metaphysical interpretation of the opening scene of Plato’s Timaeus. # PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS I.

...participates in everything toward the making of the second order. For the whole of generation <note>original: "genesis" — refers to the physical world of change and becoming</note> also requires 
<margin>E</margin> the upward-sending of things from the subterranean world. And if these things are so, it seems that the Atlantic story also possesses a **threefold** <note>original: "tritēn" (third) – the apparatus suggests "trittēn" (threefold)</note> narrative. They say that the numbers **two** <term>the dyad: representing division or movement toward the physical</term> and **three** <term>the triad: representing return, completion, or the creative act</term> are appropriate to the middle level of creation—the former because of its power, the latter because of its creative and perfecting **providence** <note>original: "pronoia" — the divine forethought that orders the world</note> over worldly things. Therefore, whether you assign a double or a triple narrative to it, you can trace it back from either of those numbers to the concept of "the middle way."

**"He then introduced a speech to us from ancient hearing, which you should tell now to Critias here, so that he may join in judging, according to the instruction, whether it is suitable or not; these things must be done, if it also seems right to our third partner, Timaeus—as indeed it does." (Page 20 D.)**

You would find here a wonderful indication, as if in images of divine things. For just as in those divine realms, the secondary powers call forth the fertile powers of the primary ones and lead them forward toward the providence of those things being governed, so too in these characters: Hermocrates calls Critias forth to speak and | fulfills the promise made to Socrates. 
<margin>F</margin> And just as in those divine realms the effects "turn back" toward the support of their causes, so in these characters Hermocrates directs himself toward Critias, while Critias looks toward the instruction of Socrates. And just as in those realms all the **demiurgic** <term>demiurgic: related to the Creator or the act of world-making</term> causes depend on the one Father and govern all things by His will, in the same way here all the speakers take refuge in Timaeus and wait for Timaeus’s nod, or his approval, or his will, so that starting from that will—as if from a root—they may arrange the speech according to | 
<margin>I</margin> his mind. In this way, the things about to be said might also contribute to the whole **construction of the cosmos** <note>original: "kosmopoiïa"</note>. Indeed, the phrase "from ancient hearing," if the story is historical, signifies what is ancient in terms of time; but if it is an indication of things that happen in the universe, it would hint at the "rational principles" <note>original: "logoi"</note> that exist in souls from eternity. And if it carries an image of divine causes, it shows that these creative causes, being filled from above by the elder gods, also share their own providence with the secondary beings.

> **"Listen then, Socrates, to a story very strange, yet entirely true, as Solon, the wisest of the seven, once said." (Page 20 E.)**

<meta>This page continues Proclus's discussion on the nature of the Atlantic story in Plato's Timaeus. On the previous page, Proclus explored the symbolic meaning of the numbers two and three in the structure of the narrative. Now, he addresses the historical authenticity of the Atlantis account and how different Neoplatonic philosophers have interpreted its deeper meaning.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...they say it is true, just as the first commentator on Plato, Crantor, asserts. He says that Plato was mocked by his contemporaries for not being the inventor of his *Republic*,
<margin>B</margin> but for merely rewriting the accounts of the Egyptians. Crantor says that Plato took these critics so seriously that he attributed this history of the Athenians and Atlanteans to the Egyptians, claiming that the Athenians once lived according to that very form of government. The high priests <note>original: "prophētai" — in this context, the ranking Egyptian priests who interpreted sacred texts</note> of the Egyptians also bear witness to this, Crantor says, stating that these things are written on pillars which are still preserved today. 

Others, however, say that the story is a myth and a fiction—something that never actually happened, but which serves as an indication of things that exist eternally or are perpetually coming into being in the cosmos. These people do not listen to Plato when he cries out that the story is "very strange, yet entirely true." For that which is "entirely true" is not true in one way and false in another, nor is it a falsehood on the surface but true in its hidden meaning; such a thing would not be "entirely" true. 

Others do not deny that these events happened in this way, but they believe they are now being used as images of the oppositions that pre-exist in the universe. For "War is the father of all things," even according to Heraclitus. Of these interpreters, some refer the analysis to the fixed stars and the planets,
<margin>C</margin> taking the Athenians to be analogous to the fixed stars | and the Atlanteans to the planets. They are said to "fight" because of their **counter-movement** <term>antiperiphora: the opposing rotational directions of the celestial spheres</term>, and the one group "conquers" because of the single, overarching revolution of the cosmos. The noble Amelius is of this opinion, and he is so insistent that this is the case—because it is clearly stated in the *Critias* <note>Plato’s unfinished dialogue that follows the Timaeus and provides details on Atlantis</note> that the island of Atlantis was divided into seven circles <note>The text of the Critias 113E actually describes concentric rings of sea and land, but Amelius interprets these as the seven planetary spheres</note>—that he defends it more than almost any other of his own doctrines.

Others refer the story to the opposition of certain **daemons** <term>daimones: intermediary spirits between gods and humans</term>, some being better and others worse, some superior in number and others in power, some conquering and others being conquered, as Origen <note>not the Christian father, but the Neoplatonist Origen who was a student of Ammonius Saccas</note> supposed. Others refer it to the conflict of souls, specifically between the more beautiful souls who are the nurslings of Athena and those other souls associated with the realm of generation, who belong to the god who presides over **becoming** <note>original: "epichōrō" — likely referring to Poseidon, who in the myth is the ancestor of the Atlanteans and a god associated with the material world</note>. This is the interpretation of Numenius. Still others, mixing the opinions of Origen and Numenius, as they believe, say it is an opposition of souls against daemons, with the daemons drawing the souls down while the souls
<margin>D</margin> are being led upward. | Among these thinkers, the "daemon" is understood in three ways. For they say there is one class of divine daemons, another which is relative—consisting of individual souls that have obtained a daemonic lot—and a third which is evil and harmful to souls. They believe these lowest daemons stirred up this war against the souls...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's discussion on the symbolic versus historical interpretation of the Atlantis story. Having previously mentioned that some see it as a literal history and others as a pure myth, Proclus now explores how the story reflects the cosmic struggle between opposing forces—a "War" that exists at every level of reality, from the gods down to material bodies.</meta>

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK I.

...souls in the descent into generation. And just as the ancient theologians—they say—referred these matters to Osiris and Typhon, or to Dionysus and the Titans, Plato refers them to the Athenians and the Atlanteans out of piety. But before the souls descend into solid bodies, he presents a war of the souls against the material demons, whom he associated with the West; since the West, as the Egyptians used to say, is the place of harmful demons. The philosopher Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist and student of Plotinus who often looked for hidden allegories in texts.</note> holds this opinion, and one might wonder if he says anything different from the tradition of Numenius.

But these men were quite nobly corrected by the most divine Iamblichus, at least in my view. It is the preference of Iamblichus and our own instructor <note>referring to Syrianus, Proclus’s beloved teacher</note> to interpret this opposition not as a rejection of the historical accounts—
<margin>E</margin> on the contrary, while those events are shown to have definitely happened, we are accustomed to refer the preliminaries of the dialogues back to the same goal as the dialogues themselves. It is pleasing, therefore, in a similar fashion, to lift this opposition from human affairs and extend it through the whole cosmos, especially the realm of generated things. We should extend our thinking to all things, observing how everything participates in opposition according to the variety of their powers.

For since all things come from the One and from the <term>Dyad<note>original: "duas" — the Pythagorean principle of "twoness" or multiplicity that follows the ultimate Unity.</note></term> that follows the One, they are somehow united with one another and yet have received an opposing nature; just as among the "kinds of being" <note>In Plato's "Sophist," these are the five fundamental categories: Being, Sameness, Difference, Motion, and Rest.</note> there is a certain opposition of Sameness to Difference, and of Motion to Rest. Since everything in the cosmos participates in these "kinds," it would be right to observe the opposition that runs through all things.

Moreover, if we have viewed the <term>Republic<note>original: "politeia" — meaning both Plato's dialogue and the concept of an organized state or "cosmic constitution."</note></term> as analogous throughout the whole cosmos, we must surely also perceive this War as being present in all of nature. For the "Republic" is analogous to the existence and the essences of things, while the "War" is analogous to their powers and, as Plato himself said, their motions. 
<margin>F</margin> And we should say that the Republic is made like the whole unification—which makes all things common—while this War is made like the cosmic division under the dominion of <term>Strife<note>original: "neikos" — the principle of separation and conflict, famously used by the philosopher Empedocles to explain the universe's diversity.</note></term>. 

Whether, then, you divide the whole of reality in two, into the incorporeal and the corporeal; and again the incorporeal into the more intellectual and the more material; and the corporeal into the heavens and the realm of generation; and the heavens into opposing revolutions, and generation into opposing powers; or whether you take this opposing life in any way whatsoever—either among the <term>encosmic gods<note>Gods who exist within the universe and govern its physical structures.</note></term>, or in demons, or in souls, or in bodies—you would have all...

<summary>Proclus argues that the war between Athens and Atlantis is not just history or myth, but a symbolic representation of the fundamental cosmic opposition between Unity (the Republic) and Division (the War) that exists at every level of existence.</summary>
<keywords>Proclus, Atlantis, Iamblichus, Porphyry, Dyad, Strife, Encosmic Gods, Neoplatonism, allegory, cosmic opposition</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s argument that Plato uses the war between Athens and Atlantis as a symbolic "pious analogy." In the previous page, Proclus discussed how earlier philosophers like Porphyry and Iamblichus interpreted this conflict not just as history, but as a representation of the fundamental oppositions found throughout the cosmos—from the gods down to the material world.</meta>

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK I.

<margin>25</margin> ...everywhere one must carry the analogies from human affairs over to the nature of things. For even the divine Homer <note>original: "ὁ θεῖος Ὅμηρος". Proclus refers to the "theomachy" or battle of the gods in Iliad, Book 20, lines 67–74.</note> creates "oppositions" among the gods themselves: he sets Apollo against Poseidon, Athena against Ares, the River <note>Xanthus/Scamander</note> against Hephaestus, Hermes against Leto, and Hera against Artemis. 

One must perceive the process of "generation" <note>the way things come into being</note> occurring in incorporeal beings, in physical bodies, and in those things composed of both. Thus, we should establish Poseidon and Apollo as the creators of the entirety of generation—the former in a universal sense and the latter in a specific, partial sense. 

Hera and Artemis are the providers of the generation of life—the former in a rational way, the latter in a physical way. 

Athena and Ares are the causes of the opposition that extends through both states of "being" and "living"—the former defining this opposition according to the Intellect, and the latter according to the more material and passive state. 

Hermes and Leto are the presiding deities over the twofold perfection of souls—the former through the powers of knowledge and the projection of reason, 
<margin>B</margin> and the latter through the smooth, voluntary, and willing ascent of vital forces. 

Finally, Hephaestus and Xanthus are the leaders of all bodily composition and the powers within it—the former presiding over the more active forces, and the latter over the more passive and material forces. 

As for Aphrodite herself, she is left alone by herself so that she may shine a light of union and harmony upon all things. She assists the "lesser" side because, in these pairings, the lesser represents the movement toward multiplicity. For every opposition is properly viewed in relation to "the One," whether the One exists before the opposition, exists alongside it in a unified way, or is somehow generated after it.

Plato, having observed these things just as the master-theologians did, correctly handed down the "multiplied" state of the world before describing the one single act of world-making. He found these parts before the wholes, and these things in images before the "paradigms" <note>the divine blueprints or original forms</note>. He observes this analogy in human affairs as something that also exists in the whole of the universe. 

In doing so, he has no need for a <term>Titanomachia<gloss>The War of the Titans against the Olympian gods</gloss></term> or a <term>Gigantomachia<gloss>The War of the Giants against the gods</gloss></term>. (For how could he say things that would please Socrates, who only the day before had accused the poets who fabricate such myths? <note>A reference to Plato’s Republic, Book II (378c), where Socrates argues that stories of gods fighting are morally harmful to the young.</note>) 

Instead, Plato took his material from history so that his discourse would not involve 
<margin>C</margin> the gods | actually fighting one another, but would rather be carried out regarding human beings. Then, through a pious analogy, the meaning is transferred to the gods themselves. 

For even to the "inspired" poets <note>such as Homer or Orpheus</note>, such wars are handed down as existing before the establishment of the single cosmic order. But that poetic style is appropriate for them, while this historical style is appropriate for Plato. Within the context of political philosophy, Plato’s way is more "temperate" <note>spiritually and socially restrained</note>, while the poetic way is more "inspired" in the context of <term>teletics<gloss>Theurgic or initiatory rituals used to connect the soul to the divine</gloss></term>. 

These things cover the general meaning of the text. As for the specific passage laid out before us, hear that the phrase "listen then" is a proverbial expression used when one wishes to call someone...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the opening of Plato's Timaeus. Having just discussed the symbolic battle between the gods as an analogy for cosmic forces, Proclus now moves into a linguistic analysis of the dialogue’s introductory words and a defense of the character of Solon, the great Athenian lawgiver.</meta>

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK I.

...will catch the listener's attention. So, the command "listen" <note>original: "ἄκουε"</note> is equivalent to saying "receive these matters which are worthy of attention." 

The word "strange" <note>original: "ἄτοπον" (atopos), literally "out of place"</note> sometimes indicates the "irrational" <note>original: "παράλογον"</note>, as when Plato says in the *Gorgias*: "Strange things indeed, O Socrates"; or it indicates the "paradoxical," as he uses it in the *Crito*: "What a strange dream, Socrates!"; or the "marvelous," as in the *Theaetetus*: "And it is not at all strange, but much more marvelous, if he were not such a man." In this present context, however, the word is taken to mean "worthy of wonder." This is made clear by what follows, when he says regarding these same things: "how great and wonderful <margin>D</margin> were the ancient deeds of this city." 

Moreover, the term "account" <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note> indicates the truth of what is about to be said; for it is stated in the *Gorgias* that an "account" differs from a "myth." 

Regarding the statement that Solon was the "wisest of the Seven" <note>The Seven Sages of Greece</note>, this was said quite appropriately: it was spoken by a relative <note>Critias</note>, addressed to another Athenian, set during the Panathenaic festival, and serves as an indication that the forthcoming discourse extends to the heights of all wisdom. One should not wonder why he was called "wisest of all," nor should one be pedantic about how he could be called the "wisest of all men" while being only "one of the wise" and "all of them together being the wisest." For what is so strange if a man is called the wisest even among those of equal rank? 

His wisdom is testified to by his legislation, his famous pretense of madness to recover the island of Salamis, and his encounter with the tyrant Peisistratus—where Solon told those who did not perceive the danger that he was the more "prudent," and told those who did understand that he was the more "courageous." His wisdom is further shown by his meeting with King Croesus and his response to the person who said Solon had established the most beautiful laws; for Solon replied that he had not established the "most beautiful" laws, but rather "those that were possible," for he knew there were better ones.

There is also a story told about the tripod that was caught in a net by some young men. | Even if not everyone tells the story the same way, it is said that when the god <note>Apollo at Delphi</note> gave an oracle that the tripod should be given to the "wisest," <margin>E</margin> it was first brought to one sage, but he sent it on to another of the Seven, and that one to another, until finally it came to Solon. All the others having yielded the honor to him, Solon then dedicated it to the god on his own accord, saying that the god was the wisest of all beings. 

It is also attributed to Solon that the lunar month is not exactly thirty days long; because of this, he was the first to call the last day of the month "the old and the new" <note>original: "ἔνην καὶ νέαν"</note>. Indeed, the entire practice of counting the days of the month backward after the twentieth day is traced back to him. Some even claim that Solon declared that "Intellect" <note>original: "νοῦν" (Nous)</note> presides over the whole of reality long before Anaxagoras did. From all these examples, it is clear that he truly shared in a profound degree of wisdom.

<summary>Proclus analyzes the linguistic nuances of the Timaeus's introduction and provides a biographical defense of Solon’s wisdom through various historical anecdotes and scientific contributions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the introductory scene of Plato’s Timaeus. Following the discussion on why Solon is called the "wisest of the Seven," Proclus now addresses the historical lineage connecting Solon to Critias and Plato, while transitioning from historical facts to their higher philosophical significance.</meta>

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK I.

...[Solon] was a kinsman of ours, and a very close friend of Dropides my great-grandfather, as he himself says in his poetry. Regarding Critias our grandfather, he said—as the old man <note>Critias the younger, the speaker in the Timaeus, is recalling what his grandfather, Critias the elder, told him.</note> in turn reminded us—that there were great and wonderful ancient deeds of this city, which had vanished through time and the destruction of men. 
(Page 20 E.) <note>This refers to the standard Stephanus pagination of Plato's Timaeus.</note>

<margin>F</margin> The history regarding Solon’s lineage and his kinship with Plato is roughly as follows: Exekestides had sons, Solon and Dropides; and Dropides’ son was Critias, whom Solon also mentions in his poetry, saying: "Tell the fair-haired Critias to listen to his father; for he will not follow an erring leader." <note>Solon’s poetry often contained moral advice; here it is used to prove the family connection.</note> The sons of Critias [the elder] were Callaeschrus and Glaucon. Of Callaeschrus, in turn, came this Critias <note>the Critias present in the current dialogue</note>. And the Critias in the *Charmides* makes this clear by calling Glaucon, the father of Charmides, his uncle. Of Glaucon, there were 
<margin>26</margin> [Glaucon] and Perictione; and of Perictione came Plato. Thus, Glaucon was the uncle of Critias, and the father of Charmides; and Charmides was the uncle of Plato, being the brother of the great-grandfather Critias. <note>Proclus is tracing the family tree to show that the characters in Plato's dialogues are often his own relatives.</note> So this is the truth of the matter. 

However, Iamblichus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher who lived about a century before Proclus.</note> gives the succession of the lineage in a different way: he directly makes Glaucon the son of Dropides. Others say that Callaeschrus <margin>K</margin> and Glaucon were both sons [of Dropides], as does Theon the Platonist. And indeed in the *Charmides*, Critias says that Charmides is the son of Glaucon, "our uncle," and—using these very words—says "he is my cousin." Therefore, Glaucon was neither the son of Dropides nor the brother of the younger Critias. 

But none of these things matter to a man who is concerned with the realities of the situation, however they may stand. You should take these [genealogies] as images to proceed toward the realities: that the whole distribution of the cosmos and the dual alignments <note>original: "συστοιχίαι" (systoichiai); a Pythagorean term for parallel columns of opposing principles like Light/Dark or Limit/Unlimited.</note> within it depend upon immediate demiurgic <note>craftsman-like or creative</note> causes and are traced back to other more intellectual and ancient causes.

...that the causes of this motion are continuous and unified <margin>B</margin> and hang from a single source, and that those things which are higher are "older" in terms of Intellect. It shows how secondary things receive the creative power of the primary ones, and how they both differ from them and yet possess a natural kinship with them. In addition to these points, [Plato shows] that forgetfulness occurs in two ways for souls regarding the nature of the whole and the "Contemplation of the Whole" <note>This refers to the soul’s pre-birth vision of divine reality.</note>—which are great and wonderful things—either by being separated from such a life for a long time, or by falling too precipitously into "becoming" <note>The physical world of birth and change.</note>. For this latter case is the "destruction of the true human" <note>Proclus believes the "real" human is the rational soul; identifying too much with the physical body "destroys" its true nature.</note>. However, newly-initiated souls, who still hold a memory of the things from that higher world, easily remember the truth despite the struggle against matter. These matters should be arranged in this way. Furthermore, if he simply called Solon a "kinsman," one should not wonder at it. For they used to call not only their close acquaintances "kinsmen," but also their actual relatives. The addition of the phrase "a very dear friend" indicates that the connection was not merely a shared lineage, but a "sameness and similarity of life" among the ancestors of Plato’s own family line. By calling the elder Critias an "old man," he signifies his wisdom and his intellectual nature, which is well-suited to "ancient" <note>original: *polia*, literally "gray-haired" or "venerable."</note> studies.

> "Of all [the city's deeds], one was the greatest, which it <margin>C</margin> 
> would be fitting for us to mention now, both to return a 
> favor to you and at the same time to justly and truly praise 
> the Goddess during her festival, as if we were singing a 
> hymn in her honor."

Longinus <note>A famous 3rd-century literary critic and philosopher.</note> used to wonder what Plato intended by inserting this narrative. He argued it was not done to give the listeners a "breather," nor because the dialogue actually needed the story. He solved the problem, as he thought, by saying that Plato included it before the "physiology" <note>The study of nature or physics.</note> to charm the listener and to "pre-treat" the dryness of the coming technical explanation through this narrative's placement. Origen <note>The Platonist philosopher, a contemporary of Plotinus, not the Christian theologian.</note>, on the other hand, claimed that the story was a "fiction" <note>original: *plasma*, meaning a constructed story or myth.</note>, agreeing to this extent with the followers of Numenius. However, he argued it was not fabricated for the sake of mere pleasure as Longinus thought, though Origen did not provide a specific reason for the fiction. We, however, have often said that this narrative contributes to the entire "Contemplation of Nature" <note>The study of the physical cosmos.</note>. Indeed, in these very words, we claim that the "one and common reason" for the two-fold "alignments" <term>sustoichia: the Pythagorean concept of opposing pairs of principles like Light/Dark or Limit/Unlimited</term> in the cosmos, and the single opposition extending through all things, is what he calls the "greatest and most wonderful" of works. It holds together the rest of creation, which is <margin>D</margin> an unbreakable structure composed of opposites—of "limiting" and "unlimited" factors, as Philolaus <note>A Pythagorean philosopher.</note> says, and as Plato himself says in the *Philebus*, stating that there is much "Limit" in the world and much of the "Unlimited," and these opposites together complete this universe. Since everything that contributes to the "world-making" <note>original: *kosmopoieia*</note> is said to "give thanks" to the universal causes, it is only natural...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the opening of Plato’s Timaeus. Having discussed the characters and the timing of the dialogue, Proclus now explores the metaphysical symbolism behind the Athenian festivals mentioned in the text, specifically how they reflect the cosmic order and the role of the goddess Athena as the weaver of reality.</meta>

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK I.
Page 60

And Critias says that it is fitting for him to return the favor to Socrates, as he has set in motion the second and third powers <note>original: "δυνάμεις" (dynameis). This refers to the secondary and tertiary levels of divine or cosmic principles following Socrates' initial discourse.</note>. These matters, then, you may understand directly from the text. But as for the Athenian festival <note>The Panathenaea, the city's most important festival in honor of Athena.</note>, would you not say that this also contains an indication of "demiurgic" or creative works? For this goddess <note>Athena.</note> holds together the entire making of the world and contains within herself intellectual lives <note>original: "νοεράς ζωάς". These are the rational principles that guide the formation of the universe.</note> according to which the "All" is woven, and unifying powers according to which she governs all the oppositions within the world. 

The Athenian festival indicates the gift that extends through all things and fills all things from the goddess, as well as the unity that has reached through all the variety of the cosmos. For it is especially in festivals that we embrace our common, <margin>E</margin> harmonious life. If we have spoken correctly about these things, it is possible to trace back from them the varied yet unified life of the world, and to observe the difference between Plato's *Parmenides* and this dialogue, the *Timaeus*. 

For both dialogues have their setting during the Athenian festivals; however, the *Parmenides* took place during the "Great" Panathenaea and this one during the "Lesser" <note>The Great Panathenaea was held every four years with more splendor; the Lesser was an annual city event.</note>—for these were celebrated around the same time as the Bendideia <note>A Thracian festival in honor of the goddess Bendis, which Socrates attends at the start of Plato's Republic.</note>. This is fitting: since the "crafting" <note>original: "ποίησις" (poiesis)</note> of Athena is twofold—being both universal and particular, above the world and within the world, intelligible and sensible—the *Parmenides* is linked to her transcendent creations, revealing the intelligible "series" of the gods, while this dialogue is linked to her lower creations, interpreting the powers of the gods regarding the physical world. 

It seems that the festival of the Bendideia signifies the opposition coming from the outside, from the "barbarian flood" <note>Bendis was a foreign, Thracian goddess; Proclus sees her festival as representing the unruly forces of matter at the edge of the cosmos.</note>, which is subdued by the gods who oversee the whole. This is why the festival is recorded as being performed in the Piraeus <note>The port of Athens.</note>, as that location is most appropriate for the furthest and most material parts of the universe. In contrast, the Panathenaea signifies the <margin>F</margin> good order descending from the goddess into the world, and the unconfused distinction of cosmic oppositions. For this goddess is both a "philosopher" and "lover of war" <note>A reference to Athena’s dual nature as the goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare.</note>. 

Therefore, another "robe" <note>original: "πέπλος" (peplos). The ceremonial robe woven for Athena’s statue.</note> containing a war in which the foster-children of Athena are victorious is offered to the goddess, just as the Panathenaic robe depicts the Giants being defeated by the Olympian gods. Thus, a hymn is offered to the goddess that is both "just" and "true." It is "just" because it is necessary for everything that has proceeded forth to return to its own origin; and it is "true" because the hymn is derived from actual things and beings. 

<margin>27</margin> Of hymns, some praise the essence <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia)</note>, while others praise the providence <note>original: "πρόνοια" (pronoia)</note> of the gods, and still others praise the works that come from them. Such a hymn [based on works] is the lowest form of praise—for praises based on divine essence lead all others, as Socrates teaches in the *Symposium*—and it is therefore fitting to praise her according to what she is. For Critias intends to praise the goddess based on the deeds performed by the Athenians. That the Panathenaea followed the Bendideia is noted by the commentators, and Aristotle of Rhodes <note>A Peripatetic philosopher and student of Eudemus, not the famous Aristotle.</note> testifies that the Bendideia in the Piraeus...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's Timaeus. Having discussed the symbolic timing of the dialogue during the festivals of Athena, Proclus now moves to the introduction of the story of Atlantis, analyzing the literary style of Plato and the historical lineage of the tale from Solon to Critias.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK I. 61

to be performed on the twentieth of Thargelion <note>A month in the Athenian calendar, roughly May-June</note>, and that the festivals concerning Athena follow^1).

**"But what sort of deed is this, Critias, not merely told as a legend, but one truly performed by this city in ancient times, as you were recounting?" (Page 21 A.)**

Socrates, rousing Critias to the discourse, demands to hear of the "greatest deed." Critias the Elder said he had heard it from Solon—a story not widely rumored, yet nonetheless true. In this, it is first worth observing that <margin>B</margin> many things happen in the universe that remain hidden from the masses (and in this way, excellent men differ from others: they see and perceive such things through those who lead them). Secondly, we see that more perfect causes delight in simplicity and move from the composite to the primary, while lower things, conversely, descend from the simple to the composite. For in this way, Socrates has run upward from below as far as Solon, whereas Critias, beginning from Solon, has descended into his own memory.

**"I shall tell an ancient story I heard, not from a young man." (Page 21 A.)**

Longinus^2) points out here that Plato cares for the beauty and variety of his vocabulary, reporting the same things in different ways. For he called the deed "ancient" <note>original: "archaios"</note>, the story "old" <note>original: "palaios"</note>, and the man "not young" <note>original: "ou neos"</note>, even though he signifies the same thing through all these and could have addressed them all in the same way. Now, Longinus was a <term>philologist</term> <note>A scholar of language and literature</note>, as Plotinus is said to have remarked of him, and not a philosopher^3). Origen <note>This is Origen the Neoplatonist, a student of Ammonius Saccas, not the Christian theologian</note>, however, did not concede that Plato aimed for engineered pleasure or certain embellishments^4), | but rather that he cared for a natural and <margin>C</margin> unadorned persuasiveness and for accuracy in his imitations—and indeed, that this form of interpretation is natural to him, as befits an educated man. 

For Aristoxenus the musician^5) was right to say that the dispositions of philosophers extend even to their spoken sounds, revealing the order that exists in all their affairs. Just as, I believe, this great heaven displays clear images of the brilliance of divine thoughts in its shifting patterns, moving in harmony with their unseen revolutions^6). But the great Iamblichus^7) considers it better for us to trace the variety of these words back to the actual "things" or realities they represent, and to see how even in nature...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the opening of Plato’s Timaeus. Following the critique of the philologist Longinus (who focused on Plato’s style), Proclus transitions into a Neoplatonic allegorical interpretation of the characters and the timing of the dialogue, specifically the festival of the Apaturia.</meta>

# PROCLUS

opposites are mastered by the One, and how the One is diversified, and how the same formative principles <note>original: "logoi"; these are the rational structures or "blueprints" of reality</note> manifest their variation—existing in one way in the Intellect of the universe, in another way in the Soul, in another in Nature, and lastly having come to be in Matter; and within the realm of Matter, they display a vast difference alongside their likeness to their sources. For these insights are worthy of Plato’s deep thought, rather than a meddlesome study of his vocabulary.

<margin>D</margin> **"For Critias was then, as he said, already nearly ninety years old, and I myself was about ten." (Page 21 B.)**

Three characters are taken up here who have arranged this history (or mythology): Solon, the elder Critias, and this younger Critias. This is because the causes of the "world-making" <note>original: "kosmopoioia"</note> and those that bring governed things to completion are preceded by a perfect triad. From Solon, the elder Critias heard the story—one from one; but from that elder Critias, both the younger Critias and Amynander heard it; and from this younger Critias, three others heard it. Thus, through the "dyad" <note>the number two</note>, the "monad" <note>the number one/unity</note> proceeds toward the providential care that completes all things. 

The numbers of their years also have a great affinity for the subject matter. For the number ten signifies the "reversion" <note>the return or turning back</note> of all worldly things toward the One; and the number ninety signifies the "restitution" <note>the restoration to a former state</note> back to the monad after the "procession" <note>the flowing out of creation</note>. Both numbers carry the symbol of the cosmos. If you wish to speak allegorically, Solon corresponds to the cause of "remaining" <note>stability</note>, the elder Critias to the provider of "processions" <note>multiplicity</note>, and this younger Critias to the cause that "reverts" <note>returns</note> the things that have proceeded and joins them back to their beginnings. Thus, one preserves the character of a "leading cause," another of a world-making cause that is freely engaged, and the third of a cause that already cares for the whole and presides over the "war" within it <note>a reference to the conflict between Atlantis and Athens described later in the story</note>.

<margin>E</margin> **"It happened to be the day of *Koureotis* for us during the festival of *Apaturia*. As many of us children as were there..." (Page 21 B.)**

**The Apaturia** was a festival dedicated to Dionysus, established following the single combat between Melanthus and Xanthus the Boeotian. Melanthus won the victory through "deceit" <note>original: "apate"; hence the name Apaturia</note> while the Boeotians and Athenians were at war over the region of Oenoe. The festival was celebrated over three days: the first was called **Anarrhysis** <note>meaning "drawing back the head," referring to sacrifice</note>, because many sacrifices were performed on it; the second was **Dorpia** <note>the "Feast of Banquets"</note>, for there were many feasts and dinners on this day; the third was **Koureotis** <note>the "Day of Youths"</note>. On this day, they enrolled the youths into the <term>phratries</term> <note>clans or kinship groups in Athens</note> when they were three or four years old. On this day, the more industrious of the children also sang various poems, and those who remembered the most poems would triumph over the others.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the introductory narrative of Plato’s Timaeus. ### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK I

...for they used to recite the works of the ancients. Concerning the members of the phratry <term>phratores; members of a kinship-based social division in Athens</term>, this much must be known: 1) <unclear>that</unclear> after Ion, there were four tribes, and after Cleisthenes there were ten; <sig>F</sig> <unclear>and</unclear> these became twelve. Each of the tribes was divided into three parts, and the "phratry-members" were those <unclear>enrolled</unclear> in the same tribe and phratry, acting as relatives to one another. The enrollment of the 2) young boys took place into these phratries. From this, the day took its name from the children being enrolled, and was called *Koureotis* <note>original: "koureotis"; the "Day of the Youth" or "Day of Shearing," the third day of the Apaturia festival when new members were registered</note>, just as we have said.

<unclear>These</unclear> details are from history; but we must look back again at the underlying realities, and <unclear>in</unclear> these historical facts, we must contemplate those realities as if in images. 4) The festival of the Apaturia <note>the "Festival of Common Fathers"</note>, having a pretext | of an Athenian victory, is appropriate to the current subject, insofar as <sig>28</sig> the <unclear>Athenians</unclear> are victorious and all intellectual principles prevail over the things within matter. Furthermore, the <unclear>diversity</unclear> <note>original: "poikilia"</note> of the festival is characteristic of cosmic forms as they depart from the indivisible and from rational <unclear>principles</unclear> <note>original: "logoi"</note>, appearing instead as things that have become "becoming" rather than "truly being." The enrollment <unclear>on</unclear> the paths mimics the descent of particular souls into their appropriate lots and their descents into various births. The aspect of the festival signifies the eternal good-order <note>original: "euthēmosynē"</note> within the universe. 6) For if we are filled with the gods, we celebrate an eternal festival 7).

The prizes for the rhapsody <note>the performance of epic poetry</note> correspond to the struggles endured by the souls who weave together their own lives with the Whole. The rhapsody itself <unclear>is</unclear> <unclear>drawn</unclear> out and woven into the life of the Whole; for it possesses an imitation of the Forms <note>original: "eide"</note>, just as epic poetry imitates heroic actions and characters, while maintaining a harmonious sequence. The many poems of the many poets represent the many <unclear>nature-principles</unclear> and the many cosmic 10) <note>translated from Latin apparatus: "Taylor thinks the word 'logoi' has fallen out; why not 'gods' or 'daemons'?"</note> powers, and in general the division of imitations. The "new poems" <note>mentioned in Plato's text</note> represent the forms that are always in their prime, <sig>B</sig> perfect and fertile, and capable of acting upon other things. So much for these matters.

<unclear>Nor</unclear> was the mention of Solon's poems accidental. He is not viewed as a "poet" in the common, demiurgic sense <note>the sense of a mere craftsman</note>, but as one who mixed philosophy with the poetic art, since the King Intellect <note>original: "nous basileus"</note> leads both divine works and universal "poems" <note>in the sense of creations</note>. And the praise is traced back to another, Amynander, because the one who praises is not far removed from the one who acts and generates, as we have <unclear>learned</unclear> in the *Phaedrus* 11). Through all the <unclear>aforementioned</unclear> things, being led back to the Whole as if from images, the argument states this: that <unclear>within</unclear> the world, a "war" is carried out by particular souls, <unclear>and</unclear> natures, and divided forms—and most of all by those that are always 13) new and <unclear>perishable</unclear>. Yet all these are held together by the gods who oversee the creation, until they are organized into one world, one harmony, and one common goal.

<margin>C</margin> Again, in these passages, those who love to observe the style of writing point out to their <gloss>1) original: "autōn"; perhaps "of themselves"</gloss> companions that Plato praises the poetry of Solon cautiously. He attributes the praise to a layman <note>original: "idiōtikon"; referring to the phratry-member rather than an expert critic</note> and as a favor to others, rather than speaking from his own mind or what is strictly reasonable. Yet, if anyone was a supreme judge of poets, it was Plato, as History itself confirms. For instance, Heraclides <gloss>2) Heraclides of Pontus; a philosopher and student of Plato</gloss> of Pontus says that Plato preferred the works of Antimachus over those of the famous Choerilus <gloss>3) original: "Choirilou"; a popular epic poet of the time</gloss>, and even persuaded Heraclides himself to go to Colophon <note>an ancient city in Ionia</note> to collect the man's poems. Callimachus and Duris <gloss>4) Note on Callimachus and Duris; Hellenistic poets and scholars who criticized Plato's taste</gloss> babble in vain when they claim Plato was not a competent judge of poets; for even the present passage reveals his philosophical <gloss>5) original: "philosophon"; though one manuscript reads "of the philosopher"</gloss> judgment. 

One might view these matters as merely historical; however, the investigator of reality will require us to see how all the <gloss>6) "the" is omitted in some manuscripts</gloss> causes of the cosmic arrangement and the governing principles of opposition are traced back to a single beginning, and how the lowest things are linked to the first through the middle ones. Thus, while the phratry-members received the story from the elder Critias, he in turn looks toward Solon. While Critias admires Solon’s poetic power, the others are led back to Solon’s poetry through the mediation of Critias; for it is to please him that they also praise the poetry. 

<margin>D</margin> But what does Critias <gloss>10) Critias says</gloss> actually say about Solon? He says that Solon is second among the "inspired" <note>original: "entheōn"; poets possessed by divine frenzy</note> poets for two reasons: first, because he treated poetry as a side-project <note>original: "parergōs"</note>, and second, because he found the city of the Athenians in a state of civil strife <term>stasis; political factionalism or uprising</term> upon his return from Egypt, and so, out of concern for his homeland, he was unable <gloss>12) "was not able"</gloss> to fully compose the account <note>original: "logon"</note> he brought from there to here. 

What this account is, he will say as he proceeds. But through these "images," he makes it clear that the primary creative <term>demiurgic; the power that shapes the universe</term> and poetic <gloss>13) "the" omitted in some versions</gloss> principle has certain primary activities, but also a secondary activity directed toward lower things. He also shows that the discordant and unstable nature of matter often does not receive the order proceeding from more divine causes, but relates to the gifts given by them disproportionately <gloss>14) original: "asymmetrōs"; corrected from "proportionately"</gloss>. For this reason, secondary and tertiary powers have come forth, which directly bring order to the formless nature of matter. Now Solon, being "most free" <gloss>15) a reference to the Timaeus 21 C</gloss> and imitating these transcendent causes, did not hand down the account of Atlantis <gloss>16) "through poetry" omitted in some versions</gloss>...

# ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK I. 65

...of causes; but Critias and those after him also bring these things out to others, imitating <margin>E</margin> the secondary and tertiary causes, which bring into the light the variety of discourses and the world-order <note>original: "diakosmēsin"; a term for the structured arrangement of the universe</note> harmonized from opposites. Furthermore, the fact that Solon is the "wisest" shows his analogy to the first principles; his "most noble" <note>literally "most free-spirited"</note> character represents a power that is transcendent, established within itself, and fills all things without being bound to them. Such a quality coincides with the "wise man" as someone immaterial, independent, and belonging to himself. The fact that the Elder Critias is proclaimed as an "old man" in these passages indicates the intellectual cause that is far removed from the realm of generation <note>the world of change and "becoming"</note>; for wisdom, as Plato says <gloss>original: "phēsi"; referring to the Laws, Book II, 653 A</gloss>, and true opinions might fortunately come to a man in his old age. Conversely, the fact that this younger Critias remembers the story so vividly reveals the preservation of eternal reasons <term>logoi; the rational blueprints of reality</term> and the stable activity of the secondary causes regarding the first. That poetry was a "side-project" <note>original: "parergon"</note> for Solon indicates that even among the first causes, those "makings" or "productions" directed toward secondary things hold a secondary place; for their primary activities are intellectual, through which they remain in contact with the principles that precede them.

<margin>F</margin> If anyone, putting aside the inner realities we have discussed, should consider the reason why Plato introduced these details on a surface level, he would reasonably find that they suit the subject at hand. Since his goal was to narrate the Atlantic War, it was necessary for the messenger of this history to be neither a deceiver nor one who is deceived. Therefore, Solon is called "wisest" and is a relative of Critias and his family; for as a wise man he is not easily deceived, and as a relative he would not be a deceiver. Moreover, the person receiving the story had to be neither of such an age that the story seemed modern,

<margin>29</margin> nor so young as to be forgetful. Therefore, the younger Critias is presented as a youth, but one capable of remembering, so much so that he could compete against others in the recitation of epic poetry <term>rhapsōdian</term>, which requires a great deal of memory. Furthermore, it was necessary that the Elder Critias did not take up such stories as a young man, lest they seem trivial or easily dismissed. It is fitting, then, that one of the members of the phratry <note>a social clan</note> is presented as inquiring about Solon and hearing the history. But it was also necessary for this man to be related to Solon in some way, so that the old man might narrate the entire history concerning him at the appropriate time. This is why the praises of Solon's poetry—which Amynander offers as a favor to Critias—precede the history itself. So much for the "economy" <note>the structural arrangement or literary management</note> of the text. Now, it is clear that Solon went to Egypt not merely for the sake of history, but so that the Athenians might live for a time under his laws; for they had sworn to him that no one would repeal the laws he had established. During this time, he met with Croesus <margin>B</margin> and sailed to Egypt. Upon his return, he found the city...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the opening of Plato's Timaeus. # PROCLUS

...disturbed by the family of Pisistratus <note>the "Pisistratids" were a dynasty of tyrants who ruled Athens in the 6th century BCE</note>. Let this much be said from history. Origen <note>original: "Igenes"; footnote 1 clarifies this refers to Origen the Platonist</note>, however, was puzzled as to why Solon was called "most noble" <note>original: "eleutheriōtaton"; this Greek word implies both the status of a free man and a generous, liberal spirit</note>, thinking such praise was not fitting for a poet. He solves the puzzle by saying that either the name comes from Solon’s "liberality" with money—being wealthy, he used words abundantly and generously—or because he was "most frank" <note>original: "parrhēsiastikōtaton"; meaning one who speaks all and holds nothing back</note> and therefore "free," showing no restraint in his poetry; or perhaps because his style was relaxed and unpretentious. 

But Iamblichus <note>a highly influential Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says that none of these are true. Rather, he says this "nobility" signifies the absolute and independent nature of Solon’s Mind, the "unmastered" <note>original: "adespoton"; a term suggesting virtue that is not a slave to passion</note> quality of his virtue, and his dignity which transcends all other things. Furthermore, this same interpreter says that the fact that Critias "smiles" indicates the perfect "bringing forth" of causes, which rejoices in its own offspring; while his "vivid memory" shows the preservation of the creative <term>logoi; the rational blueprints or principles</term> within the world-order. 

Why then was Solon eager to hand down the account of the Atlantic war in poems? It was because, as Iamblichus says, all natural works and cosmic opposition exist through "imitation" <note>the idea that physical events reflect higher, divine realities</note>. For Critias corresponds to the immediate and secondary causes, just as Solon corresponds to the primary and creative causes. And why was the work dissolved by "factions" <note>referring to political strife in Solon’s time</note>? Because material movements and "material turmoil" <note>original: "enylos thorybos"</note> become an obstacle to the creative principles of the world, as has been said before.

-> He spoke of a deed being most justly of all the greatest and most <-
-> famous, which this city performed, but through the destruction of <-
-> those who performed it over time, the account did not survive to the present. <-
<margin>21 D.</margin>

Regarding these words, Longinus <note>a famous literary critic and rhetorician</note> thinks that the phrasing is lacking; for he believes that the word "considered" should be added to "most justly," because that is what is required by the context, rather than "being." But Porphyry <note>a student of Plotinus</note> says that Longinus did not understand that because the deed *is* the greatest, but not *yet* famous, Solon added that it "most justly would be called" so. We, however, holding fast to the reality of the matter, say that he called the deed "greatest" because it carries the image of the entire cosmic opposition as it extends everywhere; and "most famous" because it contributes to the visible creation. For in this way, even in the verses of Orpheus <note>the legendary mythical poet</note>, the works of nature are called "famous":
<margin>D</margin>
> And the famous works of nature remain, and boundless eternity.

-> Tell us from the beginning; he said, what and how, and from whom, <-
-> Solon, having heard the truth, told the story. (Page 21 D.) <-

The "what" refers to the wonderful deed itself; the "how" refers to the manner in which it was performed...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, transitioning from a discussion of Solon’s lineage and the transmission of Egyptian records to a symbolic and philosophical interpretation of Egyptian geography. Proclus moves from the "universal" meaning of the setting to the "particular" details of the Nile Delta and the city of Sais.</meta>

-># PROCLUS <-

**30** These things regarding the whole account; but it is necessary also to go through the particulars. Some call Egypt an image of matter <term>hyle; the raw material of the universe</term>, while others call it an image of the whole earth, divided proportionally to it, and others call it an image of the <term>intelligible essence; the realm of pure thought and being</term>. We, however, say that in these descriptions, Egypt is made to resemble the entire invisible arrangement, which is the origin of all visible things. The **Delta** is formed where the Nile splits around the **Saitic district** <note>original: "nomos", an administrative region of ancient Egypt</note> from a single straight line to the right and left ¹), flowing out toward the sea, so that the sea becomes the hypotenuse of the triangle. This is why Plato mentioned the **Saitic district** ²) here, indicating that the stream of the Nile splits at its summit. This is analogous to the single life-generating spring of divine life, and among visible things, it corresponds to the **celestial triangle** ³) which contains all of generation. It is situated near that climate which the Egyptians honored exceptionally because of **Ammon** who is established there with a ram’s face, and because the **Ram** <note>the zodiac sign Aries</note> is the beginning of generation and is the swiftest-moving, 

**B** as it is set among the stars around the equator. It is appropriate, then, that mention was made of the **Delta** in these passages, since the **triangle** is the beginning of the existence of the cosmic elements, as we shall hear in what follows ⁴). The **Nile** is positioned proportionally to the **zodiac**, as it lies beneath it and slopes in a similar way, mimicking the zodiac's slant through its branches and its division at the equinoctial points; it bears the symbol of the **life** that is poured out upon the whole world. Furthermore, the two sides of the Nile that carry down from the summit to the sea are somewhat like the two "columns" <note>referring to the Pythagorean table of opposites</note> proceeding from a single root from the beginning of creation, of which this material generation is the recipient; thus a triangle is formed from those sides and their common base, into which they flow together ⁶). The **Saitic district** is a great portion of the Delta and participates in a great portion of the heavens. Indeed, for the priests, **Sais** ⁷) is referred back to the **North** <note>original: "Arctos", the constellation of the Bear</note>, not because it is physically located there or because of any coldness, but because it participates in a certain unique emanation <note>original: "aporrhoia"</note> of this Goddess <note>Athena/Neith</note>. For this reason, it is also unmoved ⁸) by earthquakes, because through the [spirit] of the whole region it has received a firm and stable foundation ¹⁰). |

**C** In this district, the greatest city is **Sais**, from which King **Amasis** also came. For these people, the founding deity of the city is one who is called **Neith** ¹²) in Egyptian, but in Greek, as [they say, Athena].

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK I.

...their account, Athena. And they say they are very fond of the Athenians and in a way kindred to them. (Page 21 E.)

The **district** <term>nomos; an administrative region in Egypt</term> received its name from the fact that they **distributed** ¹) the land among themselves; for this is what the Egyptians called the divisions according to the large parts of Egypt. The entire district is named the **Saitic district** after the city, just as the **Sebennytic** is named after **Sebennytus** and the **Canopic** after **Canopus**. Furthermore, **Amasis** <note>Ahmose II, a Pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty known for his friendliness toward Greeks</note> is now introduced as an analogue to **Solon**. For he, too, beyond all other kings, was devoted to wisdom and justice. Thus, Solon has this partnership with him, just as the city of Sais has with the city of the Athenians, so that you may behold both the cities and the men adorned by the one **Monad** <term>a single, unifying divine principle</term> of the Goddess, and see how secondary things are always perfected by those that are more perfect. 

**Callisthenes** <note>a historian and grand-nephew of Aristotle</note> and **Phanodemus** record that the Athenians were actually the ancestors of the people of Sais, 
<margin>D</margin> but **Theopompus** says the reverse—that they were **colonists** ²) from them. | (**Atticus the Platonist** says that **Theopompus** altered the history out of malice; for he claims that in his own time ³) certain people arrived from **Sais** to renew their kinship with the Athenians). But **Plato** said only this much about them: that the people of Sais are "fond of the Athenians" and "in a way kindred." He is able to say this because of the **Patron Goddess** ⁴) who is one and the same for both. 

Concerning the Overseer of these cities, one must know the following: proceeding from the **intelligible** <term>purely spiritual</term> and **intellectual** causes through the **super-celestial** ranks, she was allotted her own proper places in the celestial regions and the distributions of the earth. She did not receive her leadership as something accidental, but rather she pre-contained the very essence and form of the place within herself, and thus received this allotment as something kindred to her own nature. 

That the power of this Goddess extends from above down to the lowest things is shown by the Greeks when they say she was born from the **head of Zeus**, and by the Egyptians who record that this inscription is written in the inner sanctuary of the Goddess: **"I am all that is, and that shall be, and that has been. No one has ever lifted my veil. The fruit I bore became the sun."** 
<margin>E</margin> This Goddess is therefore a kind of **creative** <term>demiurgic</term> power, at once hidden and manifest, who holds her allotment in the heavens and illuminates the realm of generation with forms. Indeed, the constellation of the **Ram** <note>Aries</note> is dedicated to this Goddess, as is the **equinoctial circle** itself, where her motive power is most especially...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus (21E-22A). The previous page established the kinship between Athens and the Egyptian city of Sais, noting that both are under the protection of the same goddess (Athena/Neith). Proclus now explores why this single divine power is expressed through different names and how divine oversight interacts with physical geography to shape different nations.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...the power of the whole is established. It is with good reason, then, that Plato calls her both a "lover of wisdom" and a "lover of war," and has now addressed her as the "Foundress" <note>original: Archēgetis</note> of these lots on earth. First, he does this to honor the Goddess through her ancestral title; for the people of Athens <note>the "Attics"</note> used to call their city-protecting deity "Foundress" ¹), singing hymns to her as the one for whom the city is named and its original leader ²). Secondly, he is demonstrating that the administration of these "lots" <term>allotted regions of the world</term> is contained within her in a single, unified form. Furthermore, he makes it clear to us that the same reality can be signified through several different names, since names are merely images of the thing they signify. 

Just as there can be many statues of a single person made from different materials, the Egyptians will offer an account ³) for why they called her by this name, and the Greeks will do the same. 
<margin>F</margin> There is nothing | surprising about both naming her correctly, as if they had assigned the names according to a single science of wisdom. If, therefore, there is one guardian for both cities—Sais and Athens—it is natural that those living in Sais are "fond of the Athenians," since they are in a way kindred to them. However, this kinship is not absolute; for different people may participate more or less in the same divine providence, or they may participate in different powers within that same goddess. 

We must also understand this: the differences between various nations arise from the specific places they inhabit, from the mixture of the air, and from their relationship to the heavens <note>referring to astrological influences</note>. If you like, you can look even deeper at their "seminal reasons" <term>logoi; the underlying formative principles of a being</term>. 
<margin>31</margin> But you would say they differ most of all according to | the "divine shepherding" <term>agelaiokomikē; the way gods tend to human populations like a shepherd tends a flock</term> and the differences between their presiding deities. Because of these divine differences, you will find variations in skin color, physical shape, voice, and movement in different places. This is why colonists often change the color and voice of their ancestors when they move to other lands, just as plants change their qualities along with the nature of the soil, even if they have been transplanted into a foreign land.

->Solon said that when he traveled there, he became<-
->very honored among them, until he discovered things about such matters. (Page 22 A.)<-

Because of his own political wisdom and the dignity of his city, Solon naturally appeared honorable to the priests of Sais. Yet, when compared to the memory and history preserved by those priests, he found that neither he ⁴) nor any other 
<margin>B</margin> Greek | knew anything about the truly ancient past. Indeed, the memory of the ancients...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus. On the preceding page, Proclus discussed the shared patronage of Athens and Sais under the goddess Athena. # ON THE TIMAEUS I.
71

...it contributes to political virtue, and it also contributes to the contemplation of cosmic cycles <term>periods of time in which the heavenly bodies return to the same positions</term>—which Solon, in his pursuit of them and in his questioning of the priests, found himself ¹) entirely lacking. These matters are also symbols of divine realities. For among the theologians <note>referring here to Neoplatonic interpreters of Orphic or Chaldean lore</note> there is a certain "new creation" <note>original: nea dēmiourgia; this refers to the work of the "younger gods" who fashion the mortal parts of the soul and the physical body</note>, and this is honored in a distinct way ³) both by the Father of all and by the intelligible gods. Among those higher gods, the thoughts <note>intellectual perceptions</note> are transcendent and indeed more eternal than all others, whereas those in the second rank are more partial and lesser. There is also a distinction among the creative principles such that some encompass more universal forms and others more partial ones; some take precedence in dignity and power, while the "new" ones are subordinate to those and possess a diminished power.

->And once, wishing to lead them ⁴) into a discussion about the ancients, as far as counting the times.— (Page 22 B.)<-

<margin>C</margin> All such divine causes are provocative of more divine powers, and through this provocation, they are filled by those more divine | and more universal natures above them. This is exactly what Solon does now: by proposing the most ancient Greek traditions to the priests, he somehow draws them into a discussion regarding their own antiquity, which the Egyptians participate in to an extraordinary degree. This is because they observe the heavenly bodies without hindrance ⁵) due to the purity of the air, and because they preserve the memory of ancient times, being destroyed neither by floods nor by fires <note>original: ekpyrōseis; periodic world-conflagrations in Stoic and Platonic thought</note>. Iamblichus ⁶) says that the Assyrians have not only kept records for two hundred and seventy thousand years, as Hipparchus says, but have also handed down through memory the entire "restorations" <term>apokatastaseis; the completion of a full cosmic cycle</term> and periods of the seven world-rulers <term>cosmocrators; the planetary deities</term>. Still, much ⁷) Greek archaeology—so often discussed—must be compared against these records. From this, it is clear that the present narrative should not look toward something small, but toward the Whole and the All. Furthermore, the "archaeology" of the Greeks varies from place to place: for the Athenians, it goes back as far as Erichthonius the "earth-born" <note>a legendary early king of Athens</note>; for the Argives ⁸), as far as Phoroneus ⁹) and Niobe. These are the most ancient figures among the Greeks, since Argos was the son of Niobe, and from him came Iasus and Pelasgus, from whom | Pelasgian Argos takes its name. <margin>D</margin> The stories ¹⁰) about Deucalion and Pyrrha ¹¹)—how they were saved on Parnassus during the flood, and how they established the human race after they descended—are well known; for the Thessalians, antiquity goes back only this far. According to some, the Argive lineage begins with Inachus, and that of the Athenians ¹²) with Cecrops, both of whom lived before Deucalion. Now Solon, [recounting] these and similar things...

# PROCLUS
72

...counting some things ¹), he led the Egyptian priests into an account of the ancient traditions among them; let us observe what one of the ancient priests ²) says in response to these things. These matters will become clear through what follows. According to Egyptian histories, Solon encountered a priest named Pateneit in Sais, Ochlapi in Heliopolis, and Ethimon in Sebennytos. It is likely this Saitan priest who says the following words to him:

->O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children. An old Greek<-
->does not exist. (Page 22 B.)<-

<margin>E</margin> The priest is old so that, even when rebuking, he might not be overly offensive, and so that he might possess the authoritative speech ³) suited to teaching about antiquity. He uses a repetition of the name ⁴), not only as if he were exerting himself intensely regarding what he is about to say, but also to indicate the "recirculation" from the same things back to the same things <term>anacyclēsis; the Neoplatonic idea of the soul or cosmos returning to its origin</term>. The more universal causes of everything that happens in the universe have grasped this cycle in a stable and intellectual way ⁵) through indelible knowledge—and the priest is analogous to these causes. He accuses the Greeks of being "always children" ⁶) because they did not pursue the manifold wisdom of the Egyptians, but most among them carried "slave-like hair" ⁷) in their souls <note>original: "tēn andrapodōdē tricha"; a metaphor for a soul lacking the "grooming" of higher education or philosophy</note>. Their lack of sense, therefore, is indicated by "youth." Alternatively, it is because destructions among them ⁸) are frequent; before the existing people can become "ancient," they become "young" again through catastrophe. Or, it is because ancient deeds are not preserved among them; rather, they always know only the present and whatever their senses suggest. To the Egyptians, however, even past events are always present as "new" through memory. This memory comes through history, and history comes from the pillars ⁹) <term>stelae; stone monuments</term> on which they recorded the extraordinary and wonderful facts of reality, whether in deeds or in discoveries. But why, they ask, did | this <margin>F</margin> priest rebuke him so offensively? For what is so wonderful about knowing past events? "Much learning does not grow the mind," ¹¹) as the noble Heraclitus says <note>original: "polymathiē noon ou phyei"</note>. And if what Eudoxus says is true—that the Egyptians used to call a month a "year"—then the enumeration of these many years would hold nothing wonderful. Thus, the Egyptian would be pointlessly arrogant about these things. One must grant that while memories and sensations are not themselves the creators of science <note>referring to systematic, certain knowledge</note>, as Aristotle says, they nevertheless contribute to the "recollections" <term>anamnesis; the soul's recovery of innate divine knowledge</term> of the wholes. For by recording many similar things over a long period, we project the single "form" <term>eidos</term> within them; and having often found the "restorations" <margin>32</margin> | of many cycles to be in harmony through history, we arrive at the one | cause.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the interaction between Solon and the Egyptian priest. Having previously discussed why the priest addresses Solon twice, Proclus now moves into the metaphysical significance of the priest’s rebuke regarding the "youth" of the Greek soul compared to the "antiquity" of the Egyptian tradition.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS I. 73

...we trace back to the causes. For in this way, both the observations of atmospheric phenomena according to Callippus <note>Callippus of Cyzicus was a 4th-century BCE astronomer who refined the planetary models of Eudoxus and studied weather patterns.</note> were established, as were the predictions derived from the astrology of celestial motion. These things have been said by us in response to the one who raised the problem; but we must return again to the contemplation of the "wholes" <term>the universal or total realities</term> and observe there the "new demiurgy" <term>the secondary stage of creation involving mortal and material life</term> which is held together by Athena and fulfilled by the elder and first-born causes. For from that source, this demiurgy possesses its permanence, contributing both to what is transcendent <note>original: *to exērēmenon*; referring to the reality that exists beyond or separate from the material world</note> and to the cosmic opposition. For everything that is divided and multiplied in the progression of the "demiurgic" <term>the act of the divine Craftsman or Creator</term> process proceeds through that principle.

Since, then, there are causes in the cosmos—some productive of "palingenesis" <term>the cycle of rebirth or regeneration</term> and others protective of the stable coherence of the "ratios" <term>the *logoi*, or the underlying rational principles of the world</term>—the priest is taken as analogous to these protective causes, while Solon is analogous to the productive ones. For this reason, the priest displays a memory that excels in its antiquity <margin>B</margin>, while Solon is said to record various changes, births, and destructions. It seems to me that this also has been appropriately included in the arrangement of the whole: that the "elder" is placed before the "younger." For in the demiurgy of Zeus, things hold this order toward one another; just as the Eleatic Stranger <note>The main speaker in Plato’s *Statesman* (Politicus), who tells a myth about the world’s rotation reversing.</note> says that those living in the "Period of Cronus" <term>a golden age when time supposedly ran backward</term> proceed from the elder to the younger, but those in the "Period of Zeus" proceed in reverse. And here Timaeus will say regarding the Soul that the Demiurge produced the soul as "elder" to the body, and for this reason, he established it as more authoritative. Now, therefore, the priest—the guardian of divine laws—claims to hold power because of antiquity, even though the "younger" order <note>meaning Solon/Athens</note> comes from a higher rank, just as Solon has set out from a city that belongs more to Athena; but in the works of the cosmos, the "elder" possesses great dignity.

->“You are young in your souls,” he said. “For you hold no old opinion<-
->within them from ancient hearing, nor any learning gray with time.”<-
->(Page 22 B.)<-

These things are analogous; in those instances, <margin>C</margin> the youth of the souls corresponds to the "drawing back" of life and to the more "particular" causes... <note>original: *tais merikōterais aitiais*; Proclus is likely contrasting universal causes with those that govern specific, individual parts of the world.</note>
