<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the dialogue between the Egyptian priest and Solon from Plato’s Timaeus. It explores the metaphysical distinction between "ancient" (gray) knowledge, which views the universe as a unified whole, and "youthful" knowledge, which focuses on the changing, material parts of the world.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...to the youthful intellect and the more ancient principles <margin>Note in Manuscript A: These refer to the "absolute" or "unconditioned" causes.</margin>. The "gray" <note>original: *polion*; literally "gray-haired," used here to mean ancient or venerable wisdom</note> learning belongs to the unified and ever-constant cycle <margin>Note in Manuscript A: This refers to the crafting (demiurgy) of the universal celestial things—the first of the three stages of creation.</margin> of the nature and composition of all things in the cosmos. Because of this, the first and most divine of cosmic things contain, in a universal and transcendent way, the causes of everything that comes to be; they have grasped eternal things before they even occur in time. However, things closer to the whole <margin>Note in Manuscript A: This refers to the causes associated with the stars.</margin> possess these causes only partially and in a subordinate way, as they fall short of the unified intellect of the "wholes" <term>the universal or total realities of the universe</term>. 

For this reason, "grayness" is associated with some of the gods, while "youth" is associated with others. The "gray" is a symbol of an intellect and a pure life that exists far above the realm of "generation" <term>the world of change, birth, and physical matter</term>, whereas the "youthful" represents that more partial knowledge which already touches upon things as they are coming into being.

The cause of these things is as follows: "Many and varied destructions of men have occurred, and will occur; the greatest through fire and water, and countless others through many other lesser means." (Stephanus page 22C).

The argument seeks the reason why the Greeks are "always children" and why no "gray" learning exists among them. <margin>D</margin> Or, if you wish to consider the underlying patterns, it seeks why the "new demiurgy" <term>the secondary stage of divine crafting</term> presides over variety—given that things in the material world are always in a state of becoming and being renewed as they grow old. 

But before the text finds the cause of such puzzles, it first describes the "periods" <term>the vast, repeating cycles of time</term> within the whole universe and demonstrates their variety. This variety is known by the very first divine principles in a permanent and unified way, but the secondary principles know it only partially <note>original: *merikōs*</note> and by touching upon the nature of the things they govern. For the latter involves knowing things only as they are present, while the former involves holding even things that are absent in the memory by observing the "wholes" separately and permanently. 

What, then, are these varied periods of the things in the cosmos? One must always assume generation <term>the process of being born</term> and corruption <term>the process of decay or passing away</term> within the whole. For the sensible world is always coming to be and passing away, and never truly *is*. However, one must observe this generation and destruction differently in the heavens compared to material things. In the heavens, there exists a pre-existing change of shapes and the motion of things that are always "becoming," and through those celestial changes, the process of generation is governed as it unfolds its own circle. <margin>E</margin> 

Within this circle, sometimes one element prevails, and sometimes another. While the "wholes" always maintain the same and similar order according to nature, in the "parts," that which is according to nature or contrary to nature occurs at various times as is necessary. Or, perhaps, both the wholes and the parts are always in a state according to nature...

<summary>Proclus explains the distinction between "gray" (ancient/universal) and "youthful" (partial/changing) knowledge, linking them to the celestial cycles and the periodic destruction of human civilizations by fire and water.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the stability of the universe versus the transitory nature of its parts. Proclus is explaining why certain natural disasters (like floods and fires) are more total than others (like plagues or earthquakes) based on the physical properties of the four elements.</meta>

# PROCLUS

<note>original: ΠΡΟΚΛΟΥ</note>

...nor $^1$) <gloss>that which is mortal and sublunary</gloss> is it possible to remain [unchanging] in the whole, but the Law of Zeus $^2$) <gloss>the order within the whole universe</gloss> casts out of essence everything of such a kind $^3$) that has become, as it were, "dishonored." For it is entirely impossible for that which remains to be "dishonored" $^6$) <gloss>disordered</gloss>; and that which is utterly deprived of order is "dishonored." Now, it has been stated why both collective and partial destructions occur in various places; but next we must discuss why the greatest of these destructions happen through an excess of fire and water, rather than the other elements.

Fire holds an active and productive rank among the elements; it is capable of passing through all the others and is naturally suited to divide $^9$) them. Water, on the other hand, is more easily moved than earth, yet more resistant to being affected than air. By being easily moved, it is able to act; but by being resistant $^{10}$), it is forced not to suffer <term>to be acted upon or changed by an outside force</term> nor to become weak by being scattered like the air. Consequently, it is reasonable that the most violent and greatest destructions are carried out by flood <term>kataklysmos</term> and conflagration <term>ekpyrosis</term>.

<margin>C</margin> One might also say | that the remaining two $^{11}$) elements are more akin to us. Our nature as land-dwelling creatures makes us akin to the earth, and the fact that we are surrounded on all sides by air—living in it and breathing it—demonstrates the kinship of our bodies to that element. Therefore, because these are somehow more akin $^{12}$) to us, they are less destructive, while the elements that are in this sense "contrary" to us bring about more violent destructions. 

Furthermore, in another way, these elements—earth and air—seem to act upon us only after they themselves have suffered $^{13}$) some change. For air, having undergone putrefaction, produces plagues; and the earth, having split apart, produces mass swallowings <term>chasms in the ground</term>. Indeed, a plague is an "affection" of the air, just as chasms and earthquakes are "affections" of the earth. But fire and water are able to act upon us without first suffering themselves—the one penetrating through us, the other pushing from the outside—wherefore they work more collective destructions because they are more robust than the others, destroying without themselves being changed. 

Therefore, these are the greatest destructions: floods and conflagrations. Famines, plagues, earthquakes, wars, and other such partial "affections" might arise $^{14}$) from other causes. <margin>D</margin> The productive cause of all these things is the order of the whole, and prior to that, the "new demiurgy" <term>the secondary creation carried out by the younger gods</term> which is always making things new and producing $^{15}$) the generation of different things at different times. For this is what the myths among the Greeks say, and what the tradition of the Egyptians indicates when speaking mystically of the Sun as it changes into different forms within the signs of the Zodiac. It is no wonder, then, if while many and various destructions occur, humanity always remains—and indeed every species remains—because of the immovable [nature of the cosmic order].

### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 1

...the procession of the divine forms $^1$) <gloss>the fertile and active principles in the Creator, of the various and manifest material forms</gloss>. For because of those, the principles <note>original: "logoi" — the rational, formative structures of reality</note> in the universe stand always in the same way, because everything that comes from an immovable cause is always linked to its own cause $^2$).

It is clear that the very first principles of beings contain, in a stable manner, the things that move; in a unified manner, the things that are multiplied; in a universal manner, the partial things; and eternally, the things divided | by time $^6$), and it is well known that theologians attribute the causes of the cosmic periods <margin>E</margin> and of the descents and ascents of souls, and of all multiplied and divided life, to those powers standing immediately above the world $^7$). Therefore $^8$) <gloss>because the "new creation" presides over birth and destruction</gloss>, it seems to me that the discourse now refers the mythology concerning Phaethon back to the Greeks and to the knowledge of Solon, because all such $^9$) destructions and births are accomplished by the "new creation" <note>The "new creation" or "younger demiurgy" refers to the celestial gods who govern the realm of change under the direction of the supreme Creator</note>, from which $^{10}$) the recycling of forms is also accomplished, as well as the variety of both bodily and psychic periods. Just as the perfection of secondary beings comes to them from the primary beings while those primary ones remain [unchanging] in the divine realm, so too the Egyptian [priest], preserving the histories of the Greeks, teaches Solon from these things about what he himself already knew. What, then, $^{11}$) does this discourse hint at? It hints that even soul-lives and the nature of bodies have many-sided changes, and these are overseen by hypercosmic <term>hyperkosmioi: powers existing beyond the physical universe</term> powers $^{12}$) <gloss>those beyond the "liberated" gods</gloss>, and are held together by the intelligible ranks of the gods. A symbol of the former $^{13}$) <gloss>the oversight</gloss> is the fact that the appearance | is recorded somewhere $^{15}$ <margin>F</margin> among the **Greeks**, while a symbol of the latter is the priest's ability to trace the inner meaning of the history and to bring the truth revealed by it into the light for Solon. Let these things be said by us for the sake of the whole theory, so that these [myths] do not appear out of harmony with the subjects at hand. The myth concerning Phaethon has a varied treatment. <meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the myth of Phaethon. Having introduced the story on the previous page, he now transitions into a Neoplatonic scientific interpretation, moving away from a literal reading of the gods toward a "natural" explanation involving atmospheric physics and cosmic cycles.</meta>

# PROCLUS

<margin>34</margin> [Phaethon, the son] of Oceanus and Clymene, while driving his father’s chariot, turned aside from the path. Zeus, fearing for the whole universe, struck him with a thunderbolt. Once struck, he fell near the Eridanus river, and the fire coming from him burned the entire earth; as he fell, his sisters, the Heliades, mourned him. Now, the literal account of the story is like this; but we must assume that a conflagration <term>ekpyrosis: a periodic destruction of a region by fire</term> actually occurred—for the whole discourse is for the sake of this—and that its cause was neither impossible nor something that happens commonly.

It would be impossible if one were to think that the Sun <note>Helios</note> sometimes drives his own chariot and at other times abandons it through a change of mind, entrusting his own work to another. On the other hand, it would be a "commonplace" explanation if one were to suppose that this Phaethon was a comet which, by dissolving, creates a drought; for this is a familiar and well-trodden explanation.

Indeed, Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century scholar and predecessor to Proclus</note> says that they even took signs from the movement of comets: <margin>B</margin> when they moved toward the south, they signaled storms; toward the north, droughts; toward the east, plagues; and toward the west, prosperity. They called the disappearance of the comet a "striking by thunderbolt," as the formation of these things is quite common. There are many discussions about comets in works on natural philosophy.

But if one must resolve the Phaethon myth in a more scientific manner, it is better to follow the approach of our associate Domninus <note>A fellow student of the philosopher Syrianus and a mathematician</note>. He suggests that the explanation is this: a composition of dry exhalation sometimes arises from the earth such that it is easily ignited by the solar heat. It is not surprising that, once ignited, this exhalation should burn the region of the earth lying beneath it, and having caused such a conflagration as the myth describes, it is then extinguished and disappears.

The fact that the ignition comes from the sun is why the myth-makers called him the "Son of the Sun." They called him "Phaethon" <note>meaning "The Shining One"</note> because of the masculine and active power of fire—for fire is usually called masculine, while the earth is feminine, the latter being the matter and the former being the form.

The fact that such an exhalation occurs parallel to the sun <margin>C</note> is the reason for saying that he did not drive the chariot along his father’s path. The dissipation of the fiery cloud is the "fall" of Phaethon, and the extinguishing of the fire is the "thunderbolt." The falling of rain after this (for this usually happens after great conflagrations) is the "mourning of the sisters." These "sisters" are the exhalations <note>the Heliades</note>, insofar as those who mourn pour out moisture. Both exhalations, the dry and the moist, have the sun as their single cause; but the moist corresponds to the feminine, and the dry to the masculine. These approaches are more in line with natural philosophy...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s metaphysical interpretation of the Phaethon myth. Having dismissed a purely literal or meteorological explanation (like a simple comet) on the previous page, he now develops a Neoplatonic "theory of souls." He explains how souls are "sown" by specific gods, inheriting their qualities, and categorizes them based on how deeply they descend into the material world.</meta>

# PROCLUS ON THE TIMAEUS I.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
But the myth may also say something more sublime: that particular souls proceeded from the Father of all things, but were sown around the worldly gods, so that they might not only be intellectual and touch the intelligible world and rise above bodies, but also possess a worldly subsistence. Just as divine and daemonic souls were arranged under secondary leaders—some under the divinity of the Earth, some under the Moon, some under the Sun, some under the leadership of Zeus, and others under that of Mars <note>Ares</note>—so what is sown | everywhere <note>original: "Diogenes." The critical apparatus suggests this might be a corruption of "by necessity"</note> receives something from the nature of that in which it is sown: those sown in the earth from the earth, those in an animal from the nature of the animal. Thus, some offspring take on the character of their locations, while others take on the likeness of their mother. For this reason, souls sown around kindred <term>synnoma: stars or constellations that share a common lot or nature</term> stars also receive from those leaders a certain specific quality of life, so that each soul is not merely a soul, but a specific kind—such as "Martian" or "Jovian" or "Lunar." Whether the god is unchanging, demiurgic, or life-giving, an impression of the quality of the one who has been allotted leadership reaches the souls subordinate to him. And what is surprising in this, when the quality of the presiding gods descends even to herbs and stones? There are stones and herbs attached to the Solar power—whether you wish to call it a "heliotrope" <note>lit. "sun-turner"</note> or by any other name—and similarly for the other gods. Of these souls, some remain untainted, always attached to their own gods and helping them to govern the whole; others descend, yet are not filled with the vice | of the realm of generation; still others receive something from the things they govern. For this is the lowest form of life. The first group are truly children of the gods, as they do not depart from their fathers, being born for them (as it were) and remaining within; they are the children who precede the gods, holding the rank of bodyguards <term>doryphorikēn: a spear-bearing or escorting rank</term> or attendants. The middle group are called children of the gods, but they also take on a second life and become children of "gods and humans." The third are called children of the gods, but not "genuine" children, as they have not preserved the form of their own god, but have leaned toward matter and have forgotten their own fathers. Whether, then, the myth-makers call Tityos a son of the Earth, or Phaethon a son of the Sun, or Musaeus a son of the Moon, or some other, they call them children in this way—some in one way, some in another, according to the causes mentioned. Regarding the others, we speak elsewhere; but Phaethon, being of the Sun...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s metaphysical interpretation of the Phaethon myth. On the previous page, Proclus began categorizing souls according to the "Solar series" (those under the influence of the Sun). He now moves into the specific fate of the soul of Phaethon, explaining his "fall" not as a literal astronomical event, but as a symbolic descent into the material world of "generation."</meta>

# PROCLUS

[Phaethon] is a child, as he belongs to the **Solar series**, which is why he also bears a Solar name <note>Phaethon means "The Radiant One" in Greek</note>. Since, while remaining in the higher realms, he revolved together with his Father and joined in the pursuit of the Whole, he is said to "drive the chariot of the Father." For indeed, the vehicle of Phaethon is one of the **Solar chariots**, as that too is entirely sun-like in nature. But since he inclined toward **generation** <term>genesis: the world of change, birth, and decay</term>—for he was not among the very first-rank souls—he is said to have been "struck by the thunderbolt of Zeus." 

<margin>F</margin> 
For the thunderbolt is a symbol of **demiurgic power** <note>The power of the Creator God who shapes the world</note> that proceeds intangibly through all things and preserves all things. However, it is not the cause of the dissolution of the spirit that carries the soul. Many reassignments of souls occur, moving from some states of existence to others and from certain elements to others. 

<margin>35</margin> 
Some souls are transferred from the earth | to the sphere of fire, while others move from fire to the earth. Some of these moves happen in an orderly fashion, but others happen all at once and with much noise and disorderly movement—which is exactly what they say happened to Phaethon. For being carried down all at once from above and dragging along **fiery tunics** <term>chitones: the "veils" or energetic layers a soul wraps itself in during its descent</term>, when he came near the earth, he set fire to certain parts of it because he was moving erratically through those layers. 

Descending souls clothe themselves in many tunics—some airy or watery, and some even fiery. Of these, some have a faint fire, while others have one that is violent and striking. Some souls lay these aside upon entering the air and take on thicker ones, while others preserve those fiery tunics all the way down to the earth. 

Now, I know that **Plutarch of Chaeronea** <note>A famous Middle Platonist philosopher and biographer (c. 46–120 AD)</note> records a story about the islands around Britain. He says there is one island considered sacred and inviolable, which the rulers leave alone for this reason. Often, when extraordinary storms or thunderbolts occur there, the locals—being accustomed to these events—say that one of the **superior beings** <term>kreittones: higher souls, heroes, or daemons</term> | has passed away. 

<margin>B</margin> 
They use the term "superior beings" for souls that are migrating into bodies or leaving some state of generation. Nevertheless, one must not rule out that such things happen to souls descending into bodies, especially those of great works and those who have been allotted a more **daemonic essence** <note>A nature intermediate between gods and humans</note>, which is what this myth hints the soul of Phaethon to be. 

It is not surprising that descending souls are more affected by those elements which are analogous to their presiding gods. They drag along and clothe themselves in more of those "tunics," so that **Saturnian souls** <note>Souls in the series of Cronus/Saturn</note> delight more in the moist and humid, and **Solar souls** in the fiery. Instead of immaterial things, both tend to material and heavy bodies, and the gods use these souls as **instruments**, just as they use material things.

<summary>Proclus interprets the myth of Phaethon’s fall as a symbolic descent of a "Solar soul" into the material world, wrapping itself in energetic "tunics." He compares this metaphysical event to local legends in Britain about the passing of higher beings during great storms.</summary>

...pertaining to earthly creations, and through these they bring about both conflagrations <note>original: *ekpyroseis*</note> $^1$) or other such experiences $^2$) for those destined to undergo them. In doing so, they use the celestial causes of what occurs, acting as assistants to their own souls. 

<margin>C</margin>
For it is no wonder that many things have the same causes, some acting in one way, some in another. At any rate, Phaethon, being carried around the earth and burning those places $^4$) he approaches with a certain divine fire of a fiery stream—for partial souls do many things outside the body, acting as the instruments of either purifying or punishing spirits <term>daimones: intermediate spirits between gods and humans</term>—the Heliades <note>The daughters of Helios, the Sun</note> mourned him. 

They are indeed "Solar" spirits, which is why they were called the sisters of Phaethon $^5$). They mourned him not only because they pitied him due to his descent into **generation** <term>genesis: the realm of physical birth and decay</term>, but also because they provide care $^8$) so that they might keep their oversight of things that come to be and perish **pure** <note>original: *achranton*</note> $^7$). 

For the river Eridanus and his fall there indicates the movement of the soul into the moisture of generation. Having arrived there, the soul needs the foresight of its own kin and the assistance of those souls that remained above. Indeed, the theologians signify the Solar providence even toward mortals through tears: 

*Tears of yours are the race of much-enduring mortals.* <note>Proclus quotes an Orphic poem here; the "tears" of the god are the source of human souls</note>

<margin>D</margin>
So, the myth concerning the Solar souls' providence for Phaethon | symbolically revealed this through tears. Again, a conclusion <term>porisma: a secondary finding or logical deduction</term> must be taken from this myth: that the descents of souls are accomplished through weakness. For Phaethon wants to drive the chariot [of the Sun], but he is unable and falls because of this inability. 

Furthermore, it shows that not only the souls, but also their **vehicles** <note>original: *ochemata* - the "astral bodies" that carry the soul</note> share in the designations of the leading gods, so that they are called "Solar," or "Martial," or after some other god. It also shows that even destructions occur according to providence from the gods; for Zeus is the cause of the conflagration by striking Phaethon with the thunderbolt. Finally, it shows that the descents of souls depend upon the one **Demiurgy** <note>The work of the Creator God</note> $^{10}$), and Timaeus will teach us not only about their essence $^{11}$), but also about their descents $^{12}$) and their various lives and choices.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s metaphysical commentary on the myth of Phaethon from the Timaeus. # PROCLUS
### PAGE 82

<margin>E</margin> The Egyptian priest revealed only as much of the myth as was relevant to the subject at hand: that sudden, mass destructions of things on earth occur by fire due to the **deviation** <note>original: *parallaxis*. In this context, it refers to a shift or variation in the movement of celestial bodies</note> ¹) of bodies moving around the earth and in the heavens. What does he mean by "deviation"? He means the **asymmetry** of things on earth in relation to the heavenly realms. For when all things are in symmetry with the "outflowings" from above, they are able to endure; but when they are asymmetrical, they are destroyed. 

For those things able to withstand the **divisive power of Ares** <note>Mars, the god of planetary force often associated with heat and separation</note> ²) are preserved, while those that are too weak to bear its action are easily dissolved. This is like our eye ³) being blinded because it cannot bear the solar rays, whereas another eye might be able to look directly ⁴) at them without pain. The same applies to the other gods and their configurations. 

For the Whole is one single Living Being, and since its parts are in "sympathy" with one another, it preserves some things in one way and others in another. Nothing that happens within it is "against nature" for the Whole. For what happens within it happens through it; the Cosmos itself is the actor, looking into itself ⁵). 

<margin>F</margin> Thus, we should either define this "deviation" in this way—as when a good father, out of affection, might occasionally strike his son for the boy's own good, appearing to deviate from his usual habit—or we should define it as the **varied configuration** of the heavenly bodies. For these are the ones moving around the earth in the heavens, showing different patterns at different times due to the diverse thoughts of the souls. 

For those configurations are the "letters" <note>An ancient philosophical metaphor: the stars are a script written in the sky</note> of those souls, and certain active patterns created through them. Both of these explanations are true. Both the deviation of those heavenly bodies and the asymmetry of things around the earth bring about such destructions. 

If we must call the fall of Phaethon to earth from heaven a certain "deviation" of those things moving in heaven, it is no wonder. 

<margin>36</margin> For there is one kind of "deviation" belonging to the heavenly gods themselves—which is a change of form without suffering—and another belonging to the souls that travel with them, which is a relationship toward earthly things from a life that is otherwise detached. There is yet another "deviation" of earthly places, which is a destructive change, during which neither the souls nor (certainly) the leading gods of those souls themselves deviate. 

Such destructions of earthly things occur through "partial" souls, and they also occur through **spirits** <term>daimones: intermediate beings between gods and mortals</term> alone. Just as these spirits bring about the destructions appropriate ⁶) to their **chains** <term>seirai: lineages or "series" of divine influence connecting the highest gods to the lowest matter</term> ⁷), so too do the souls. For the souls above, while rejoicing ⁸) in immaterially illuminating this realm, "run over" (oversee) the conflagrations. 

But why do these mass destructions happen after long intervals of time? It is because many factors must coincide for such a destruction to occur. One must consider the state of those who "suffer" <note>those undergoing the change or destruction</note> ⁹), the...

### PAGE 83

...the whole and the common state, as well as the concord <note>original: *sympnoia*, literally "breathing together" or synergy</note> of those who act. For what if the destruction of one thing were the preservation of another? We must also consider the suitability of the matter, the preparation of the instruments, and the timing of the seasons. These factors exist in cases of partial destruction, but they occur more rarely in universal destructions, and for good reason. For it is necessary for nature to proceed from the indestructible to the easily destructible by way of things that are difficult to destroy. <margin>B</margin> If the "Wholes" <note>The major components of the universe, like the heavens and the elements in their totality</note> are always indestructible, while more particular things are easily destroyed, then those things in the middle are rightly ranked among the difficult to destroy, enduring for long periods before their loss.

For while the Wholes remain indestructible and imperishable throughout a cosmic cycle—since no configuration of the stars is destructive to them, all being wound together in the total cycle of the universe—particular and individual things admit an easy dissolution. Yet, <gloss>1) but</gloss> the collective groups of these particulars endure for long periods, even if they are eventually dissolved. For there is a "life" for a specific race just as there is for an individual man, a city, or a nation; these have their cycles, some with longer paths and others with shorter, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>A reference to Aristotle’s view that human civilizations and even geographic features undergo cyclical growth and decay over vast timescales</note> says.

**"Then all who live in mountains and high and dry places perish more than those who live near rivers and the sea."** <margin>C</margin> <margin>(Page 22 D)</margin>

In the case of visible destructions, what is expected occurs: those living near water defend themselves against damage from fire. However, the philosopher <term>Porphyry</term> <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist who often sought deeper symbolic meanings in Plato's texts</note> transfers these arguments from visible phenomena to the soul. He says that sometimes the "spirited" part <note>original: *thymoeides*, the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and fire</note> boils over within us, and this "conflagration" <note>original: *ekpyrosis*</note> is a destruction of the "human" within us. <gloss>2) they whose [eyes]</gloss> Homer described <gloss>3) regarding the angry <term>Agamemnon</term></gloss> as being "like blazing fire." <note>Homer, *Iliad* 1.104</note>

This is another kind of death for the parts of the soul; for "it is death to souls," says <term>Heraclitus</term>, <gloss>4) to become wet</gloss>. <note>Heraclitus, Fragment 77/36; the philosopher famously associated soul-health with "dryness" or light, and vice with "wetness"</note>

If these things are correctly arranged, then those whose spiritedness is tempered and measured for the care of lesser things remain untried by the passions of anger—this is what the "hollow places" and "neighbors of water" signify. <margin>D</margin>...matter; for this is what the high places reveal. For it is natural for the [active part] to be mobile and energetic, while the part of desire is relaxed and <unclear/>. It would belong to a musician to loosen the tension of the spirited part <note>original: *thymos*, the "lion-like" or emotional part of the soul</note>, and to tighten the <unclear/> of desire into a proper melody. However, the philosopher Iamblichus <note>A major Neoplatonist teacher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized the physical and ritual aspects of philosophy</note> thinks these things should be understood physically, rather than ethically. Therefore, when a conflagration <note>original: *ekpyrosis*, a cosmic destruction by fire</note> occurs, those living in high mountains are more likely to perish, as they are farther from the [moist] vapors. For these vapors do not rise very high due to the weight of the moisture. Thus, the air surrounding them is not damp, but dry, and becomes fuel <unclear/> for the fire, which naturally moves upward. Conversely, when floods <unclear/> occur, those living in the hollows perish more, since all flowing water naturally moves downward.

->But for us, the Nile, our savior in other respects, also saves us then from this difficulty by being released. (Page 22 D)<-

On the surface, it is because the Nile is the cause of many and diverse goods for the Egyptians—<margin>E</margin> geometry, the growth of crops, and indeed it is the cause of escaping conflagrations. Both the water is [cleansing] to their bodies, and the deity who holds this together is an "elevator" <note>original: *anagogos*, meaning it leads the soul upward back toward the divine</note> for their souls. One might [conclude] from these things that the primary causes, being full of life and generative power <unclear/>, both hold themselves together and remain eternally, and they deem those things that flow and are [scattered] worthy of their own cohesion, so that even the name of "savior" <unclear/> and transcendent providence is mirrored, from which providence <note>original: *hes*, referring to *pronoia* or divine foresight</note> light shines forth in all the gods, both intellectual and demiurgic <note>The "demiurge" is the divine craftsman of the universe in Plato's philosophy</note> causes.

> "But when, on the other hand, the rains—which cleanse the earth with waters—flood it, those in the mountains are preserved, the herdsmen and shepherds, but those in the cities among us are carried away into the sea by the rivers." (Page 22 E)

In these words, the efficient cause is explicitly attributed to the gods, <unclear/> and the same can be said regarding the conflagrations; for there is a cleansing, one [happening] through water, the other through fire. Everywhere, purity comes to the secondary things from the primary ones. For this reason, in Orpheus <note>A mythical poet and the legendary source of the Greek mystery religions</note>, Zeus commands that "purifications be brought <margin>F</margin> from Crete." For he ranks Crete in place of the intelligible realm <unclear/>.

...the theologians; but they attribute the material cause <note>original: *hylikēn aitian*</note> to the flow of water. For each of these elements acts without choice, being carried along by its own natural impulse. There must, therefore, pre-exist that which uses them well and acts for the sake of the Good—which the discourse rightly assigned to the gods. If indeed there are certain purifications <note>original: *katharmoi*</note> even in the universe as a whole, then surely there are also overseers of these purifications, acting as purifiers for the whole of things before they act on the parts. Indeed, there are divine rites where some act as initiators and others are initiated, and these never fail the universe. The priest, knowing this, has called the destructions by water and fire by the priestly name "purifications," <margin>37</margin> rather than "destructions," as one might say if they were speaking only as a natural philosopher.

**In this land, neither then nor at other times does water flow over the fields from above. On the contrary, it is natural for all of it to rise from below. From which cause and for which reasons the things preserved here are said to be the oldest. (Page 22 E)**

Even if rain ever occurs in Egypt, it does not happen over the whole land, but usually occurs around the lower part; and this lower part is clearly the "work of the river," as Aristotle says; but the upper part does not receive such overflows. From where, then, does the Nile rise? Porphyry says that it was an ancient opinion of the Egyptians that the water gushes up from below during the rising of the Nile, which is why they called the Nile the "sweat of the earth," and that the "rising from below" means the same to the Egyptian as "saving by being released" <note>The Greek word *lyomenon* can mean both "melting" (like snow) and "releasing" or "solving" a problem</note>. It is not that melting snow <margin>B</margin> creates the volume of water, but that the river is "released" from its own springs and proceeds into the open, having been held back before. 

We, however, shall understand "released" in relation to the "difficulty" <note>original: *aporia*, meaning a deadlock or lack of resources</note>. For the word is used in the Attic sense: that the Nile "releases" us from our difficulty. For it is not true that the Nile increases from melting snows; for where in the southern regions, from which it flows, would snows accumulate? Nor does it rise because it is under the earth and the earth is becoming porous; for the porosity of the earth will not give the water an upward movement—there must be something else pushing it entirely, even from the hollows to the heights. These arguments, then, are directed against the Egyptian opinion; but others say that the Nile increases from certain rains pouring into it, as stated explicitly by Eratosthenes <note>A Greek polymath (c. 276–194 BC) who was the first to correctly explain that the Nile's floods were caused by heavy tropical rains in Ethiopia</note>. Therefore, "rising" here does not mean gushing up from somewhere below, but that the water, increasing from elsewhere, proceeds higher than the land because waters are breaking forth into it from other regions. # 86 PROCLUS

### ON THE TIMAEUS

...to seek, but rather to understand more simply the return of the water from below, which 
<margin>C</margin> they are accustomed to call the "ascent." Giving a twofold cause for why the Egyptians escape both droughts and floods, he clearly approves of the cause originating from rainfall. For he says the primary cause of the Egyptians' safety is the will of the gods who have been allotted to them and the original boundary <note>The "limit" or "definition" established at the moment of the world's making.</note> of the creation <note>original: *demiourgia*</note>, while the second cause is the temperament of the air. For the seasons are reversed among the <term>Antoikoi</term> <note>Those who live in the opposite hemisphere or temperate zone; literally "opposite-dwellers."</note> from where the Nile flows, relative to the regions here, and the occurrence of droughts and heavy rains alternates among them. And if someone finds fault with this explanation because the increase of waters fed by rain is not usually regular, it must be said that there are indeed many "descents" <note>decreases in water level</note> of the Nile. Nevertheless, the continuity of the rains is the cause of the uninterrupted increase of the water, as are the sizes of the mountains where the sources of the Nile lie. For these mountains, receiving the rains from the clouds that are driven against them by the <term>Etesian winds</term> <note>Strong, seasonal Mediterranean winds that blow from the north in summer.</note>, flow down from all their slopes into the sources without interruption, and these sources, being filled, cause the river to rise. For even <note>original: *Theophrastos*</note> Theophrastus says this is one cause of rain: the filling of clouds against certain mountains. Furthermore, even if clouds are not seen around the <term>Catadupa</term> <note>The great cataracts or waterfalls of the Nile.</note>, it is not at all surprising; for the Nile does not first flow from there, but from the **Moon Mountains**, which were so named because of their height. The clouds gathered near those mountains, passing by the Catadupa, pour down upon them. Now, these arguments are directed against the Egyptian discourse of <note>original: *Aristeidou*</note> Aristides; but Eratosthenes says it is no longer even necessary to seek the cause of the Nile’s rise, since certain people have clearly reached the sources of the Nile and have seen the rains occurring there, so that the explanation of Aristotle is confirmed. We note these things briefly concerning these matters. From these points, the Egyptian account established that neither conflagration <note>destruction by fire</note> nor flood happens to them. However, it is not surprising if the water should fail in other ways, if Aristotle is correct in saying that every part of the earth, in the infinity of time, becomes sea, and the same place becomes both mainland and, at other times, sea. For he did not rule out that the water of the Nile itself would fail, 
<margin>E</margin> looking toward the infinity of time. For what if the Etesian winds, blowing more weakly, should fail to push the clouds there? And what if the <unclear>rē</unclear> <note>A corrupt or abbreviated term in the Greek manuscript.</note> should collapse, a wind having broken them from the underground places—the kind of wind by which the <term>oracles</term> <note>original: *logia*</note> say even cities are destroyed along with their inhabitants—in the places where the gathering of clouds occurs? If these do not gather, the water remains <note>Textual note: "remains" might be a mistake for "diminishes."</note>...

# 87 PROCLUS

### ON THE TIMAEUS A. 87

...the stream becoming less and less, being swallowed up by the dry earth.

->**The truth is that in all places, wherever excessive cold or heat does not prevent it, there is always a race of humans, sometimes more, sometimes fewer.** (Page 22 E.)<-

He has spoken about the cosmic periods and the various shifts, and how for the Egyptians, safety is guaranteed both by the physical position of their land and by the providence of the Nile. Now, therefore, he introduces a general statement concerning the regions of the earth as follows: every place that is not being submerged by flood or consumed by fire always has a surviving race of humans, whether in greater or fewer numbers. For the greatest destructions occur through fire and water, as was said previously. And yet, someone might say, the human race could perish in other ways as well. For those who now inhabit these regions of Attica <note>The region surrounding Athens.</note> are not the same as those of old, even though no flood or conflagration occurred; instead, a certain "terrible impiety" <note original: "deinēs tinos asebeias">A scholar's marginal note in a historical copy suggests this "impiety" refers to the rise of Christianity, which Proclus—as a defender of the old Platonic and polytheistic tradition—saw as a spiritual force that wiped out the ancient Greek way of life.</note> utterly vanished the affairs of those people. 

Or perhaps we should interpret "places" here as <term>climates</term> <note>original: "klimata" — In ancient geography, these are the latitudinal zones of the Earth.</note>. He says, therefore, that every climate has humans, unless a flood or fire should occur, sometimes more, sometimes fewer. And some might be saved even in a flood, just as Deucalion was saved when the climate throughout Greece was flooded. <margin>F</margin> Some have explained the text in this way; but as **our companion** <note>Likely referring to the philosopher Domninus of Larissa, a contemporary of Proclus.</note> suggested, Plato might mean that every place on earth always has humans, either more or fewer, provided it is not excessively cold or parched. For the **mathematicians** <margin>38</margin> <note>In this context, Proclus refers to "mathematical geographers" who used geometry to map the habitable world.</note> also say that certain places are uninhabitable due to an excess of heat or cold. Every place, then, that is suitable for human habitation and every climate has more or fewer humans. And this is both reasonable and in harmony with the text. 

For the phrase **"wherever excessive cold or heat does not prevent it"** seems to mean wherever one of the opposite extremes does not make habitation impossible. Generally, since he said before that the traditions of the Egyptians are the oldest, he rightly added that, in truth, every climate balanced for human habitation always has more or fewer humans. For not only do the mathematicians say that not every climate of the earth has humans, but Orpheus also defines it thus:

> He marked out for humans a seat to dwell apart from the immortals,
> where the middle axis of the Sun turns, being observed <note original: "potineumenos">A rare term in the Orphic fragments suggesting the sun is watched or directed in its course.</note> as neither
> too cold above the head nor fiery, but in the middle...

This is what Plato has just said: that where there is neither extraordinary winter nor excessive heat, the human race always exists in greater or lesser numbers. Forgetfulness <term>lethe</term> occurs among others regarding ancient events, not because of the total disappearance of humanity, but because of the continuous <insert>2</insert> destructions that occur, leaving behind some who are illiterate and uncultured. Among us <note>referring to the Egyptians</note>, many things are said to be most ancient because of the recording of everything in the temples.

->“Whatever has happened among us or here, or even in another place <insert>3</insert>, that we know by hearsay—if anything beautiful or great has occurred, or anything possessing some other distinction—all these things have been written down from of old here in the temples and preserved.” (Page 23 A.)<-

->“Just as the goddess of the land provided salvation <term>soteria</term> for the Egyptians, and the god who was allotted the land provided it as well, so too they ensure the salvation of events through their own diligence. By this diligence, they find comfort against the forgetfulness brought by time, and they find sufficiency in the records within their temples. In these, they record all great and wonderful deeds, both their own <margin>C</margin> and those of others, or the extraordinary outcomes of affairs; for this is what constitutes having some other distinction. The history of these things contributes to their knowledge of similar events—from which comes the recollection <term>anamnesis</term> of the whole—and toward the knowledge of the future. For through such observations, they discover the productive powers of the celestial configurations. By knowing what conditions led to certain events, they are able to reason out the causes of future events from the same signs. It seems to me <insert>4</insert> also that the doctrine of the Pythagoreans imitates this kind of Egyptian history, as it prepares souls to remember their previous lives. For just as one might consider different lives for a single man, or rather for a single soul, so it is fitting to consider different cycles for a single nation. If, therefore, in the former case, the recollections of previous lives are perfecting for souls, so too in the latter, the histories of previous cycles provide the greatest contribution to wisdom. Furthermore, such observations are likened to the arrangement of the universe. For they imitate the standing principles <margin>D</margin> of nature, which remain unmoved while governing those things that change or come into being. If, then, the most holy temple is the cosmos, in which the principles that hold the whole <insert>6</insert> together remain eternally, the record of ancient deeds in the temples would be an image of this constitution. The account of the Egyptians would say that whatever is permanent in the realm of the senses <term>aistheta</term>, fixed and always the same, comes from the intelligible <term>noeta</term> gods <insert>7</insert>; but whatever is moved and changes from time to time, coming into being and perishing <insert>8</insert>, this comes from the younger...”<-

# PROCLUS

"And it left those of you who were **illiterate** and **unrefined**, as many as existed in ancient times." (Page 23 B.)

<margin>B</margin> For he said <note>The Egyptian priest speaking to Solon</note> that from the **flood**, herdsmen and shepherds were left behind, while those in the cities perished. Therefore, those remaining were **illiterate** <term>agrammatoi: literally "without letters" or unlearned</term> and **unrefined** <term>amousoi: literally "without the Muses," meaning lacking in arts, music, and culture</term>. Because of the former <note>illiteracy</note>, they are unable to hand down the memory of the previous cycle through writing; because of the latter <note>lack of culture</note>, they do not happen to be capable of preserving past lives even in songs or melodies. Hence, everything naturally falls into **oblivion**, and through this oblivion, they return to the life of **children**. For as **Aristotle** says, it makes no difference to life whether one is young in years <note>original: "διαφέρει δ᾽ οὐδὲν νέος τὴν ἡλικίαν ἢ τὸ ἦθος νεαρός" - Nicomachean Ethics 1095a</note>.

Such a thing also happens to **souls** that have recently descended into the realm of generation. For having exchanged their previous **intellectual** <insert>intellectual: corrected from "younger" in the manuscript</insert> cycle for a second, generative one, they possess an **oblivion** of the intelligible world due to the "flood" arising from **matter**. Even if they once held impressions of those things from their vision of them, they lose them as time proceeds. In this way, everything in the cosmos returns to youth through **rebirth** <term>paliggenesia: the cycle of being born again</term>, being carried from youth in different ways at different times because their nature holds its form within constant motion.

Furthermore, when changes occur, the fact that the "illiterate and unrefined" are left behind indicates to those looking at it **physically** <note>i.e., through natural philosophy</note> that the dissolution reaches down to the **formless** and **shapeless**. The loss of "letters" signifies the destruction of the **elements** <note>In Greek, 'stoicheia' means both letters of the alphabet and physical elements</note>, and the loss of "harmony" also occurs. Yet, the gods who oversee **renewal** easily heal these things and lead them back to their natural state.

<margin>C</margin> "At any rate, these genealogies of yours, **Solon**, which you have just recounted about your people, differ but little from the **myths of children**." (Page 23 B.)

The Egyptian compares the solemn and ancient narrations of Solon to the myths of children. For the myths of the **wise** concern **eternal** things, while those of children concern **temporal** and small things. The former contain a hidden **intellectual truth**, while the latter are "earth-bound" <note>original: "χαμαιπετῆ" - literally "falling on the ground," meaning low or trivial</note> and show nothing lofty. Therefore, Solon’s histories are analogous to these sorts of [children's] myths, while those of the Egyptians are analogous to the myths of the wise. For the former look toward the small, while the latter extend toward the greatest; the former are merely **histories**, while the latter contribute to **scientific knowledge** <term>episteme: certain, philosophical knowledge</term>. From these, one must also view their **paradigms**: that the things arising from the "recent" <note>lower</note> craftsmanship are called the "playthings" of the gods and resemble myths, for they are **images** <term>eidola</term> of true beings and participate in the Forms only in the most distant way; whereas the things from the **intelligibles**...

...thus existing things are intellectual <note>original: "noera"</note>, eternal, stable, and possess their own essence in a hidden manner.

**"You remember only one deluge of the earth, though many occurred before it." (Page 23 B.)**

For they used to chatter about the deluge in the time of Deucalion <note>The Greek equivalent of the Noah figure, survivor of a great flood</note> incessantly, though many others had occurred previously, as the Egyptian says. In this same way, within the universe as a whole, the "new" demiurgic creation <note>The ongoing process of world-ordering</note> produces the whole in a partial and multiplied way, and through rebirth <note>original: "palingenesia"</note> it sets the present state in good order; however, in the realm of the Intelligibles <note>The higher divine reality</note>, the causes of both the primary substance and the cyclic revolution of the Forms are pre-contained in a unified manner.

**"Furthermore, the finest and noblest race among men once lived in your country... until you were left as a people without letters or speech." (Page 23 C.)**

He wishes to link the second period to the former one, and to show that there is one continuous life of the Athenians—both those of the first age and those of the present—through the "seed" which he calls "small." This is because in the cosmos, the seeds of a prior period link the beginnings of the one following it, due to the essence of the causes, the unceasing motion of the whole, and the "unchanging change," as someone once called it. Let us not wonder if he calls Solon himself a descendant of those excellent men, while we, on the other hand, <margin>B</margin> place him as the cause of all cosmic opposition. For as a living being, he derives his lineage from them; but as one who received the particular accounts concerning the war, he is analogous to the divine power that conveys the principle of cosmic opposition from above, from the heights <note>original: "krētōn" - likely referring to the summits or sources</note> down to the sensible world. One should not be disturbed by such objections, but rather recognize the nature of analogies: that the same things become first, last, and middle through the power of analogy.

**"For there was once, O Solon, before the greatest destruction by waters, the city that is now Athens, which was the best in war and in all respects exceptionally well-governed. To her are attributed the most beautiful deeds and the most beautiful systems of government of all those under heaven of which we have heard." (Page 23 C.)**

By "greatest destruction," he does not mean the one in the time of Deucalion, but perhaps one of the deluges that happened even earlier. He calls the city of the Athenians "most warlike" and "best-governed" because it is an imitation of its presiding Goddess <note>Athena</note>, whom he calls both a lover of wisdom <note>original: "philosophos"</note> and...

**F** He will call them **war-loving** 1) as he proceeds; for they inherited the warlike quality from being "war-loving," but their law-abiding nature from being "wisdom-loving" <note>original: *philosophou*</note>. Their "noblest of deeds" was the victory over the **Atlanteans**; and their "noblest of polities" <note>or "constitutions"</note> is so called, not because he changed it many times, but because one might call this single polity a "number of many polities," just as the one Cosmos contains many worlds within it. For if the life of each individual is a kind of polity, and the common life is a communion of many partial lives, then it would be a union of many polities according to the **One Beautiful**. And of all things <margin>40</margin> known to us under the heavens, it is the first **imitation** <note>original: *mimema*</note> of the polity of the universe, so that you might say it is the best of those under heaven; for its **paradigm** 4) <note>the ideal model</note> exists in heaven. These things concern the particulars; but again, regarding the whole work of the Athenians, we must remind ourselves that it is neither a **myth** being told nor **bare history**, though some have accepted the account as history and others as myth. Some say, first, that it seems even to **Plato** 6) himself that the unfolding of these and similar accounts is laborious and not entirely fortunate; second, that Plato’s tradition is not of such an enigmatic nature as that of **Pherecydes**, but clearly teaches most **doctrines**; therefore, one should not 8) force 9) an analysis when the man has clearly set out to teach us; third, that the unfolding is not even necessary in the present circumstances, for the recognized cause for introducing this narrative is the **B** entertainment of the listeners; fourth, in addition to these, that if we analyze everything, we will fall into the same trivialities as those who laboriously dwell on the settlements in **Homer**. But those who claim—starting from the narrative concerning **Phaethon**, which Plato says has the "form of a myth" but "signifies something else" regarding natural events—that the unfolding of this history should also be led back to a **physical application** 10), since even the **Egyptians**, whom he says 11) are the fathers of this account, hinted at the secrets of nature through myths 12), so that the unfolding of this narrative would be fitting 14) for the character of the Egyptian. For just as **Timaeus** himself will make his arguments in a way suited to the **Pythagorean** philosophy, interpreting nature through **numbers** and **geometric shapes** as if through images, so also the **Egyptian priest**, in a manner appropriate to himself, would teach the **truth** concerning reality through **symbols**. In addition to these, Plato himself in other works 16) sought out those who speak everything in a superficial way, so that, as he says, they might make their **wisdom** clear even to the cobblers; thus, it is not foreign **C** to Plato to deliver true accounts through enigmas. | These things then...

...others say; but we have said <note>original: "ὡς" (as)</note> that all these things are both history and an indication of the cosmic opposition and the total order. It narrates events that happened among men, but symbolically it contains within itself the things contained in the universe and the cosmic opposition. For from above, starting from the first intelligible beings, the procession [of reality] also divided the world by opposing powers.

And if you wish, let us next divide the whole theologically according to the divine ranks, and let us observe the "co-ordinate series" <note>term: "συστοιχίας" (systoichias) — a Pythagorean concept of parallel columns of opposing principles, like Light/Dark or Limit/Unlimited</note> within it according to the Pythagoreans. 

Therefore, starting from the two principles, it makes use of **Limit** and **Infinity**, or rather, the things related to Limit and those related to Infinity; for among mixed things, some belong to the former principle and others to the latter. 

From the **Triad** <note>The "triple-manifest" (τριττοῦ φανέντος) refers to the third rank of the intelligible world</note> appearing after those principles, the division is into **Unified** and **Multiplied**; for it is there that multiplicity first exists in a unified way. 

From the next Triad, the division is into **Eternal** and **Perishable**; for the measure of being for all things comes from there. 

From the third Triad, into **Male** and **Female**; for each of these exists there for the first time. 

From the first of the intermediary ranks, the division is according to **Odd** and **Even** <margin>D</margin> — for the unitary number is there. 

According to the second, into **Particular** and **Universal**. 

According to the third, into **Straight** and **Circular**. 

Furthermore, among the Intellectual beings: 
* According to the first rank, into **Things existing in themselves** and **Things existing in others**. 
* According to the second, into **Animated** (living) and **Inanimate**, and into **Stationary** and **Moving**. 
* According to the third, into **Same** and **Other**. 

And from the "Leading" gods <note>The "Hegemonic" or ruling deities who preside over the planetary spheres</note>, the division is into those **Rejoicing in Likeness** and those **Akin to Unlikeness**. 

From the "Absolute" gods <note>The "Apolutoi" or liberated gods who are not bound to physical bodies</note>, into the **Separate** and **Inseparable**. 

These matters have been arranged elsewhere, and are now merely recounted by us as a history. For in every distinction, the side of the superior beings—desiring to fill the inferior ones and to eliminate the base—works upon the ancient [order]; while the desire of the inferior beings to tear away a certain portion of the better ones rouses the apparent...

...into total <note>universal</note> essences and partial ones; and of the totals into divine and angelic; and of souls into the divine and those that follow them; and of the divine into the celestial and those providing for generation <note>the world of change and becoming</note>; and of those following the gods into those following them eternally and those that often fall away; and of those that fall away into the pure ones presiding over generation <margin>F</margin> and those that are distressed. For the descent <note>the "kathodos" or journey of the soul into the body</note> reaches as far as these. Of celestial bodies, they are divided into the fixed and the wandering; and these into those moving with a simple motion and those with a complex one; and the complex into the specific properties of their powers. In general, for all the aforementioned divisions, there is that which adorns and that which is adorned, that which fills and that which is filled. If one must not look at a part, but grasp the contemplation of the whole, this opposition must be assumed everywhere. For it exists among gods, and in intellects, and in souls, and in bodies. For there <note>among the gods</note> is the Limit <margin>41</margin> and the Infinite; in intellects, Sameness and Difference; in souls, the circle of the Same and the Other; and in bodies, heaven and generation. But secondary things are always arranged before <note>original: "pro". Proclus argues that the lower is ranked "in front of" or "subordinate to" the higher</note> the better ones. Therefore, we say this myth is useful for the whole theory of nature, as it demonstrates to us through actions and motions the cosmic opposition. For all those who have demonstrated anything about nature begin from opposites and make these their principles. Plato, knowing this, delivers to us through symbols and riddles the opposition of the genera in the universe—what it is, and how through the intellectual energy of Athena the worse is subordinated to the better. Reasonably then, Plato called these the "deeds" and the "citizenship" <note>or "polity"</note> of the Athenians, because he knew such an analogy proceeded through all things, which the new demiurgy <note>the creation of the physical world</note> contains, but much earlier the total powers, from which Athena herself, being filled, establishes the mundane intellects, souls, and bodies according to her own specific character.

B Having heard this, Solon said he wondered, and possessed every eagerness, entreating the priests to relate everything in order with accuracy concerning the ancient citizens. (Page 23 D.)

And this is a characteristic of divine beings: that secondary natures cling eagerly to the first and are established in their pure intellections, while the first natures, through ungrudging powers and goodness, shine upon the secondary ones the fullness from themselves. Wonder, then, leads the way, because in us also this is the beginning...

of the knowledge of the whole; but in divine matters, it joins the one who wonders with the object of wonder. <note>original: "τῷ θαυμαζομένῳ τῷ θαυμάζον"</note> For this reason, those wise in divine things have sung hymns to Thaumas <note>The personification of "Wonder" and father of Iris, the messenger of the gods.</note> as a certain great god, who through wonder subordinates secondary things to the primary. There follows earnest prayer, which makes that which is to participate in more perfect goods fit for that participation.

**"The priest then said: 'I will not refuse you, Solon; but for your sake and for the sake of your city I will tell you; and most of all for the sake of the Goddess.'"**
(Page 23 D.)

Through these names, the discourse sufficiently indicates the divine causes of visible phenomena. For Solon, being an Athenian, bears the images of the city-protecting Goddess <note>Athena</note>, insofar as he lays hold of a more perfect <margin>C</margin> | intellection. And the priest, speaking as if from some inner sanctuary (for he teaches what has been recorded in the temples), bears an imitation of the middle ranks of both the new <term>demiurgy</term> <note>The creative or world-making power.</note> and the whole paternal cause. These ranks convey the gifts of the higher cause to the lower, filling the divine order as if from a certain fountain; and everything is harmoniously accomplished by the speaker. For Solon is perfected, the city is praised, and the Goddess is hymned. The ascent proceeds from Solon, through the mediation of the city, up to the Goddess, imitating the "reverting" power of the Goddess. <note>In Neoplatonism, "reversion" is the process by which a created thing turns back toward its divine source.</note>

This too is of the nature of the Good: to perform activities for the sake of the perfection of secondary things—for he exercises providence and is overflowing with divine powers. But it is a greater thing to do so for the sake of the city, for it possesses a broader activity and lays hold of a greater power. Yet even more divine than these is to direct the entire exposition toward the Goddess, and to let the end of the whole activity terminate in her. All these things regarding Solon are clearly presented to the priest, showing not only the absence of envy <margin>D</margin> | but also the divine and ready generation of good things.

Again, let us not be misled by these words if the priest is now said to represent a greater and more divine cause as the arranger of the discourse, while the Athenians—being ancestors of Solon and older than the inhabitants of Sais—are ranked according to the cosmic order of the whole opposition. For as they appear in the narrative, they hold this rank; but according to the natural progression, they bear the image of certain superior and divine orders. And if you wish to say it: since the whole creation and the cosmic opposition are pre-contained in the Father of all things—both the things that order and the things that are ordered—you might also take there, by analogy, the ancestors of the Athenians...

***

<margin>42</margin> seating the things that are held together within those that hold them | and hanging all things from the goddess according to a single cosmic bond and chain.

**"She was allotted both your city and this one, and she nurtured and educated them." (Page 23 D.)**

In a wonderful manner, the Egyptian turned all things back to the goddess; he both brought them forth from her and turned them back again. For from the political arrangement of the city, he made a certain return to the city-protecting goddess; and from her again, he imitated the procession from her toward both those things that participate in her primarily and those that participate secondarily in her goods, and again the things that participate and are nurtured...

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK I.

And having established that he is being educated by the Goddess <note>Likely referring to Athena or Neith, mentioned in the Timaeus regarding the origins of Athens and Sais</note>, he turned these matters back toward her. How, then, does he not marvelously imitate the demiurgic powers? For these powers themselves are established upon those that precede them, and they both generate the things that come after them and turn them back <note>original: "ἐπιστρέφουσιν" - a technical term in Neoplatonism where an effect returns to its cause to achieve perfection</note> toward their own causes. So much, then, regarding these matters. But what is this "allotment," and when does it occur? And in what sense are the gods said to have "divided up" the whole? Of these lots, <margin>B</margin> some belong to particular souls, some to the undefiled ranks <note>referring to higher classes of beings like heroes or demi-gods</note>, some are of the nature of spirits <term>daimonic: intermediary spirits between gods and men</term>, some are angelic, and some belong to the gods themselves. If indeed...

--- Page 111 ---
<meta>This page continues Proclus's discussion on the nature of divine distributions or "allotments" (kleroi), moving from their general definition to the specific problem of how divine providence governs the changing world of generation.</meta>

# PROCLUS
### Page 98

Of **essences**, just as with **powers** and **activities**, the progressions generate a multitude. Thus, regarding the **allotments** <note>Greek: *kleroi*; these are the specific realms or "lots" assigned to different deities or powers</note>, the very first are superior in power but diminished <margin>1) The manuscript A reads "diminished" in the dative case.</margin> in quantity, insofar as they are closer to the **One Father** and to the total and single **Providence**. However, the second orders have received a diminished power but an increased quantity. These things, then, should be considered generally regarding allotments.

But since, according to the division into two, we have distinguished between **celestial** allotments and **sublunary** <note>The region below the moon, i.e., the Earthly realm subject to change and decay</note> allotments, no argument would be raised concerning the former—what kind they are and if they always remain the same. But concerning the sublunary ones, it is worth wondering whether one should call them **eternal** or not. For if they happen to be eternal, how is this possible? For how, when all things in the realm of **generation** <note>The physical world of birth and death</note> are changing and flowing, could the allotments of those exercising providence be called eternal? For the things in generation are not eternal. But if they are not eternal, how can the matters of divine oversight be different at different times?

For the **allotment** <margin>2) Note in margin: "What an allotment is."</margin> is neither a **separated activity** of the gods—such that we might say it is set apart <margin>3) Manuscript B and the correction in A read "set apart" or "exempt."</margin> and remains immutable while these things fall away—nor is it | the **governed object** alone, so that there would be nothing strange in the allotment flowing away and being carried along in all sorts of changes. Rather, it is a **divine distribution** <note>Greek: *lexis*</note> and a **providence** concerning these things, and an **unattached oversight**. 

On account of the governed object, it does not admit the logic of eternity; but on account of the **presiding power** <margin>5) The text reads *enestos* (present), but the translator Taylor suggests *ephestos* (established over/presiding), which matches the term "oversight" used previously.</margin>, it rejects corruption. This is so that we do not attribute to the gods the qualities of **partial souls**, assigning them different allotments at different times <margin>6) This phrase is omitted in manuscript A.</margin>. What reasoning, then, could explain the allotment by both preserving immutability for the gods and explaining change for the things in generation? How must we understand it?

Perhaps the explanation will be easier for us if we pursue the inquiry in this way, which we have often approved elsewhere: namely, that one must not think all things in generation, and generation itself, consist only of changing and flowing affairs. Rather, there is something even in these things that is **immutable** and by nature always remains the same. 

For the **extension** <margin>7) Note in margin: "The separated extension/space."</margin> <note>Greek: *diastema*; referring to the spatial interval or "place" that holds the cosmos</note> which has received all the parts of the cosmos and contains them in itself and is stretched <margin>9) Some readings suggest "ordered" rather than "stretched."</margin> through all bodies is **immovable**. This is so that, if it were among the things that move, it would not itself require another space, and this would proceed to infinity unnoticed. Furthermore, the **ethereal vehicles** <note>The "astral bodies" or subtle envelopes that carry souls</note> of the divine souls, which they have put around themselves, imitate the lives in heaven and possess an **eternal essence**. They are eternally joined <margin>11) Confirmed in manuscript B.</margin> to the divine souls, being full of **generative power** <margin>12) Taylor suggests "generative powers" in the plural.</margin> and making a **circular motion** according to a second order of the celestial poles...

<summary>Proclus examines the paradox of how eternal gods can govern a changing, sublunary world through "allotments." He proposes that even within the realm of change, there are immutable elements like spatial extension and the ethereal vehicles of souls.</summary>

<page-num>99</page-num>
# ON THE TIMAEUS I.

...and thirdly, in addition to these, there is the way in which the **wholeness** <note>original: "helotes"</note> of these **elements** <note>original: "stoicheion"</note> remains the same, while the parts perish in every possible way. For it is necessary that every **form** <note>original: "eidos"</note> be inexhaustible within the whole, so that the universe may be perfect, and so that what has come into being from an immovable cause may be immovable in its **essence** <note>original: "ousia"</note>. Every wholeness is a form, or rather, it is a complete **participation** <note>original: "metousia"</note> in a single form. And you see how the nature of bodies proceeded in an orderly fashion. For one type is immovable regarding every motion, while another has accepted only motion according to place; for this is furthest removed from a change in essence. Yet another has accepted the other motions in its parts, while the whole remains entirely unchangeable.

And the heavenly **lots** <note>original: "kleroi" - divine assignments or territories</note> divided the interval and simultaneously divided the heaven itself; but those below the **moon** first received their portions in the interval, then made their distribution according to the defined **vehicles of souls** <note>the "ochēmata" or subtle bodies that carry souls</note>, and thirdly, they remain always in the same way according to the whole portions of **generation** <note>the realm of birth and decay</note>. Therefore, the lots of the gods do not change, nor do they exist differently at different times; for they do not have their **subsistence** <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> directly in that which is subject to change.

How then do the **illuminations** <note>original: "ellampseis"</note> of the gods come to be in these things? How do the dissolutions of **sacred rites** <note>original: "hieron"</note> occur? And how is the same place occupied at different times by different **spirits** <note>original: "pneumaton"</note>? It is because the gods possess eternal lots and have divided the earth according to divine **numbers**, just as the divisions of the heaven are illuminated, and these things are illuminated insofar as they possess **fitness** <note>original: "epitedeiotes" - the capacity or receptivity of a material thing to receive divine influence</note>.

This fitness is produced both by the **revolution** of the heavenly bodies—which, through these **configurations** <note>astrological aspects</note>, provides a **power** superior to the present nature—and by the whole of nature itself. Nature implants in each of the illuminated things divine **tokens** <note>original: "synthemata" - hidden symbols or signatures in nature</note> through which these things naturally participate in the gods; for as nature is suspended from the gods, it implants different **images** of them in different things. The powers around us also act—those by which the compositions of other things are governed, as well as the successes of those beyond, and generally everything around us contributes to the **increase** and **decrease** of this fitness.

When, therefore, through the **concurrence** of these many **causes**, fitness arises in something naturally subject to change for the participation in the gods, the divine then shines forth in these things—having previously been hidden by the unfitness of the recipients. The divine holds its own lot eternally and proffers its own participation, but it is not participated in by those things that are unfit, just as with partial souls...

<margin>...providing a divine illumination <note>Note: Taylor suspected "divine illumination" fell out of the text here.</note></margin>

<summary>This page explains how eternal divine influences (lots) interact with the changing material world through the concept of "fitness." It argues that while the gods are unchanging, their presence in the world fluctuates based on the receptivity of physical locations and objects, influenced by celestial cycles and hidden natural tokens.</summary>
