<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing the divine allotment of cities and the nature of the goddess Athena across different levels of reality.</meta>

# PROCLUS
<page-num>100</page-num>

...souls choosing different lives at different times, some choose those suited to their **kindred gods**, while others choose different ones through a forgetfulness of their own origins. In the same way, among **sacred places**, some are naturally allied to the god who received them by lot <note>original: *klēros* — a divine "allotment" or portion of the world</note>, while others are attached to a different rank <insert>of being</insert>. Because of this, some people have lived their lives more fortunately, and others more unfortunately, as the **Athenian Stranger** <note>A reference to the lead character in Plato's *Laws*</note> says. Whether it was through **theurgic art** <term>telestikē — the ritual art of consecrating statues or cities to draw down divine presence</term> or through **legislation** that this city was dedicated to the god who, according to the original allotment, received this eternal portion, the result is that its life is more closely conformed to its **overseeing god**. Its deeds are also more likely to be great and wonderful than those of a city that does not set out upon its actions from such a divine beginning. Indeed, the person who has chosen the life of the god who holds the lot is more successful than the one who has shifted themselves to a different rank.

In this very manner, the **Egyptian** <note>The priest speaking to Solon in the Timaeus</note> says that **Athena** received by lot both the city named after her and his own city, **Sais**. He perhaps infers this from the great similarity of the citizens' lives to the goddess herself, but perhaps he also perceived such an allotment through **theurgic art** and **priestly works**. For just as with other gods, there is an allotment of Athena which proceeds from above, from the **intellectual causes**, down into the region of the earth. 

Indeed, she exists first in the **Father** <note>Referring to Zeus/the Demiurge</note>; secondly, she holds a rank among the **leading gods**; thirdly, she makes a **progression** <term>proodos — the Neoplatonic concept of divine energy flowing outward from a source</term> among the **twelve rulers**; and after this, she manifests her **absolute authority** in the heavens. She is present in one way in the **fixed stars**—for a certain multitude is suspended from this goddess there, whether it be the region around **Aries**, or **Virgo**, or one of the **northern stars**, as some say of **Electra** there. She is present in another way in the **Sun**; for there, according to the **theologians**, a wonderful power and **Athenian rank** creates the whole of things in conjunction with the Sun. She is present in another way in the **Moon**, being the **monad** <note>The unifying principle</note> of the **triad** there <margin>This triad consists of Minerva, Proserpine, and Diana.</margin>. She is present in another way in the **Earth**, according to the similarity of earthly allotments to the heavenly distributions; and around the Earth, she is present differently in different places, according to the specific characteristics of her **providence**. 

It is therefore not at all surprising if one goddess is said to have received both **Athens** and **Sais**. For we must not think of the gods as we do of **particular souls**, which are not naturally able to inhabit two bodies because they exercise their **providence** through a specific relationship <note>i.e., they are "tied" to one body at a time</note>. On the contrary, there is a participation in the same power across different places. Within the **One**, there is also **Multitude**; the goddess is participated in one way by this place, and in another way by others. In some cases, the **identity** <note>sameness</note> is greater, and in others, the **alterity** <note>difference</note>. These things we speak of as true: the **allotments of the gods** stand eternal within the **Universe**.

<summary>Proclus explains how the goddess Athena governs multiple cities and levels of the cosmos simultaneously, from the intellectual realm down to the stars, the sun, and specific earthly locations like Athens and Sais.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing the divine allotments (estates) of the gods and the nature of Hephaestus as the craftsman of the physical world.</meta>

<page-num>101</page-num>
<header>ON THE TIMAEUS I.</header>

## ON THE TIMAEUS I.

...while these things are eternal, there are also manifestations according to time in different places. Indeed, ancient theology <note>Referring to the Orphic or Homeric traditions</note> also recognizes the everlasting essence of these divine allotments, just as when in Homer <note>original: "Ὅμηρος"</note> it is said: *“In truth, I was allotted to dwell forever in the hoary sea.”* <note>Homer, Iliad 15.190. The translator notes that the Greek word "aei" (always) signifies eternity.</note> Generally, since there must be things that always participate in the gods before those that participate only occasionally, it is necessary that eternal allotments exist before those that exist in time. For just as guardian spirits <term>daimones: intermediary beings between gods and men</term> follow the gods before partial souls do, so too the "estates" <term>lēxeis: assigned portions or realms</term> of the gods are always suspended from their particular illuminations. The gods of the world maintain these estates: the terrestrial gods maintain the terrestrial, the aquatic maintain the aquatic, and the aerial maintain the aerial. Even before the visible bodies, they ride upon ethereal vehicles <note>The "okhema" or subtle body of a deity or soul</note> among the celestial gods. Whether there are other allotments under the moon <margin>44</margin> that proceed together from above with light has been examined elsewhere; for the present, this suffices.

**[The Goddess said:] "I founded your city a thousand years earlier, receiving your seed from the Earth and Hephaestus, and the later city [Athens] afterwards." (Page 23 E.)**

Regarding the craftsmanship of Hephaestus <note>The god of fire and smithing</note>, how might one describe it without falling entirely short of the god's power? The stories told by the many concerning these things are utterly contemptible; but the views held by the more recent philosophers, while true, require no small amount of systematic support. Let us, therefore, bring the beliefs of the ancient theologians concerning him to bear upon our own interpretations from a higher perspective. The theologians show that he belongs to the "demiurgic" <term>demiurgic: the creative or world-building rank of gods</term> series, and not the life-generating or connecting series, by depicting him as a blacksmith, working the bellows, and generally as a master craftsman. That he is the craftsman of *sensible* things <note>Physical things perceived by the senses</note>, but not of psychic or intellectual works, is also shown by the same authorities. For the construction of the mirror, the smithing, the lameness <note>Hephaestus's traditional physical disability is interpreted here as a symbolic trait</note>, and such symbols represent his production concerning the realm of the senses. And that he is the maker of all sensible things is clear from the same sources, which bring him down from above, from Olympus to the earth, and which make the "seats" <note>The physical foundations or bodies</note> of the worldly gods to be "Hephaestus-wrought." If, then, we say it is so, this god would be the universal craftsman of the entire bodily constitution, preparing the visible seats for the gods, and fulfilling all things into the single harmony of the cosmos, filling all his handiwork with bodily life and organizing the resistant and dense nature of matter. <margin>B</margin>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing the mythical origins of Athens and the roles of Hephaestus and Athena in the creation of the physical world.</meta>

# PROCLUS

<page-num>103</page-num>

...uniting and containing them within the Forms. For these reasons, he is said by the theologians <note>Proclus refers to Orphic or Homeric traditions</note> to **forge**, as he is the worker of solid and resistant materials, and because the **brazen heaven** <note>original: *chalkeos ouranos*</note> is an imitation of the Intelligible realm, and the maker of the heaven is a smith. He is said to forge with **both feet** <margin>C</margin> because he is the craftsman of the lowest things in the progressions of Being (for such are bodies) and because he is no longer able to proceed to another rank, and because the maker of the universe is "without legs," as the *Timaeus* says. He is said to be **carried from above to the earth**, as he extends his craftsmanship through the whole of sensible substance. Whether, therefore, some speak of "physical principles" or "seminal principles" <term>seminal principles: *logoi spermatikoi*, the formative forces that govern the growth of matter</term> in the universe, the cause of all these must be referred to this god. For what Nature does by sinking into bodies, this divine being fashions divinely and in an exalted manner, moving Nature and using her as an instrument for his own craftsmanship. Indeed, the innate heat is **Hephaestian**, produced by him for the sake of bodily creation.

The discourse has thus referred the productive cause of things generated to this god; but since there is also a need for **matter** for things that are generated (for even the gods in heaven "borrow parts from the universe to be paid back again" <note>A reference to *Timaeus* 42e regarding the composition of mortal bodies</note> for the generation of mortal living things), he has most wonderfully handed this down through the **Earth**. For in the seed itself there are both formative principles and a substrate; the former come from the art of Hephaestus, the latter from the Earth. <margin>D</margin> For all the material cause must now be understood as "Earth," not because the Athenians are "earth-born" <note>autochthonous</note>, but because people are accustomed to call the whole of generation "earth," and every material instrument "earthy." Fire, then, is the Hephaestian instrument, while Earth is the matter moved and quickened by the fire, being in itself lifeless. Therefore, Earth is now included as fulfilling the material rank for Hephaestus, and for these reasons it is said that the **seed of Hephaestus** together with the Earth established the generation of the Athenians. For according to the myth, Hephaestus, being in love with Athena, cast a certain seed upon the earth, and from there the race of Athenians sprouted.

Hephaestus is always and entirely in love with Athena, imitating her **intellectual nature** in his craftsmanship. Athenian souls especially receive their activity according to this power of Hephaestus; they receive their "vehicles" <note>the subtle body or 'astral' shell of the soul</note> from him and are settled into bodies from the formative principles of Hephaestus and the Earth, the principles having received **Athenian tokens** <note>symbols or signatures of the goddess</note> for their substance. For he is the one who, prior to Nature, <margin>E</margin> perfects bodies, imposing different symbols of the divine upon different things. But what is the **thousand years** according to which the Athenians were prior to the citizens of Sais? Let these things be spoken of historically, but they also seem to signify the seniority of the Athenian life, meaning that their life ought to be entirely superior to that of the Saitic people...

<summary>Proclus provides a Neoplatonic allegorical interpretation of Hephaestus as the divine craftsman of the physical world and explains the mythical "earth-born" origin of the Athenians as the union of divine formative principles with matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic commentary on Plato's Timaeus, specifically discussing the divine origins of Athens and Sais, and the nature of how gods "allot" or govern specific earthly locations over time.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS I.

<page-num>103</page-num>

Just as in the invisible ranks of the same leader there are many classes—some closer to the source and others subordinate—in the same way, among the Athenian souls descending into generation <note>The process of souls entering physical bodies</note>, some possess a supreme likeness to the Goddess <note>Athena</note>, while others are next in line after them. The "thousand years" mentioned signifies this excellence; for a thousand is the measure of a perfect generative period because it is a cubic number <note>10x10x10; in Pythagorean thought, cubic numbers represented stability and completion</note>. Therefore, it appropriately fits the superior life within generation which is more closely likened to the presiding Goddess. 

If you wish to apply these concepts to the whole universe, you will see that the entire visible arrangement is "Hephaestian" <note>original: Ἡφαίστιον; referring to Hephaestus as the craftsman of the physical world</note>, including both the things being ordered and the ordering principles. Among these ordering principles, some are more universal and others more particular; some are analogous to the Athenians and others to the inhabitants of Sais. For nothing prevents us from viewing these accounts as analogous within the creative causes, within the universe as a whole, and within historical tradition.

But the divine Iamblichus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) often cited by Proclus</note> raised a difficulty: how can the gods be said to be allotted certain places according to defined times—for instance, Athena receiving Athens first, and Sais later? For if they ever begin their filling of a place, they might also one day cease; everything measured by time is of such a nature. Furthermore, when they receive an allotment, do they receive a place that was previously masterless, or one presided over by other gods? If it was masterless, how could any part of the universe be entirely deserted by God? How could any place remain totally unguarded by the higher powers? And if the body of the universe is self-sufficient, how could it later become the "lot" <term>kleros: a portion or territory assigned to a deity</term> of a specific god? 

If, on the other hand, it was under another leader and then a different god receives it, that too seems irrational. A second god does not push aside the authority and allotment of a predecessor, nor do they take over each other's places; even the <term>daimones: intermediary spirits between gods and men</term> do not exchange their assigned stations. 

Having raised these doubts, he solves them by saying that the "fillings" <note>The divine presence or influence</note> of the gods remain eternal, but the things participating in them sometimes receive the influence of the leaders and sometimes are deprived of it. These are the "participations" measured by time, which the sacred laws often call the "birthdays of the gods" <note>original: γενέθλια θεῶν</note>. 

We have said that this is similar to what happens with souls. Every soul certainly has a presiding god, and some choose lives suited to other gods. In this way, every place is the allotment of some god, and sometimes it becomes the allotment of another through certain cycles that make the place suitable, or through some rite established by men. In such cases, the allotment is twofold: one according to essence, and the other according to relation. But let us proceed to what follows.

**"But in our sacred writings, the number of years for the arrangement here in Sais is recorded as eight thousand."** (Page 23 E.)

# PROCLUS
<page-num>104</page-num>

To the Athenians, he <note>Plato</note> assigned the number nine thousand, taking this from history; but to the citizens of Sais, he gave eight thousand, according to the records in the sacred writings. He measures the lives of cities by the millennium <note>original: "χιλιάδι" (thousand)</note>, for it is in this way that even the spirits <note>term: "daimones" (intermediary spirits between gods and men)</note> are said to measure time, as the philosopher Porphyry says. Or perhaps, making this narrative based on the sacred writings, it reveals the permanent guardianship of the divine watchers of the world, as Iamblichus might say.

Furthermore, these numbers correspond to the types of lives according to a likely reasoning. The number eight thousand is a cube upon a cube <note>8,000 is 20 cubed</note>, while the other <note>9,000</note> is a square plane multiplied by a cube. Therefore, while the one deepened the plane—and did so through the "indefinite dyad" <note>term: "dyad" (the principle of duality or division)</note>—the other preserves the plane within itself in the likeness and perfection of the triad <note>term: "triad" (the number three, representing stability and return)</note>.

<margin>C</margin> Now, a symbol of a superior life is that which remains within itself and brings order to secondary things; whereas a more imperfect life is that which descends into those secondary things, becoming like them and being filled with a certain indefiniteness. Yet, since even the secondary life does not entirely depart from its likeness to the Goddess <note>Athena</note>, the descent happens through cubes, in which likeness resides, or through more composite forms; for the square is simpler than the cube.

If you do not find these reasons sufficient, consider that the number nine thousand is appropriate for those who arose from the earth and from Hephaestus. For the number one thousand is "of the earth" <note>original: "χθόνιος" (chthonic)</note> as a cube, but the number nine belongs to Hephaestus. As the poet <note>Homer, Iliad 18.400</note> says: "For nine years I forged many intricate works of bronze." Thus, you would not be speaking out of turn. In general, the cube is fitting for the earthly allotments of Athena, since they assign the decad <note>term: "decad" (the number ten, representing the heavens)</note> to the heavens, but the final progression of the decad produces the solid number one thousand. For the gods have made their progression from the heavenly lots down to the final earthly ones.

These things, then, we must say. But the philosopher Porphyry, in explaining these matters, 
<margin>D</margin> supposes Hephaestus to be the "artistic intellect" <note>term: "technikos nous" (the creative mind)</note> and the earth to be the lunar sphere; for he says that among the Egyptians, this is called the "ethereal earth." He says that souls which have their substance from the Goddess, but participate in the artistic intellect, are sown into the body of the moon, living there as "artistic souls," yet having bodies that are outpourings of the ethereal bodies. The nine thousand fits these souls in the following way: there is a ten-thousand-year period of the soul, as he says, which ascends and descends through the five planets, so that each planet has two thousand years—though not in a continuous sequence. However, the time is continuous and...

Indeed, people perform the **ninth-day rites** <note>original: "enata" — traditional Greek funerary offerings made nine days after death</note> for the dead, and similarly, some give names to the newborn on the **ninth day**, using these periods as symbols of birth and passing away. <margin>E</margin> The divine **Iamblichus** <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized theurgy and ritual</note> rejects this, saying that the discourse here is not about lives, but about the different measures of **Athenian participation** <note>The way the soul or city partakes in divine reality</note>. All these principles are in the manner of **Hermes**, for Hermes is the overseer of natural principles. Through these, the soul is bound to the body. 

And again, all at once, the body first lives naturally, with the soul being the **protector** of the body's nourishment and growth; then it lives desirously, awakening the **generative powers**; then with spirit, having settled these but sufficing for the ambitious life; then politically, having measured the passions; and finally, intellectually. If, therefore, it is not restored to its source, it lives intellectually, and the **myriad** <note>The number 10,000, symbolizing completion or the return to the One</note> reaches its limit. But in the realm of generation, even when it governs excellently, it lives according to the number falling short of the thousand <note>i.e., 9,000 instead of 10,000</note>. The number **nine thousand** is a symbol of this, being appropriate for the **excellent constitution of the Athenians**.

-> Concerning the citizens who lived **nine thousand** years ago, I will declare to you briefly the **laws**; and of their **deeds**, that which was most beautiful was performed by them. We shall go through the exact details about everything in order later at our leisure, taking up the **writings** themselves. (Page 24 A.) <-

If you wish to refer these matters to the whole arrangement of the universe, the number **nine thousand** will reveal the entire progression | reaching down to the **cube** <note>Symbolizing the three-dimensional physical world</note> and earthly works, and the life that extends through all things. The phrase **"briefly"** indicates the unification of the many principles and their containment within the Intellect. For the "brief" is a visible image of **intellectual indivisibility**, while the "progression into multitude" belongs to the **productive power** which fills, leads forward, and **fragments** the forms through **otherness**. The **laws** represent the divided craftsmanship known to the Intellect, and the **"most beautiful deed"** represents that which reaches upward toward the **One Beauty**.

Just as things that are secondary by nature are not called "primary," so it is with patterns. They become patterns for those who are sent up from them and who, through them, come to know the things that precede them. Here too, the affairs of the Athenians display a more universal order, while those of the people of Sais display a more particular order. For every law is said to be a "distribution of intellect" <note>A pun on the Greek words 'nomos' (law) and 'nous' (intellect/mind)</note>, and the laws of the Athenians, established under the supervision of the gods, manifest the distribution of the Athenian Intellect. That this entire arrangement is in some way more particular than Socrates’s Republic and more divided than that one, imitating the middle level of creation <note>original: "μέση δημιουργία"</note>, can be understood both from the number of classes in the city and from their quality. For in the former <note>The Republic</note> there are three classes: the guardian, the auxiliary, and the mercenary; for the triad is appropriate to the demiurgic monad <note>The "monad" refers to a single, unified principle</note>. But here <note>In the Timaeus</note> there are double these: the priestly, the warrior, the artisanal, the pastoral, the hunting, and the agricultural. For the middle level of creation possesses both the nature of the dyad (two) and the triad (three); and both numbers | are E appropriately related to Athena, though the one here is directly so, as a triad, while the other is so by way of generation. For the number six is a "triangular" number derived from the triad <note>1+2+3=6</note>. Thus, by being both triangular and derived from the triad, it demonstrates both its subordination to and its kinship with the Goddess. For either all of creation participates in Athena, or rather the first and highest parts of the universe are specifically allotted to her. Both the primary creation and the first Father <note>Referring to the Demiurge</note>. If, then, you take only these classes, you will find the number appropriate to the Goddess; but if you add the class concerned with wisdom, you will certainly find it to be the Athenian heptad <note>The number seven</note>; and this is one of those things famously celebrated. Both the "unrevealed" nature of the heptad is hymned, and its existence from the monad alone, and that the monad is most especially an image of Athena, the triad around the six: the one as intellectual, the other as turned back toward the monad itself, and the third as proceeding from the Father alone. From the numbers, then, you might consider it thus. But one must also see the subordination and superiority from the quality of the classes themselves. For the priestly class is subordinate | to the guardian class which ascends to the primary cause, just as he <note>Plato</note> himself in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Πολιτικῷ"</note> F subordinated the priests to the statesman and did not give them a share of political power; and the warrior class is subordinate to the auxiliary; for the latter is properly and sufficiently educated in the affairs of the city itself, while the former pursues only wars and the things within them, participating in this exercise alone; and the mercenary class...

...it is divided into the remaining <term>classes</term> <note>original: "γένη" (genē); refers to the social divisions in Plato's Republic</note>. It differs, therefore, both in being more comprehensive and in being harmonized in a specific manner with the classes that precede it. Thus, from both their number and their quality, it has become clear to us that the details handed down regarding the <term>Socratic constitution</term> <note>The ideal state described by Socrates in Plato's Republic</note> are owed their place and should hold the second rank after that primary model. And indeed, in that case, we established the analogies to the Whole in this way: the **guardian** class <note>original: "φυλακικὸν"</note> is analogous to the celestial gods; the **auxiliary** class <note>original: "ἐπικουρικὸν"</note> to the higher beings who provide for the goods of the celestial ones and guard the Whole; and the **mercenary** class <note>original: "θητικὸν"</note> to those who hold together material nature and to partial souls—the first corresponding to the fixed stars, the second to the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>, and the third to material things. We also took all things by analogy even among the celestial gods themselves.

<margin>47</margin> But here, it is worth observing how and in what manner these classes are to be understood within the Whole. For on the one hand, the philosopher **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist scholar</note> arranges them thus:
*   The **priests** correspond to the **archangels** <note>original: "ἀρχαγγέλοις"</note> in heaven who are turned toward the gods, whose messengers they are.
*   The **warriors** correspond to the souls descending into bodies.
*   The **shepherds** <note>original: "αὐτονόμας"</note> correspond to those appointed over the herds of living beings; and they say—not without some secret meaning—that these are souls who have failed to attain the **human intellect** <note>original: "ἀνθρωπικοῦ νοῦ"</note> but have a disposition toward animals. For there is a certain guardian of the human herd, and certain partial ones: some over nations, some over cities, and some overseeing individuals.
*   The **hunters** correspond to those who hunt souls and shut them up in bodies; there are also those who delight in the hunting of animals, such as they assign to **Artemis**, and another multitude of hunting spirits <note>original: "δαιμόνων"</note> with her.
*   The **farmers** correspond to those appointed over the fruits of the earth.

<margin>B</margin> Porphyry claims this entire political arrangement and the host of spirits beneath the moon, divided into many creative roles, was spoken of by **Plato** because he was looking toward a result that was already coming into being.

However, the divine **Iamblichus** <note>A later Neoplatonist who often disagreed with Porphyry's more psychological interpretations</note>, having censured these views as being stated neither in a Platonic nor a true manner, argues:
1.  Archangels are nowhere deemed worthy of mention by Plato.
2.  The warrior class cannot consist of souls inclining toward bodies; for one must not contrast these against gods or spirits. Indeed, it would be absurd if we were to station these in the middle class, while placing gods and spirits among the lowest creative ranks.
3.  Those "shepherds" are not beings who failed to achieve human intellect yet held a sympathy for animals; for the existence of the spirits who superintend **mortal nature** <note>original: "θνητὴν φύσιν"</note> does not derive from human beings.
4.  Nor are the hunters those who shut the soul in the body as if in a cage; for the soul is not joined to the body in that way.

<margin>C</margin> This mode of **contemplation** <note>original: "θεωρίας" (theōrias); philosophical investigation</note> is not truly philosophical.

At any rate, having criticized these views, he establishes the **priests** by analogy, through their similarity to all the secondary substances and powers that serve and attend to their own prior causes. He assigns the **shepherds** to all those who have been allotted oversight in the cosmos over the life that inclines toward the body and the irrational powers, distributing these in an orderly fashion. The **hunters** he assigns to the universal powers that adorn secondary things through the "hunting" of true Being. The **farmers** <margin>D</margin> he assigns to those who provide the perfection of the seeds brought down from heaven to earth. For no one, looking at it correctly, would place the pastoral or the hunting class under the demiurgic. 

Perhaps, then, it is better to make the explanation as our own teacher <note>Likely referring to Syrianus, the teacher of Proclus</note> divided it: by establishing one pair as the **priestly** and the **warrior**, a second as the **demiurgic** and the **agricultural**, and a third as the **pastoral** and the **hunting**, and having adopted such an order, to pursue their divine models. 

For the **priestly** element exists among the gods of elevation; the **warrior** among the guardian gods; and the **demiurgic** among those who distinguish all the forms and the rational principles of the worldly things. The **agricultural** belongs to those who move nature from above and sow souls into the realm of generation—for even Plato <margin>E</margin> calls the fall of the soul into generation a "sowing," and "to sow" is most appropriate for farmers, just as "to conceive" is for the births of nature. The **pastoral** belongs to those who oversee in a distinct manner all the forms of life that revolve in the realm of generation; for in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politikos," a dialogue by Plato</note> he himself handed down to us certain "divine shepherds." The **hunting** belongs to those who arrange all the material spirits—for it is perhaps always the custom of theologians to call those activities "hunts." 

All these classes belong to the middle demiurgy: the power that converts, the power that guards, that which manages the allotments of souls, that which governs the generative forms of life, that which is entirely demiurgic and gives form to immaterial things, and that which brings order to the lowest spirits. Aside from all these classes, one must place that which cares for **wisdom** <note>original: "phronesis"</note> and the **contemplative**, which he himself will celebrate above all others, having first mentioned the priestly class as a priest would. ...in the one Mind, which holds together the entire <term>demiurgy</term> <note>original: "δημιουργίαν" - the act of world-making or divine craftsmanship</note> of generated things; while the other division belongs to the more particular nations within them, acting as elevating, guarding, form-giving, and life-giving principles of civilized life, and as powers that hold mastery over <note>original: "κρατητικοῖς"</note> the wilder nature. After this comes the class of craftsmen, noting that each performs its craft by itself without mixing with others; then the class of shepherds, the hunters, and the farmers. (Page 24 A.)

This entire <term>tetrad</term> <note>a group of four</note> holds the third rank according to the threefold division of the classes, yet it has now been numbered second by Plato, so that through this arrangement the discourse might imitate the Universe, in which the lowest part is in the middle, surrounded on all sides by more divine things. For that which is most material and dense has been placed in the center by the divine craftsmanship; for only in this way could it be preserved by being ordered, and not perish if it were not guarded by all the surrounding powers. Again, in these matters, the principle is added that the crafting class should not mix with the others, nor should those others mix with them, but each should remain by itself and in its own purity. For this not only achieves accuracy in their occupations and their proper works, but also produces a "fellow-feeling" <note>original: "συμπάθειαν" - sympathy or interconnectedness</note> among the citizens. For all will have need of all because each individual does not pursue many trades. The craftsman will need the farmer, the farmer the shepherd, the shepherd the hunter, and the hunter the craftsman; and thus, each being in need of the others, they will not be unmixed in their social relations. Therefore, alongside "otherness" there is "sameness," and alongside "union" there is "distinction."

And indeed, you have perceived that the warrior class here is separated from all other classes, to whom nothing else was assigned by law except to care for the affairs of war. (Page 24 B.)

Everywhere, but especially in the case of the warrior class, the principle of being unmixed and distinct is appropriate. For this class has a kinship with the highest order and with the...

From above, from the archetypes down to the lowest kinds, the discourse extends the activity <note>original: *energeia*</note> of Athena. For she herself is both more universal, having shared in the innate things of the pure powers, and more particular and worldly kinds, being ordered by the middle demiurgy, containing things analogous to that and being mastered by the Athenian activities, and remaining always likewise pure through her in the universe. But the divine Iamblichus <note>A later Neoplatonic philosopher who emphasized theurgy and divine ritual.</note>, speaking with divine inspiration, since everything divine must both act and not be acted upon—so that by acting it may not have the weakness similar to matter, and by not being acted upon it may not have the activity resembling material things, which act with passion—posits that the shields are powers through which the divine remains impassive and pure, surrounded by an ineffable guard within itself; and the spears are powers according to which it proceeds through all things without contact <note>original: *anaphos*</note> and acts upon all, cutting away the material and warding off every generation-producing form. These things are seen first concerning Athena; and her shield and spear are received in her statues; for she imitates all things and remains unswerving according to the theologians and pure in the [universe].

# PROCLUS

...order, or the Goddess, having first established you in your dwellings. (Page 24 C.) <note>Proclus is quoting Plato’s Timaeus here, where the Egyptian priest describes how Athena founded Athens before Sais.</note>

The phrase "the whole" indicates the unified containment within the Goddess of all things ordered by her, and that nothing is left out, nor is there any divided <note>original: "διῃρημένως"</note> multitude within her. The term "arrangement" <note>original: "διακόσμησιν"</note> indicates the distribution occurring within the order of Athenian Providence <term>Providence: the divine care and guidance of the gods over the universe</term>; while "composition" <note>original: "σύνταξιν"</note> indicates the unification of the whole through its kinship to a single world-order. Furthermore, "arrangement" signifies the procession of material things from the Goddess, while "composition" signifies their return back to her. Since among the things in the universe some are universal and others are particular, and some correspond to unities <note>monads</note> and others to numbers, both participate in Athenian Providence; however, the universal and unitary things participate primarily. For this reason, the present discourse assigns the older and leading rank to the Athenians, and the second and subordinate rank to the inhabitants of Sais. <margin>F</margin>

Choosing the place in which you were born, having observed in it the temperate climate of the seasons, that it would produce the most prudent men. (Page 24 C.)

Previously it was said that the Goddess "received by lot" <note>original: "λαγχάνειν"</note> the land, but now she "chooses" <note>original: "ἐκλέγεσθαι"</note> it. Both coincide: for neither is the "allotment" on her part involuntary, nor is the "choice" disordered, as is the case with a particular soul. For divine necessity coincides with divine will, and choice with the lot, and choosing with receiving by lot. What this "place" is has been stated before: that it is the extension <note>original: "διάστημα"</note> and the truly real place. For according to this, the divisions of the divine lots exist, having their being eternally before those things that exist according to time. It must be added now that the Soul of the Universe, possessing the formative principles <note>logoi</note> of all divine things and being suspended from the beings prior to her, possesses an affinity and certain symbols <note>original: "σύμβολα"</note> of the different ranks among the gods in different parts of space. For this space is suspended directly from her and is an organ natural to her. Being herself a rational and psychical world-order, she also renders this spatial and vital world complete through divine tokens <note>original: "συνθημάτων"</note>. <margin>F</margin> Thus, space itself, even if it is said to be continuous and immovable, is not entirely indifferent <note>uniform</note> to itself, just as the Soul of the Universe is not entirely indifferent to herself; rather, one part of her is the Circle of the Same, and another the Circle of the Different. And why do I speak of the Soul? Not even the much-hymned Intellect <note>original: "νοῦς"</note> is indifferent to itself, even if all things in it are, as it were, of the same color <note>original: "ὁμόχροα"; the text notes a variant "of the same time"</note>. For not all things in the Intellect possess equal power...

<summary>Proclus explains the metaphysical meaning behind Athena's "choice" of Athens, arguing that divine will and destiny are the same. He describes how the Soul of the World uses space as an organized instrument to reflect divine hierarchies.</summary>

...but some are more spiral-like, while others are more partial, and even this is not surprising. For even the Demiurge <note>The "Craftsman" or creator deity in Platonic philosophy.</note> himself possesses primary, middle, and ultimate orders. Hence, I believe, Orpheus also described the order of the powers: "His head," he says, "is the radiant heaven," <note>original: "κεφαλὴ μὲν... οὐρανὸς αἰγλήεις"</note> and his eyes are the sun and the reflecting moon, and so on in order. If, therefore, even this spatial interval were uniform and indifferent, yet the distributions of the soul, the ranks of the daemons <note>Intermediate spirits between gods and mortals.</note> who have received their lots, and before these the gods—dividing it according to the demiurgic order and the allotments of Justice—have demonstrated a great difference of parts within it. 

We must consider, then, that the choice comes from within and from the very essence of the gods, but it is not of such a kind as we see in the case of partial souls. For the former is essential, while the latter is defined according to the present life alone; and the former is eternal, while the latter is temporal. Furthermore, by "place" <note>original: "τόπον"</note> we must not understand the earth or this air, but rather the immovable Body <note>The celestial or ethereal realm.</note> prior to these, which is always received in the same way by the gods and divided by the allotments of Justice. For these material things are sometimes suitable for the participation of the gods and sometimes unsuitable; but prior to those things which participate only "sometimes," there must be those things which are always suspended from the gods in the same way. 

Regarding these matters, let this suffice. But as for the "temperate mixture of the seasons" <note>original: "εὐκρασίαν τῶν ὡρῶν"</note> which brings forth wise men, Panaetius and certain other Platonists understood this in terms of visible phenomena—that because the seasons of the year are well-blended in Attica, the region is suitable for the birth of wise men. Longinus, however, raises a difficulty against them: first, that they are not speaking the truth (for on the contrary, a great disproportion of droughts and winters is seen around this place); and second, that even if the place were such, they could no longer preserve the immortality of souls if wisdom is implanted in them by the temperament of the air. For a "mixture" <note>original: "κρᾶσιν"</note> is the perfection of those who declare the soul to be a result of bodily blending. 

Longinus himself says that this "temperate mixture" does not refer to the condition of the air, but is a certain unnamable quality of the spatial interval contributing to wisdom. For just as some waters are purgative, and certain places are disease-inducing or destructive, so it is not at all wonderful that a certain quality of a region contributes to wisdom. Origen, however, referred this temperate mixture to the circulation of the heaven; for he saw that there are "bearings" and "barrennesses" <note>original: "φορὰς καὶ τὰς ἀφορίας" - referring to the cycles of fertility and infertility of souls mentioned in Plato's Republic.</note> of souls, as Socrates says in the *Republic*. But while Origen touches upon the truth in a more partial way, Longinus misses it by making the quality something corporeal and becoming entangled in difficulties.

...strengthened <note>original: "enischymenos"</note>, which are the same points that Porphyry brings against him. For if a single quality of the air makes people fit for different pursuits, then while that same quality remains, why is the same natural excellence no longer present in the inhabitants? <note>Proclus is questioning why a region like Athens might produce geniuses in one era but not in another if the climate remains the same.</note> And if this quality is perishable, what should we say is the cause of its destruction? It is better to say that since the gods have divided the entire world-space according to the creative order, each part of a place receives the souls that are appropriate to it: the portion of Ares receives the more spirited souls; the portion of Apollo, the prophetic ones; the portion of Asclepius, the medicinal ones; and the portion of Athena, the wise ones.

This occurs through a certain quality, or rather, the place possesses such a power from the god who was allotted it. He <note>Plato</note> called this "well-ordered harmony" a **temperate climate** <note>original: "eukrasia," literally a "good mixing" of elements</note>, since many powers—natural, psychic, demonic, and angelic—reside in each portion. The unity of the single god who was allotted each part <margin>I would prefer "of each god"</margin> unifies all these powers and blends them together, joining them all in an indivisible way. 

Because the Hours <note>The Horae, goddesses of the seasons and cosmic order</note> have received from the Father the guardianship of these portions and allotments, Homer says:
-> "To them is entrusted the great heaven and Olympus," <-
just as the harmonious fittings of similar souls to their places are also brought to completion. For this reason, he linked this "temperate climate" to the Hours, seeing it as being held together from that source. Therefore, the Goddess <note>Athena</note>, seeing that the portion of space was fitted by the Hours and always guarded by them for the reception of prudent souls, chose it for herself. It is not as if the place once existed without Athena and was later allotted to her (for the argument has shown the opposite), but rather that in that very part of space, there are certain fitnesses for the reception of divine illuminations <column-break/> in different measures. These were instilled by the universal Creator <note>The Demiurge</note>, who contains within himself in a unified way the powers of all the gods who come after him; these powers are strengthened and perfected, or rather, they proceed forth from the presiding gods. 

Just as in the "choices of lives" <note>A reference to the Myth of Er in Plato's Republic</note> a soul succeeds by choosing its own proper life, in the same way, a soul assigned to its proper place according to its choice of life acts more effectively than one sown into a foreign place. The circulation of the heavens also contributes to this arrangement, bringing about periods of fertility and barrenness <note>original: "phoras kai aphorias"</note> for souls. Even in the fertile periods, the holistic quality of wise souls prevails during that flow; and in the barren periods, there is less of a scarcity in this place than elsewhere. 

Just as a good farmer might select a piece of land for the perfection of his seeds, knowing that when there is a harvest he will have more, and when there is a failure he will suffer less during that cycle because of the inherent power of the earth—so too the argument says that the Goddess chose this place as one holistically suited for prudent men, so that even during a fertile period, she might have more for the sake of generation...

# PROCLUS

...the race of heralds, as he says; but the divine Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a hugely influential Neoplatonist who emphasized theurgy and the harmony of ancient traditions.</note>, having rebuked these [interpreters] and beautifully preserved the proper analogy, explains that "war" refers to that which is utterly destructive of all disordered, discordant, and material nature, while "philosophy" refers to immaterial and separate intellection. He considers the Goddess <note>original: "τῶν θεῶν" (of the gods), but the translator Taylor suggests "τὴν θεὸν" (the goddess), referring to Athena.</note> to be the cause of both, <margin>C</margin> and it is this nature which the Athenians imitate through their prudent and warlike life. Furthermore, the Athenian region is well-fitted for the reception of such souls.

But if it is necessary to make the clear thought of these men manifest, and before them to reveal the Platonic tradition—which is in perfect harmony with the theologians—one must speak from the beginning in this way: In the Father and Creator of the entire universe, many ranks of unified gods appear—protective, creative, elevating, connective, and perfecting. But there is also this one among the first intellectual unities <note><term>unities (henads)</term>: In Neoplatonism, these are the highest principles of being, existing just below "The One."</note> within him: the pure and unsubdued deity, according to which the Creator himself remains unswerving and immutable, and all things proceeding from him partake of an unyielding power, through which he perceives all things and is separate, set apart from the whole of existence.

All the theologians call this deity **Athena**, as being born from the summit of the Father and remaining in him as a creative intellection, separate and immaterial. Therefore, <margin>D</margin> Socrates in the *Cratylus* <note>Plato's dialogue on the origin of names; see Cratylus 407B.</note> praised her as "God-Mind" <note>original: "θεονόην" (Theonoē), a pun on "Theou noēsis" or "God's thought."</note>. Because she leads all things back to the one Creator along with the other [gods] and orders the whole together with the Father, they call her "Philosophical" because of the former, and "Warlike" because of the latter. For she who unifiedly contains all the paternal wisdom is "Philosophical," and she who governs all opposition in a uniform manner might reasonably be called "Warlike."

Regarding this, Orpheus <note>The legendary poet-prophet; Proclus frequently cites "Orphic" verses as sacred authority.</note> says of her birth that Zeus brought her forth from his head:
> "Gleaming in brazen armor,
> A flower to behold." <insert>original: "Ὅπλοις λαμπομένην χαλκείοις / ἄνθος ἰδέσθαι."</insert>

Since it was necessary for her to proceed into second and third ranks, she appears in the Maiden <note>original: "Κόρῃ" (Kore/Persephone). Proclus is linking Athena's essence to other divine manifestations.</note> according to the pure number seven; she generates all virtue from herself and elevating powers, and sheds the light of intellect and pure life upon secondary beings. Therefore, the Maiden is also called "Thrice-born" <note>original: "τριτογενὴς" (Tritogeneia), a traditional epithet for Athena.</note>, and she obtained this choral and pure character from the Athenian quality. She appears also among the liberated gods, instilling the Lunar <margin>E</margin> rank with intellectual and creative light, making it pure for the sake of generations, and revealing their single unity as unmixed by means of these set-apart powers. She appears both in the heavens and beneath the moon, everywhere putting forward this dual power—or rather, providing the cause for both according to her unified gift. For her unyielding nature is intellectual...

Everything, therefore, that is suspended from the gods, originates from the gods, and returns to the gods, displays a superior virtue. Since there is a multitude of deeds, but also a single encompassing unity according to which the entire form of the state is displayed, he promises to teach the greatest deed, differing in virtue—not just one among many, but the "one before the many." For such a method of discourse is appropriate both to the Whole, in which all things complete one continuous life, and to the Goddess who brings many oppositions together into a single union. Therefore, while the city's deeds are many and great, he reasonably recounts the one deed recorded in the sacred texts. For there is an intellectual paradigm <note>original: "παράδειγμα νοερόν"</note> of it, insofar as it is contemplated in the cosmos, surpassing in magnitude and virtue; magnitude manifesting its universality, and virtue manifesting its intellectual nature. # PROCLUS

53 ...completes a life and a way of being, according to which she rules over all things placed beneath her under the leadership of Athena. These matters should be stated in this way. However, Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus; Proclus often engages with his earlier interpretations.</note> says that she possesses great and wonderful works of souls, as many as are performed toward matter and material ways; he calls the "daemons" <note>original: "daimones" — in this context, intermediary spirits or powers, not necessarily evil "demons" in the modern sense.</note> "material ways." For he says there are two kinds of daemons: some are souls, while the other kind are "ways," and these are material powers that are harmful to the soul. Indeed, regarding these doctrines, he [Porphyry] was held to account by the commentator who came after him.

The text says: **"How great a power your city once stayed, which was marching insolently against all Europe and Asia at once."** (Page 24 E.)

Plato has omitted none of the laudatory exaggerations in these lines, if one were to accept the war of the Athenians against the Atlanteans as a plain historical narrative. Nor has he fallen short of a certain theological precision combined with reverence, if one wishes to transition from the particular to the universal and to move toward the *paradigms* <note>The eternal, perfect models or "blueprints" of things in Neoplatonic thought.</note> from the *images*. 

<margin>B</margin> While many are accustomed in the Panathenaic orations <note>Speeches given during the Panathenaea, the great festival in honor of Athena.</note> to chatter up and down about the Persian fleet and the Athenian victories by land and sea—in which even the more recent historians have entangled their own accounts—Plato himself, when praising Athens, does not hand down the story of the Persians or any other such deed. Instead, bringing in the Atlantic war from somewhere outside our inhabited world into our own—a war capable of utterly destroying these things—he records the Athenians as the best and the victors in this conflict, having conquered such a great and massive power. 

Since the Persian fleet set out from the East against the Greeks, and specifically against the Athenians, Plato himself introduced the Atlantic war from the West. By doing so, he views the city of the Athenians as a center point, bringing to order the barbarian element that moves in a disorderly fashion on either side. 

Furthermore, in the ancestral rites of Attica and in the Mysteries, the Giant War is a common theme, telling how Athena excelled in the battle against them, because she, along with her Father, overcame both these [the Giants] and the Titans. However, Plato did not think it safe to introduce war directly among the gods. For this very thing—this "living"—was what he used to accuse the ancient poets of; and it would have been absurd for Critias or Timaeus to become practitioners of the very things for which Socrates blamed the poets on the previous day, by once again attributing wars and factions to the gods. 

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, through the analogy of human affairs to divine ones, he hands down this war as occurring before the creation of the world <note>original: "kosmopoiias" — the making of the cosmos.</note>, taking the Athenians as substitutes for Athena and the Olympian gods.

<summary>Proclus discusses Porphyry’s view of "material daemons" before explaining why Plato uses the story of the Atlantic war instead of the historical Persian wars: it serves as a theological allegory for divine order overcoming material disorder without disrespecting the gods.</summary>

## ON THE TIMAEUS I.

Instead of the Titans and Giants, he uses the Atlanteans; for it is possible to observe the same things in images as exist in the whole of reality. And so that I may remind you of the analogy: through the name of the Athenians, he directs his listeners to the Olympian "co-ordinate" <note>term: *systoichia* (co-ordinate series) — a Pythagorean and Neoplatonic concept where realities are arranged in parallel columns of opposing principles (e.g., Light/Dark, Limit/Unlimited)</note> which is commanded by Athena; but through the name of the Atlanteans, he refers to the Titanic gods. For Atlas, the greatest of them, is surely one of the Titans. Indeed, the theologians <note>referring to Orphic traditions</note> say that after the dismemberment of Dionysus—who represents the division of the indivisible creation into the whole by <margin>D</margin> Zeus—the other Titans were allotted various stations, but Atlas was established in the regions toward the west, holding up the heavens:
> Atlas holds the wide heaven under powerful necessity, at the 
> boundaries of the earth. <note>Quoting Hesiod, Theogony 517</note>
Furthermore, the trophies of victory for Athena are celebrated among the Athenians, and they hold this festival because Poseidon was defeated by Athena—meaning that the generative order was mastered by the intellectual order <note>term: *noera* (intellectual/noetic) — relating to the higher realm of pure Mind or Intellect</note>, and that after the establishment of the necessities of life, those inhabiting this land hastened toward the life according to the Mind. For Poseidon is the overseer of generation <note>the realm of becoming and physical birth</note>, while Athena is the guardian of the intellectual life. You have here, then, the greatest contribution to the matters at hand. For the Athenians, bearing the name of the goddess, are analogous to her; and the Atlanteans—both because they inhabit an island and because they are said to be descendants of Poseidon—preserve the analogy to that god. Thus, it is clear from these points that the Atlantic war indicates the "middle" <margin>E</margin> demiurgy <note>the process of world-making</note>, through which the second Father <note>likely referring to the Demiurge or a secondary creative power</note>, being filled by Athena and the other invisible causes, guides mortal things more powerfully and subordinates all that is multiplied, divided, and more material in its substance to the intellectual principles. For the gods themselves are eternally united, but the things governed by them are filled with such division. These things should be understood in this way.

However, so that we may grasp certain defined patterns of the present analysis, we must place the dwellings within the Pillars of Hercules <note>the Strait of Gibraltar, marking the boundary of the known Greek world</note> as analogous to the entire superior "co-ordinate" series, and those outside as analogous to the entire inferior series—this latter being a single life, continuous and proceeding in various ways. Whether you prefer to speak of gods as Olympian and Titanic, or of the essence of Mind as rest and motion (or "Same" and "Different"), or of souls as rational and irrational, or of bodies as heaven and generation, or however else you might divide the levels of being: in all these divisions, the entire race within the Pillars of Hercules will correspond to the better side, and those outside to the worse. For the true "sea" is that of unlikeness <margin>F</margin> and all material life, which proceeds into distance and multiplicity away from the One. Whether, therefore, you wish to arrange these oppositions in the Orphic manner...

## PROCLUS

<margin>54</margin>Whether one chooses to hymn the Olympian races and the Titanic races, and how some hold power over others; or to observe the two Pythagorean "columns" <note>original: *systoichias*. These are the two opposing lists of principles, such as Light/Dark or Limit/Unlimited</note> extending from the highest heights down to the furthest extremes, where the superior column organizes the inferior; or to view it in the Platonic manner, seeing much of the "Unlimited" in the universe and much of the "Limit," as we learned in the *Philebus* <note>Plato, *Philebus* 30C</note>, and how the whole of Unlimitedness, when combined with the measures of the Limit, has produced "Becoming" <note>generation or the physical world</note> stretching through all things in the world—from all these views you might grasp this one truth: that the entire constitution of the cosmos is harmonized out of this opposition. And if the noble Heraclitus, looking toward this, said "War is the father of all," even he did not speak out of place. 

Now, Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist scholar</note> in these matters refers the theory to spirits <note>daimones</note> and souls, and at times makes mention of the mythical Titanic war; in some ways he speaks persuasively, but in others he does not reach the heart of the subject. However, the divine Iamblichus <note>A highly influential Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, in a marvelous way, took up the analysis more specifically regarding the explanation of causes. He decided to listen to the account not merely according to its outward appearance, even though he himself provided us with the starting points for such discourses in his introductions. But while this divine man has instructed us in many other things and indeed in these as well, let us now turn to the explanation | of Plato’s words. 

Let us deem ourselves worthy to recall the topics written previously: we should rank the Atlanteans according to the "inferior column" in its entirety. For even among these there are wholes and parts. We should understand their "insolence" <note>original: *hybris*</note> according to their progression <note>the way divine power flows outward into lower forms</note>, their division through decline, and their proximity to Matter. For Matter is truly "Unlimitedness" and "Ugliness"; therefore, they say that whatever approaches it or exists within it in some way acts with "insolence." Indeed, the archetype of these beings is revealed by the Theologian <note>Orpheus</note> through these names: *Titans of evil counsel, possessing a violent heart.* 

We should understand their "outward assault" according to their distance, being settled far away from the gods and from the more divine things in the universe. For the term "outward" does not imply a surrounding of powers, but rather a substance <note>hypostasis</note> that has gone out from all that is stable, immaterial, pure, and unified. The "Atlantic Sea" refers to Matter itself—whether you wish to call it an "abyss," or a "sea of dissimilarity," or by any other name. For | Matter receives the titles of the inferior column, being named "Unlimitedness," "Darkness," "Irrationality," "Lack of Measure," "Principle of Alteration," and "Duality"—just as the Atlantic Sea took its name from Atlantis. For taking the analogies in order, we shall say that the entire inferior column...

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing the metaphysical principles of Sameness and Difference, and the mythological struggle between the Olympian and Titanic orders as a metaphor for cosmic structure.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK I.

The more universal kinds within it, as well as the more particular, are characterized according to their progression, their equality, and their turning toward matter. In this way, the principle pervades through all things, appearing appropriately to each and manifesting according to each nature <note>The text suggests a principle of "analogy" where the divine manifests differently at different levels of reality.</note>—divine and intellectual, psychic and bodily. Being of such a nature, it is established and ordered by the superior power, which you might reasonably call "Athenian" <note>Referring to Athena as the goddess of wisdom and orderly power.</note>, since she is pure and dominates the lower orders through her own power.

When this power is present, the great division and infinity cease. The Titanic race <note>original: "Τιτανικὸν γένος" — representing the principle of division and fragmentation in Greek mythology.</note> is held together by the Olympian gods, and Difference is unified by Sameness. Motion is governed by Rest, the irrational souls by the rational, and the realm of generation by the celestial bodies; and so it is similarly for all things. <margin>D</margin>

Let us not suppose this account implies that we must set down two entirely separate first principles of things. For we say that these two "columns" <note>term: "συστοιχίας" (systoichiai) — a Pythagorean concept of parallel columns of opposites, such as Light/Dark or Limit/Unlimited.</note> belong to the same family. For the "One" precedes every opposition, as the Pythagoreans also say. But since, after the Single Cause, the Duality of principles appeared, the Monad <note>The principle of unity.</note> within these principles governs the members of the Duality. Or, if you wish to speak in the Orphic manner, Aether governs Chaos.

In the gods who exist before the world, divisions are completed in this way, and they continue through the worldly gods down to the very last things. For there, under the one principle, sits the intellectual and the demiurgic <note>The "crafting" or creative power.</note>; under the other, the generative and life-giving. Here, under the Monad is the Olympian race, and under the Duality is the Titanic. Under the elder principle are Sameness, Rest, Reason, and Form; under the remaining principle are Difference, Motion, the Irrational, and Matter. For the descent of the two principles proceeded even as far as these.

But since the One is beyond the primary Duality, even things that seem to be opposites are led back and arranged toward a single cosmic order. <margin>E</margin> For in the universe, there are both the two kinds of gods and the divided kinds of Being, the various kinds of souls and the opposite kinds of bodies. The lower things are governed by the more divine, and a single world is perfected, "fitted together from opposites" <note>original: "ἐξ ἐναντίων ἡρμοσμένος"</note>, consisting of "limiters and infinites" according to Philolaus <note>A Pythagorean philosopher who argued the world is a harmony of limited and unlimited elements.</note>. According to the "infinites" within it, its nature comes from the Indefinite Duality or Infinity; according to the "limiters," it comes from the Intellectual Monad or Limit; and according to the one, whole, and perfect Form arising from all these, it comes from the One Being. For God is the one who established the "mixture," as Socrates says in the *Philebus*.

<margin>F</margin> That such an island once existed, and of such a great size, is made clear by certain writers who have investigated matters concerning the outer sea. For they say that in their own times there were seven islands in that sea sacred to Persephone <note>The daughter of Demeter and queen of the Underworld</note>, and also three others of immense size, one of which was sacred to Pluto, another to Ammon <note>An Egyptian deity often identified with Zeus/Jupiter</note>, and the middle one of these to Poseidon, being a thousand <term>stadia</term> <note>A Greek unit of distance; 1,000 stadia is roughly 115 miles</note> in size. They also state that the inhabitants of this island preserve the memory from their ancestors of Atlantis, an island that truly existed there and was of vast proportions, | which for many periods held dominion over all the islands in the Atlantic sea, and was itself likewise sacred to Poseidon. These things Marcellus has written in his *Ethiopian History* <note>original: *Aithiopikois*</note>. But since, even if these things are so and such an island once existed, it is possible to accept the account of it both as a history and as an image of a certain reality existing in the whole of nature, we shall explain its correspondence, gradually accustoming those who are unpracticed in such contemplations <note>original: *theamaton*</note> to the universal theory of the world-order. (For it is possible to contemplate the same proportions both in a more particular and a more comprehensive way.) Indeed, instruction must proceed from the generalities and end the contemplation at the <insert>activity</insert> of the particular parts. Therefore, do not be surprised if we previously took this proportion in one way—speaking of it in terms of place—but now we shall arrange it in another way, yet still the same, with the precision appropriate to the subject matter.

<margin>B</margin> | For as there is a twofold <term>co-ordination</term> <note>original: *systoichias*; a Pythagorean term for a series of related concepts or "columns" of reality</note> in the universe, as we were saying, beginning from the gods and ending in matter and the material form; and as each of these has its most universal aspects and its most particular aspects (for we have said this before) and the middle ground between both (for the divine orders are all-encompassing, while the final elements are the most lowly <note>original: *atimotata*</note>, and between them are the intellectual and psychic orders); we think it right first to divide the lower co-ordination into three parts. We take the most universal kinds within it, then the middle, then the final. We assign the Atlanteans as analogous to the first, those on the other islands to the second, and the entire opposite continent to the third; and we assign the ocean and the Atlantic sea to matter <note>original: *hyle*</note>. For the entire lower co-ordination is a "procession" <note>original: *proodos*; the Neoplatonic concept of reality flowing outward from the One</note> advancing into multiplicity and division, yet it possesses its own primary excellence and deficiency. ## ON THE TIMAEUS I.

<note>original: "κεῖν μεῖζον Λιβύης ἅμα καὶ Ἀσίας"</note> ...larger than Libya and Asia combined, as they proceed into bulk and extension. For all things further removed from the One, while diminished in power, exceed in quantity; just as those things which are closer <note>original: "ἐγγυτέρω"</note>, being contracted in quantity, possess a marvelous power. Therefore, in this context, magnitude is indicative of a decline <term>hyphesis: a "subsidence" or lowering of ontological status</term> and of the procession and expansion toward the all. He says the sea is "navigable" because the fewer things proceed as far as the last things and adorn matter; but having reached the limit of the world-ordering, they stop, and what lies beyond is infinite. For that which in no way "is" follows immediately upon the limits of Being. The addition of the word "then" <note>referring to the time when the sea was navigable</note> suggests that while the universal causes pass through matter without hindrance and adorn it, we ourselves must not be mastered by it, nor be "baptized" <note>immersed or overwhelmed</note> into its infinite and indefinite nature. Since the procession of things is continuous, and nowhere does any "void" <note>original: "κενόν"</note> intervene, but a well-ordered decline is observed from the most unified things to the intermediate—containing and being contained—and from the intermediate to the last and most indivisible things; | for this reason, he says the passage for the Atlanteans was from Atlantis to the other islands, and from these to the continent lying opposite <note>original: "κατακτικρήν" - likely meaning the "opposite" mainland</note>. He says Atlantis is one, the other islands are many, and the continent is the greatest. For the Monad <note>the principle of Unity</note> befits the first of each genus, number and plurality befit the second (for plurality appears with the Dyad), and magnitude befits the third, because of the progression of magnitude toward the Triad. Since the last things of the inferior series tend toward the most material, he indicated their greatest distance from the <margin>superior things through the term "opposite" <note>original: "κατακτικροῦ"</note>; and it was not enough to use only the word "outside," as he did for the Atlanteans to show they belonged to the other portion, but he added "opposite" to indicate the ultimate decline. By saying it was "around the true sea," he signaled their existence around matter and the final subsistence of worldly things. For the "true sea" is analogous to the "true lie" <note>A Platonic concept from the Republic, referring to ignorance in the soul</note> and to "true matter," which he called the "sea of dissimilarity" | in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Πολιτικῷ"</note>. Furthermore, to show that these two series must be distinguished from one another, kept unconfused by the demiurgic boundaries, he said the Pillars of Hercules distinguish the inner inhabited world from the outer. For they represent the vigorous demiurgic <note>creator-like</note> activity and the distinction of the kinds of things in the universe, which is divine, stable, and always masculine...</margin>

This Hercules is indeed of the lineage of Zeus; but the one before him, being divine, was allotted a protective rank over the generative series. From both, therefore, we must understand the demiurgic division which guards the two portions of the universe as distinct.

**"For these things which are within the mouth of which we speak, appear to be a harbor having a narrow entrance, until it might most rightly be called a continent." (Page 25 A.)**

The things within the "mouth" indicate the classes of the superior coordinate <note>The "coordinate" or *systoichia* refers to the Pythagorean table of opposites; here it refers to the higher, more divine realm</note>, as being turned toward themselves and rejoicing in their permanent and unifying power. For the "mouth" symbolically reveals the cause that limits and distinguishes the two <margin>F</margin> portions of the world; while the "narrow harbor" signifies their coiled-up existence, inclining toward itself, ordered, and immaterial. For through the "narrowness," the distance and extension belonging to the inferior coordinate are cast away; and through the "harbor," the separation from the discordant and disordered calamity of material things is shown. For such are harbors: they provide shelter from the disturbances at sea. And if someone were to say that a "harbor" is created for souls through the more intellectual and divine elevation of the whole, he would not <margin>56</margin> fall far from the truth.

**"But in this Atlantic island, a great and wonderful power of kings was established... even unto tyranny." (Page 25 B.)**

In these matters, one must remember the **Platonic hypotheses** concerning the earth: that he does not measure its magnitude in the same way as the mathematicians, but has assumed its extent to be something much greater, as **Socrates** says in the *Phaedo* <note>referring to Phaedo 109a, where Socrates describes the earth as vast and the Mediterranean world as only a small "hollow"</note>, and that he posits many habitations similar to our inhabited world. Therefore, he also records such a great island and continent in the outer sea. For generally, if the earth has a spherical form according to nature, it must be such according to the greater part of itself. Yet our inhabited world shows much irregularity with its inlets and outlets. There are, therefore, elsewhere on the earth level plains and dimensions extending to a great height. Indeed, the story goes that **Hercules**, having traveled through much impassable <margin>B</margin> land, arrived at the **Atlantic mountain** <note>Mount Atlas</note>. Those who have written the *Ethiopian Histories* <note>original: *Aithiopika*</note> record its magnitude as such that it touches the very air and casts a shadow for five thousand stadia <note>A stadium was roughly 600 feet; 5000 stadia is approximately 600 miles</note>; for from the ninth hour of the day, the sun is hidden by it until its final setting. ## ON THE TIMAEUS I.

Indeed, it is a marvelous thing. For Mount Athos, the Macedonian mountain, casts its shadow as far as us <note>The author likely refers to Lemnos or the surrounding Thracian sea</note>, though it is seven hundred stadia <term>stadium: an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters</term> distant. And it is not only Atlas that Marcellus—who wrote the *Ethiopic History*—recorded as being of such great size; Ptolemy also says that the Mountains of the Moon possess an immeasurable height, and Aristotle says that the peaks of the Caucasus are illuminated by the sun’s rays for a third part of the night after sunset and a third part before sunrise. And if one were to look toward the whole magnitude of the earth as defined by its depressions, one would consider it truly immeasurable according to the report of Plato. Thus, we do not fear certain mathematical methods in our current explanation of the earth, nor shall we attempt to overturn them. For those methods measure the earth as a flat plane according to the inhabited portion (though Plato says we dwell in a hollow <note>original: "en kolpō"; a reference to the Phaedo 109b where humans are said to live in a cavity of the earth like ants around a pond</note>), while he suggests the whole earth is elevated, which is also what the sacred tradition of the Egyptians has handed down.

Regarding the stated size of Atlantis, one should not be skeptical, even if one accepts the account as mere history. Concerning its power—that there were ten kings in it, born as twin children, and that they ruled over the other islands and certain parts of the continent and the lands within the Pillars of Hercules—this is explicitly recorded in the *Critias*. Now (since our purpose is to provide an analysis of these things according to their reference to the Whole), its power is called "great and marvelous" because it extends over the entirety <note>original: "epi pan"</note> and has embraced the whole of the second "co-ordinate series" <term>systoichia: a Pythagorean concept of paired opposites, such as Light/Dark or Limit/Unlimited</term>. For ten kings hold it together, because the decad <term>the number ten</term> encompasses the leading principles of the two series; as the Pythagoreans also say, through the decad all things are included within the opposites.

They were born as twins, so that there are five pairs—five times twins being born to Poseidon and Cleito—because the arrangement of this series is according to the measures of Justice <note>The number five was associated with Justice in Neoplatonic numerology</note>, of which the pentad <term>the number five</term> is the image; but its procession <margin>D</margin> is through the dyad <term>the number two</term>, just as the superior series proceeds through the monad <term>the number one</term>. They are all descendants of Poseidon, because the entire weaving together of opposites and the cosmic war belongs to the realm of the Demiurge <term>the divine craftsman of the universe</term>. For this god is the overseer of everything that exists through opposition, generation, decay, and every kind of motion. They rule Atlantis as those who hold together all the primary and most universal genera of the inferior series; they rule the other islands as having embraced the middle regions through their wholeness; they rule the parts of the continent as those who adorn even the furthest reaches as far as possible; and they dominate certain parts of the inner inhabited world because even the lowest parts of the superior series serve the first parts of the inferior series. This is not surprising, just as certain spirits <note>daimones</note> are subordinate to certain heroes, and partial souls, falling away from the intelligible world, often serve Fate. For such is the Titanic order among the gods, to which Atlas also belongs, and these ten kings...
