# PROCLUS

The first of the kings was called Atlas, and he gave his name to the island, as is said in the *Atlantic* <note>original: "τῷ Ἀτλαντικῷ" — referring to the dialogue *Critias* 114A</note>. Now, the highest parts of the second coordinate series <term>coordinate series: "συστοιχία" (systoichia), a Pythagorean concept of paired opposites like Limit/Unlimited or Light/Dark</term> are ordered by the Olympian gods, led by Athena; but this series also rules over all the lower and divine essence which falls under the inferior coordinate series—such as irrational souls, material masses, and matter itself. It seems that for this reason Plato called the power of the Atlanteans "great and marvelous," since in this rank of beings, a certain "Terror" and "Force" <note>original: "Βίας" (Bias)</note> have been handed down by the ancient theologians. Perhaps it is also because the entire second coordinate series is the offspring of "Infinity," which we say is the very first principle above, or rather superior to "Limit." For this reason, they ascribe "power" to the Atlanteans, just as they ascribe "virtue" to the Athenians, which stands before Limit <note>original: "πρὸ τοῦ πέρατος"</note>. For virtues are the measures of those who possess them. In this way, naturally, I believe we shall understand the entire analysis according to Pythagorean principles.

The account also possesses an "increase" <note>rhetorical amplification</note> in order to show the work of the victors as greater and more illustrious. For he said that its "power" increased through union, and he further added "great and marvelous." Each of these is distinct: for a thing is "great" even if it were nothing else, but it is called "marvelous" in relation to others. By as much as the defeated party is wondered at, by so much greater is the victor shown to be. Furthermore, by indicating the multitude of divisions, he showed that the power which was mastered by Athens was manifold and superior to all things.

-> **"This entire power, gathered into one, both in our region and yours, once attempted to enslave the entire region within the mouth [of the strait] with a single impulse."** (Plato, *Timaeus* 25B) <-

He does not mean that there was ever a literal rebellion in divine affairs, nor that the lower things sought to master the better, he says; rather, while these things may be true among men, the present account indicates that among the universal kinds of the second coordinate series, this power has traveled through all things. For there is in heaven and everywhere a power that is both distributive and unitive, and nothing is without a share in them. But in the higher beings, it exists not dividedly nor according to a "multiplication," but gathered into one and with a single impulse—that is, unitedly and according to a single, continuous life. For just as in the inferior coordinate series even the "one" is multiplied, so in the superior series the "multitude" is unified. Therefore, the multitude is everywhere, but it is mastered through union. The fact that the Atlanteans wished to rule the entire inhabited world within the straits by gathering into one, yet were nonetheless mastered by the Athenians, bears an image of these truths. For even if multitude and distinction are observed in the better coordinate series, they are observed in a unified manner...

where it is not the multitude that holds power, but rather identity and, in general, the superior kinds.

**Then, O Solon, the power of your city became conspicuous to all men for both its virtue and its strength.** (Page 25 B.)

He <note>Proclus, the commentator</note> contrasts the power of the Athenians with the power of the Atlanteans, placing this name <note>Athens</note> before the others as befitting the central demiurgic <term>demiurgy: the work of the divine creator or craftsman</term> power, and as relating to the superior power in both virtue and strength. He does this so that through **virtue** he might demonstrate the city's kinship with the philosophical nature of Athena herself (for indeed, another tradition of theology, not only the Orphic, has called her Virtue itself), and through **strength** its kinship with her lover of war. He calls this power **conspicuous** because it is cosmic and contributes to the creation of sensible things. To the Atlanteans, he assigns only "power," and this continually, as they are ranked under the principle of **Infinity** <note>the Indefinite Dyad</note>; but he says the Athenians "master" power through their total **virtue**. For belonging to the series of **Limit** <note>the Monad</note>, they are characterized by virtue, | which both measures the passions and employs powers as is necessary. <margin>C</margin>

**For standing at the head of all in courage and all the arts of war... until it liberated everyone.** (Page 25 C.)

Just as we divided the inferior series <term>sustoichia: a Pythagorean 'column' or series of opposing principles</term> into three—the first, middle, and last limits—so we shall divide the superior series into totality, the most partial parts, and the intermediates subsisting between them. Having made this division, we shall rank the Athenians analogous to the first, the other Greeks who were not yet enslaved to the middle, and those already enslaved to the last. For according to these paths, the Athenian powers master the powers of Poseidon <note>original: "the things of Poseidon," representing the Atlantean/material realm</note>; the first master the first, the monadic <term>monadic: relating to the One or unity</term> masters the dyadic <term>dyadic: relating to duality or division</term>, and simply put, the better masters the worse. They eternally preserve the middle powers which guard their own rank and their state of being mastered by the inferior series through their own union and the stable nature of their power; they also rescue those in slavery from their servitude, calling them back to union and stability. For some things are always in matter, others are separate, and others are sometimes under the material kinds | and sometimes raised up toward a separate life. Such indeed is the drama <note>original: "drama," referring to the soul's journey</note> concerning us: sometimes we are ranked under the **Titanic** order, and sometimes under the **Olympian**. <margin>D</margin>

The phrase "to stand at the head of all" signifies the universal embrace of the primary classes of the more divine portion. The reference to "nobility of soul" and "skills in war" is identical to the character of Athena; for through nobility of soul, they imitate her philosophical nature, and through the skills of war, her love of combat. The phrase "at one time leading the Greeks, and at another time standing alone in danger" <margin>E</margin> signifies that the primary and universal causes sometimes act in conjunction with secondary and intermediate causes, and at other times act by themselves, transcending the production of these others and remaining solitary in their activity. For the race of gods and the race that follows the gods <note>referring to daemons or heroes</note> do not act equally; rather, the creative power of the gods extends further, since the more divine elements everywhere act before their effects, with their effects, and after them. This can be confirmed from many sources. The "extreme dangers" signify the final or most distant creative act of the primary causes. The word "trophy" <note>original: τρόπαιον (tropaion) - a monument to an enemy's defeat</note> signifies both that the second series of beings is perfected under the first, being ordered by it, and that it is in some way "turned" <note>a wordplay on 'trope' (turning) and 'trophy'</note> according to the power of that first series; it also signifies that there are always constant signs of the "turning" or defeat of the inferior elements even in the lowest realms, reaching down from the primary causes. That these statements follow a natural sequence is clear to those who are not entirely inexperienced in natural theory <note>original: "φυσικῆς θεωρίας" - the study of the physical world</note>; for it is not surprising that an earthquake of such magnitude occurred as to destroy so great an island. Indeed, the earthquake that happened shortly before our time shook both Egypt and Bithynia in a single day; and it is not at all incredible that a flood should follow the earthquake. For this usually happens in the case of great earthquakes, as Aristotle also notes, adding the cause at the same time. For wherever a flood occurs along with an earthquake, a wave is the cause of the suffering. For when the wind <note>term: "πνεῦμα" (pneuma) - in ancient physics, this refers to trapped air or "spirit" within the earth believed to cause seismic activity</note> that produces the earthquakes—not yet flowing beneath the earth—is driven from the opposite direction and cannot push back the sea (which is being moved by the force of some contrary wind) because of the wind rushing against it, it stands still, hindering its progress. This causes a great mass of water to be gathered up by the wind contrary to it. Then, when much of the sea has been accumulated because of the force pushing from the opposite side, the wind itself, having rushed all at once beneath the earth outside of the flow, produces the earthquake, and the sea floods the place. For it was in this manner that the earthquake occurred around Achaia, along with the onset of the wave that flooded the coastal cities of Boura and Helike. Thus, no one looking correctly at natural phenomena would doubt this. Furthermore, that the same region can become at one time passable, at another mainland, and at another sea, is among the things confirmed by natural philosophers, as Aristotle believes and history demonstrates. C It is not surprising if "very shallow" signifies a marshy place; for even now people call underwater rocks and those where the water is near the surface "shallows" <note>original: *brachē*</note>. Why then should one trouble themselves by contending over these matters? We shall prove that even these things possess a marvelous quality regarding the arrangement of the whole universe <note>The *diakosmēsis* or world-order</note>, by reminding ourselves of those "descents into the underworld" <note>original: *katartarōseis* — literally, being thrust into Tartarus</note> mentioned by Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and prophet of the Orphic mysteries</note> at the conclusion of the creation. For he, having handed down the creative opposition between the Olympian gods and the Titans, completes the entire arrangement down to the furthest extremities of the universe, granting even to those realms a share of the gods' untainted providence. Plato, knowing these things and delivering the whole truth through images, extends and leads down these two classes of beings beneath the invisible realm, and through this disappearance he imitates the Orphic descent into the underworld. For in order that even the furthest things might be ordered and enjoy divine providence, it was necessary for both the superior and the inferior series <note>The *systoichia* or "coordinates" of being</note> to extend their own making from above down to the cosmic bottom, each in a manner appropriate to itself. One series is shaken and sinks into the earth—which is the same as saying it proceeds in a permanent and solid fashion—while the other disappears, which would be the same as becoming material, disordered, and formless. The former follows the symbol of the permanent and stable, while the latter follows the symbol of the sea: the changeable, disordered, and flowing. For even in the furthest things, stability and generation come from the better series, while decay, change, and discordant motion come from the worse. Since these too are ordered as the invisible and visible creations are fulfilled, he says for this reason that there was a "day" and a "grievous night," with the night indicating the invisible causes and the day the visible ones, and the "grievousness" indicating that which is irresistible, unswerving, and pervading through all things. Because all these things are accomplished according to creative powers, the earthquakes and floods were brought down, being appropriate to the middle region. For if he wished to signify the powers or activities of Zeus, he would have spoken of thunderbolts and fire-storms; but since he delivers the creative activities of Poseidon, he likened them to earthquakes or floods. For they are accustomed to call this god the "Earth-shaker" and "Dark-haired." Because time also signifies the progression in order and the well-ordered...

<margin>B</margin>

This indeed pre-exists in the Paradigm <note>The "Paradigm" refers to the eternal model of the universe in Platonic thought.</note>, being filled from the first principles and filling the things after it with demiurgic <note>creative or world-making</note> power. Moreover, if you approach the text in another way, the Athenians are wonderfully praised and the 

<margin>C</margin> 

polity <note>or "form of government"</note> of Socrates is fittingly celebrated. For it shows that it is possible through the life of the Athenians, and that in whomever it arises, it is a savior of the greatest things. Socrates deemed these things worthy of demonstration in those [Athenians]; and they, having lived according to the best form of polity, are shown to be worthy of the greatest wonder. For to be modeled according to the first paradigm is truly wonderful; and among worldly things, those that are more divine perfectly preserve their whole form and are called (and are) "monadic" <note>unique or singular</note>, while the material things, having the same form in many subjects, hold the lowest rank. This, then, which belongs to the gods in their craftsmanship—namely, attaining the peak of their own paradigm—the city of the Athenians also displayed by practicing the best measure of life to the highest degree. Furthermore, the cycle of benefits imitates the worldly cycle. For the Egyptians were well-treated by the Athenians through their deeds in war, and the Athenians by the Egyptians through their priestly <note>original: *hieratikon*</note> discourses. It was 

<margin>D</margin> 

already a return of the favor to have the deed itself recorded, but the instructional narration of their ancestral deeds shows the repayment to be many times greater. In addition to these things, the attributing of "fortune" <note>original: *tyche*</note> and "divine intervention" to the movement of our intellect is worthy of Plato’s theory. For fortune and the gift from her are not aimless or indefinite, but a power that gathers together the many and scattered causes and brings order <note>original: *kosmike*, though the translator notes suggest "beautifying/ordering"</note> to the disordered.

## ON THE TIMAEUS I.

...is the fulfillment of the portions allotted to each from the whole. Why then was Socrates brought into harmony with the words of Solon? I would say it is both because of the gathering together of the many and scattered causes <note>original: "αἰτίων"</note>, and because of the one Goddess <note>Athena</note> who possesses their common intellect. For being Athenians, they are moved as if from a single spring by their presiding Goddess toward identical inner thoughts.

->**"I was not willing to speak immediately; for because of the passage of time, I did not remember it sufficiently... until I could speak thus." (Page 26 A.)**<-

These things must also be observed in the context of the universe. Before particular things <note>original: "μερικῶν"</note> come into being in time, the Demiurgic Cause <term>Demiurgic Cause: The "Craftsman" or Creator-God in Platonic philosophy who shapes the material world according to eternal patterns</term> establishes its own offspring. And just as the sustainer of all generated things, being the primary Intellect, sees within himself the causes of things produced, so he grants the procession from himself to all others. Being himself sufficient and perfect, he thus shares his own power with secondary beings. Therefore, the "inner thought" and the "recollection" and all such terms signify the containment of the Demiurgic principles <note>original: "λόγων" - logoi</note> within the One.

->**"Wherefore I quickly agreed to your instructions... until I took them up again during the night." (Page 26 B.)**<-

<margin>•</margin> Because he remembered in a general way, he promised to fulfill the instructions; but because <margin>•</margin> he did not remember with precision, he first examined the arguments within himself. He considered that in such instructions—just as Socrates commanded to see the Republic <note>original: "πολιτείαν"</note> in motion—it is a very great task to find a premise upon which one can render what is fitting to the commands. This is exactly what he has done by taking the war of the Atlanteans and the Athenians from history, as being able to demonstrate the life that provides the best Republic. He took these things up again during the night so that he might share the account with his companions without distraction. Again, one must transfer these points to the whole of reality; for there, the Demiurgic Cause, being filled from the unmanifest cause (for it possesses primarily all the intellectual causes and is united in supreme excellence), thus brings forth its own power into the manifest according to the will and judgment of those higher causes. Furthermore, the fact that he did not speak "immediately" but "later" is a symbol of the pre-arranged preparation of things, from which perfection comes to natural effects. You might say...

<margin>§</margin> There is also something ethical in this sense of "caution." For one must not rashly undertake 1) such great matters without first examining the whole task within oneself, as if we were bringing forth from a storehouse 2) a spoken word that is merely a messenger 4) for the inner reasons <note>original: "logoi," meaning both words and rational principles</note> lying within. Indeed, to take up the discourse within oneself and then speak mimics the "reversion" <note>term: epistrophe - the Neoplatonic concept of a thing returning to its source or looking inward to find its true nature</note> of the creative principles toward themselves; it also demonstrates the soul's wise turning back upon itself 6), through which it contemplates the reasons of all beings within itself. Furthermore, to propose a discourse fitting for the divine intentions demonstrates the connection in the act of creation between visible things and their causes.

-> "As the saying goes, the lessons of childhood possess a wonderful memorial; until, like indelible encaustic paintings, they have become ingrained in me." (Page 86 C.) <-

The fact that children have better memories is observed in practice and could have many persuasive causes. One, as Porphyry <note>A famous 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> says, is that the souls of children have no experience 10) of human evils. Since they are neither distracted <margin>B</margin> nor troubled | by external things, they possess an imagination <note>term: phantastikon - the faculty of the soul that receives images</note> that is not yet distorted, though their intellect is somewhat slower; for experiences are what make the intellect sharp and quick-moving 11). A second reason 12) is that the rational life in them 13) is more thoroughly blended with the imagination. Just as when the soul thickens and mixes itself with the body, the body becomes stronger 14) and more vital, in the same way, the imagination is strengthened through its relationship with reason. Being strengthened, it holds its impressions <note>term: typoi - literally "stamps" or "imprints" left on the mind</note> more permanently, perceiving them more clearly 15) through its own power. Just as the body has more control over the things within it 16) when it is more vital through a greater communion with the soul. A third reason besides these 17) is that the same things appear greater to the imaginations of children; thus, they are more wondered at by them, so that they "thicken" <note>meaning they become more intensely focused or concentrated</note> with them, which is why they remember them best 18). For we store in our memory things that have greatly grieved us or greatly delighted us; at any rate, such things look more directly at us. Just as that which is more affected by <margin>C</margin> fire | preserves the heat given to it for a longer time, in the same way, the faculty of imagination, being more affected by external things, holds the impression more firmly. And indeed, the imagination of children is more affected because the same things appear larger to us when we are young.

...it is reasonable that children retain the impression <note>original: "typon"</note> more firmly, as they are more easily affected by the same things. This is what Critias seems to me to indicate when he says he listened to the story from the old man with great pleasure, and for this reason, the "indelible ink" <note>original: "anekploutou graphes" - literally an un-washable writing or dye</note> of the story remained within him. Just as Socrates, in the summary of the *Republic*, handed down to us the cause of memory as being the **unfamiliarity** <note>original: "aetheian" - the novelty or strangeness of a thing makes it stick in the mind</note> of the things we hear, so Critias here points to the **imitation** <note>original: "mimian"</note> of children. It seems that the former is also the cause of the latter—unfamiliarity being the cause of the memory of Forms <note>term: Forms (Eide) - the eternal, perfect archetypes of all things in Platonic philosophy</note>. For all things seem unfamiliar when they first strike the minds of children.

Perhaps this also indicates that the **prolific demiurgy** <note>term: Demiurgy - the act of world-creation or "crafting" by a divine intellect</note> of secondary things depends upon the **permanent identity** of the primary things, just as the cause of memory is also the cause of the memory of children mentioned by Critias. If anyone, in addition to these explanations, should hold fast to the higher contemplation of these matters, let him hear **Iamblichus** <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who influentialized the mystical interpretation of Plato</note> saying that the memory of children refers to the ever-young and flourishing permanent production of Reason-principles <note>original: "logon"</note>, while the "indelible" nature of the writing or the dye (for it is spoken of both ways) refers to the **ever-flowing** <margin>Iamblichus</margin> supply from the elders to the secondary levels of reality. For these interpretations also possess the grace of the aforementioned explanations.

-> **"And indeed, I was telling these very things to them early this morning... until we must seek someone else in his place." (Page 26 E.)** <-

Previously, Critias made them partners in the discourse, but now he invites them to be spectators, because in the **Paradigms** <note>The eternal models used by the Creator</note> above, all things are united and fill one another with intellectual powers; but in the world, the Creator <note>original: "demiurgei"</note> acts upon things through one another according to a certain divine and **universal sympathy** <note>original: "sympnoia" - literally a "breathing together" or cosmic harmony</note>, through which all things are in all things in a manner appropriate to each. In heaven, the paradigms pre-exist those in the realm of generated things, and in the realm of generation, there are images of the heavenly things. Since the **wholeness** <column-break/> always precedes the parts, this must also be observed in the secondary demiurgy. For this reason, he first went through the war in summary, but afterwards he will attempt to teach the particulars, recounting the entire constitution of the **Atlanteans** and the origin of their birth, how they turned toward **injustice**, and how the Athenians behaved toward the war...

...they passed through, from what kind of preparation, from what embassies <note>original: "πρεσβειῶν"</note>, through what means and joined with whom, and all that follows from these things. Therefore, the hypothetical state is an imitation of the primary <term>demiurgy</term> <note>The act of world-creation by a divine craftsman</note>; wherefore, revealing its mystical nature and that which pre-exists in pure reason, he says it was arranged as if in a myth. Since this [secondary state] is linked to the former and is continuous with it, he says, "they will certainly speak, and we shall not reject them."

<margin>F</margin> **And whom, O Critias, should we rather receive in exchange for this... until... it is not.** (Page 26 E.)

Socrates accepts the discourse, first as being appropriate to the festival of Athena; for the war was an image of the cosmic wars. He also accepts it as a hymn to Athena, suitable for the sacrifice; for if there is any use for the voice among men, it must be used for hymns to her. Moreover, since the Goddess is the cause of both contemplation and action, through the sacrifice we imitate her practical activity, <margin>61</margin> while through the hymn we imitate her contemplative activity. Secondly, he accepts it as witnessing to the possibility of the state. For he himself claimed to demonstrate this in his discourses concerning it. For this form of the state was sufficient for him, existing both in the heavens and in a single man—for all things that are without are also within—and the law that is truly so-called begins from the inner life itself. But if it could be shown to have once prevailed among the Athenians, its possibility is absolutely demonstrated. This, then, has such causes; and again, from these things we must grasp that the story concerning the Atlanteans is not a mere fiction <note>original: "πλάσμα"</note>, as some have thought, but a history <note>original: "ἱστορία"</note>, yet one having an affinity to the whole <term>cosmopoeia</term> <note>The making of the world</note>. Thus, even the things he related concerning the magnitude of Atlantis should not be condemned as mythical and fabricated by those who shut up the magnitude of the earth into a very narrow space.

**But with good fortune you must speak; and I, in return for yesterday's words, must now keep silence and listen.** (Page 27 A.)

<margin>B</margin> Plato does not say, as those from the <term>Stoa</term> <note>The Stoic philosophers</note> do, that the virtuous man <note>original: "σπουδαῖον"</note> is granted nothing by fortune, but rather that even our intellectual activities [depend upon it]...

# ON THE TIMAEUS I.

When [the souls] are entwined with bodily things during their outward progression, [the author] wishes them to be inspired <note>original: *epipneisthai*</note> by **Good Fortune**, so that they may make their progression successful and their activity toward others beloved by the gods. Just as **Nemesis** <note>The goddess of retribution, here acting as a guardian against "light words" or careless speech.</note> is the overseer of frivolous words, so too does **Good Fortune** steer words for the benefit of both those who receive them and the one who gives them, so that the former may receive them with gratitude and sympathy, while the latter, knowing <note>The Greek text here is slightly damaged; it likely implies "knowing how to give."</note> what is appropriate, may render to each their due. This is how it works in particular cases; but in the case of the whole universe, **Good Fortune** signifies the divine allotment <note>original: *diaklerosin*</note>, according to which each thing has obtained the rank suitable to itself from the one Father and the entire **Demiurgy** <note>The "work of the Craftsman" or the creation of the world.</note>. Furthermore, the fact that **Socrates** listens to these discourses while remaining silent <note>original: *hesychian agonta*</note> involves a reciprocal return of duty. For the others did the same when he led the discussion on the **Republic** <note>original: *politeia*</note>, so much so that it was not even clear from that writing that they were present. It also shows by analogy how the demiurgic causes, though all united with one another, nevertheless possess distinct modes of production. <margin>C</margin> Listening is indicative of their penetration through one another, while remaining silent while another speaks signifies the unmixed **purity** by which each thing, from its own specific character, acts upon and generates secondary things.

**"Consider then, Socrates, the arrangement of the hospitality-gifts we have prepared for you..." until "...to make the remaining discourses as if they concerned citizens and Athenians." (Page 27 B.)**

This order of speakers intends to make **Timaeus** both the summit and the middle; for he speaks after Socrates and Critias, and before Critias and Hermocrates. <note>The commentator is analyzing the symbolic order of the speakers in the dialogue.</note> He is silent in the middle, but in another sense he is the summit, both according to his knowledge and because he generates the men whom Socrates nourishes and Critias arms. This is also a clear symbol of the entire **Demiurgy**: being simultaneously the summit and the middle. For [the demiurgic causes] transcend all **inter-cosmic** <note>original: *egkosmion*; things existing within the physical world.</note> beings and are equally present to all; both the summits of the universe and the center are consecrated to the Creator, as the doctrine of the **Pythagoreans** says—for there, as they say, is the "Tower of Zeus" <note>original: *Zanthos pyrgos*; likely a corruption of *Dios pyrgos* (Tower of Zeus), the central fire in Pythagorean cosmology.</note>. And **Critias** is the middle, speaking now in summary after Socrates, and later speaking before Hermocrates. <margin>D</margin> For the "dyadic" <note>The number two, representing division or mediation.</note> nature and the "whole-with-parts" belong to the middle demiurgy, just as the "whole" belongs to the first and the "parts" to the last. Therefore, Socrates delivered the **Republic** in summary, and Hermocrates contributes to the parts of the **history** that is to be delivered by Critias. These things, then, concerning the whole...

# PROCLUS

Let this be said regarding the order. One might ask <note>original: "ἀπορήσεις δ᾽ ἄν τις"</note> what role is left for Hermocrates, given that Timaeus has been assigned the generation of men, Socrates their upbringing, and Critias their deeds. For there is nothing left in the discourse, unless Hermocrates is a collaborator with Critias in the narratives. For the narration of history consists of both deeds and words; and while Critias himself promised to provide the account of the deeds, he also called upon Hermocrates to join him in the journey of the discourses. For the explanation of these things is difficult, as was said previously. This is why in the *Atlantic* <note>The *Critias*, which deals with the story of Atlantis.</note> he portrays the gods as gathering to deliberate concerning the judgment of the Atlanteans, where <margin>E</margin> Zeus speaks, and he concluded the gathering as if handing over the imitation of the speeches to Hermocrates. And if he did not reach the rest of the works, it is not at all unlikely. For having gathered the gods for the purpose of chastening <term>chastening: "σωφρονίσαι", to bring to one's senses or moderate</term> the insolence of the Atlanteans, he holds within this all that follows: the preparation of the Athenians, the expedition, and the victory. Therefore, Timaeus produces the men, Socrates educates them, Critias leads them forth into deeds, and Hermocrates into words. The first imitates the paternal cause; the second provides stable intellection; the third provides the cause of motion and the second progression; and the fourth provides the cause that turns the lowest things back to their principles through the imitation of words.

These things should be heard symbolically and perhaps not with excessive curiosity. But one might ask why the *Republic* <note>original: "Πολιτεία"</note> was not placed before the *Timaeus*, in which the account of the rest of the universe and the race of men is handed down. For they ought first to be born, as Timaeus says, and then be educated, which Socrates does in the *Republic*, and then <margin>F</margin> act in a manner worthy of their upbringing, which the *Atlantic* somehow indicates. And if he had started from the end itself and come down to the *Timaeus*, which is first by nature, we would have the usual thing to say: that for the sake of teaching, the things that are first to us are handed down first, even if they are later by nature. But now the middle seems to be placed first, and the first in the middle. And if this order had been handed down by editors, it would be less surprising to us; but now it seems Plato himself arranged it this way. Here, then, | he summarizes the *Republic* as having already been stated in its main points through...

# ON THE TIMAEUS I.

<margin>Solution</margin> In response to this <term>aporia</term><note>A philosophical puzzle or contradiction.</note>, it must be said that if all the <term>hypotheses</term><note>Foundational assumptions or starting points of an argument.</note> were taken from the nature of things that exist or have come to be, then the puzzle would hold, and the *Timaeus* would be incorrectly placed second. Furthermore, if they were all fashioned entirely by reason, then the primary things should likewise be taken first. But since the hypothesis of Socrates follows reason alone and fashions through contemplation both the nourishment and the education of the men—of which they discourse as both existing and having come to be—it is reasonable that while the others are organized as wholes, the Socratic hypothesis, as if subsisting according to reason alone and through precision, is placed before the rest. 

Perhaps this was also intended by the author to show us that whatever divine souls project while looking toward the <term>intelligible</term><note>The realm of pure thought and forms, beyond physical perception.</note>, these things once actually occurred during certain favorable revolutions of the cycles upon the earth. This, at least, Critias testified to Socrates <note>original: "μαρτυρήσας" (having testified); see Plato, *Critias* 28D</note> regarding the citizens: "We shall say that those citizens you imagined are these very ancestors of ours whom the priest spoke of." They certainly harmonize, and we shall not be mistaken in saying they are the ones who lived in that time. 

And if the *Republic* should fall short of the *Timaeus* in particular details—by dealing with mortals and lingering upon an image—yet it precedes it in the universal. For the same form of life displays justice in the soul, order in the city, and <term>demiurgy</term><note>The act of world-creation or divine craftsmanship.</note> in the cosmos. Furthermore, while the choice of life is free, the activity directed outward requires the cosmic order. This is why the war is described in the *Atlanticus* <note>The *Critias*, which deals with the story of Atlantis.</note> after the *Timaeus*. The life of the citizens, while still following the "unmastered" <note>original: "ἀδεσπότην" (without a master/free)</note> life, shows through these things that Plato believes the soul, when remaining within itself, is superior to every physical substance and transcends <term>Fate</term>. But when it inclines toward outward actions, it is mastered by physical laws and subjected to Fate. 

In addition to what has been said, one must also know that the continuity of the dialogues follows the order of human life delivered in the *Republic*. For there, those men were first nourished and educated in the mathematical sciences, then they ascended to the vision of true beings, and finally descended from there to the providential care of the city. According to this sequence, the *Republic* is placed before the *Timaeus*, and the *Timaeus* before the *Atlanticus*. For having been educated by the *Republic* and led upward by the *Timaeus*, they will wisely arrange such actions as the *Atlanticus* teaches through images, living happily. We, therefore, have met the puzzle in this way; however, the philosopher Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and scholar (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote extensively on Plato.</note> does not start from the puzzle itself...

It also touches on the soul's relationship to Fate and the transition from internal contemplation to external action.</summary>

# PROCLUS

...not merely for the sake of this story, but while arranging another matter, he provided such an opportunity for a solution: those who are to genuinely grasp the whole of the contemplation <note>original: "theoria"</note> must first have their character educated, so that being similar to the object of understanding, it may be fittingly harmonized for the knowledge of the truth. Indeed, this very order of the dialogues demonstrates this. For those who listen to the discourses in the *Timaeus* ought to have previously enjoyed the *Republic*, and having been ordered <margin>D</margin> through that work, | they should thus come to listen to the doctrines concerning the universe, having rendered themselves most similar to the good order of the whole through their education. Let so much be said regarding this difficulty.

We must also examine the specific details of the text. Now, Timaeus is called "most skilled in astronomy" <note>original: "astronomikotatos"</note> not as one who has merely investigated the speeds of motions, nor as one who has collected the measures of the sun's courses, nor as one who lingers over the works of fate, but as one who "surveys the heavens from above" according to the "leading man" in the *Theaetetus* and who contemplates the unseen causes—which are also stars in the primary sense (which is why Socrates revealed man not as the visible one, but as the one purely substantialized in reason)—and as one who imitates the universal Creator, in whom both the heaven and the stars exist; for "all things are light," as the theologian says.

He begins from the generation of the cosmos and ends with human beings, because man is a "little cosmos" <note>The concept of the microcosm.</note>, possessing in a partial way everything that the whole possesses universally, just as Socrates demonstrated in the *Philebus*. And some are preeminently <margin>E</margin> educated by Socrates—not yet the whole city, | but the guardians and the auxiliaries. For in the whole, that which preeminently participates in Intellect is the heaven, which also imitates Intellect through its motion.

They are introduced by Critias according to the law and speech of Solon, because Solon recorded that the Athenians once lived under such a constitution and established laws regarding how children must be introduced into the state, how they enter the clans <note>original: "phrators"</note>, and how they are entered into the public register <note>original: "lexiarchikon grammateion"</note>, before which judges—in some cases the clansmen, in others the appropriate officials. Having himself established that those educated by Socrates were Athenians, he follows both the speech and the law of Solon, according to which certain people are introduced into the state.

# ON THE TIMAEUS I.

"I seem likely to receive back the feast of discourse perfectly and brilliantly. It is your task then to speak, O Timaeus, what comes next, as it seems, after having called upon the gods according to the law." <note>original: "Τελἐως τε καὶ λαμπρῶς... κατὰ νόμον θεούς." This is a quote from Plato's Timaeus 26e–27c.</note> (Page
<margin>67 B.Y</margin>

The "perfect" and "brilliant" nature of the repayment indicates the supernatural and all-pervading creation for those who refer these words of Socrates back to the <term>Paradigms</term> <note>The eternal blueprints or Forms upon which the physical world is modeled.</note>; the "feast of discourse" signifies the fulfillment of the <term>Demiurgic Forms</term> <note>The creative ideas used by the divine craftsman to shape the universe.</note>; the summoning of Timaeus signifies the return of particular causes toward the Whole and the invitation of the goods from that higher realm; and the invocation of the gods signifies the creation led down from above, from the <term>Intelligible</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and being, beyond physical perception.</note> realm. For "according to the law" is not such as the many understand regarding Italian or Attic customs, but rather as it is accustomed to be said among the **Pythagoreans**: *Honor the Immortal Gods first, by the law as they are established.* <note>original: "Ἀθανάτους μὲν πρῶτα θεοὺς νόμῳ ὡς διάκεινται." A reference to the Pythagorean Golden Verses.</note> For "law" reveals the divine order, according to which secondary things are always suspended from the primary and are filled by them. Thus the Law, beginning from the Intelligibles, descends even into the <margin>63</margin> **Demiurgic Cause** <note>The divine agency responsible for "making" the world.</note> and proceeds from it, being distributed throughout the universe. At the same time, Socrates indicates through this that he demands the "study of nature" <note>original: "φυσιολογία" (physiologia).</note> to become **Pythagorean**, beginning from the divine cause, and not such as he himself rejected in the *Phaedo*, which blinds the eye of the soul by attributing causes to "airs and ethers" according to **Anaxagoras**. For one must attach true natural philosophy to **theology**, just as Nature itself is suspended from the gods and is distributed according to their whole orders, so that the accounts of things may be imitators [of reality], not merely signs. For even **Hephaestus** himself, who presides over Nature, is handed down by the myth-makers as being in love with **Athena**, who weaves the arrangement of the intellectual forms and is the provider of insights for all beings within the cosmos.

Up to this point, the prologue of the *Timaeus* is completed, which **Severus** did not even deem worthy of explanation at all, and **Longinus** did not speak of in its entirety, but only so much as is introduced concerning the **Atlanteans** and the narrations of the **Egyptian**; so that he was even accustomed to join the report of **Critias** to the request of Socrates—I mean the passage "I am present then, [duly] prepared..." <margin>B</margin>

The introduction of the *Timaeus* <note>original: "Τιμαίου"</note> has provided a tradition consisting of two main chapters: a summary of Socrates’s <term>Republic</term> <note>original: "πολιτείας" - referring here to the ideal state or constitution described by Socrates</note> and a brief narrative of the battle of the Athenians against the inhabitants of Atlantis <note>original: "Ἀτλαντίδας"</note> and the victory achieved over them. Each of these contributes greatly to the complete contemplation of the universe <note>original: "κόσμου"</note>. The form of the Republic, when understood in and of itself, was adapted to the ordering of the heavens <note>original: "οὐρανοῦ"</note>, while the narrative of the war and the victory symbolizes the cosmic opposition. The former outlined the primary <term>demiurgy</term> <note>the act of divine creation or "crafting" the world</note>, and the latter the secondary—or, if you prefer, the former represents the formal cause and the latter the material cause. For all natural philosophers establish the universe by harmonizing opposites. This harmony arises from the "form," which the discourse on the Republic revealed as a common principle proceeding in order over every multitude. For the republic in the soul is one thing, that among men another, and the cosmic republic yet another. The summary of the Republic, by outlining the very form of every state, shows us primarily the "republic" within the All, to which the discourse was ultimately hastening to refer. Furthermore, if you wish, one should station the Republic as analogous to the heavens, and the war to the realm of <term>generation</term> <note>the sublunary world of change and decay</note>. For the Republic extends to the furthest limits, since all things have been ordered by the Creator <note>original: "δημιουργοῦ"</note> in a series reaching down to the things within the world. Indeed, there is a kind of opposition even in the heavens, whether according to the two-fold revolutions of the bodies—to the right and to the left—or according to the two-fold circles of the souls—that of the Same and that of the Other—or according to the <term>genera of being</term> <note>referring to Plato's "Great Kinds" from the Sophist</note>, namely rest and motion, or according to the divine properties of male and female, or some other such division of opposites. Rather, the Republic is directed toward...

### ON THE TIMAEUS II.

In short, he has led us through various opinions, saying that neither those suffering from the first kind of atheism <note>The denial of the existence of the gods.</note> claim any benefit from prayer—since they say the gods do not even exist—nor those suffering from the second kind, who utterly subvert providence <note>original: "pronoia"</note>; for while they grant that gods exist, they do not think they exercise providence. Nor do those who concede both their existence and their providence, but claim that everything happens by necessity <margin>B</margin> <note>original: "ananke"</note>; for if there is no possibility for things to happen otherwise, the utility of prayer is destroyed. But those who say that gods both exist and exercise providence, and that many things that happen are capable of being otherwise, these people reasonably accept prayers and acknowledge that they set our lives upright.

And he adds that prayer especially befits virtuous men <note>original: "spoudaioi"</note>, because it is a connection with the divine, and like naturally loves to be joined to like; and the virtuous man is most like the gods. Furthermore, because those who cling to virtue are "in custody" and are confined by the body as if in a prison, they ought to petition the divine for their migration <note>original: "metastasis"; referring to the soul's departure from the body</note> from here. It is also fitting to pray as children snatched away from their fathers, concerning our return to our true fathers, the gods. Those who do not think it worthy to pray or to turn back toward their superiors seem to be, in a sense, both fatherless and motherless.

Among all nations, those who excelled in wisdom were diligent concerning prayers: the Brahmans among the Indians, the Magi among the Persians, and among the Greeks, the most theological <note>Those most deeply versed in the knowledge of the gods.</note>, [who also established rites and mysteries; and the Chaldeans <margin>C</margin> served the rest of the divine realm and worshipped the very virtue of the gods, calling it "of the gods"], many being far from looking down upon sacred worship because of their own virtue. And above all these reasons, because we are parts of the universe, it is fitting to petition the universe; for to everything, the turning back <note>original: "epistrophe"; the Neoplatonic concept of the soul returning to its source</note> toward the whole brings about salvation. Therefore, if you possess virtue, you must invoke that which has previously grasped the whole of virtue; for the universal Good will be the cause of the specific good that befits you. Or if you seek some bodily good, there is a power in the world that holds every body together; from there, of necessity, perfection reaches down to the parts.

This is what Porphyry says, to speak briefly. But the divine Iamblichus thinks that such a historical account is not at all relevant to the matters at hand. For Plato’s discourse now is not about atheistic men, but about those who are sober-minded and able to commune with the gods; nor is it about those who dispute the works of holiness, but about those who wish to be saved by the saviors of the whole. <margin>D</margin> He hands down the power of prayer and its perfection as something marvelous and supernatural and...

<page-num>150</page-num>

...surpassing every hope. It is fitting for us to shift the discourse to what is more customary and familiar to our listeners <note>original: "metagagontas"</note>, so that we may both make his thought clear and render the teachings concerning prayer in harmony with Plato. We must, therefore, begin from this point: All beings belong to the gods; they are produced by them immediately and are established within them. For the progression of things is not only completed according to a continuous sequence—where subsequent things subsist from their proximate causes—but all things are also generated directly from the gods, even if a thing is said to be most distant from the gods, even if you speak of matter itself <note>original: "eipēs"</note>. For the divine is absent from nothing, but is present to all equally <note>original: "ex isou paresti"</note>. Therefore, even if you take the lowest of things, you will find the divine present even there. For the One is everywhere, insofar as each of the beings has its subsistence from the gods <note>original: "uphestēke"</note>.

And though all things have proceeded from the gods, they have not gone out from them, but are rooted within them. For where could they even "go out" <note>original: "exelthoi"</note>, 
<margin>E</margin> since the gods have encompassed and pre-occupied all things and hold all things within themselves <note>original: "autois"</note>? That which is "beyond" the gods is that which in no way exists. For all beings are encircled by the gods and exist within them. In a wonderful way, then, all things have both proceeded and not proceeded. They have not been torn away from the gods, nor could they exist if they were torn away; for just as all offspring, when torn away from their parents, immediately sink toward the non-existence of the unborn, so too are these things established somehow in the gods. To speak generally, they have proceeded <note>original: "proelēluthe"</note> in relation to themselves, but they remain in the gods. 

But since it was necessary that those things which proceeded should also return—imitating the gods' own manifestation and their turning back toward their cause—so that these things, ordered according to the perfecting Triad <note>The "perfecting triad" refers to the Neoplatonic cycle of Remaining, Procession, and Return.</note>, might again be contained by the gods and the primordial Unities <term>Henads: the highest "units" or gods in Proclus's system, existing above Being</term>, they receive from them a certain second perfection. By this perfection, they are able to turn back toward the goodness of the gods, so that having been rooted in the gods from the beginning, they may, through this return, once again rest firmly in them <note>original: "apereidētai"</note>, completing a kind of circle that begins from the gods and 
<margin>F</margin> ends in the gods. | All things, therefore, both remain and return to the gods, having received this power from them and having accepted two "tokens" <note>or "signatures"</note> according to their essence: one so that they may remain there, and the other so that they may return after proceeding. 

And one can observe these things not only in souls, but even in the inanimate things that follow them. For what else is it that works within these things a sympathy <term>Sympathy: the cosmic "resonance" or connection between earthly objects and celestial/divine powers</term> toward various powers, and causes them to receive "symbols" from Nature—some making them akin to one 
65 divine | chain <term>Series/Chain: the vertical lineage of power descending from a specific god down to minerals and plants</term>, and others to another? For Nature herself is suspended from above, directly from the gods.

# ON THE TIMAEUS II.
<page-num>151</page-num>

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, discussing Nature's role in distributing divine signs.</note> Nature, having been distributed according to the ranks of the gods, also assigns to physical bodies certain "tokens" <note>original: "sunthemata" — symbolic signatures or physical imprints of divine power</note> of their kinship to the gods. To some bodies she gives Solar tokens, to others Lunar tokens, and to others the tokens of some other god. She turns these bodies back toward the gods—some toward the gods in a general sense, others toward specific gods—having perfected her own offspring according to the various distinct characteristics of the gods. 

Therefore, much earlier than this, the Creator <note>The Demiurge, the divine craftsman of the universe</note> also worked within souls the tokens of their remaining in Him and their turning back toward the gods. He established them according to their "One" <note>The highest, most unified part of the soul</note> and granted them the power of turning back through the Intellect. 

Toward this "turning back," prayer provides the greatest contribution. By using the ineffable symbols of the gods, which the Father of souls sowed within them, prayer draws the goodness of the gods into itself. It unites those who pray with the very beings to whom they pray; it joins the Intellect of the gods <margin>B</margin> with the words of those who pray. It moves the will of those who possess the fullness of good things within themselves toward a generous sharing of those goods. Prayer is the "craftsman of divine persuasion" and establishes everything within us firmly in the gods.

The leadership of perfect and true prayer consists of several stages:
1. **Knowledge:** First is the knowledge of all the divine ranks to which the one praying approaches. For one cannot approach in a fitting way without knowing their specific characteristics. For this reason, the Oracle <note>Likely the Chaldean Oracles</note> commanded that the "fire-heated" <note>original: "pyrithalpe"</note> rank should hold the very first place in sacred worship.
2. **Assimilation:** Second is the making of ourselves like the divine through bodily purity, holiness, education, and order. Through these, our affairs are brought before the gods, drawing out their favor and bowing our souls beneath them.
3. **Contact:** Third is contact <note>original: "synaphe"</note>, through which we touch the divine essence with the highest peak of the soul and incline ourselves toward it.
4. **Approach:** After this comes the "nearing" (for so the Oracle calls it: *By nearing the fire, the mortal shall have light from God*). This provides us with a greater communion and a clearer participation in the light of the gods.
5. **Union:** Finally, there is Union <margin>C</margin>, which establishes the "One" of the soul into the "One" of the gods. It makes our activity and the divine activity one and the same. In this state, we no longer belong to ourselves but to the gods, remaining in the divine light and surrounded by it in a circle. 

This is the best end-goal of true prayer: that it might join the "turning back" <note>original: "epistrophe"</note> to the "remaining" <note>original: "mone"</note>, and establish everything that proceeded from the One of the gods back into that One again, encompassing the "One" within us with the light of the gods. Therefore, prayer is no small part of the whole...

<summary>This page outlines the Neoplatonic theory of prayer as a five-stage process (Knowledge, Assimilation, Contact, Approach, and Union) that returns the soul to its divine source. It emphasizes that the Creator sowed "tokens" or symbols within the soul to facilitate this mystical ascent.</summary>

of the entire ascent of souls, nor is the one possessing virtue without need of the goods that come from prayer; on the contrary, the ascent is accomplished through it, and along with it, the very summit of virtue, which is holiness toward the gods. In general, it is not fitting for anyone else to pray except the good person in an exceptional way, as the **Athenian Stranger** <note>original: "Ἀθηναῖος ξένος" — a reference to the lead character in Plato's *Laws* (716d)</note> says. For to such a person, conversing with the gods becomes the most holy path toward the blessed life, whereas for the wicked, the opposite is natural. For <margin>D</margin> it is not lawful for the **unclean to touch the clean** <note>original: "μὴ καθαρῷ γὰρ καθαροῦ ἐφάπτεσθαι οὐ θεμιτόν" — a famous quote from Plato's *Phaedo* (67b)</note>. Therefore, the one who intends to take up prayer in a noble manner must make the gods gracious and awaken within themselves the true conceptions concerning the gods. For the kinship with the higher beings is the very first starting point for participating in them. And one must pray without ceasing in the service of the divine; for **to the lingering mortal, the blessed ones are swift** <note>A poetic or oracular fragment suggesting that divine help is immediate for those who are diligent</note>, and one must keep the order of divine works unshaken, putting forward virtues that are both purifying and elevating from the world of generation—namely faith, truth, and love, that famous triad—and an unwavering hope for the goods, a reception of the divine light, and an ecstasy <note><term>ecstasy</term> (ekstasis): literally "standing outside" oneself; a state of mystical union where the soul transcends its ordinary limits</note> from all other pursuits, so that one may be alone with the God alone, even if one attempts to join the divided self to the One while in the midst of a multitude. For such a person does the exact opposite and separates himself from the gods. Just as it is not lawful to converse with Being while in the company of non-being, so it is impossible to be joined to the One while in the company of the multitude. Such, then, are the forms of prayer and what its primary nature must be. Its essence is <margin>E</margin> collective and a bond | of souls to the gods, or rather, a unifying force of all secondary things to their priors; for "everything prays except the First," says the **Great Theodore** <note>Theodore of Asine, a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Iamblichus</note>. Its perfection begins from the more common goods and ends in divine union, gradually winding the soul toward the divine light. It is an active energy, fulfilling of goods and making our affairs common with the gods. We account for the causes of prayer as follows: as **productive causes**, we see the active powers of the gods which turn us back and call us toward the gods themselves; as **final causes**, we see the pure goods of souls which they harvest when established in the gods; as **paradigmatic causes**, we see the primary causes of beings which proceeded from the Good and live toward it according to a single, ineffable union; and as...

...assimilating the souls to the gods and perfecting the whole [soul], while regarding as material <note>original: "hylikas"</note> the tokens <note>The "synthemata" or divine symbols implanted in the soul by the Creator</note> placed within the essences by the Creator <note>original: "demiurgou"</note> for the sake of remembering the ones who established them. Furthermore, we define the modes of prayer as being of many kinds, according to the genera and species of the gods. For there is a creative <note>original: "demiurgike"</note> prayer, a purifying one, and a life-giving one. The creative kind, for instance, is for the sake of rains and winds—for the creators are the causes of the generation of these—and the prayers for favorable winds <margin>1) material 2) 65, 50 her (the soul) 3) 65, 51 concerning the [nature] of 4) 65, 52 favorable winds; [variant] of abundance 5) 66, 5 performed 6) 66, 7 defining</margin> were made by the Athenians to these gods. The purifying prayers are for the sake of averting pestilential diseases or all sorts of defilements, such as those recorded in the sacred rites. The life-giving prayers are like those for the sake of the fruits of the earth, serving those superior to us who are the causes of life-generation. And there are perfecting prayers, because they raise us up toward these orders of the gods. And he who falls away from the judgment of these things misses the correctness of prayers. We also define prayers by the objects <note>original: "pragmata"</note> about which the prayers are made: for the first are those for the sake of the salvation of the soul, the second are for the sake of the good temperament of bodies, and the third are those performed for the sake of external things. We also define these many-sided prayers according to the division of the gods to whom we make the prayers, or according to the seasons of the year, or according to the cycles of the solar revolution, or according to other such intercalations.

**Socrates, this at least all those who partake even in a small measure of temperance <note>original: "sophrosynes"</note> do: at the beginning of every undertaking, whether small or great, they always call upon a god.** (Page 27 C.)

We have seen what kind of hypothesis Plato referred to in the *Timaeus*, what kind of listener he brought to him in Socrates, and what kind of beginning of the discourses he wrote. For the hypothesis pertains to the whole of creation, and the listener was brought in so that he might be gathered into a single intellect and a single contemplation of the whole. For this reason, he himself aroused Timaeus to prayer. The beginning of the discourses, starting from the invocation of the gods, thus imitates the procession of beings; for just as beings, remaining first in the gods, thus obtained their generation from them, so too let us observe how this beginning ordains that all who partake even in a small measure of temperance must always call upon a god at the start of every small or great matter. For from what kind of conception do these people make this invocation in every instance? For it is surely not likely that those who are temperate should fail to aim at reality and the truth of the things themselves. I say, therefore, that all [possess a conception] concerning the gods...

--- Page 167 ---
Those who apply a pure intellect to contemplation and place the Beautiful and the Good within the soul's own excellences—rather than in human affairs or external fortunes—attain genuine <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "episteme"; here meaning certain, scientific understanding</note>. They perceive the power of <term>Providence</term> <note>original: "pronoia"; the divine foresight and care that governs the universe</note> reaching through all beings and | harmonizing everything with the Whole, so that the whole and the parts are in the best possible state, and nothing is without a share of the divine care that reaches down to every individual.

<margin>C</margin> Seeing this in every action and every activity, they rightly call upon Providence as a helper in their own impulses. They align their own creations with the Whole and with universal things, establishing themselves within the goodness of the gods. For even things that seem small enjoy Providence and are great insofar as they depend upon the gods; conversely, things that are great according to their own nature appear tiny and worthless when they fall away from the divine.

Temperance <note>original: "sophrosyne"; often translated as "soundness of mind" or "moderation"</note> provides these things to souls. It is not merely a human habit, nor is it close to what is called "self-control," but it is a divine activity of the soul that has turned back toward itself and the divine. It sees the Cause of all things among the gods and contemplates from that vantage point both other things and those that proceed from the gods. Through these things—which serve as starting points <note>original: "aphormai"</note> granted to us by the gods—we are able to ascend back to them. This temperance finds the <term>symbols</term> <note>original: "symbola"; tokens or signatures of divine power hidden in the material world</note> of the gods even in the smallest things and, through these, brings each thing into kinship with the gods.

<margin>D</margin> Since the gods produced our entire essence and granted us the power of self-motion <note>original: "autokineton"; the soul's ability to move and choose for itself</note> for the choice of good things, their creative work is shown to be superior in our external activities. Even when we deliberate, we need the foresight that comes from them (indeed, the Athenians show this by honoring "Zeus of the Council"). When we make choices, we need their assistance so that in deliberating we may find what is beneficial, and in choosing we may not slide toward the worse through passion. Rather, in acting and initiating impulses, we see that our self-moving power has the least strength, while the Whole depends on the Providence of the gods. For this reason, Timaeus <note>A reference to Plato's dialogue, the *Timaeus* (27c)</note> says that those who are temperate always call upon a god at the start of every undertaking.

We are unable to distinguish Providence from "what is up to us" <note>the sphere of human agency</note> in our choices, but we can do so more easily in our impulses, because the self-moving element is less prominent in them. For "what is up to us" does not extend as far as the Providence of the gods reaches. Instead, as | has been said, the higher causes often act before the secondary causes, alongside them, and after them, encompassing the activities of subordinate beings from every side. But...

<margin>E</margin>

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II

The Epicurean Hermarchus <note>Hermarchus was the successor to Epicurus as head of the school; the Epicureans were famously skeptical of the efficacy of prayer</note> asks: "Do we not proceed into infinity if we require a prayer for every impulse and even for a small matter? For if we pray, we shall then need another prayer for that prayer, and we shall never find a place to stop." We must resolve this objection as Porphyry <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> does, by noting that it was not said that a prayer is required for every single thing <margin>67, 1</margin> <insert>but rather for the beginning of significant works</insert>.

<column-break/>

For the soul does not require an infinite series of prayers to reach the Divine, but rather a turning of its own will toward the source of all good. As the philosopher says, the act of prayer is itself a stabilization of the mind, not a task requiring a secondary justification. 

<margin>67, 3 to him <note>original: "αὐτῷ"</note></margin>

If we were to follow the logic of the skeptics, no action could ever begin. However, the beginning of a discourse on the universe <note>The "Timaeus" is Plato's primary work on the creation of the physical world</note> is a task of such magnitude that it demands we align our intellect with the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the "Craftsman" or creator-god in Platonic thought</term>. Therefore, the prayer is not a "small matter" but the very foundation of the work.

<summary>This page addresses an Epicurean critique of prayer, specifically the "infinite regress" argument posed by Hermarchus, and defends the Platonic practice of beginning philosophical works with an invocation.</summary>

...separated, insofar as it is generated from the gods <note>original: *theōn*</note>, it possesses a divine sort of existence. And this must be defined in such a way. However, people are often puzzled as to why Plato here adds the word "somehow" <note>original: *pē* (in some way/to some extent)</note>. For he says that those who are about to make discourses concerning the universe "somehow" <note>Plato, Timaeus 27c</note>. 

<margin>B</margin> Now, the more superficial of the commentators say that because the universe is in one sense ungenerated and in another sense generated, the discourse about it is naturally in one sense as if about an ungenerated thing, and in another as if about a generated thing. And yet, Plato did not link the "somehow" to the "ungenerated" and "generated," but rather to the "making of the discourses." 

The divine Iamblichus <note>A highly influential Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) whom Proclus often cites as an authority.</note>, however, says that the discourse will "somehow" be about the universe, and "somehow" not. For he leaves aside Matter <note>original: *hylē*</note>, insofar as it is indefinite and formless and therefore ineffable, but he will examine all the formal variety within the Cosmos. 

But it must be said against this explanation as well, that the "somehow" is joined to another word and not to "the universe." Perhaps then, as our teacher <note>Likely referring to Syrianus, Proclus's predecessor as head of the Academy.</note> used to say, since "discourses" <note>original: *logoi* - this term means both spoken words and the underlying rational principles or "blueprints" of reality.</note> are spoken of in many ways—for some are the demiurgic <note>creative or world-building</note> powers proceeding from the Intellect, such as the Creator will speak to the young gods, and indeed he says the Soul speaks when moving within herself; and others are those contemplated in science; and others still, having received a third-degree removal from the Intellect, are those moved in outward speech for the sake of instruction and social communication—

<margin>C</margin> Timaeus, knowing that the Creator establishes the demiurgic discourses, and that he is not now about to generate the scientific ones (but has already brought them forth within himself), but will only produce the discourses in outward speech for the sake of power, for this reason said he would "somehow" make discourses about the universe. For it is one thing to speak intellectually, another scientifically, and another instructionally; the "somehow" indicates these differences in the types of discourse. 

Again, regarding the phrase "whether it has been generated or is ungenerated," some have explained it by marking the first "or" <note>original: *ē*</note> with a rough breathing and the second with a smooth breathing <note>A grammatical distinction in Greek that changes the meaning from "or" to "in the way that."</note>, as many as say that he will speak about the universe insofar as it has been generated from a cause, or even is ungenerated, so that by contemplating it as having been generated we might perceive the nature within it. And the Platonist Albinus <note>A 2nd-century AD philosopher; his view was that the world is eternal (ungenerated) but has a logical "beginning" of existence from a cause.</note> maintains that according to Plato the world, being ungenerated, has a beginning of generation, which...

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing the ontological status of the universe—whether it is "generated" or "unbegotten"—and the necessity of divine invocation before philosophical inquiry.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II.

...from that which truly exists, that alone <note>original: "μόνου"</note> always being, while the world, in addition to its eternal existence, also possesses a beginning of generation <note>term: *genesis* (generation/becoming) — the process of coming into being as opposed to eternal, unchanging existence</note>, so that it might be both "always being" and "generated." It is not "divided" in a temporal sense (for it did not once "not exist" if it is always being), but it possesses the character of generation entirely because of its composition from many and dissimilar parts. This composition necessarily refers its substance back to another cause more ancient than itself <margin>D</margin>, through which it is the first of things that always exist; it is itself in a way "always being," and not only generated, but also unbegotten. And yet, Plato in the following passages nowhere explicitly states how the whole is generated and how it is unbegotten. Others, however, have held both opinions, so that he might be said to conduct his discourses about the universe on the basis of whether it has come into being or is unbegotten, falling into the same errors as those who came before them. Unless, perhaps, they should say the whole is "generated" and "unbegotten" in this way: generated according to its **Form**, but unbegotten according to its **Nurse** <note>The "Nurse" or *Receptacle* is Plato's term for the underlying material or space that receives the Forms.</note>. For in this way Timaeus will also say that the one is unbegotten, while the world is generated, as receiving its Form from God. But Porphyry and Iamblichus <note>Two major Neoplatonic philosophers; Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) and his student Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD).</note> favor both views, so that the question is: "Has the whole come into being, or is it unbegotten?" For he will examine this before all other things. Indeed, it provides the greatest contribution to the whole of natural philosophy <note>original: "φυσιολογίᾳ"</note> to correctly hypothesize whether the world is generated or unbegotten. We shall be able to perceive its essence and its powers from this hypothesis, of what sort they are, as will be clear to us a little later. Therefore, the discourses concerning the universe will proceed for the sake of instruction, starting from this beginning: whether the world has come into being or is unbegotten, and from this, weaving the rest in logical succession. <margin>E</margin>

> **It is necessary that those who call upon the gods and goddesses pray to be able to speak everything according to their mind especially, and consequently for us.**

The division of **male** and **female** has embraced within itself all the fullnesses of the divine orders. For that which is the cause of stable power and identity, the provider of being and that which gathers the primary principle of return for all things, is contained in the **male**. But that which produces from itself all kinds of progressions and distinctions, measures of life, and generative powers, is contained in the **female**. Wherefore Timaeus, reasonably referring himself to all the gods according to this division into these kinds, embraced the totality of their **Ideas**. Moreover, such a division is also suited to the present theory...

Reasonably, then, he who is about to compose a discourse concerning the universe invokes both **gods** and **goddesses**, by both of whom the whole has been filled, so that the things about to be said may be spoken in a manner pleasing to the gods themselves according to their Mind. For this is the highest end of contemplation: to run back up to the **Divine Mind**, and just as all things are contained there in a **uniform** <note>single-form or unified</note> manner, so to arrange the discourse concerning reality. Second and following this is to complete the whole contemplation according to the **human mind** and the light of **science** <note>original: <term>episteme</term>, meaning certain or demonstrative knowledge</note>. For the whole, the perfect, and the uniform pre-exist in the Divine Mind; but that which is partial and falls short of divine simplicity belongs to the mortal mind. But how is it that Timaeus says one must pray, and magnificently proclaimed that we should call upon gods and goddesses, yet passed over <margin>B</margin> this | very act and, without praying, turned immediately to the proposed discourse? We shall say that some things have their end contained within the **will** itself, while others, after the will, incline toward another activity and accomplish what was willed through **action**. The life according to **philosophy** depends upon our will, and any deficiency in it is due to those who are deficient in their will; but the acquisition of external things requires a second activity after the will, for their end does not lie within us. Therefore, among those things that have their entire perfection in the act of willing, we should rightly place the matter of **prayer**.
