<header>ON THE TIMAEUS II.</header>

## ON THE TIMAEUS II.

the soul which desires it and joins it to the divine, which is indeed the very first instrument of prayer <note>original: "euchēs". The translator notes a correction from "psychēs" (soul) in the manuscript</note>. It is not necessary, therefore, to wish first and then to pray, but as soon as one wishes, one also possesses the prayer, though the one is more a matter of the will, and the other less so. This is also a work of true prayer: to recognize that those things for which we pray already exist within the gods, according to their powers and their activities, and that we ourselves complete these things together with the gods. For example, if someone <margin>C</margin> prays to the gods to cut away the "matter" <term>hylē: the raw, chaotic physical substance of the universe</term> and to vanish the stains resulting from "becoming" <term>genesis: the realm of changing, physical existence</term>, and he himself pursues this especially through the purifying virtues, such a person completes the release from material bonds together with the gods. This is exactly what Timaeus does here. For the things he prays for the gods to accomplish, he also fulfills himself, arranging the whole discourse according to the human intellect in a way that follows the Intellect <term>Nous: the divine, cosmic Mind</term> of the gods.

-> Let the matters concerning the gods be invoked in this way; but our own part must be called upon so that you may learn most easily, and I may best demonstrate what I intend regarding the subjects before us. (Page 27) <-

The conversion of the listeners follows naturally upon the prayers. For it is necessary for that which is suspended from its proper causes to awaken in advance the things that will receive them, and to extend itself toward them before the fulfillment, so that becoming more fit, they may richly lay hold of the insights being granted. For this perfects the participation for the listeners themselves, and makes the giving easier for the giver. And this very quality of "ease" is appropriate to those who look toward the material craftsmanship <note>The demiurgic work</note>, from which all things <margin>D</margin> proceed while it remains within itself and rejoices in its own moving results. Furthermore, the fact that the second parts form a single chain of connection with the first parts mimics the creative power that extends through to the very last things. For if the listeners require the discourse according to the manner of Timaeus, and Timaeus conducts the whole treatment according to the Intellect of the gods, then the gathering will happen quite simply from one Intellect and one act of Intellection. In addition to these things, he demonstrates the self-moved nature of souls, because being moved by the gods and by themselves, they also project the sciences from themselves. For the phrase "either we think" <note>referring to the Greek "ē dianooumetha"</note> shows an activity starting from a life that possesses its own authority.

***

<summary>Proclus explains that prayer is a collaborative act between the human soul and the divine, where the soul must prepare itself to receive divine insights. He emphasizes the continuity between the divine Intellect, the teacher (Timaeus), and the students as a single chain of being.</summary>

1) It is therefore necessary, in my opinion, first to make the following division. <note>original: "Ἔστιν οὖν δὴ κατὰ γε ἐμὴν δόξαν, πρότερον διαιρε τάδε." Referring to Timaeus page 27 D.</note>

Timaeus is a Pythagorean, and he maintains the character of the Pythagorean discourses even from the very beginning. He did this very thing in the *Philebus* <note>A Platonic dialogue concerning pleasure and the good life</note> as well. For seeking the nature of the Intellect and the mixed life, and which is better, he took up their kinds: the Limit, the Unlimited, and the Mixture. In this way, the rank of each would become clear, and he revealed the unique character of these kinds. But in that case, the Limit and the Unlimited, starting from the gods, proceeded through all things that exist in any way whatsoever. For these were present even in the Intelligible gods, according to the stable and generative cause; and in the Intellectual gods, according to the paternal and maternal principle of the Intellectual gods; and they were in the <term>hypercosmic|Deities existing 'above the world' or beyond the physical universe</term> gods, according to the creative Monad and the life-generating Dyad; and finally according to the productive and fertile powers. The other gods are unities, not participated in by Being, but those after them are called "participated" by it and exist under Being. Nor does this division reach to the lowest things. For they say it is not possible to call Matter "Being"—which we are accustomed to call "non-being"—nor "Becoming," for if it were not even able to be acted upon, it would vanish entirely. This, then, shall be discussed again later. Therefore, this is not a division of some single thing, but it is necessary that the present inquiry into these kinds takes precedence over all others, just as the discourse proceeds from geometric hypotheses to the examination of what follows, so that it may discover the nature of the universe and its paternal and <insert>paradigmatic</insert> cause. Some have claimed that all existing things, whether as models or as images, are included through this distinction; others say not all, and there have been not a few disputes among the commentators against one another concerning this. But we would not know which way it is proper to speak unless we examine each of the words themselves on their own. Come then, let us understand from the beginning what power each of the terms has in itself. First, then, what does the "**What**" <note>original: "τὸ τί"</note> mean for us? For we are accustomed to place the "what it is" first in definitions, and not "how it is," as **Severus the Platonist** <note>A 2nd-century AD Middle Platonist philosopher.</note> thinks, saying that this "What" is a genus of Being and Becoming, and that the "Whole" is signified by it. For in that way, both the becoming and the always-being would be the "Whole." However, this creates a difficulty, which he also passed down to those before us: why on earth did he not provide "that it is" <note>existence</note> before "what it is" <note>essence</note>? one. For this is what belongs to the gods: to be unified, and not that which is becoming and perishing <note>original: ἀπολλύμενον</note>, which in reality never truly exists. Rather, even before these arguments, the concept of "that which always is" <note>the eternal Being</note> is stored within our common notions. For from where does that which becomes arise, if not from that which always is? For if that source were also becoming, it would have to be produced by some other being, which would itself be either always existing or becoming. Thus <margin>Note in manuscript A: That natural philosophy proceeds from hypothesis.</margin> we would either proceed to infinity, or the process of becoming <note>original: γένεσις</note> would move in a circle, or there exists that which always is. But it is not lawful to proceed to infinity, for all things come from one and from a single principle <note>original: ἀρχῆς</note>; nor can becoming be a circle, lest <margin>C</margin> the same things become both superior and inferior, both causes and effects. | It remains, therefore, that Being always exists. 

Why then, someone might ask, does becoming not proceed directly from the One? Because, we shall say, it is absurd to produce a multitude entirely outside of Being directly from the One. There must, therefore, be "Truly Existing Being" <note>original: ὄντως ὄν</note>. This is the first to proceed from the One, so that the First Cause is not the cause of the lowest things alone, but prior to these, it is the cause of Being, from which becoming also derives. The greatest truth regarding what has been said is this: that now, taking it as a hypothesis, he defined "that which always is," but after the discourses on the creation of the world <note>original: κοσμοποιίας</note>, he takes this up again and demonstrates that "that which always is" exists. Maintaining the methods appropriate to natural philosophy <note>term: physiology/physiologia — here meaning the study of the natural world</note>, he proceeds from this hypothesis and demonstrates the consequences following from it. For this science too is based on hypothesis, and it is necessary for its hypotheses to be grasped prior to the demonstrations. 

In the discourses concerning matter, he will demonstrate not only that matter exists, but also Being; and a little later, from one of the hypotheses—the third—he shows that there is a Creator <note>term: Demiurge/dēmiourgos — the divine craftsman of the universe</note> of the cosmos. Because of this, "that which always is" must exist prior to that which is generated; and again, from the fourth hypothesis, he reveals that <margin>D</margin> the Creator <margin>Note in manuscript A: Mark this: what is "that which always is."</margin> has crafted | the whole in relation to an eternal model <note>term: Paradigm/paradeigma — the eternal blueprint used by the Creator</note>. That "that which always is" exists in itself prior to generated things, he will demonstrate in those discourses we mentioned. 

So much for that. But as for "Being Always" itself, does it signify the entire intelligible world <note>original: νοητὸν κόσμον</note>, or the Creator, or the Model of the universe? For different thinkers have taken it in different ways. If it is the Intelligible, where does the intelligible breadth begin and where does it proceed? If it is the Model, how is the Creator not "always being," if the Model and the Creator are different? And if it is the Creator, what of the Model? That the Model-cause must be placed within "that which always is," Plato clearly says: "To which of the models did the craftsman work it out? To that which is self-same and stays the same, or to that which has come into being?" And he judged immediately: "If the world <note>original: κόσμος</note> is beautiful and the Creator is good, it is clear that he looked toward the eternal <note>original: ἀΐδιον</note>; but if—which is not lawful to say—he looked toward that which has come into being." If, then, it is not lawful to say this, the Model of the universe is "that which always is."

That the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator deity in Plato's philosophy</note> also belongs to this same rank is clear from the following: the <term>soul</term> <note>Greek: psychē</note> <margin>E</margin> which the Demiurge brings into existence, he himself explicitly calls the first among generated things <insert>at page 34C</insert> and describes its coming-into-being. But the Demiurge exists before the soul, so that he belongs among the things that always are. Therefore, he will also say <insert>at page 34A</insert> concerning him: "Such then was the entire eternal reasoning of the god." And how could he, being the Divine <term>Mind</term> <note>Greek: Nous</note>, not belong to this rank?

Is it then the case that the entire <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of Forms or Ideas, accessible only to the intellect</note> is that which "always is"? But the divine Iamblichus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who influenced later interpretations of Plato</note> vigorously contests this argument, declaring that "Being Always" is superior both to the genera of being and to the <term>Forms</term> <note>Greek: eidē; the perfect archetypes of all things</note>, and stands at the very summit of intelligible essence, being the first to participate in the One. The writings in the *Parmenides* concerning the "One Being" and those in the *Sophist* <insert>at page 14D</insert> bear witness to these points. For there, he places the "One Being" at the head of the whole and before the entire intelligible universe, even though both the One and the Whole are intelligible. 

But here, at least, Plato clearly addressed the <term>Paradigm</term> <note>The model used by the Demiurge to create the world</note> as "Always Being," and as "Whole" and "Perfect." This is evident from the text itself; for he calls it the "Perfect Living Creature" <note>Greek: zōon</note> and "Whole" when he says <insert>at page 30C</insert>: "For it contains and embraces within itself all the intelligible living creatures." Thus, if the Paradigm is a whole <margin>F</margin> and perfect, but that which is "Primarily Being" is above the whole and the sum of things, then the Paradigm and that "Being" would not be the same. 

Perhaps, then, it is better to say that there is indeed such an order of Being as that divine man [Iamblichus] handed down and such as Plato observed in other places, but that now the entire eternal world is named in this way. And this is not surprising. For the term "intelligible" is sometimes used for the entire <term>unseen</term> <note>Greek: aeidous; literally "formless" or "invisible"</note> and invisible nature—as when they say the soul is intelligible, as Socrates does in the *Phaedo* <insert>at page 80B</insert>—and sometimes for all those things superior to the essence of the soul, as the division in the *Republic* <insert>Book VI, page 509</insert> | shows. 71 At other times, it refers to the very first triads of Being, as Timaeus will call them a little later <insert>at page 28</insert>. In the same way, "Being" in the *Sophist* indicates the rank of the "One Being," but here it indicates the entire eternal world. For it is clear that the "Primarily Being" is the highest peak of the intelligible breadth and the <term>monad</term> <note>The single, unifying principle</note> of all beings. For everywhere, that which is "Primarily Being" holds the highest rank in its own series; if it were second, it would no longer be that specific Form in its primary sense. Just as "Virtue-itself" <note>Greek: autoaretē; the absolute Form of Virtue</note> holds the highest place...

rank in the series of virtues, just as the <term>Self-Equal</term><note>original: "αὐτοΐσον" - the Platonic Form of Equality itself</note> is among equals, and the <term>Self-Living</term><note>original: "αὐτοζῶον" - the Form of Life or the Living Being</note> is among living things, so surely also <term>Being-Itself</term><note>original: "αὐτόον" - the Form of Being</note>, which is primarily Being, is the summit of all beings, and from it <insert>all beings</insert> proceed. If, then, I must state what appears to be the case, Plato has now primarily included everything that is eternally being, beginning from the nature of the <term>Self-Living</term>; for this is the primarily eternal; and ending at the <term>particular intellects</term><note>original: "μερικῶν νόων" - individual minds or souls</note>. At any rate, a little further on, he will call the <term>Self-Living</term> the most beautiful of the <term>intelligibles</term><note>original: "νοουμένων"</note>, as those things prior to it are superior to the intelligible through their excess of unity. 

<margin>C</margin> Unless, indeed, the <term>Self-Living</term> is the most beautiful of | all intelligibles, since there are intelligibles and Eternity prior to the Living Being and the One Being—the one existing always by way of cause, the other as the substance of Eternity, and the third by way of participation in the eternal. And if these views prevail, then in "Always Being," both Eternity and the <term>Self-Living</term> and the <term>Demiurge</term><note>original: "δημιουργὸς" - the divine Craftsman of the universe</note> would be contained, as well as Being itself, which holds the hidden cause of Eternity. 

So it is clear from these points that "Always Being" encompasses the entire nature prior to souls, whether intelligible or intellectual, beginning from <term>Being-Itself</term> and ending in the particular intellect, but not only the highest of all beings, as <term>Iamblichus</term><note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher who preceded Proclus</note> used to say—such as the <term>One-Being</term>, through which all beings are said to be beings. For it is not only the One itself and the principles of Being that are superior. The One and the <term>unsubstantiated</term><note>original: "ἀϋπόστατον" - that which does not have a separate lower existence</note> are superior because they are exempt from all multiplicity; but "Always Being" is indeed unsubstantiated, yet it possesses this power through the One. That which comes after it is both unsubstantiated and at the same time subsists from another productive cause, as is the case with our own <note>intellects</note>...

<summary>Proclus analyzes the hierarchy of Being, Eternity, and the "Self-Living" Form, arguing that "Always Being" encompasses a range of divine realities from the highest Being down to individual intellects. He engages with the interpretations of earlier philosophers like Iamblichus regarding the relationship between the One and the realm of Forms.</summary>

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.

It proceeds <note>original: "πρόεισι". A correction from "πάρεσι" (is present) suggested by the scholar Thomas Taylor.</note> from a superior cause into existence, yet it is not self-subsistent <margin>D</margin> but—let us not discuss these things yet. That which is **always Being** must not be assumed to be Being in one respect and non-being in another, nor as a composite of such things, in this way: an unlike composition, nor at one time Being and at another time non-being. For this very thing has been stated: it is **always Being**. Rather, it is simply and eternally Being, unmixed with anything whatsoever that is its opposite. For this seems to me to indicate the fact of "not having a beginning" <note>original: "γένεσιν μὴ ἔχειν". This refers to the lack of a temporal origin or a process of coming-into-being.</note>, namely the unmixed and stainless purity of the **always Being**, according to which it is set apart from all the subsistence found in images and that which changes according to time. 

It is not, as some say, that he explains "always Being" through "having no beginning" for the sake of clarity; nor, as others say, that he wished to state the same thing both affirmatively and negatively. Rather, it is because one must conceive of the **always Being** in itself, apart from any change according to time. For even the Soul participates in time <note>original: "χρόνου μετέχει"</note>, and the World-Soul has been allotted a life that unrolls according to time; but only the Intelligible nature <note>The realm of pure forms/ideas.</note> is eternal in its own right. 

Therefore, some of the ancients call the Intelligible breadth "Truly Being," but the nature of the Soul "Not-Truly Being," and the physical world "Not-Truly Not-Being," and Matter "Truly Not-Being." <margin>E</margin> How they arrange these things, we shall examine later. But that the phrase "having no beginning" is added to indicate the separate essence of the **always Being**, I believe has been made clear through what has been said. 

Next, regarding "that which becomes" <note>original: "τὸ γιγνόμενον"</note>: does he mean the entire universe, or the material and changing constitution? For some of the ancients explained this one way, and others another. We, however, say that everything corporeal is "becoming," insofar as it is unadorned by itself, but is at some time ordered by another. But this does not apply to the Soul of the All; for it is in a sense "always Being," and much more so is the Intellect, for that is "always Being" directly. Only the body is "becoming" and "truly never Being." For it is that which is always receiving the reflection of existence from the world-making cause. 

Why then did he add "always" to "becoming," just as he did to "Being," and then add "at some time" <note>original: "ποτέ"</note>, so that it might stand in total antithesis to the "always Being"? Or did Plato, looking at the varied nature of that which becomes, devise this by removing the "always" from the "becoming"? <margin>F</margin> For wholes "become" always, but the parts "become" at some time. And in another sense, some forms are inseparable from matter...

# PROCLUS
<page-num>168</page-num>

And that which is "always becoming" <note>original: *ginetai*</note> derives from that which "always is," <note>original: *ontos*</note> while that which is in time also passes away. For while **corporeality** <note>The state of having a physical body</note> is always becoming and is always around **matter**, the specific **form** <note>original: *eidos*</note> of fire or of air enters into matter and departs from it, being separated and removed due to the mastery of an opposing nature. If, then, that which always occupies matter is "always becoming," it never truly "is"; and if that which becomes at some time is "becoming" because it is not yet, and when it is not becoming it does not exist, then even that which becomes at some time never truly "is." But everything that becomes | either becomes always, or at some time. Therefore, everything that becomes is never truly Being. Having said these things, let us run back to the beginning and ask whether "Being" refers to all things that exist, or not to all. For if we should wish "Being" to indicate only the **eternal nature** <note>original: *aionion physin*</note> which possesses eternity throughout its whole self, it would not apply to all things. For neither that which is **before eternity**, nor the order of eternity itself, nor again those things which have an eternal **essence** <note>original: *ousian*</note> but perform their **activities** <note>original: *energeias*</note> according to time, would be stationed under this "Being." But if we take "Being" to mean everything that is in any way eternal—whether strictly, universally, or partially—then the **Soul** is among the eternal things, as is that which contains the causes of all things in a unified and primary way within itself, as they say. For the situation is thus: one thing is **supra-eternal**, another is **simply eternal**, and another is **partially eternal**, yet each of these is "always being." The first is as the **power** <note>original: *dynamis*</note> and **fountain** of the "always"; the second is "always" as primary Being and "self-always" <note>Being eternal by its own nature rather than by participation</note> and not by participation; the third is "always" as **participating** in the "always" and is primarily a whole | eternal thing; and the last is that which has merely shared in such a quality. For each thing exists in three ways: either by **cause**, by **subsistence**, or by **participation**. <margin>B</margin> That which is "Being" in its subsistence is only Being, and is the cause of the "always being." **Eternity** <note>original: *aion*</note> is "always being" by subsistence, but is "Being" by participation; whereas the "eternal" is "always being" by participation, but in its subsistence it is something else—either **intelligible**, or **intelligible and intellectual**, or **intellectual**; and if the latter, it is either **universal** or **particular**. And if this, it is either **supracosmic** or **encosmic** <note>Existing within the physical universe</note>. And if this, it is either **divine** or existing after the gods; and each of these is so either in its **being** alone, or in its **power** and its **activity**, reaching down to the "always being" of those things that are only partially eternal. Again, then, regarding "that which becomes": if we take it in the strict sense, we shall understand **Generation** <note>original: *genesin*</note> as that which is changing in every way; but if we mean everything that is in any way "generated," we shall say even the **heaven** is "becoming," insofar as it participates in **motion** and **change**; and we shall say the **Soul** is the first of things that "become," insofar as it lives in time and time is innate to its activities. And so, from below, the...

<margin>C</margin>
...descending into the **soul** <note>original: *psychē*</note>, we shall end at it as the first of generated things; and ascending from below toward it, we shall find rest in it again as the last of eternal things. For even if someone says that the **heaven** <note>the physical cosmos</note> always exists—speaking correctly—yet its being is always dependent upon another; whereas the soul possesses its own essence from itself. This is why Socrates in the *Phaedrus* <note>referring to Phaedrus 245e</note> called it both **unbegotten** and **generated** at the same time, and self-moving, as being the principle of all generation, yet generating itself and making itself alive. Therefore, we shall speak correctly by calling it both unbegotten and generated, both eternal and not eternal. For this reason, the **Athenian Stranger** <note>the lead character in Plato's *Laws*</note> thought it right to call the soul "imperishable" but not "eternal" <note>original: *aiōnion*</note>, using these very words because "everlasting" <note>original: *aidion*</note> is eternal, but the soul is not so in its entirety, as is **True Being**. There was a difference between "always being" and "always becoming"; the heaven is always becoming, for it does not have being from itself; but the soul also "is" always, for it has being from itself. That which is prior to the soul does not "become" from a cause, but "is" from a cause; for **generation** <note>original: *genesis*</note> belongs only to those things that receive their existence from others. How it is, then, that he has encompassed all things, and how he has not encompassed all things in the aforementioned divisions, should be clear through these points. He has not encompassed all, because the "solely eternal" has been taken and 
<margin>D</margin>
the "primarily generated," which are respectively before the soul and after the soul. But since the extremes have been taken, it is possible to find the middle from these, which is simultaneously "being" and "becoming." Furthermore, it is easy to learn, by considering that this is the very first of the **problems** <note>or "inquiries"</note>, why he has necessarily placed these definitions of "that which always is" and "that which becomes" before all other axioms. Regarding the whole, one must consider at the beginning whether it always was, having no principle of generation, or whether it has come into being. For if this is the first of the things to be examined, it reasonably holds the first rank among the axioms: what is the "generated" and what is the "eternal." For then the other axioms follow, just as the remaining problems follow the premise concerning whether it has come into being. And if we must again take up the account of the **hypotheses** <note>foundational assumptions</note> to state our view at greater length, it seems that Plato—just as geometers take up **definitions** and hypotheses before their **demonstrations** <note>original: *apodeixeis*</note> through which they will make their proofs—is laying down the principles 
<margin>E</margin>
of the whole of **natural philosophy** <note>original: *physiologias*</note>. For just as there are certain principles of music and others of medicine, and others of arithmetic and mechanics, so too there are principles of natural philosophy—those of the whole—which Plato now hands down: **True Being** is that which is grasped by the intellect with a rational account. The **generated** is that which is grasped by opinion with irrational sensation. Everything that is generated comes into being from a **cause**; that which does not subsist from a cause...

# PROCLUS

It is not right <note>original: "Themis"</note>, lest it be more imperfect than the secondary things, nor is it an activity <note>term: *energeia* (activity/actuality) — the state of being in operation as opposed to mere potential</note>, lest it possess differences. It would be better to say it is altogether set apart from both power and activity, so that there would be no division at all in the One. Or rather, we shall say that Plato has not made a division here, but a definition <note>original: "aphoristikon"</note> of that which always *is* and that which *becomes*, to show what each of them is. For "that which is to be divided" seems to me the same as "that which is to be distinguished." Since he is discussing the cosmos, the Creator <note>term: *demiurge* — the craftsman-god who shapes the material world</note>, and the Model <note>term: *paradeigma* — the eternal blueprint of the world</note>, he wishes to define Eternal Being separately, and separately 
<margin>D</margin> that which becomes, so that through these given definitions we may know where to place the cosmos, where the Creator, and where the Model, and not confuse their respective ranks, but distinguish them from one another as they are by nature. He did this same thing in the *Philebus* as well. For seeking there whether the Intellect or the "mixed life" is better, he took up their kinds: the Limit, the Infinite, and the Mixed; for thus the rank of each would become clear. And he revealed the specific character of these kinds. But in that work, the Limit and the Infinite, beginning from the gods, proceeded through all things that exist in any way whatsoever. For these were in the first beings according to the stable and generative cause of the Intelligibles; they were in the Intellectual beings according to the paternal and maternal principle of the Intellectual gods; they were in the super-cosmic beings according to the creative Monad and the life-generating Dyad; and they were in the lowest beings according to the productive and fertile powers. But here, "Being" and "Becoming" do not even begin from the gods; for the Unities <note>term: *henads* — the highest, most unified principles of the gods</note> of the gods are superior to Being, 
<margin>E</margin> | and before these, Being itself has been explained as the first of all beings—which is why it is the first Being—while the other gods are Unities. Nor is it participated in by them, but those who come after it are called participants and are under Being. Nor does this division extend to the lowest things. For we can neither call Matter "Eternal Being"—since we are accustomed to calling it "non-being"—nor "that which becomes," since it is not even capable of being acted upon; otherwise, it would vanish entirely. This, then, will be discussed again later: that this is not a division of a single thing, and that it is necessary for the present inquiry to have this definition of these kinds before all others, so that the argument may proceed from "geometrical hypotheses" <note>note: Proclus refers to the method of starting from self-evident axioms to reach a conclusion</note> to the examination of what follows, and may discover the nature of the universe and its paternal and formative cause. For if the whole is generated, it has come to be by a cause. It is, therefore...

# ON THE TIMAEUS II.

<page-num>171</page-num>

...and this we shall discuss again. But why is it that Plato, though he is accustomed to use both the terms "the thing itself" <note>original: *auto*</note> and "that which is" <note>original: *to hoper*</note> regarding the Intelligibles <note>The "Intelligibles" are the eternal Forms or Ideas that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses.</note>, has here taken up neither of these, but instead preferred the term "always" <note>original: *aei*</note> as being more naturally suited to Truly Existing Being? For this also poses a difficulty: why did he consider "always" to be more authoritative than the other three terms for signifying the nature of that which primarily exists?

Perhaps it is because "the thing itself" reveals the simplicity of the Intelligibles—their primary existence and primary essence. This is said according to that specific characteristic by which they are primarily the things that they are, and by which they fill secondary things through their own participation. On the other hand, "that which is" <note>original: *to hoper on*</note> signifies purity, the unmixed, and that which is not infected by the opposite nature. Finally, "always" signifies the eternal, the unchangeable, and the immutable according to its substance.

For example, when we speak of "the Beautiful itself" <margin>C</margin> <note>original: *autokalon*</note> and "the Just itself," we do not see something that is beautiful by participating in beauty, nor just by participating in justice, but we see that which is primarily Beautiful and primarily Just. But when we speak of "that which is beautiful," we mean that which is not mixed with the ugly nor stained by its opposite—unlike the beauty found in physical things, which, residing in the ugly <note>i.e., in the material world</note>, is itself infected by the underlying nature of matter. And when we say "always beautiful," we mean that which is not beautiful at one time and not at another, but is eternally beautiful.

Thus, one term reveals the simplicity of the Intelligibles and their primary provision to all things—for "the Beautiful itself" is that from which all beautiful things come, and "the Equal itself" <note>original: *autoison*</note> is that from which all equal things are equal, and so on for the rest. The second term reveals their isolation, purity, and their unmixed and undefiled nature; for this is "that which is"—something that is not other than itself and does not drag along anything foreign to it. The third term reveals immutability; for this is the "always." And it does not simply mean immutability, but permanence in eternity.

For the "always" of time is one thing, and the "always" of eternity is another. The latter exists as a whole all at once, while the former is filled out by the entire continuity of time and is infinite. <margin>D</margin> The one exists in the "now," while the other exists in extension—an extension that is unceasing and always coming into being.

Therefore, the "itself" comes to beings from the Paradigm <note>The "Paradigm" is the eternal model the Creator uses to fashion the universe.</note>; for that is the cause of simplicity for beings and of the distribution to others of those qualities it possesses primarily. "That which is" comes from the One-Being; for that is what is primarily set apart from non-being and from "passing away," because it is primarily Being, and all things subsist in it occultly and indivisibly. But the "always" comes from Eternity; for just as the One-Being is the provider of existence, so Eternity is the provider of perpetuity to the Intelligibles.

If, then, Plato were making his argument about participants and things participated in, and needed "Being" for this purpose, he would have said "what is Being itself." And if he were speaking about the unmixed...

<page-num>164</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS</header>

being. For this is what is united to the gods, but not that which is becoming and perishing <note>original: ἀπολλύμενον</note>. But in reality, it is never truly being. Rather, even before these points, it is stored within our common notions that there is something which is *always being*. For from where does that which becomes arise, if not from that which always is? For if that source were also to become, it would be generated by some other being, and that would be either always being or itself becoming; thus we would either proceed to infinity, or generation <note>term: genesis | the process of coming-into-being</note> would move in a circle, or there is indeed that which is always being. But it is not lawful to proceed to infinity, for all things come from one and from a single principle; nor is generation a circle, lest <margin>C</margin> the same things become both superior and inferior, both causes and effects. It remains, therefore, that being is eternal. 

Why then, someone might ask, does generation not proceed directly from the One? Because, we shall say, to produce plurality entirely outside of being from the One is strange; therefore, "truly being" <note>original: ὄντως ὄν</note> must exist, which proceeds primarily from the One, so that the First is not the cause of the last things alone, but prior to these, it is the cause of Being, from which generation also flows. 

The truest point regarding what has been said is this: that now, taking it as a hypothesis, he defined what is "always being," but after the discourses on the creation of the world, he takes this up again and demonstrates that the "always being" exists. Maintaining the methods proper to natural philosophy <note>term: physiologia | the study of nature and its principles</note>, he proceeds from these hypotheses and demonstrates the consequences following from them. For this science too is based on hypotheses, and it is necessary for its hypotheses to be grasped prior to the demonstrations. In the discourses concerning matter <note>term: hyle | the underlying "stuff" of the universe</note>, I demonstrate not only that matter exists, but also Being; and a little later, having shown from one of the hypotheses—the third—that there is a Craftsman <note>term: demiourgos | the divine architect of the cosmos</note> of the world, it follows through this that the "always being" exists prior to the generated, and again from the fourth declaration, that the <margin>D</margin> Craftsman has fashioned the whole according to an eternal model <note>term: paradeigma | the perfect "blueprint" or Form used by the Creator</note>. That the "always being" exists in itself prior to generated things, he will demonstrate in those discourses we have mentioned. 

And this is so. But does this "always being" signify the entire intelligible world <note>term: noetos kosmos | the realm of pure thought and Forms</note>, or the Craftsman, or the Model of the whole? For different thinkers have taken it differently. If it is the intelligible, where does the intelligible breadth begin and where does it proceed? If it is the Model, how is the Craftsman not "always being," if the Model and the Craftsman are different? And if it is the Craftsman, how is the Model not such? That the model-cause must be placed within the "always being," Plato clearly says: **"To which of the models did the one who fashioned it work? Toward that which is always the same and in the same state, or toward that which has come to be?"** And he judged immediately: **"If the world is beautiful and the Craftsman good, it is clear that he looked toward the eternal; but if—which is not lawful to say—he looked toward that which has come to be."** If, then, this is not lawful to say, the Model of the whole is "always being."

<summary>Proclus argues for the necessity of an eternal, unchanging "Being" as the source of all generated things, distinguishing between the Craftsman and the eternal Model used in creation.</summary>

<page-num>173</page-num>

<header>->ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK II.<-</header>

Of Plato. Some commentators have divided the text and identified the "defined" <note>Greek: *horiston*</note> and the "definition" <note>Greek: *horiston* (with a slight accentual shift in the Greek philosophical tradition to distinguish the two)</note> in each of the two clauses. For in the first clause, they declare that "that which is graspable by intellect with the aid of reason" is the definition, while "that which always is in the same state" is the thing defined. In the second clause, they provide "that which is the object of opinion with the aid of irrational sensation" as the definition, and the remainder as the primary subject itself. Among these men who speak thus, our own teacher <note>Likely referring to Syrianus, Proclus' predecessor as head of the Academy</note> is also found. For if we were to slightly rearrange the phrasing, the whole matter would become immediately clear: "That which always is in the same state is graspable by intellect with the aid of reason, while that which is becoming and perishing, but never truly is, is the object of opinion with the aid of irrational sensation."

These points follow from what was said previously: "What is that which always is, having no beginning in generation, and what is that which is becoming, but never truly is?" For "always in the same state" signifies that which has no beginning in generation, while "becoming" and "perishing" <margin>B</margin> and "never truly being" signify the same thing. This has been expressed somewhat more obscurely through the addition of the word "truly" <note>Greek: *ontōs*</note> in Plato's text, indicating that insofar as a thing is "becoming," it is not; but insofar as it is removed from "Being" in this context, to that extent it is "not-becoming." 

In the opening sections, he clarified the things defined even further through these additions. For where he said "always," he added "always being in the same state," so that we should not understand "always" as merely perpetual time, but as the **Eternal** <note>Greek: *aionion*</note>. For the Eternal is "all at once" and "being in the same state," whereas the "temporal" is ranked alongside the infinity of time. And where he said "becoming," he spoke of it alongside "perishing," so that we should not understand the "processions of generation" <note>A technical Neoplatonic term for how divine realities emanate or "proceed" downward</note>—which is a term even applied to the gods who are beyond Being—but rather those generations that have "destruction" as their counterpart.

The definitions provided are, therefore, something like this: "Always Being is that which is graspable by intellect with the aid of reason"; "Becoming Being is that which is the object of opinion with the aid of irrational sensation." Regarding these, people are accustomed to bring charges against Plato: first, that he did not include a "genus" <note>A standard requirement in Aristotelian logic for a formal definition</note> as the rules of definitions require, and second, that he did not reveal the nature of the defined things <margin>C</margin> themselves, nor did he consider the things in themselves apart from this relationship. But we must demonstrate that those who wish to raise these difficulties are completely in error. For what kind of "genus" has a place in the case of **Being**, which encompasses the entirety of intelligible substance? For if **Substance** <note>Greek: *ousia*</note> has no genus prior to itself, nor a definition...

<summary>Proclus defends Plato's definitions of Being and Becoming against critics who claim they lack proper logical structure. He argues that Plato's specific phrasing distinguishes eternal, intellectual reality from the perishing world of the senses.</summary>

# PROCLUS

rank in the series of virtues, just as the <term>Living-Being-Itself</term> <note>original: "αὐτοζῶον" (autozōon); the archetypal Form of Life</note> is among equals, so surely the <term>Being-Itself</term> <note>original: "αὐτοόν" (autoon); the primary Form of Being</note>, which is Being in the first degree, is the summit of all beings and proceeds from it <note>original: "ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ πρόεισι"</note>. Everything that is an <term>intelligible being</term> <note>original: "νοητὸν ὄν" (noēton on)</note> and an <term>intellectual being</term> <note>original: "νοερὸν ὄν" (noeron on)</note>, appearing as being in any way whatsoever, has participated in the title of "Being," yet "Being" and "Always Being" are not the same. For "Being" is beyond <term>Eternity</term> <note>original: "αἰών" (aiōn)</note>, 
<margin>B</margin> which participates in Being; | therefore, all things that have participated in Eternity also have a certain share of Being, but not all things that participate in Being have also participated in Eternity. For instance, even things in time participate in Being; thus, that which is "Primarily Being" is beyond the rank of Eternity. But "Always Being" is eternal; so the argument has demonstrated the opposite: that everything should rather be understood from "Always Being" than from "Being" as such. For the former is superior to the latter, being between the One and Eternity, and is called "Being before Eternity." If, then, I must state what appears to be the case, Plato has now primarily included everything that is <term>eternally being</term>, beginning from the nature of the Living-Being-Itself—for this is the primarily eternal—and ending at the partial intellects. But he perhaps left out "Being" as the <term>monad</term> <note>original: "μονάδα" (monada); the single source or unit</note> of these, as it is unutterable and joined to the One. And in this way, his discourse would be about the whole intelligible realm, unless you take "the intelligible" to be the hidden, highest, and ungraspable aspect of the One. At any rate, he will say that the Living-Being-Itself is the most beautiful of <term>intelligible objects</term> <note>original: "νοουμένων" (nooumenōn)</note> as he proceeds, since those prior to this are superior to being known due to their excess of unity. 
<margin>C</margin> Unless, perhaps, he called the Living-Being-Itself the most beautiful of all | intelligible objects because Eternity exists before the Living Being, and the One exists before that—the one as a cause forever, the other as the existence of Eternity, and the third by participation in the eternal. And if these points hold, then "Always Being" contains both Eternity and the Living-Being-Itself, and the Demiurge <note>The Creator-God in Plato's philosophy</note> would be contained within it, and Being itself, which possesses the hidden cause of Eternity. Thus it is clear from these things that "Always Being" encompasses the entire nature prior to souls, whether intelligible or intellectual, beginning from Being-Itself and ending in the partial intellect, but not only the highest of all beings, as **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who influenced Proclus</note> used to say—such as the "One-Being," which all beings are said to be. Indeed, the One itself and the principles of Being are alone superior. Now, the One is superior even to being <term>self-subsisting</term> <note>original: "αὐθιδύποστατον" (authidypostaton); existing by its own power</note>, for it is exempt from all multiplicity; but "Always Being" is self-subsisting, possessing this power through the One; and that which comes after it is both self-subsisting and simultaneously subsists from another productive cause, as is the case with our own [soul]...

# ON THE TIMAEUS II.

...proceeds <note>original: *proeisi*</note> from a superior cause into existence, but it is not self-subsistent. But let us not dwell on these things yet. We must not suppose that **that which always is** <note>The Platonic *aei on*</note> is in one way being and in another way non-being, or that it is composed of such and such elements of dissimilar quality, nor that it is at one time being and at another time non-being; for this very thing has been stated: it is *always being*. Rather, it is simply and eternally being, unmixed with anything whatsoever that is its opposite. <margin>D</margin> For this, it seems to me, is also indicated by the addition of the phrase **having no generation**, which shows the unmixed and undefiled purity of that which *always is*, according to which it is suspended above all that subsistence found in the images of being and that which changes according to time. It is not as some say, that he explains "that which always is" by "having no generation" for the sake of clarity; nor as others say, that he wished to speak both affirmatively of its being and negatively; but rather because one must conceive of "that which always is" as being in itself exempt from temporal change. For even the **Soul** <note>original: *psychē*</note> participates in time, and the **World** <note>original: *kosmos*</note> has been allotted a life that unfolds according to time; but only the **Intelligible nature** <note>The realm of pure forms/ideas</note> is eternal in itself. Therefore, some of the ancients call the Intelligible breadth "truly being," the psychic "not truly being," the sensible "not truly non-being," and **Matter** <note>original: *hylē*</note> "really non-being." But how these thinkers arrange these things, <margin>E</margin> we shall examine elsewhere. That the phrase "not having generation" is added to indicate the separation of that which *always is* from the world of change has, I think, been made clear through what has been said.

Following these points: when he speaks of **that which becomes**, does he mean the entire world, or the material and ever-changing constitution? For on this point, some of the ancients explained it one way, and others another. We, however, accept that everything **body-like** is "becoming," insofar as it is unadorned by itself, but is ordered by another or at some time. But this is not true of the **Soul of the All**; for it is in a way "always being." Much less is it true of the **Intellect** <note>original: *nous*</note>; for this is directly "always being." Only the body is in a state of flux and is "truly never being." For it always stands in need of the world-making cause of the **Forms** <note>original: *eidōn*</note> and must receive from it the reflection of existence. Why then, one might ask, did he not add "always" to "that which becomes," just as he did for "being," or "at some time," so that it might be antithetically balanced in every way against "that which always is"? Perhaps Plato, looking at the varied nature of that which becomes, devised this by <margin>F</margin> removing both "at some time" and "always" from "that which becomes." For some things [the wholes] are becoming **always**, while the parts are becoming **at some time**. And in another sense, some of the forms are inseparable from matter...

For the corporeal nature is always coming-to-be and is always centered around matter <note>original: *hylēn*</note>, but the <unclear>procession</unclear> of the form <note>original: *eidos*</note> enters into the matter and departs, being separated and destroyed through the mastery of the contrary nature. If, then, that which always occupies matter is always coming-to-be, it never truly *is*; and if that which comes-to-be at some time <margin>72</margin> | never truly *is*, then everything that comes-to-be either does so always or at some time. Therefore, everything that comes-to-be never truly possesses Being. Having said these things, let us run back to the beginning and ask whether "Being" belongs to all things that are, or not to all. For if we should posit that the "Always" indicates only the eternal nature <note>original: *aiōnion physin*</note> which possesses eternity according to its whole self, it would not belong to all things. For neither that which is before eternity, nor the rank of eternity itself, nor again those things which have an eternal essence but perform their activities <note>original: *energeias*</note> according to time, will be stationed under this "Being." But if we take everything that is in any way eternal—whether strictly <note>original: *kyriōs*</note>, or universally, or partially—to be "always being," then the soul <note>original: *psychē*</note> is also among the eternal things, as is that which contains the causes <note>original: *aitias*</note> of all things united in itself and strictly, as they say. For it holds thus: one thing is supra-eternal <note>original: *hyperaiōnion*</note>, another is simply eternal, and another is eternal in a certain respect; and each of these is "always being"—the first as the power <note>original: *dynamis*</note> and source <note>original: *pēgē*</note> of the "always," the second as primarily being the "always" and "itself-always" and not by participation <note>original: *metochēn*</note>, <margin>B</margin> and the third as participating in the "always" and being primarily a whole | eternal thing, and the last as having shared in such a characteristic. For each thing exists in three ways: either according to cause, or according to subsistence <note>original: *hyparxin*</note>, or according to participation <note>original: *methexin*</note>. That which is "One" exists according to subsistence as only Being, and is the cause of "always being." But Eternity <note>original: *Aiōn*</note> is "always being" according to subsistence, but "Being" according to participation; whereas the "eternal" is "always being" according to participation, but according to subsistence it is something else: either intelligible <note>original: *noēton*</note>, or intelligible and intellectual, or intellectual <note>original: *noeron*</note>; and if this, either universal or partial; and if this, either supra-cosmic or intra-cosmic; and if this, either divine or existing after the gods; and each of these either in its being alone, or in its power and its activity, even down to the "always being" of things that are eternal in a certain respect. Again, then, regarding "that which comes-to-be": if we take it strictly, we shall understand "becoming" <note>original: *genesin*</note> as that which is changing in every way; but if we mean everything that is in any way generated, we shall say even the heaven is "coming-to-be," insofar as it participates in motion and change, and the soul is the first of things "coming-to-be," insofar as it lives in time and time is connate with its activities. ## ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II

...ending at the Soul as the first of generated things, and from above we shall cease all things back into it again as the last of eternal things. For indeed, he <note>Plato</note> says that the heaven is always "being," speaking correctly, but its being is always coming to it from another; whereas the Soul possesses its own essence from itself. But in the *Phaedrus*, Socrates called it both ungenerated and generated at the same time, and also eternal, as being the principle of all generation, yet generating itself and making itself alive. Therefore, we shall speak correctly by calling it ungenerated and generated, both eternal and not eternal. For this reason, the Athenian Stranger <note>The primary speaker in Plato's *Laws*</note> deemed it right to call the Soul "more" <note>original: μᾶλλον (mallon); implying more akin to being than becoming</note>, yet not strictly eternal, using these very words because it is not eternal in every part of itself, as is Truly Real Being <term>Truly Real Being: a technical term for the unchanging realm of Forms</term>. For there was a difference between "being always" and "becoming," and the heaven is always "becoming," for it does not possess being from itself; but the Soul also "is" always, for it possesses being from itself. And that which is prior to the Soul <note>The Intellect or the One</note> does not "become" from a cause, but "is" from a cause; for generation exists among those things produced by others...

# PROCLUS
### Page 174

...being most generic, what could you say about **Being** itself <note>original: *autou tou ontos*</note>, which encompasses all powers and all activities? Therefore, neither is Being [simply a genus]. For if it were, it would be the genus of "that which always is"; but then this would be a specific kind of being, not Being simply. [We must also consider] **Non-Being**, lest we inadvertently create "that which always is not." For in every case, the genus is predicated of its own species. Therefore, [Being] is not a genus. 

Is it not appropriate to the whole inquiry and the proposed definitions to ask: what is the definition of these modes of knowledge? For if, as we said before, we must use these as axioms and hypotheses for the demonstrations that will be spoken, these definitions must be known and clear to us. If he <note>Plato</note> had commanded us to hunt for the nature of things in itself, he would have filled the entire teaching with obscurity. But since he wishes to make **Being** and **Becoming** <note>original: *to on kai to gignomenon*</note> known through definitions—so that he may proceed with demonstrations from known principles—he clearly presents their unique characteristics to his listeners. By awakening and initiating ourselves, we shall behold those truths more transparently. 

Since every cognitive faculty either is the known object itself, or sees it, or possesses it (for **Intellect** <note>original: *nous*</note> is the **Intelligible** <note>original: *noēton*</note>, **Sensation** <note>original: *aisthēsis*</note> sees the **Sensible** <note>original: *aisthēton*</note>, and **Reason** <note>original: *dianoia*</note> possesses the **Object of Reason** within itself), and since we are not by nature the Intelligible itself, we know it through the power within us that is yoked to it. It is through this power, then, that the nature of Being becomes known to us. 

Regarding the difficulties, we shall meet them through these points. But we must observe how, in setting the objects of both before himself, he indicated them both **negatively** and **affirmatively** <note>original: *apophatikōs kai kataphatikōs*</note>. In responding to each: 

| Object | Mode of Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Eternal Being** | He took up the affirmative alone. |
| **Becoming** | He took up both the affirmative and the negative. |

He added to Becoming the term "perishing," and interpreted "that which is never" through the transition into "that which is never truly being." Since Being is characterized by **Existence**, and Becoming by **Non-Existence**, in defining the former he used only the affirmative, saying it "is always the same." For the latter, he included the negation—not the negation alone (since definitions are of affirmations, signifying what belongs to each thing), but he also called it "perishing," which is not surprising. Just as he added "being the same" to Being (and not just "always being"), so he added "perishing" to Becoming. For as "becoming," it is different from "always being"; as "perishing," it is different from "being the same." Indeed, that which becomes, insofar as it is becoming, is also perishing, being unable to sustain itself; for [if it could], it would be able to produce itself. Taking each in turn, **Being** and **Becoming**, he saw the one as above **Generation** <note>original: *genesin*</note>, and the other as...

<page-num>175</page-num>
<header>ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK II.</header>

# ON THE TIMAEUS BOOK II.

<note>original: "ιον"</note> ...not being; for whenever the reflection of "being" is added to that which is "becoming," then opinions, following a wandering path, [regard it] as always becoming. But come, let us examine each of the words themselves by which he constructs his explanations, and let us first of all observe how many ways "intellection" <note>original: "νόησις" (noesis) - the act of direct mental apprehension or intuitive thought</note> exists, and let us calculate its other progressions.

First, then, is the **intelligible intellection**, which arrives at the same point as the "intelligible" <note>original: "νοητῷ" (noeto) - the object of thought, the Forms</note> and is nothing other than the intelligible itself; it is both essential intellection and **self-subsisting essence**, because everything in this intelligible realm exists in a formative and intelligible manner.

<margin>75</margin> Second is the intellection that joins the "intellect" <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun) - the faculty of the mind</note> to the intelligible; it possesses a cohesive and unifying quality for the extremes and is **life and power**, proceeding from the intelligible toward the intellect, and establishing the intellect within the intelligible.

Third is the **yoked intellection** within the intellect itself, being the "activity" <note>original: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia)</note> of the intellect, through which it has grasped the intelligible within itself and according to which it thinks and is what it is. It is an activity and a **self-intellection**, yet not as an "intelligible intellection" <note>the first type</note> nor as a mere potentiality, but as an activity, as has been said: an **intellectual intellection**.

Fourth in order is the intellection of **partial intellects**; for each of these also has something intelligible yoked within itself and an intellection—or rather, each partial intellect has all things: intellect, intellection, and the intelligible—through which it is joined to the wholes and thinks the whole intelligible world and each of its parts.

Fifth is the intellection of the **rational soul**. For just as the rational soul is called "intellect," so too its knowledge is called "intellection"—a **transitive intellection** <note>meaning it moves from one thought to another, unlike the static intuition of higher intellects</note> which has time innate within itself.

Sixth, if you wish to count this as well, is **imaginative knowledge**, which is also addressed by some as "intellection"; and the "imagination" <note>original: "φαντασία" (phantasia)</note> is a **passive intellect** <note>A reference to Aristotle's De Anima</note>, because it knows whatever it knows internally and by means of types and shapes. For it is common to every intellection to have the object of knowledge within itself. This is clear, and it is how intellection differs from "sensation" <note>original: "αἰσθήσεως" (aistheseos)</note>. 

But in one case, the objects of knowledge are present **universally**; in another, the second is present but sees the first universally; in another, the object of knowledge is present **partially**, but sees the wholes through the part; in another, it sees the wholes, but partially and not all at once; and in another, the vision occurs alongside "passion" <note>or "impression"</note>. Such then are the differences of intellection. But for now, we must not take up imaginative intellection; for it is not of a nature to know **truly existing being**.

# PROCLUS
### Page 176

For the **imagination** <note>original: *to phantaston*</note> is indefinite, because it knows through shape and form, whereas **Eternal Being** is without shape. In general, no irrational knowledge is able to contemplate Being itself, since it is not even naturally suited to see the universal. Nor can the knowledge in the **rational soul** <note>original: *logikē psychē*</note> do so; for it does not possess the quality of being "all-at-once" <note>simultaneous, non-discursive grasp</note> nor that which is coordinate with eternal things, but rather it proceeds according to time. Nor can **universal intellections** <note>the higher, divine thoughts</note> do so; for those are beyond our modes of knowing, yet Timaeus joined **Intellection** <note>original: *noēsis*</note> together with **Reason** <note>original: *logos*</note> in his account. 

Instead, we must now take this to mean the intellection of the **particular intellect**. For it is with this that we at some time behold Being. For just as **sensation** <note>original: *aisthēsis*</note> is in the second dyad below the rational soul, so Intellection is above it in this same way. For the particular intellect is established immediately above our essence, leading it upward and perfecting it; toward this we turn ourselves when we have been purified through philosophy and have joined our own intellectual power to the intellection of that higher source. 

What this particular intellect is, and how it is not "one" in a singular sense, but exists through those entities that are always active according to it—through which particular souls sometimes participate in the **intellectual light**—has been articulated at greater length elsewhere. For now, let this much be understood: that this intellect is participated in by other proximate, more numerous **daemonic souls**, but it shines into our own souls whenever we turn toward it and make the reason within us "intellectual." As in the *Phaedrus*, Plato called this the **"pilot"** of the soul and said that it alone intellects Being, while the soul, following after it, is nourished by intellect and knowledge. 

In this way, then, this too is Intellection; it exists prior to the soul and is Intellection in the true sense, but it is participated in by the soul whenever the Reason acts intellectually. Therefore, in the following passages, he will say that **Intellect** <note>original: *nous*</note> belongs to the gods, but the race of men participates in it only to a small extent. And the account, in revealing the knowledge of Eternal Being, seems to call the primary form "Intellection" itself; but so that one does not assume it is Intellection alone, he adds "Reason" to "Intellection," in order to distinguish it by its **discursive** <note>original: *metabatikō* - moving from one point to another</note> nature. For whenever Reason intellects Eternal Being, as Reason it acts discursively, but as an intellecutal thing, it acts with simplicity—intellecuting each thing as a simple unity at once, yet not all things at once, but passing from some to others; yet it intellects everything it passes through as a single and simple thing.

After the definition of Intellection, he clarifies what **Reason** is and how it is grown together with Intellection. In the *Theaetetus*, Reason is said to have three meanings: vocal expression, the passage through the elements <note>syllables/parts</note>, and that which presents the differences of each thing in relation to others. But all these meanings concern **composition** and **division**, and they happen to be ill-suited for the grasping of Eternal Being. For like is naturally chosen by like, and Eternal Being is simple and indivisible, set apart from all things related to these...

<summary>Proclus explains that human reason (logos) can only grasp Eternal Being when it is elevated to "Intellection" (noēsis) by a higher, particular Intellect. He distinguishes between the discursive nature of human thought and the simple, simultaneous grasp of the divine.</summary>

<page-num>177</page-num>
<header>ON THE TIMAEUS II.</header>

## ON THE TIMAEUS II.

...contrary. Furthermore, it is spoken of in another way: one [reason] is **opinion-based**, another **scientific**, and another **intellectual**. For since there is in us opinion, and discursive reason, and intellect (and by "intellect" in this context I mean the very summit of discursive reason), and since our entire essence is <note>original: "ρος" - likely "partible" or "rational"</note>, we must view "reason" differently in each of these. But opinion is not able to connect with the intellection of the active Intellect; on the contrary, it is yoked to irrational <note>original: "ώσει" - likely "perception"</note>. Nor is discursive reason, insofar as it proceeds into multiplicity and division, able to run back up into Intellect; rather, it stands apart from intellectual impartibility through the variety of its <note>original: "ων" - likely "objects"</note>. It remains, therefore, that the summit of the soul—the most unified part of discursive reason—is established in the intellection of the partial Intellect, being joined to it through kinship. This, then, is the "reason" <term>logos: here meaning the rational faculty</term> that intuits the <insert>intelligible</insert> things in us, and of which Socrates in the *Republic* <margin>Book VI, Page 511 D</margin> called the activity "intellection," while calling <note>original: "ροιαν" - likely "dianoia"</note> the knowledge of the intermediate objects of thought and opinion. If its activity is intellection, it would be a kind of intellect. This reason, he says in the following passages <margin>Page 37 A, B, C</margin>, comes to be in the soul as it moves around the intelligible, just as science does; but science has a more varied activity, pressing upon different things through others, whereas intellect has a simpler activity, beholding beings by direct vision. This most partible and most impartible part of us is what Plato has now called "reason," as being the intellect within us and our intelligible nature. For when the soul is purified of imagination and opinion and varied and indefinite knowledge, and runs back to the <note>original: "76"</note> state of impartibility—by which it is rooted in the partial Intellect—and having run back, joins its own activity to the intellection of that Intellect, then indeed it thinks the intelligible along with it. The activity is then single yet twofold, and both identity and difference exist within the intellections. For at that time, the soul's intellection becomes more collective and closer to eternal realities, so that it may grasp the intelligible together with the Intellect, and act like a smaller light with a greater light, with the intellection of the reason within us following the lead of the Intellect, so that the intelligible becomes comprehensible to the soul along with reason. For our reason sees the intelligible by means of intellection, but the intellection of the Intellect always both is and sees the intelligible, and does not need reason for itself, even when reason becomes intellect-like. But how is "that which truly is" <term>ontos on: true reality</term> comprehensible to the partial Intellect or to reason? For this is even more wonderful. Perhaps the intelligible itself cannot be grasped by the intellect and reason because it is beyond all containment and has embraced all things in an exempted way, but...

# PROCLUS
<page-num>178</page-num>

**B** Therefore, while the **Intellect** <note>original: *nous*</note>, possessing its own **intelligible object** <note>original: *noēton*</note>, is said for this reason to grasp the whole, **Reason** <note>original: *logos*</note>—receiving the things that are through the Intellect that corresponds <margin>76, 10: *systoichou* (corresponding) in B; *systoichōs* (correspondingly) in A.</margin> to it—is thus said to encompass **Being** through these means. Perhaps you might also say that Reason, by running around the intelligible and acting as if around a center, beholds it in this way; for while **Intellection** <note>original: *noēsis*</note> knows it immutably and without mixture, Reason dances around it in a circle, unfolding the essence that is united within it of all things.

Now, let us consider the nature of **Opinion** <note>original: *doxa*</note>. That it is the limit of the rational life and that it connects to the highest point of the irrational life is a frequently repeated point. But let us state what is unique to the **Platonic tradition**: that the faculty of Opinion contains the "reasons" <note>the formative principles or definitions</note> of sensible things, and that it knows their essences but only the "fact" <note>original: *to hoti*</note> of their existence, not the "cause" <note>original: *tēn aitian*</note>. For while **Understanding** <note>original: *dianoia*</note> knows both the essences and the causes of sensible things, **Sensation** <note>original: *aisthēsis*</note> knows neither (for it has been shown in the *Theaetetus*

**C** that Sensation is ignorant of essence and only learns through the experience | of the cause of what it knows). It is necessary, then, that Opinion, being stationed in the middle, knows the essences of things through the reasons within itself, but remains ignorant of the causes. In this way, **Right Opinion** differs from **Science** <note>original: *epistēmē*; systematic knowledge</note>, in that the former knows only the "fact," while the latter is able to behold the "cause."

Sensation is attached to Opinion, being itself a product of both the sense organ and Opinion. For the sense organ perceives the "affection" <note>the physical impact or sensation</note> of sensible things—which is why it is destroyed by excesses <note>e.g., a light too bright for the eye</note>—but Opinion possesses a knowledge pure of affection. Sensation, however, participates in affection in some way. Yet it possesses something cognitive, insofar as it is established in the perceptive faculty and is illuminated by it, becoming **reason-like** <note>original: *logoeidēs*</note>, though it is irrational in itself. Into this faculty, the series of cognitive powers terminates: first is **Intellection**, being above reason and immutable; second is **Reason**, which is the intellection of our soul as it touches beings transitively <note>moving from one thought to another</note>; third is **Opinion**, being a knowledge of sensible things according to reason; and fourth is Sensation, being an irrational knowledge of the same. For Understanding is the middle.

**D** Being between Intellection and | Opinion, Understanding is cognitive of the middle forms, which require a clearer intellection than that found in Opinion. And **Socrates** <margin>76, 31: *Republic*, Book VII, Page 533 D.</margin> said this on the previous day when defining the types of knowledge for those who know. We must, therefore, address Opinion as being "according to reason," because it possesses cognitive reasons.

<summary>Proclus defines the hierarchy of knowledge, distinguishing between Intellect (direct grasp), Reason (discursive unfolding), Opinion (knowing the fact but not the cause), and Sensation (irrational perception). He emphasizes that Opinion acts as a bridge between the rational and irrational souls.</summary>

# PROCLUS

<page-num>170</page-num>
<header>PROCLUS</header>

...is not a thing of generation. That which is the eternal model is beautiful; that which is a generated model is not beautiful. The universe is the heaven, and thus the cosmos. For from these principles, he brings forward everything that follows. It seems that for this reason, he states what the "always existing" <note>eternal Being</note> is and what "generation" <note>the world of change</note> is, but he does not state *that* each of them exists <insert>1</insert>. For even the geometer reminds us what a point is and what a line is before the demonstrations, but he in no way teaches *that* each of these exists <insert>2</insert>. For how could he be <insert>3</insert> a geometer if he were to discuss his own principles? In the same way, the natural philosopher <term>physikos</term> <note>one who studies 'physis' or nature</note> will say what eternal Being is for the sake of what is to follow <margin>F</margin> | but he will by no means demonstrate *that* it exists; for that would be beyond the scope of natural philosophy. 

However, since—as we said before—Timaeus is not a natural philosopher in the same way as others, being a Pythagorean, and since Plato displays the highest science even in these matters <insert>4</insert>, he will later establish with total mastery that "Truly Existing Being" exists. But for the present, it is sufficient for him to define what it is as he sets the boundaries of natural philosophy. And he seems <insert>5</insert> to seek the definition of eternal Being and of generation in order to find the causes that complete the universe: Form <margin>73</margin> | and Matter. For generation has need of these. He takes up the third hypothesis in order to find the productive cause <note>the Demiurge or Creator</note>; the fourth, so that he may show that the universe was made according to a model <insert>8</insert>; and the fifth, regarding the name, so that he may hunt down the participation of the Good and the Unutterable in the world, as will be shown in what follows <insert>9</insert>. 

It seems to me that Aristotle <insert>10</insert> also imitated him; in his *Physics*, he took up one hypothesis: "let it be assumed by us that things which exist by nature are either all or some of them in motion." For there must certainly be motion if the arguments of natural theory are to proceed well <insert>11</insert>, since nature is the principle of motion. But in his work *On the Heavens*, he took up those hypotheses before all other arguments, about which Plotinus <insert>12</insert> said: "Aristotle would find no difficulty if one were to grant him his hypotheses concerning the fifth body" <note>the aether or quintessence</note>, stating five of them: 
1. Simple motion belongs to a simple body. 
2. A simple body <margin>B</margin> has a certain motion according to nature. 
3. Simple motions are of two kinds. 
4. One thing exists in one. 
5. That which has no contrary has nothing that can destroy it. 

From these, he demonstrates facts about the fifth body. But while that thinker [Aristotle] shows from his hypotheses that the heaven is ungenerated, Plato shows that it is generated. Whether they disagree or not, we shall consider a little later.
