26. And this again: why indeed <margin>Why the terms "itself," "that which," and "always" are used.</margin> is it that Plato, though accustomed to use both the term "itself" <note>original: *auto*</note> and "that which" <note>original: *hoper*</note> in relation to the intelligible forms, has here taken up neither of these, but instead preferred the term "always" <note>original: *aei*</note> as being more naturally united to Being? For this also poses a difficulty <note>original: *aporia*</note>: for what reason did he suppose "always" to be more authoritative than the other three for signifying the nature of Truly Existing Being?

Is it because "itself" <margin>The solution.</margin> indicates the simplicity of the intelligibles and that they are primarily the things which they are, filling secondary things with their own participation? While "always" indicates the eternal, immutable, and unchangeable character of their subsistence <note>original: *hypostasis*</note>. For example, when we say "Beauty-itself" <note>original: *autokalon*</note> | or "Justice-itself," we see a beauty or justice that is not so by participation in beauty, nor by sharing in justice, but that which exists as the primarily beautiful and primarily just. But when we say "that which is beautiful," we mean that which is not mixed with the ugly nor stained by its opposite—just as a mirror's beauty, lying as it does in the ugly <note>i.e., in the material world</note>, is itself infected by the underlying nature. But when we say "always beautiful," we mean that which is not at one time beautiful and at another time not, but is eternally beautiful.

So, the term "itself" indicates the simplicity of the intelligibles and the abundance they provide to all other things; for this is "Beauty-itself," by which all equal things are equal, and "Equality-itself" <note>original: *autoisos*</note>, by which all equal things are equal, and similarly for the others. The term "that which" <note>original: *hoper*</note> indicates the isolation, purity, unmixed, and unstained nature; for this "that which" is so by not being anything else nor being dragged down by anything foreign. But "always" indicates immutability. For this is the "always"—and not simply immutability, but a remaining in eternity <note>original: *aion*</note>. For the "always" of time is one thing, and the "always" of eternity is another <margin>That "always" is twofold.</margin>; the one being the whole at once, the other being constituted by the entire continuity of time and being infinite; | and the one exists in the "now," the other in extension, its subsistence being unceasing and always coming-into-existence.

Therefore, the term "itself" reaches the things that exist from the Paradigm <note>The divine model of the universe</note>; for that is the cause of simplicity for beings and of the gift to others of those things which it possesses primarily. But "that which is being" <note>original: *hoper on*</note> comes from the "One-Being"; for that is what is primarily set apart from non-being and privation, because it is primarily Being, and all things subsist in it secretly and indivisibly. But the "always" comes from Eternity; for as the "One-Being" is the source of existence, so Eternity is the provider of everlastingness to the intelligibles. If, then, Plato were making his argument about participants and things participated, and needed "Being" for this purpose, he would have said "Being-itself"; and if he were speaking of the unmixed and the mixed, he would have said...

If the "One" is above Being; since he <note>Plato</note> is discussing generation and the ungenerated state, and requires these definitions for that purpose, he reasonably asked: "What is that which always is?" For this distinguishes the eternal from that which subsists according to time. <margin>1) <note>original: "κατὰ χρόνον"</note></margin> For that which is generated has time as its coordinate, just as the ungenerated has eternity. Therefore, the nature of the Living Being <note>The "Intelligible Animal" or the Paradigm of the universe</note> which encompasses all intelligible living things is eternal, while time | came into existence along with the heavens, as he himself will say <margin>2)</margin> further on. However, even if that which "always is" is said to proceed from a cause, one must say that according to all its causes it does not "become," but "is." For the "reason why," the "goal toward which," and the "agent by whom" are not the same. For it is impossible for that which always is to be "becoming" by its own agency, lest it should at some point become "non-being"—for that which is becoming, while it is becoming, is not yet. Nor is it "becoming" toward itself <margin>3)</margin>, lest it be composite, nor "becoming" because of itself <margin>4)</margin>, lest it be incomplete. But the generated is suspended from another and has its passage into existence from other causes, such as is the case with everything corporeal. But <margin>4)</margin> <note>original: "ἀπορία" (difficulty/problem)</note> how is that which is becoming "never being," about which the *Sophist* explicitly said that this too "really is"? Or will he himself say this a little later <margin>5)</margin> <note>original: "λύσις" (solution)</note>—not that it is "non-being," but that it is "really never being"? Now, however, it is called "never being" because "Being" was previously assigned to the eternal nature, and that which is becoming is never that which "always is." If, therefore, "to be" or "Being" is unreceptive to "not being," it is clear that the generated—having been intertwined <margin>8)</margin> with non-being in whatever way—is impossible to ever be "Being" in the sense of being purely Being and Being in itself, which belongs to "to be" alone <margin>11)</margin>, rather than being together with "to be" and "not to be" in some way, being simultaneously | Being and non-being.

That which is graspable by intellect with a rational account <margin>12)</margin>, must be according to the same things <note>i.e., self-consistent/unchanging</note> Being; and that which is the object of opinion with irrational sensation, being generated and perishing, but really never Being.

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.

<page-num>173</page-num>

Of Plato. Some, having divided the matter, have presented the definition on one hand and the object of definition on the other in each of the two regions. For in the former region <note>the intelligible realm</note>, they show that "that which is graspable by intellect with the aid of reason" is the definition, while "that which is always the same" is the object defined. In the second region <note>the physical world</note>, they present "that which is the object of opinion with the aid of irrational sensation" as the definition, and the remainder as the essential subject itself. Our own teacher <note>likely Syrianus, Proclus' mentor</note> is also found to agree with what these men say. For if we were to slightly rearrange the phrasing, the whole matter will become immediately clear: "That which is always the same is graspable by intellect with the aid of reason," while "that which is becoming and perishing, but never truly is, is the object of opinion with the aid of irrational sensation."

For when is it consistent with what was said before? "What is that which always is, having no beginning <note>original: γένεσιν, 'genesis' or 'becoming'</note>, and what is that which is becoming, but never truly is?" Since that which is always the same does not have a beginning, and that which is becoming never truly is, the phrase "to that which is becoming and perishing" <margin>B</margin> signifies the same thing as "that which never truly is." Or perhaps it has been expressed even more clearly through the addition of "truly," indicating in Plato's style that insofar as it is "becoming," it *is not*, but insofar as it carries an image <note>original: ἔνλημα, a trace or reflection</note> of Being, to that extent it is "not-becoming." For in the ancient texts, he made the objects of definition even clearer through these additions. For when he said "always the same," he added "always" to "being the same" so that we would not understand "always" as a temporal duration, but as the eternal <term>aeonic: relating to eternity (aion) rather than linear time</term>. For this is "all at once" and "being the same," whereas the temporal is ranked with the infinity of time. And what he called "becoming," he spoke of alongside "perishing," so that we would not understand "processions" <note>the flowing out of divine principles</note> as simple "becomings"—which is a term even applied to the gods who are beyond Being—but rather those things which have "destruction" as their counterpart.

The definitions provided are therefore something like this: "Eternal Being is that which is graspable by intellect with the aid of reason"; "Becoming is that which is the object of opinion with the aid of irrational sensation." Regarding these, people are accustomed to bring charges against Plato: first, that he has not included a "genus" <note>a general category</note> as the rules of definition require; and second, that he has not revealed the nature of the defined objects <margin>C</margin> as they are in themselves, but has defined them based on our ways of knowing them. They argue one ought to examine things themselves according to their own nature, apart from this relationship to us. But we must accept the opposite: that those who wish to raise these difficulties are entirely mistaken. For what kind of "genus" has a place in the case of Being, which encompasses the entirety of intelligible substance? For if Substance <note>ousia</note> has no genus prior to itself, nor a definition...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato's Timaeus (27d-28a). Proclus is analyzing the formal definitions of "Being" (eternal reality) and "Becoming" (the physical world), debating whether "Being" should be considered a "genus" and how the human mind approaches these two distinct realms.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...being most generic, what would you say about Being itself, which encompasses every single power and all activities? Therefore, "Being" is not the genus <note>original: γένος</note> of "that which always is"; for this would be "a being" (a specific instance), not "Being" simply. Nor is it the genus of non-being, lest we inadvertently create "that which always is not." For in every case, a genus is predicated of its own specific kinds <note>original: εἰδῶν, 'species'</note>. Therefore, Being is not a genus. How then is the definition of these types of knowledge appropriate to the whole investigation and the proposed distinctions? For if, as we said before, we must use these as axioms and hypotheses for the demonstrations that are to follow, these definitions must be 

<margin>D</margin> well-known and clear to us. But if he <note>Plato</note> had merely commanded us to hunt for the nature of things on its own, he would have left us in obscurity, and his entire teaching would have been [unfinished]; but since he wants to make "Being" and "Becoming" known through their definitions, so that he may proceed from known things to demonstrations, he clearly presents their distinct characteristics to his listeners. Once we have awakened and perfected these concepts, we shall behold the nature of those things more clearly. 

Since every cognitive faculty either is the known object itself, or it sees it, or it possesses the known object (for Intellect <note>original: νοῦς, 'nous'</note> is the intelligible <note>original: νοητόν</note>, sensation sees the sensible, and discursive thought <note>original: διάνοια, 'dianoia'</note> possesses the object of thought within itself), and since we are not by nature the intelligible itself, but we know it through the power within us that is yoked to it, we must use this power; for through it, the nature of Being becomes known to us. We shall meet the difficulties in this way. 

But one should observe how, in proposing the problems to himself, he expressed each both negatively and affirmatively, yet in responding 

<margin>E</margin> to each, he employed only the affirmative for "that which always is," but for "becoming" he also used the negative, adding the term "perishing" and interpreting "being" as "never being" through its change into "really being" <note>Proclus refers to the Timaeus 28a: "becoming and perishing, but never truly being"</note>. For since Being is characterized by "to be" and Becoming by "not to be," in defining the former he used only Being, saying it is "always the same," but for the latter he used the negation—not merely the negation, since definitions consist of affirmations, indicating what belongs to each thing. 

And if he called it not only "becoming" but also "perishing," it is not surprising. For just as he added "always being the same" and "not having a beginning" to Being, so he added "perishing" to Becoming. For as "becoming," it is different from "always being," and as "perishing," it is different from "being always the same." For that which becomes, insofar as it is becoming, also perishes, being unable to sustain itself; for [if it could] it would be able to produce itself. Thus, having taken each one, 

<margin>F</margin> Being and Becoming, he saw the one as above generation, and the other...

### ON THE TIMAEUS II

[...imperishable] <note>original: ἀνώλεθρον; the start of the word is cut off in the margin</note> not being; for whenever a reflection of "Being" is added to that which is "Becoming," it is able to remain, in some sense, always "Becoming." Come then, let us examine each of the terms by themselves through which he <note>Plato</note> composes these definitions, and let us first of all observe how many ways intellection <term>noesis: the highest form of rational or intuitive grasp</term> is understood, and let us reason out its various progressions.

First, then, is the **Intelligible Intellection**, which arrives at the same point as the "Intelligible" <note>original: νοητόν; the object of thought</note> and is nothing other than the Intelligible itself; it is also an **essential intellection** <margin>75</margin> and **self-essence** <note>original: αὐτοουσία</note>, because everything in the Intelligible realm exists in this manner: essentially and intelligibly. 

Second is the intellection that **joins the Intellect to the Intelligible**; it possesses a connective and unitive property that brings the two extremes together, and it is entirely Life and Power, filling the Intellect from the Intelligible and establishing the Intellect within the Intelligible. 

Third is the **Intellection yoked within the Intellect itself**, which is the activity of the Intellect. Through this, it has grasped the Intelligible within itself; it is according to this that it "thinks" and is what it is. For it is both activity and **self-intellection**, yet it is not the "Intelligible Intellection," nor is it merely a potentiality, but an activity, as has been said: an **intellectual intellection**.

The fourth rank is held by the **intellection of partial intellects** <note>individual minds or spirits rather than the Universal Intellect</note>. For each of these also possesses something Intelligible yoked within itself and an intellection; or rather, each possesses all things in a partial way—Intellect, Intellection, and the Intelligible—through which it joins itself to the wholes and understands the entire Intelligible world and each of its parts. 

The fifth is the **intellection of the rational soul**. Just as the rational soul <note>original: ψυχή</note> is called "intellect," so too its knowledge is called "intellection"—a **transitional intellection** <margin>B</margin> that has time as something innate to itself <note>meaning human thought happens in a sequence over time, unlike the timeless flash of divine Intellect</note>. 

Sixth—if you wish to count this as well—is **imaginative knowledge** <note>original: φανταστική γνῶσις</note>, which is also addressed by some as a kind of "intellection." Imagination <note>original: φαντασία</note> is a **passive intellect** <note>original: νοῦς παθητικός; a term from Aristotle's "On the Soul"</note>, because it knows whatever it knows in a material way, involving impressions and shapes. 

For it is common to every kind of intellection to hold the objects of its knowledge within itself. This is surely how intellection differs from sensation. But in one case, intellection *is* the known objects themselves; in another, it is secondary but sees the primary object as a whole; in another, the known object is present partially, but the mind sees the wholes through that part; in another, it sees the wholes, but partially and not all at once; and in yet another, the vision occurs alongside a state of being affected <note>original: πάθους; passion or passive reception</note>. These, then, are the many differences of intellection. However, we must not now take "intellection" to mean the imaginative kind, for that is not of a nature to know **that which truly is**.

<summary>Proclus categorizes six levels of "intellection" (noesis), ranging from the divine identity of thought and being to the human soul's temporal reasoning and the "passive intellect" of imagination. He emphasizes that true intellection contains its objects within itself, unlike sensory perception.</summary>

<keywords>Proclus, Timaeus, noesis, intellect, intelligible, self-essence, rational soul, imagination, passive intellect, epistemology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s detailed breakdown of the definitions in Plato’s Timaeus. On the previous page, he categorized different levels of intellection (noesis). Here, he focuses on the "particular intellect" that connects human souls to the divine, and begins to define "reason" (logos) as it relates to eternal Being.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...for the imaginative faculty is indeterminate, because it knows with shape and form, whereas that which "Always Is" is shapeless; and generally, no irrational knowledge is able to contemplate Being itself, <margin>C</margin> since it is not even naturally suited to see the universal. Nor [can the knowledge] in the rational soul [see it]; for it does not possess the "all-at-once" quality nor that which is coordinate with the eternal, but it proceeds according to time. Nor [can] the universal intellections [see it]; for those are set apart from our forms of knowledge, but Timaeus joined **intellection** <term>noesis: a direct, non-discursive grasp of truth</term> with **reason** <term>logos: here meaning discursive or logical thought</term>.

But we must now take up the intellection of the **particular intellect**. This is the one through which we are able at times to see "Being." For just as sensation is in the "second dyad" below the rational soul, so intellection is above it in this same way. For the **particular intellect** <term>merikos nous: an individual manifestation of the divine Mind that acts as a guardian and goal for the human soul</term> is established immediately above our own essence, leading it upward and perfecting it; we turn back toward this intellect after being purified through philosophy and joining our own intellectual power to its intellection.

What this particular intellect is <note>original: τίς δὲ ὁ μερικὸς ἐστὶ νοῦς οὗτος</note>, and how it is not one in a numerical sense, but acts through those powers which are always active according to it—through which the particular souls sometimes participate in the intellectual light—this has been articulated at length elsewhere. For now, let this much be grasped: it is participated in by all other nearby **daemonic souls** <term>daemonic: in Neoplatonism, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense</term>, but it shines into our souls whenever we turn toward it and bring the intellectual reason within us to completion. 

And as in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato, Phaedrus 247C</note>, he <margin>D</margin> called this the "charioteer" of the soul and said that it alone thinks "Being," while the soul is nourished by intellect and knowledge along with this. In this way, then, this is also "intellection" and is both prior to the soul and is "Truly Being" intellection, but it is participated in by the soul whenever the reason acts intellectually. Therefore, in what follows, he will say that intellect is indeed in God, but the race of men participates in it only to a small degree <note>Plato, Timaeus 51E</note>.

And it seems that the argument, in revealing the knowledge of that which "Always Is," calls this first "intellection"; but so that one does not suppose it is the only kind, he added "reason" to "intellection," going through it in a transitional way. For when reason thinks that which "Always Is," as reason it acts transitionally, but as thinking, it acts with simplicity—thinking each thing as a simple whole at once, yet not thinking all things at once, but passing from some things to others. Yet, it thinks everything it thinks as one and simple while it passes through them.

After this definition of intellection, let us look at **reason** <note>original: λόγος (logos)</note>, what it is and how it is naturally joined to intellection. Reason is spoken of in three ways in the *Theaetetus* <note>Plato, Theaetetus 206C</note>: as vocal expression, as the progression through the elements [of a thing], and as the representation of the difference of each thing relative to others. But all these <margin>E</margin> meanings concern composition and division and happen to be ill-suited for the grasp of that which "Always Is." For by nature, "like is chosen by like," but that which "Always Is" is simple and indivisible, set apart from all things related to these [compositions].

<summary>Proclus explains that humans grasp eternal "Being" through a "particular intellect" (the charioteer of the soul) which mediates between our discursive reason and the divine. He also begins to analyze why standard definitions of "reason" (logos) are insufficient to describe the simple, indivisible nature of eternal reality.</summary>

<keywords>particular intellect, noesis, logos, Being, Phaedrus, Theaetetus, Neoplatonism, charioteer of the soul, daemonic souls</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the definitions of "Being" and "Becoming" in Plato's Timaeus. Having previously discussed the "particular intellect," Proclus now distinguishes between different levels of human cognition—opinion, discursive thought, and the "summit" of reason—and explains how the human soul can eventually grasp eternal Being by aligning itself with a higher, divine Intellect.</meta>

# ON TIMAEUS II.

->**[BOOK 2]**<-

<note>The left margin of this manuscript is heavily shadowed, leading to missing letters at the start of many lines. These have been reconstructed based on the philosophical context.</note>

...Further, [the soul's activity] is spoken of in another way: one as related to opinion, another to scientific knowledge, and another to intellect. For since there is in us opinion, discursive thought, and intellect, <unclear>and before the</unclear> intellect in these faculties, there is the highest point <term>akrotaton: the "summit" or "flower" of a faculty</term> of discursive thought; and since our entire essence <unclear>consists</unclear> of these, one must view "reason" <term>logos: here, the rational principle or discourse</term> differently in each of these cases. 

But opinion is not naturally <unclear>suited</unclear> to be joined with the intellection <term>noesis: a direct, non-discursive grasp of truth</term> of the active intellect; for on the contrary, it is yoked to the irrational <unclear>life</unclear>. Nor is discursive thought, insofar as it moves toward multiplicity and division, <unclear>such</unclear> as to run back up into the intellect; instead, it stands apart from noetic indivisibility due to the variety of its <unclear>arguments</unclear>. It remains, then, that the highest part of the soul <unclear>and</unclear> the most intellect-like part of discursive thought is established in the intellection of the particular intellect, being joined to it through its <unclear>essence</unclear>. 

This, then, is "reason"—that part of us which thinks the <unclear>intelligible objects</unclear>, and <note>original: οὐ "not"</note> Socrates in the *Republic* <note>Book VI, 511d</note> called this activity "intellection," <unclear>viewing</unclear> it as having knowledge of intermediate things, both intelligible and opinable. But if its <unclear>activity</unclear> is intellection, it would be a kind of intellect. <margin>F</margin> He <unclear>says</unclear> that this reason arises in the soul in what follows as the soul moves around the intelligible, just as scientific knowledge does; but <unclear>scientific</unclear> knowledge has a more complex activity, pressing upon things through other things, while the intellect has a simpler activity, contemplating beings as an eyewitness. 

This <unclear>unified</unclear> and most indivisible part of us is what Plato has now called "reason," in relation <unclear>to</unclear> our intellect and our intelligible nature. For when the soul stands <unclear>apart from</unclear> imagination and opinion and from complex | and indefinite knowledge, and runs back into its <margin>76</margin> own indivisibility—through which it is rooted in the particular intellect—and having run back, joins its own activity to the intellection of that [higher intellect], then indeed it thinks the intelligible along with that intellect. In this state, the activity is both one and dual-natured, and both sameness and difference exist within these intellections. For at that time, the soul's intellection becomes purer and closer to eternal realities, so that it may grasp the intelligible together with the intellect; it acts like a lesser light with a greater light, the reason within us running beneath the intellection of the intellect, so that the intelligible becomes comprehensible to us in conjunction with reason. 

For while our reason sees the intelligible along with intellection, the intellection of the [higher] intellect always *is* and sees the intelligible, and it gives reason to the soul whenever the soul also becomes intellect-like. But how has it encompassed "Truly Existing Being" by the particular intellect or by reason? For this is even more wondrous. Or is it that the intelligible itself cannot be encompassed by the intellect and reason, because it is superior to all encompassing and has encompassed all things in a transcendent manner?

Following the previous discussion on how the "summit" of discursive thought connects to a higher Intellect, Proclus now moves down the scale of the soul’s faculties to define the roles of Opinion (doxa) and Sensation (aisthesis), using Plato’s Republic and Theaetetus as foundational guides.</meta>

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, while the Intellect <term>nous: the highest intuitive faculty</term> possesses its own intelligible object within itself, and for this reason is said to encompass the whole of reality, Reason <term>logos: discursive or step-by-step thinking</term> is said to encompass Being by receiving notions from the Intellect that is coordinate <gloss>1) <note>original: systoichou</note></gloss> with it. Perhaps this also signifies <gloss>2)</gloss> that Reason, by "running around" the intelligible and acting and moving as if around a center, views it in this way; for while Intellection <term>noesis: the act of the Intellect</term> knows the object without transition or division <gloss>3)</gloss>, Reason dances in a circle around its essence and unfolds the unified substance of all things contained within it. Following these points, let us consider <gloss>4)</gloss> the nature of Opinion <term>doxa</term>. That it is the limit of the entire rational life and that it joins with the highest point of the irrational life is a matter frequently discussed. But let us now state what is unique to the Platonic tradition: that the faculty of Opinion contains the "reasons" <term>logoi: the formative principles or definitions</term> of sensible things, and it is this faculty that knows their essences <gloss>5)</gloss>. It observes the *fact* <note>the "that it is"</note> but remains ignorant of the *cause* <note>the "why it is"</note>. For while Discursive Thought <term>dianoia</term> knows both the essences and the causes <gloss>6)</gloss> of sensible things, Sensation knows neither <gloss>7)</gloss> (for it has been clearly shown in the *Theaetetus* <margin>C</margin> that Sensation is ignorant of essence and entirely unlearned regarding the cause of what it knows). It is therefore necessary that Opinion, being stationed in the middle, knows the essences of sensible things through the "reasons" within itself, but remains ignorant of the causes. In this way, right opinion would differ from scientific knowledge <term>episteme</term>, in that <gloss>8)</gloss> it knows <gloss>9)</gloss> only the *fact*, while the latter is also able to contemplate the *cause*. Sensation is attached to Opinion, being itself in the middle between the sense-organ and Opinion. For the sense-organ perceives sensible things through a "passion" <term>pathos: a physical impression or suffering</term>, which is why it is destroyed by their excesses; but Opinion <gloss>10)</gloss> possesses knowledge pure of passion. Sensation, however, participates in passion in a way, yet possesses something cognitive, insofar as <gloss>11)</gloss> it is both established in the faculty of Opinion and is illuminated by it, becoming <gloss>12)</gloss> "reason-like" though it is irrational in itself. Into this faculty terminates the series of cognitive powers: Intellection leads the way <gloss>13)</gloss>, being above reason and unchanging; Reason holds the second rank, being the intellection of our soul as it touches upon beings transitionally <note>moving from one thought to the next</note>; third is Opinion, which is a rational knowledge of sensible things; and fourth is Sensation, which exists as an irrational knowledge of those same things. For Discursive Thought, being in the middle of Intellection <margin>D</margin> and Opinion, is the knower of the "middle forms" <note>mathematical objects or concepts</note>, which require a projection that is dimmer than that of Intellection, yet clearer than that of Opinion—just as Socrates <gloss>14)</gloss> said on the previous day when distinguishing the types of knowledge by their objects. Thus, Opinion must be addressed as being "according to reason," because it possesses the rational principles that know the...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s investigation into the hierarchy of the soul's faculties. Having previously discussed the higher intellect and discursive reason, he now descends to the level of Opinion and Sensation to explain how we perceive and identify objects in the physical world.</meta>

### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II

...irrational in another way, as it is also <note>original: kai</note> ignorant of causes. For how could knowledge be irrational? This is what Socrates says in the *Symposium* <note>original: Symposio; specifically Plato, Symposium 202a</note> regarding it. Sensation must certainly <note>original: pantos</note> be considered irrational. For in general, while each of the senses recognizes a "passion" <term>pathos: a physical impression or "undergoing" of an external stimulus</term> produced in the living being by the object of sense—for instance, when an object is brought near, the sight knows it is red from the passion in the eye, the smell knows it is fragrant from the passion in the nostrils, the taste knows it is sweet, and touch knows it is smooth—what is it that says, "this thing brought near is an apple"? It is not any of the particular senses; for each of these knows only one specific quality of the object, not the whole. Nor is it the "common sense" <term>koine aisthesis: the faculty that coordinates different sensory inputs</term>; <margin>E</margin> for this faculty only distinguishes the differences between the various impressions, but it does not know that the whole thing is of such-and-such an essence. It is clear that there is some power superior to the senses which knows the whole and, as it were, contemplates its form <term>eidos: the internal blueprint or "idea" of the object</term> without dividing it into parts, acting as a unifying bond for the many sensory powers. This power, then, Plato has called Opinion <term>doxa</term>, and for this reason the sensible object is called "that which is subject to opinion" <term>doxaston</term>. Furthermore, since the senses often report impressions <gloss>passions</gloss> as being of a certain kind when they are not actually so, what is it in us that judges and says that the sight is deceived when it claims the sun is only a foot wide, or that the taste of the sick is wrong when it declares honey to be bitter? It is completely clear that in all these cases, the senses report the physical impression and are not entirely lying; for they report the experience regarding the sensible objects, and that experience is indeed as they say. But the power that speaks of the cause of the impression and passes judgment on it is something else. There is, therefore, a certain power of the soul superior to sensation, which no longer knows through a physical organ, but through itself, correcting the "coarseness" of sensation. <margin>F</margin> And while this power is "rational" in relation to sensation, it is "irrational" in relation to the knowledge of things that truly exist <note>Meaning it lacks the absolute certainty of divine or mathematical knowledge</note>.

...while sensation is simply irrational. Therefore, in the **Republic** ¹) he [Plato] declared opinion to be a middle ground between knowledge and ignorance. For opinion is indeed a rational form of knowledge, but it is blended with irrationality, as it knows sensible things by means of sensation. Sensation itself, however, is purely ²) irrational, just as the **Timaeus** addressed it. First, this is because sensation exists even in irrational animals and is the identifying characteristic 
<margin>77</margin>of all irrational life; for by this ³) the argument in the **Theaetetus** ⁴) distinguished sensation from science <term>episteme: certain, demonstrative knowledge of truth</term>. Second, because among all the parts of the irrational soul, sensation is the one that is disobedient ⁵) to reason. For the spirited part <term>thymoeides: the seat of anger and courage</term> and the desiring part <term>epithymetikon: the seat of physical appetite</term> are obedient to reason and its commands and can receive education from it; but sensation, even if it hears a thousand times from reason stating that the sun is larger than the earth, still sees it as a foot across and would not report it to us in any other way. Third, then, sensation does not even know the very thing it perceives; for it is not its nature to see its essence <term>ousia: the underlying reality or "whatness" of a thing</term>. It does not know *what* "white" is, but through the affection <term>pathos: the physical impression or "undergoing" of a stimulus</term> it has known ⁶) that something is white, and the sense organ has made a distinction ⁷); on this account, therefore, it is irrational. For in the **Gorgias** ⁸) he defined irrational knowledge in this way: as that which does not know, but merely guesses. Fourth, because sensation is the boundary of the entire series of knowledges; it has its essence furthest from reason ⁹) and intellect, belongs to the realm of external things, and 
<margin>B</margin>achieves its perception through the body. All these points demonstrate its irrationality. It is the case, ¹⁰) then, that everything generated <term>geneton: physical things that come into being and pass away</term> is graspable by opinion combined with sensation—the latter reporting the physical affections, while the former projects the reasons for them from itself and knows their essences ¹¹). And just as ¹²) reason, when joined ¹³) with intellection, sees the intelligible world, so also opinion, when coordinated with sensation, knows ¹⁴) the generated world. For since the soul is of a middle essence, it fills the gap between intellect and irrationality. By its highest part, it is joined with intellect, but with its lowest part, it leans toward sensation. Therefore, the **Timaeus**, in the first pairing, placed intellection before reason, as it is superior; but in the second pairing, he placed opinion before sensation. For in the first case, reason follows intellection as being a lesser kind of intellect ¹⁵), but here, opinion precedes sensation as being a kind of "rational sensation." The entire breadth of the rational essence is defined by opinion and reason; but our King is Intellect, and Sensation is the Messenger, as says the...

Plotinus ¹). And reason <term>logos: the discursive reasoning power</term> indeed together with the mind <term>nous: the higher intuitive intellect</term> sees the intelligible <term>noeton: the realm of true being and forms</term>, but by itself it contemplates the inner reasons <term>logoi: the formative principles or "blueprints" within the soul</term>; but opinion <term>doxa</term> together with sensation sees the generated <term>geneton: anything that comes into being and passes away</term>, but by itself <margin>C</margin> it examines all the forms within it. | Regarding these matters, it has been said elsewhere how it <note>opinion</note> subsists, and how the opinionative part of the soul is their place. And for that [the mind], the intelligible is graspable, but for this [opinion], the generated is "opinable." For the object of knowledge is outside of it and not within, just as the intelligible is for that [the mind]; it is not "graspable" <note>in the sense of certain, intellectual apprehension</note>, but is called "opinable," and yet it is not called "sensible," because opinion knows the essences <term>ousiai: the underlying reality or "whatness"</term> of things, but sensation does not. From the superior knowledge it also takes its name—the knowledge that knows *what* a thing is and not only *what sort* of thing it is, which we said was the work of sensation. It is reasonable, then, that Timaeus addressed it as both "generated" and "opinable"; for this is its characteristic. For even the one in the **Parmenides** ⁸) for this reason titled the treatment of sensible things as being "according to opinion," since sensible things are "opinable" in their very nature. Therefore, one should not call the generated only "sensible," because sensation is not knowledgeable of the essence of anything, nor should one call it "opinable" without sensation; for opinion knows the reasons within itself and generally knows itself—things which are certainly not among the generated. Fittingly, then, he previously called it "opinable with sensation" ¹⁰). These are the things we have to say regarding the Platonic words. But Aristotle ¹²) seems in these matters to have particularly criticized the second argument; for [he asks] is it truly the case that what is opinable by opinion with sensation is that which is "becoming" and | <margin>D</margin> "perishing"? For the heaven <note>ouranos: the cosmos or the celestial sphere</note> is ungenerated and indestructible ¹⁴), yet it is opinable by opinion with sensation. Timaeus, as he proceeds, will indeed investigate whether the whole heaven has come into being; but let it be said by us even now, that "becoming" and "perishing" exist by analogy even in the heaven, not only regarding the motions and the changes of shapes, but also because the heavenly body is not generative of itself ¹⁷), but subsists from another cause alone ¹⁸). For this reason...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the Timaeus. Having just discussed how Opinion and Sensation relate to the "generated" world of change, Proclus now moves into a metaphysical analysis of what it means for the physical universe (the "heaven") to be "generated" and "corporeal," contrasting it with the "truly existing" eternal realm.</meta>

### PROCLUS

...is generated, in the sense that it has the cause of its existence suspended from another. Since it not only subsists from something else ¹), but is also held together by something else—being unable to hold itself together—it therefore perishes according to its own nature. This is because "becoming" <term>genesis: the process of coming-into-being</term> is taken as the counterpart to "perishing." For those things which truly exist and always exist both beget themselves and are held together by themselves; for this reason, they are called "ungenerated" ³) and "imperishable" ⁴) according to their own nature. If that which truly exists is ungenerated and subsists from itself ⁵), then that which does not subsist from itself would not be truly ungenerated. Likewise, if that which is truly imperishable is naturally inclined to hold itself together ⁶), then that which is not naturally inclined to hold itself together is not truly imperishable ⁷). However, the heaven (and by "heaven" I mean ⁸) only

<margin>E</margin>
its corporeal nature) | is naturally capable of neither producing itself ⁹) nor sustaining itself. For everything of this sort—that which is capable of producing itself and sustaining itself—is impartite <term>amerês: without parts, indivisible</term>. Therefore, the heaven is not truly ungenerated ¹⁰) nor truly imperishable ¹¹); rather, insofar as it is corporeal, it is both generated and fashioned. Furthermore, as Aristotle ¹²) himself says and demonstrates clearly and nobly, no finite body possesses infinite power. The heavenly body is finite; therefore, it does not possess infinite power. But the imperishable, insofar as it is imperishable, possesses infinite power. Therefore, the body, insofar as it is body, is not imperishable ¹³). Thus, this point is demonstrated even according to the logic of Aristotle. In what way the heaven is ungenerated and eternal ¹⁴) will be made clear to us a little later. For now, only this is evident from what has been said: that according to itself, everything corporeal is in a state of becoming and perishing, and "never truly is," just as he <note>Plato</note> himself says in the **Politicus** ¹⁵).

> To exist forever in the same state and to be the same belongs only to the most divine of all things, but the nature of body is not of this order. That which we have named "heaven" or "cosmos" has received many blessed gifts from its begetter ¹⁸);
> <margin>F</margin>
> however, | it also participates in body, which is why it is impossible for it to be entirely free from change ¹⁹).

It has been stated, then, how the heaven also falls under the aforementioned definitions. But if the divine Aristotle ²⁰) <note>original: "daimonios Aristoteles" — here meaning "divinely brilliant" or "superhuman"</note> should again raise difficulties regarding the definition of that which "always exists," refusing to say that everything which "always exists" is "graspable by the mind with the aid of reason," because there is... ²¹)

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus. Having distinguished between the eternal and the temporal, Proclus now addresses how the physical universe participates in eternity through "becoming" and begins a crucial discussion on the "criteria" (the standards of truth) used to perceive different levels of reality.</meta>

...the most divine of visible things, we shall deem it right that he does not <note>original: μὴ (mê). A textual correction discussed in the footnotes.</note> confound the eternal and that which subsists through the whole of time. For he [Plato] himself distinguishes eternity and time, assigning eternity to the Intellect, and time to the heaven and the motion <margin>78</margin> of the heaven. That which is "always being"—the eternal—is of the kind that Timaeus has described. But the most divine of visible things are eternal in another way, according to an eternal duration; yet they are produced throughout all time from their own causes, and their whole being consists in "becoming" <term>genesis: the process of coming-into-being, as opposed to static existence</term>. It has been said by him that eternity is connatural with the intelligibles, containing and encompassing infinite time, and that the eternal is truly intelligible <note>original: νοητὸν ὄντως (noêton ontôs)</note>. But if this "always" signifies the eternal, why is it necessary to trace the nature of the heaven back to this "always," rather than saying it is "always becoming," as if extending alongside the eternity of time? 

Thus we have resolved both objections, based on his own words, which he brought against these definitions. But since we are weary of this inquiry, we must move on from these matters; for they will be spoken of directly. In general, however, one must grasp the opinion Plato holds regarding the criteria <term>kritêria: the standards or faculties by which we judge truth</term>. For while others have established different criteria—some sensation, as the <margin>B</margin> Pythagoreans say; some opinion, like the one who says "opinion is built upon all things" <note>A reference to the philosopher Xenophanes, who argued that human knowledge is merely "opinion" (doxa).</note>; some reason, and some intellect—Plato divided the essence of the criteria appropriately to the objects of knowledge. He assigned intellect <term>nous</term> to the intelligibles, discursive reason <term>dianoia: step-by-step logical reasoning</term> to the objects of thought, opinion to the objects of opinion, and sensation to the objects of sensation. 

And do not think these criteria exist as fragmented things according to him. For the soul is both one and many. If, therefore, that which judges is the soul (for surely our body does not possess a judicial power), and the soul is one and many, then the judicial faculty is also both one and many; the power of judgment is both uniform and multiform. Someone might ask: what is this one power? We shall say: Reason <term>logos</term>. For this power, when it sets itself to the contemplation of the intelligibles, uses itself and intellection—not that intellection is an instrument while the reason is the user, as Severus the Platonist <note>Severus was a 2nd-century Platonist whose works are mostly lost; Proclus often cites him to disagree with his more "mechanical" views of the soul.</note> thinks, placing intellection as inferior to reason, but because intellection is the light of reason, being its perfection and the means of its ascent, brightening the judicial power within it. But when it enters into the judgment of intermediate reasons, it uses discursive reason and uses only itself, turned toward itself through this; but for the objects of opinion...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "criteria" of truth and the faculties of the soul. Proclus is now moving from how we perceive physical objects to the metaphysical distinctions between Being and Becoming, and how the "middle" entities like the Soul and Time fit into this framework.</meta>

## ON THE TIMAEUS II.

->185<-

<note>The text begins mid-sentence</note> [...] things he proposed previously, such as that which **always is** and has no **generation** <term>genesis: the process of coming-into-being</term>, and again that which is **generated** and **never is**. He does this so that through affirmations he might set apart those things that belong to neither <note>original: "μηδετέρου"</note> <gloss>Perhaps "participating" (original: μετέχοντα), as the scribe’s eyes may have strayed to the following words.</gloss>, and through negations he might distinguish <note>original: "διαστήσηται"</note> those things that have participated in both in some way. 

Since these are the extremes—the entire **intelligible** and **intellectual** essence on one hand, and the **sensible** on the other—one must also observe the nature that lies in the middle. For Timaeus calls both **time** and the **soul** "generated," and it is clear that since these are not sensible objects, they are in one sense "beings" and in another sense "generated," and they belong entirely to neither | category. <margin>F</margin> Therefore, Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> was correct in saying that Plato is now defining the extremes: that which is primarily "always being" and that which is "only generated." He passed over the middle terms, such as that which is simultaneously "becoming and being," or "being and becoming." Of these, the "being and becoming" belongs to the breadth of **souls**, while the reverse—"becoming and being"—belongs to the highest <note>original: "τῇ ἀκροτάτῃ"</note> of generated things. 

Such also is the nature of the **Universe**, which gives life to the whole. For this nature, insofar as it is divisible among bodies, is entirely "generated," but insofar as it is completely incorporeal, it is "ungenerated." | To say that **matter** <term>hyle: the underlying "stuff" of the universe</term> is also <margin>79</margin> "becoming and being" is absurd. For in that way, matter would be superior to sensible, generated things, if the latter were only "generated" while matter also participated in "being." 

If you wish <note>Margin of manuscript A: "How the middle things are known"</note>, take the "only always being" and the "only generated" as separate, and by removing **Intellect** <term>nous: the highest intuitive mind</term> from one of the terms and **Sensation** from the other, you will create the definition of the middle. For this middle is known by **Reason** <term>logos</term> and **Opinion** <term>doxa</term>. Reason knows both itself and Opinion, and Opinion knows itself and Reason—the former knows both along with their cause, while the latter <note>original: "ἡ", corrected from "ὁ"</note> knows both without the cause. It is in this way that Reason and Opinion are distinguished. Opinion is known by Reason, and Reason by Opinion, and the whole soul is known through both of these as they are middle faculties. 

Just as you might take the "worse" of the two higher faculties—for example, **Reason**—and turn it into a **bastard reason**, and take the lower faculty—**Sensation**—and turn it into an **insensible sensation**, you will understand <note>original: "πῶς", manuscript B reads "πως"</note> how Plato thinks **Matter** is known <note>Reference to Plato's Timaeus 52B</note>: by a "bastard reason" and an "insensible sensation." | And proportionally, by taking the "better" from each and making a "bastard" according to the better part, you will have <margin>B</margin> <note>Margin of manuscript A: "How the One is known"</note> how **the One** is known: for it is known by a "bastard intellect" and a "bastard opinion." Therefore, it is not "simple" in the strict sense, nor is it known from a cause. It is "bastard" because it is known in a way that transcends each faculty. For it does not know from a cause, and that object [the One] is not known from a cause, but by its not having a cause. Intellect knows that which is simple, but a "bastard intellect" knows that [the One].

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Plato’s Timaeus. Having previously defined the "extremes" of Being (the eternal) and Becoming (the physical), Proclus now moves to the logical axioms that govern the creation of the world, specifically the necessity of a Cause.</meta>

# PROCLUS

->186<-

...because it is **superior** <note>original: κρεῖττον (kreitton)</note> to intellection. Therefore, that which is superior is "bastard" in relation to the intellect, because even that [the One] is superior to being simple—such as the **intelligible** which is truly for the intellect—and the intellect is of the same kind, but not "bastard." That [the One] therefore "thinks" with its "non-intellect," while this [the soul or intellect] is one in itself, according to which it is also **god**.

**Everything that becomes, of necessity becomes by some cause. For it is impossible for anything to have its generation without a cause.** (**Plato, Timaeus 28 A.**)

Truly, according to the **geometrical method**, he introduces these **axioms** after the **definitions**. For having stated what **Being** is and what **Becoming** is, he adds these other "common notions": that everything that becomes is produced by a cause. <margin>C</margin> And that which is not produced by a cause is not even able to have **generation** <term>genesis: the process of coming-into-being</term>. It is clear | from these points that the "thing to be divided" <note>original: διαιρετέον (diaireteon)</note> did not indicate a method of division, but rather that the **hypotheses** are to be clearly defined. For the statements that "everything that becomes becomes by some cause of necessity," and "it is impossible to have generation without a cause," and subsequently "that which is produced according to an **eternal model** is completed as beautiful"—all these are given for the purpose of definition, being axioms and not parts of a division. 

Since one of these statements just mentioned is more evident, and the other is less familiar and clear, he positions the one as a **middle term** and the other as a **conclusion**. For the statement "everything that becomes becomes of necessity by some cause" is a **conclusion**, while "it is impossible for anything to have generation without a cause" is the **middle term**. This is so that the **syllogism** <term>a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term> might be **categorical** in the **first figure**, as follows: 
1. That which becomes is impossible to become without a cause. 
2. This [the thing becoming] must of necessity become by some cause. 
3. Therefore, everything that becomes becomes by some cause of necessity. 

For it is better to conclude in this way, just as the **divine Iamblichus** <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher whom Proclus deeply admired</note> <margin>D</margin> judged, | rather than to make it a **hypothetical syllogism**, as some others do. 

But is every middle term more familiar than the conclusion? For to be clear that something is "impossible not to be" is not the same as it being "necessary to be," and "necessary to be" is not the same as "impossible not to be." Or perhaps they are the same, but often the "necessary to be" is not familiar, while the "impossible not to be" is familiar. For example, a doctor says it is "necessary to be nourished," and he might persuade the sick person less; but if he says it is "impossible to live without being nourished," this immediately humbles <note>original: συστέλλει (systellei) - literally "contracts" or "draws in," meaning the statement strikes home or forces the listener to accept the truth</note> the listener. Again, we say death is **necessary** for a certain cause, for it is **impossible** not to die; and it is **necessary** for a debtor to pay back money to a tyrant, for it is **impossible** not to pay it back; and so it is with other things...

<summary>Proclus explains Plato's use of the "geometrical method" in the Timaeus, framing the claim that everything created must have a cause as a formal logical syllogism. He highlights the distinction between necessity and impossibility as a rhetorical and pedagogical tool used by Plato.</summary>

### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.

->187<-

...in many <note>original: [πολλ]ῶν; reconstructed from context</note> cases you might see one thing as less clear and the other as better known, even if the same word <note>original: [ὑ]πὸ (hypo), likely referring to the underlying meaning</note> seems to signify the same thing. How then is one clearer than the other in the present case? For what if this is true in some instances, but in others not true? Or is it easy to understand even here, how that which **becomes** <term>gignomenon: the physical world in flux</term>, when separated from its **cause** <term>aition: the source of existence</term>, is impossible and weak? For that which is unable to preserve itself or to be held together by its own power, | but which receives both its preservation and its <margin>E</margin> cohesion from the cause alone—if it were to be separated from that cause, it is clear that it becomes impossible in itself and departs into **non-being**, scattering away. This very fact proves that it is impossible for the thing that becomes to come into being without a cause. For if it is becoming, it is brought into being by something that acts upon it. It was therefore correctly stated in the *Philebus* <note>Plato, Philebus 26E</note> as well, that "that which is becoming" is "that which is being made," and "that which is making" is the cause for the thing being made. And if this is so, it either becomes by its own power or by another. But if it were by its own power, it would result in the same thing as **True Being**, and it would be the same thing—both becoming and **eternally being**—and it would be among those things that exist eternally. But if it is not by its own power, it is certainly by another. For that which becomes must be brought into being by something, since it is a thing that "becomes" and is not "Being" itself. For that which does not hold itself together by its own active power will be affected by another, and being weak in itself, it receives its power from another. Furthermore, even if the same thing were to act and be acted upon, insofar as it is **passive**, it is acted upon by another, and insofar as it is **productive**, it acts upon another. And that which becomes, insofar as it is becoming, is passive; | but if it is passive, it is acted upon by another. <margin>F</margin> For it is not in its nature to generate itself. For then it would have to exist before it came into being, and be in "actuality" <note>original: ἐνεργείᾳ (energeia)</note> before it was in "potentiality" <note>original: δυνάμει (dynamei)</note>. For that which acts upon the potential must itself exist in actuality. It is with good reason, then, that Plato, when linking the "thing that becomes" to its cause—which he did in his conclusion—used the phrase **"by necessity."** For permanence and stability, along with **persuasion** <note>original: πειθοῦς (peithous); some manuscripts read "suffering" (pathous)</note>, come to the thing that becomes from its cause, just as he says in the *Politicus* <note>Plato, Politicus 270A</note> that an "acquired immortality" is granted to the world | by the **Father**. <margin>80</margin> But when he separated the thing that becomes from its cause—which he did in the middle of the sentence by setting the thing that becomes apart—he used the word **"impossible."** For seen by itself, it is vanishing and incomplete. Furthermore, in saying "cause," he indicates the unified power of the **Demiurgic** <term>demiurgic: the "craftsman" or creator god</term> principle, calling the creative power "cause," and not simply that which gives existence to something else. For Socrates also said that **The Good** is the cause of the **intelligibles** <note>Plato, Republic VI, 509B</note>; but the Good is not "demiurgic." For the demiurgic is assigned to **Generation** <term>genesis: the realm of change</term>, as he said in the *Philebus*, that the "worker" <note>the demiurge</note> belongs to the "becoming"; hence there are causes prior to the world, but they are causes of other things, and are not "demiurgic."

And since, as Aristotle says, all things are ordered toward the Form, there must also be an end to the ordering, and "that which is in vain" <margin>**E**</margin> should have no place in the whole; for even that which seems to be in vain in the part is beneficial to the whole. These things he says elsewhere; but it seems that the statement made in the *Philebus* <note>Plato's Philebus 23D</note> is more universal than this axiom: that **everything mixed has its existence from some cause of the mixture.** For whether the things being mixed are to be mixed by chance or however it happens, there must be one cause of the divided things and a unifying one, providing the form to the mixture. 

And this [cause] is in one place a god, in another an intellect, in another a soul, in another nature, and in another some art imitating nature. Everything that comes into being is mixed, but not everything mixed is a thing that comes into being. For even the very first of beings consist of things mixed with one another: the **Limit** <term>peras: the principle of definition and boundary</term> and the **Unlimited** <term>apeiron: the principle of expansion and multiplicity</term>. From these, at least, he says, beings and bodies consist. Therefore, everything here is analogous to everything there: the creative power to the One, the form to the Limit, the power to the Unlimited, and the generated thing to the mixture. But those things there are more universal than these, for the former are observed in all things, while the latter only in worldly things. For even the Intellect is a <margin>**F**</margin> mixture, as knowledge and as infinite power, and the soul as both indivisible and divisible. 

So the cause is the cause of the thing that comes into being, just like something being mixed, but not everything [mixed is generated]. From which it is also clear how the **Demiurge** <term>Demiurge: the divine Craftsman of the world</term> is second [after the One], making the mixture, but a generated mixture. Since these things are causes...

The following syllogism <term>syllogism: a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term> arises: the world has come into being. Everything that has come into being has a creator as its cause. Everything | having a cause in a creator also has a paradigmatic cause <term>paradigmatic cause: an eternal model or blueprint</term>. <margin>C</margin> The world has both a creative cause and a paradigmatic cause. And just as with the axioms <note>referring to the philosophical principles established earlier in the text</note> there were two hypotheses—what is that which always is, and what is that which becomes—and of the secondary ones another two—everything that becomes has a cause, and that which does not have a cause is <unclear>not</unclear> generated—so too regarding these matters there are two common notions: that which is made in relation to what is truly real is beautiful, while that made in relation to what is generated is not beautiful. And each <unclear>of these</unclear> is entirely true. For the one who creates in relation to the intelligible <term>intelligible: the realm of eternal Forms that can only be grasped by the mind</term> either <unclear>creates</unclear> it similarly or dissimilarly. If indeed he creates it similarly, he will make the imitation beautiful, for the model was primarily beautiful; but if dissimilarly, he does not create in relation to the intelligible, for the opposite of similarity occurs. And the one who creates something in relation to a generated thing—if he truly looks <unclear>toward</unclear> that—it is clear that he does not create something beautiful. For that thing itself is full of <unclear>dissimi</unclear>larity and is not the primarily beautiful; thus, the generated object will be far removed from beauty. Even Phidias, who made the statue of Zeus, did not look at a <unclear>gen</unclear>erated thing <note>original: "gegonos"; meaning a physical person or mortal model</note>, but rather reached a conception <margin>D</margin> of the Zeus found in Homer. If he were able to stretch himself toward the intellectual god himself, it is clear that he would have produced his own work even more beautifully. From the model, the quality of <unclear>being</unclear> beautiful reaches the image; but from the maker comes the similarity or dissimilarity to the arch<unclear>etype</unclear>. The image is called an "image" in relation to the model, but in relation to the <unclear>maker</unclear>, it is called a "work" and a "result." Wherefore Plato himself, whenever he speaks of a "model," joins to it its <unclear>ima</unclear>ge. Thus, one must speak of the model and the <unclear>ima</unclear>ge in this way; but when he speaks of the "Demiurge" <term>Demiurge: the divine craftsman of the universe</term>, he speaks of the "work," as in: "The works of which I am the demiurge <unclear>and fa</unclear>ther, are indissoluble, so long as I will it." <note>original: "ὧν ἐγὼ δημιουργὸς πατήρ τε ἔργων, ἄλυτα ἐμοῦ γε ἐθέλοντος"; quoting Timaeus 41a</note> Now, there being <unclear>three</unclear> kinds of models (for a model is either eternal of an eternal thing, or eternal of a generated thing, or <unclear>generat</unclear>ed of a generated thing): when the model of an eternal thing is eternal, the entirely eternal is the model of that which is eternal in a certain respect, just as the Intellect is the model of the Soul. When it is the eternal of the generated, this too is <unclear>eter</unclear>nal, according to infinite time. But when it is an entirely generated model of a generated thing, it has fallen away <unclear>from</unclear> eternity. For it is not possible for that which is generated in its essence to be productive <margin>E</margin>. Therefore, those things participate in beauty and order from their models, insofar as they are imitations of a stable nature; but these things, arising as if from changes and moving things, are not beautiful—yet they are not entirely ugly, but are defined only by the negation of beauty. And whatever beauties are "offspring," these too are not beautiful in comparison to that Beauty; rather, they are drawn from the beauty that reaches sensible likenesses from the eternal model. And perhaps for these reasons Timaeus did not say [the model] in relation to the generated...

...is the provider of beauty, holding the highest rank among eternal beings and belonging to the first rank of the intelligibles <term>intelligibles: eternal realities that can be grasped by the mind rather than the senses</term>.¹⁾ Therefore, the beauty-making cause exists there,²⁾³⁾ which is the reason why all things are beautiful: intellect, soul, and the nature of the body. Again, the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the "Craftsman" or Creator of the physical world</term> is the cause of form, while the Paradigm is the cause of beauty, and the Good is the cause of unity. This Good is simultaneously the provider of all things, while the paradigmatic cause provides both beauty and form, and the creative cause, being intellectual, provides form and essence.

Indeed, the creative cause, as it looks toward the intelligible, is multi-faceted.⁴⁾ For the total Demiurge creates in one way by looking toward that paradigm⁵⁾ (and in this way⁶⁾ he is unified with it in supreme transcendence), while the creative triad creates in another way. In this triad, the first member acts in a unifying way, the second in a generative <note>original: γενητικῶς; meaning "producing or giving birth to"</note> way, and the last in a returning <note>original: ἐπιστρεπτικῶς; referring to the way created things "turn back" toward their source</note> way. 

This creation is seen differently among the "ruling" gods, differently among the "absolute" gods, and differently among the "cosmic" gods. Following these, one must observe the creative process proceeding in another manner into the many creative gods, who receive the paternal powers from their superiors and divide them among themselves. <margin>F</margin> Together with⁷⁾ these, one finds the creative angels, and in another way the demons who are the attendants⁸⁾ of this order. Furthermore, there are the "unstained forms of life" that contribute to the creative chain, and the ranks of partial souls that follow the creative choir. For the specific character and manner of "making"—and of looking toward the intelligible—descends through all of these, differently from one to the next.

One must also admire this point in Plato: how he did not say that what comes into being according to an eternal paradigm⁹ is beautiful, <margin>83</margin> but rather that what is made by the Demiurge *looking* toward that paradigm is beautiful.¹⁰⁾ For even the "discordant and unordered" pre-cosmic state—which was a "generated" thing (since it was visible and sensible, and as Plato will say later, everything of that sort is generated and has come into being)—had received certain "traces" of forms from the intelligible¹¹ before the actual creation began. Yet, it was not beautiful,¹²⁾ except perhaps in a limited sense compared to the formlessness of raw matter. 

Therefore, it is not simply that which is made according to an eternal paradigm that is beautiful (such as that unordered and discordant state), but specifically that which was made by the Creator while he was looking toward that paradigm. For the Demiurge was absent from that earlier state, even though the Intelligible was present before the Demiurge and was already shining down upon it. But whatever has come into being from the Demiurge has also come from that Paradigm¹³⁾ toward itself¹⁴⁾ through the mediation of the active Demiurge. Insofar as a thing comes from the Paradigm, it receives its form; insofar as it comes from the Demiurge, it is set in order. For the Demiurge is the cause of order, whereas the Paradigm is simply the cause of form for those things that participate in it. Furthermore, from <margin>B</margin> the Paradigm itself, one must grasp the difference between the various creative powers. For some look toward the whole intelligible realm and¹⁵⁾ create according to the whole, and of these...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's detailed analysis of the Demiurge’s relationship to his "model" or "paradigm." Following the discussion of the beauty-making cause on the previous page, Proclus here examines why Plato uses specific Greek phrases like "such a model" or "a certain intelligible" to describe the blueprints of creation.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II

->185<-

...they act, while others act partially. Some view the model through unity, others through [distinction], and others again do not act according to the whole of the intelligible realm. Instead, some have divided it into four primary causes, while others have proceeded to a greater number. Still others take the lowest forms as the model for their own offspring; and through these, there is one shepherd for men and another for horses, as stated in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politicus", 267D; a dialogue by Plato</note>, and similarly for the other species. 

Since the creative series is manifold and there are different models—some more universal and others more partial—it is for good reason that Timaeus did not say that the one who uses "this" specific intelligible model makes the thing becoming beautiful, but rather he who uses "such a" model. For even the one who uses the "Human-itself" <term>Human-itself: the eternal, perfect Idea of a human being</term> uses "such a model." At any rate, the "Whole" is somehow present in those partial forms because of the unity of the intelligibles, and the multitude is most similar to the Monad <term>Monad: the principle of oneness</term> because of the dominance of Sameness. 

<margin>C</margin> Indeed, the whole Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the divine Craftsman of the universe</term> looks toward the intelligible and perfect Living Being, but he uses the intellectual paradigm within himself, possessing the intelligible in an intellectual manner. This internal model is "such a thing" as that [greater one], due to its similarity to it, yet it is also more partial than it. For this reason, Plato added the word "certain" <note>original: "tini"</note>. For these intelligibles participate in that [Perfect Living Being] and are more partial than it. Therefore, he called the Idea "a certain something" <note>original: "ti"</note>, making the thing produced similar to the intellectual model. 

Creation provides both essences and powers to the things brought into being. Why, then, when speaking of that which "always is," did he use the phrase "using such a model," but for that which has "come into being," he no longer added "such a," but instead introduced the term "generated" <note>original: "gennēton"</note>? Or is it because that which "always is" had something similar to itself, being at the very peak, whereas the "generated" has nothing else similar to it? For that which is produced in relation to it is "generated." To the one [the eternal], "the similar" and "the same" are natural, but to the other [the generated], "the dissimilar" is characteristic. 

So much for these matters. The word "always" should be joined with "that which is the same," as in: "looking toward that which is always the same." This is how the philosopher [Plato] judged it, and rightly so. 

<margin>D</margin> For he does not say that every demiurge is "always looking"—as Atticus <note>Atticus: a 2nd-century Platonist who argued for a more literal, temporal reading of Plato</note> thinks—but rather that the intelligible "is always in the same state." Unless, perhaps, he included "always" with "looking" to prevent the idea that by seeing at one time and not at another, any unfitness might creep into the beauty of the creation. Therefore, wherever a demiurge may be among us, let him look toward the eternal, so that he may make his work similar to it and beautiful.

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on Plato's Timaeus, specifically moving to the section where Plato defines the names of the universe—"Heaven" or "Cosmos"—and explains why such definitions are necessary for a rigorous philosophical demonstration.</meta>

# PROCLUS

->196<-

> "Now, let the whole **heaven**, or **cosmos**, or whatever other name it may most prefer to be called, be named by us thus." (Timaeus, Page 28 B.)

This is the last of the axioms according to the geometers: assigning a name to a subject, just as they do when they speak of the **gnomon** <term>gnomon: in geometry, the L-shaped part of a parallelogram that remains when a smaller similar parallelogram is removed from one of its corners</term> in parallelograms, saying: "in any [parallelogram], let it be called a **gnomon** along with the two complements." For since he is about to call it both "heaven" and "cosmos" throughout the same work, he pre-defines the terms so that you do not think he is confusing the teaching by using different names. 

Indeed, one must know this very thing: that these names held much ambiguity among the ancients. Some called only the region below the moon the **cosmos**, and that which is above it the **heaven**. Others said the heaven was a part of the <margin>E</margin> **cosmos**, defining it as everything up to the moon itself. Still others addressed the heights of the realm of generation in this way, as in the verse: 
*"Zeus was allotted the wide heaven in the ether and the clouds."* <note>original: "Il. XV. 192"; Homer, Iliad 15.192</note>

Therefore, Plato reasonably defines these names before the whole contemplation of the subject, addressing the whole as "heaven" and "cosmos." He says "the whole heaven" (so that you do not think he is speaking only of the divine body) and "let it be named by us **cosmos**, or whatever else it may rejoice in being named." It seems he calls it "heaven" as it appears to all, but "cosmos" as it appears to himself. For he says, "let it be named by us also **cosmos**." 

For the name **cosmos** <term>cosmos: Greek 'kosmos' means both 'world' and 'order/ornament'</term> is appropriate for it as a crafted work of the Demiurge, even if it is possible to call it both: "heaven" insofar as it "sees the things above" <note>original: "horōn ta anō"; a wordplay from Plato's Cratylus 396b connecting 'Ouranos' (Heaven) to 'seeing the things above'</note> and contemplates the **intelligible** <term>intelligible: the realm of pure, eternal ideas accessible only to the mind</term> and participates in intellectual essence; and "cosmos" insofar as it is always being seen and "ordered" <note>original: "kosmoumenon"</note> by the things that truly exist. It is "heaven" as that which has turned back toward its source, but "cosmos" as that which proceeds forth. For it is both generated from there and has turned back toward Being. 

But just as with the **statues** <term>agalmata: specifically cult statues or shrines inhabited by a divine presence</term> established by the **telestic** art <term>telestic: the ancient Greek priestly art of consecrating statues to make them 'alive' with a god's presence</term>, some parts are visible, while others are hidden within <margin>F</margin> symbolically as signs of the presence of the gods—which are known only to the consecrators—in the same way, the **cosmos**, being a statue of the **intelligible** and having been consecrated by the Father, contains both the visible signs of its own divinity and the invisible **tokens** <note>original: "synthēmata"; divine 'passwords' or 'symbols' implanted in the world</note> of its true participation, which it received from the Father who consecrated it, so that...
