<meta>This page continues Proclus's analysis of the names "Heaven" and "Cosmos." On the previous page, Proclus discussed how these terms are used as foundational axioms, similar to geometry. Here, he explores the deeper metaphysical and theurgic significance of names, distinguishing between how gods and humans name the same reality.</meta>

# ON TIMAEUS II.

->197<-

...is rooted through these names eternally in Being. The names **heaven** <note>original: "ouranos"</note> and **cosmos** are significant of the powers made manifest within it—the former according to its procession from the source, and the latter according to its return. One must also recognize the divine name of its "staying" power <note>Proclus refers to the Neoplatonic triad: remaining/staying, proceeding, and returning</note>, which is a symbol of the **Demiurge's** <term>Demiurge: the "Divine Craftsman" who shapes the material universe</term> "token" <note>original: "synthema," a divine seal or signature</note>. Insofar as this power never departs from Being, it is ineffable, unspoken, and known only to the gods themselves. Indeed, names appropriate to every level of reality exist: divine names for divine things, intellectual names for intellectual things, and names based on opinion for objects of opinion. 

Plato himself says this in the *Cratylus*, accepting **Homer** as an authority when he assigns different names for the same things among the gods and among human opinions: *“The gods call it **Xanthus**, but men call it **Scamander**,”* and *“The gods call it **Chalcis**, but men call it **cymindis**.”* <note>original: "Il. XX. 74; Il. XIV. 291"; these refer to a river and a bird, respectively</note> This occurs in many other instances as well. For just as the knowledge of the gods is different from that of partial human souls, so too are names: divine names reveal the whole essence of the things named, while human names only grasp them partially. 

<margin>B</margin> Knowing, therefore, that this principle pre-exists in the universe—that there is another divine name besides the one that is apparent—Plato declared it ineffable and approached it with the greatest reverence as a symbol of the divine "token" within it. For the phrase *"whatever [name] it may prefer"* is a hidden type <note>a mystical pattern or blueprint</note> of the cosmic name, since it has received an unspoken and divine essence, and what is signified by it is of a corresponding rank. 

For this reason, divine cosmic names have also been handed down to **theurgists** <term>theurgists: "god-workers" or practitioners of ritual magic intended to achieve union with the divine</term>, some of which they call "ineffable" and others "effable." The ineffable ones belong to the invisible powers within the world, while the effable ones belong to the visible elements from which the world is completed. 

Through these concepts, as if through hypotheses, the cosmic form, the creative cause, the paradigm <note>the eternal Model</note>, and the name (both visible and invisible, both dual and unified) are handed down. For the phrase *"whatever [it is]"* is significant of unity. Thus, you might say the **ineffable name** signifies the universe's permanence in the Father; the name **cosmos** signifies its procession; and the name **heaven** signifies its return. Through these three, we find the "Final Cause," because of which the world is full of **the Good**—remaining ineffably, proceeding perfectly, and returning toward <margin>C</margin> **the Good** as the object of its desire. It remains for us now to touch upon the actual contemplation of these things, bringing to a conclusion what follows from these principles.

**"We must therefore consider concerning it first, that which is foundational to consider regarding everything at the beginning."** (Timaeus, Page 28 B.)

<meta>This page continues the commentary of Proclus on Plato's Timaeus. It follows a discussion on the naming of the universe by divine and human standards, moving here into a specific definition of terms like "Heaven" and "Cosmos" as foundational axioms for the dialogue.</meta>

# PROCLUS

->196<-

> Now, let all the heaven—or "cosmos" or whatever other name it might most properly accept—be named by us. (Page 28 B.)

This is the last of the "axioms" <term>axioms: self-evident truths used as a starting point for reasoning</term> according to the geometers, which is established as a definition, just as they do when speaking of the "gnomon" <term>gnomon: the part of a parallelogram that remains after a similar parallelogram is removed from one of its corners</term> in parallelograms: "in any such figure, let the gnomon be so called along with the two complements." For since Plato intends to call the same thing both "heaven" and "cosmos," he defines these names beforehand so that you do not think he is confusing the teaching by using different terms. 

One must also know that these names were the subject of much ambiguity among the ancients. Some called only the region beneath the moon the "cosmos," <margin>E</margin> while calling the region above it <note>original: "ten hyper auten"</note> the "heaven." Others said the heaven was merely a part of the cosmos, defining it only as far as the moon; still others applied these names even to the extremes of the realm of generation, as Homer says: *“Zeus obtained the wide heaven in the ether and the clouds.”* <note>original: "Iliad XV. 192"</note> 

Therefore, Plato reasonably defines these names before his entire investigation, calling the whole thing "heaven" and "cosmos." He says, "all the heaven" (so that you do not think he means only the divine body) "let it be named by us 'cosmos,' or whatever else it might rejoice in being called." It seems he calls it "heaven" as it appears to all, but "cosmos" as it appears to himself. For he says, "let all the heaven be named by us 'cosmos.'" 

The name "cosmos" <note>original: "kosmos," meaning "order" or "ornament"</note> is appropriate to it as a "work of the Demiurge," even if it is possible to call it by both names: "heaven" <note>original: "ouranos"</note> insofar as it "sees the things above" <note>original: "horon ta ano"; a wordplay typical of Neoplatonism where "ouranos" is derived from "seeing what is above"</note> and contemplates the Intelligible realm and participates in intellectual essence; but "cosmos" insofar as it is always being ordered and beautified by the things that truly exist. We call it "heaven" as it is turned toward its source, and "cosmos" as it proceeds outward. For it is both generated from that source and turned back toward Being. 

Just as in the sacred rites established by the "telestic" <term>telestic: the "perfecting" art of theurgy and divine initiation</term> art, some things are manifest <margin>F</margin> while others are hidden within, acting as symbolic signs of the presence of the gods—which are known only to the initiators—in the same way, the cosmos is an "image" <note>original: "agalma," a cult statue or divine representation</note> of the Intelligible. Having been perfected by the Father <note>the Demiurge</note>, it possesses some manifest signs of his divinity, and other hidden tokens <note>original: "synthemata"</note> of its superior participation, which it received from the Father who perfected it...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's line-by-line commentary on Plato's Timaeus. Having established that "Heaven" and "Cosmos" are the primary names for the universe, Proclus now explores the metaphysical significance of naming itself, drawing on the Neoplatonic triad of Remaining, Procession, and Reversion.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II.

...rooted through these names, it might be eternally established in Reality. The names "Heaven" and "Cosmos" are indicative of the powers visible within the universe: "Heaven" represents its **procession** <term>procession: the way a divine effect flows out from its cause</term> from its source, while "Cosmos" represents its **reversion** <term>reversion: the way a created thing turns back toward its divine source to find perfection</term>. | It is also necessary to know the divine name of its <margin>84</margin> **remaining** <term>remaining: the aspect of a thing that stays unified with its cause even as it acts</term> power, which is the symbol of the Creator's own seal. Insofar as it never departs from Reality, this name is ineffable, unspoken, and known only to the gods themselves. For there are names appropriate to every rank of things;¹) there are divine names for divine things, intellectual names for intellectual things, and names based on opinion for things perceived by opinion.

Indeed, Plato himself says this in the *Cratylus*,²) accepting the authority of Homer, who assigns one set of names among the gods for the same things and another set in the opinions of men:

> Whom the gods call the Yellow One <note>original: "Xanthos"</note>,³) but men call Scamander.
> And the gods call the Bronze-voiced bird <note>original: "Chalkis"</note>, but men call it the Night-hawk <note>original: "Kymindis"</note>.⁴)

This occurs in many other instances as well. Just as the knowledge of the gods is one thing and that of partial souls is another, so too are their names different. Divine names manifest the entire essence of the things named, whereas human names only touch upon them partially. Therefore, because Plato knew that this universe possessed a divine name prior to its visible one, | he left it unspoken <margin>B</margin> and introduced it⁵) with the greatest reverence as a symbol of the divine seal within it. By using the phrases "whatever [name]" and "it might accept," he hints at the cosmic name as having an ineffable and divine essence, so that his designation might be coordinate with the thing itself.

For this reason, theurgists <term>theurgists: "god-workers" or practitioners of ritual who used sacred names to communicate with the divine</term> have been handed down divine cosmic names, some of which are called "ineffable" and others "effable" among them.⁶) The former belong to the invisible powers within the universe, while the latter belong to the visible elements from which it is composed. 

Through these concepts, as if through preliminary assumptions, he transmits the cosmic form, the creative cause, the paradigm <term>paradigm: the eternal model after which the world was fashioned</term>, and the name—both the visible and the invisible, the dual and the singular. For the phrase "whatever it might be" is indicative of its unity. You might say that the **ineffable name**⁷) belongs to the "remaining" of the whole in the Father; the name **"Cosmos"** belongs to its "procession"; and the name **"Heaven"** belongs to its "reversion." Through these three, we see the final cause through which the world is full of the Good—remaining ineffably, proceeding perfectly, and reverting toward the Good | as toward its object of desire.⁸) It is now fitting to grasp the actual study of the facts, completing the sequence of principles. <margin>C</margin>

***

We must therefore first consider about it that which must be⁹) considered about everything at the start. (*Timaeus* Page 28 B.)

<meta>This page continues Proclus's detailed commentary on the Timaeus. Proclus is specifically analyzing Timaeus's opening question (27c): "Whether [the universe] always was, having no beginning of generation, or has come into being, starting from some beginning." Proclus is here defining the "middle ground" between purely eternal things and purely temporary things.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...before, that the extremes are defined as that which simply always exists and that which is simply generated, while the middle states are encompassed within these. That which does not have its essence <term>essence: 'ousia', the fundamental reality of what a thing is</term> or its activity ¹) <note>original: 'energeia'</note> standing all at once as a whole in a unity is called **generated** <term>generated: 'genēton', meaning something that comes into being through a process</term>, and such a thing subsists entirely through a process of generation ²), and its being is something that is "becoming," but not "being." Such is this sensible world, and the **time** that exists within moving things, and the **transitive thinking** <note>thinking that moves from one step to the next, unlike divine intuition which sees all at once</note> of souls. 

Now, it is clear that every motion exists part by part and never exists as a whole all at once; but if the essence of the world also involves generation, and its perpetuity exists according to an infinite stretch of time, one might pause to consider this. 

<margin>C</margin>
And having paused, | one might reason: first, that between those things that are eternally everlasting and those things that are generated in a specific part of time, there must be a **generated subsistence** that is infinite. This exists in two ways: either having the whole as everlasting throughout the whole of time, while its parts exist in parts ⁶) of time—such as the elements here on earth—or both the whole and the parts extending along with the perpetuity of all time, such as the heavenly bodies. For the perpetuity found in **Eternity** <term>Eternity: 'aiōn', the realm of unchanging, timeless reality</term> is not the same as that found in **total Time**; neither is the infinity of Time the same as that of Eternity; for Eternity and Time are not the same thing. 

Second, that which is measured by Eternity and exists within Eternity must be **indivisible**; for how can that which is divisible stand within the indivisible and have its essence firmly established? 

Third, since the soul acts according to time, the body must certainly also exist according to time; for the activity of the soul is closer to Eternity than the essence of the body is. 

What then shall be our proof that the essence of heavenly things is "everlasting" in a way that aligns with time? I would say it is the fact that, if it were separated ⁸) from the one who grants it order, it would no longer exist. This makes it clear that 
<margin>D</margin>
it obtained an **acquired perpetuity** | and is always "becoming" ⁹) from another source. For if it had received its own essence as a whole all at once, it would have been self-sufficient ¹⁰) in its existence, even if separated from the Creator who makes it and gives it its essence. 

Plato’s goal is to show that the world is "simply generated," including its essence ¹²), its power, its activity, and its very perpetuity, which extends along with the whole of time. He seeks from the beginning whether it "always was" or is "generated"—which is the same as asking whether it belongs to the rank of eternal beings ¹⁴) or those that fall under the domain of time ¹⁵). For the phrase "it always was" indicates the **intelligible** <note>the realm of pure thought/forms</note> to him, as we said before: "What is that which always is, and has no generation?" ¹⁶) If, as he proceeds ¹⁷), he says that "it was" is not strictly appropriate for eternal things, but rather "it is," we should not be troubled. For this is said before the strict distinction of terms.

***

<summary>Proclus argues that the physical universe is "generated" because its existence relies on a continuous flow of time and the sustaining power of a Creator, distinguishing its "acquired" perpetuity from the absolute, indivisible Eternity of divine realities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s systematic analysis of Plato's *Timaeus*. Specifically, Proclus is examining the linguistic and philosophical distinctions Plato makes when describing the "goodness" of the Creator and the "eternal" nature of the universe's model. This section serves to bridge the gap between pure, unchanging Being and the world of change we inhabit.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II

...by habit. Wherefore also, in hymning the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: 'dēmiourgos', the divine craftsman or creator of the universe</term>, he [Plato] says, "He **was** good" ¹) <note>original: 'agathos ēn'; Plato, Timaeus 29e</note>. The Demiurge is **eternal**, and regarding the **Paradigm** <term>Paradigm: the eternal blueprint or "Living Being" that the creator looks upon</term> he said both at once, stating: "The nature of the **Living Being** ²) was eternal." He joined the word "was" with the word "eternal" to show a unique kind of existence. And above all, 

<margin>E</margin>
within a finite body, the power is also not infinite, as **Aristotle** ⁴) showed; but **Eternity** <term>Eternity: 'Aion', a state of existence that is complete all at once, without past or future</term> is infinite power. Thus, every finite body is incapable of receiving eternity. It must, therefore, not *be* always [in a static sense], but **always become** <note>Proclus is explaining that the physical world stays "eternal" only by constantly renewing itself through time, rather than standing still like a divine thought</note>, receiving its existence in a flowing succession. That which *is*, then, as I said, and "always being," signifies the **eternal**; while "having been generated" signifies a reality that has received a **subsistence** <term>subsistence: 'hypostasis', the underlying reality or foundation of a thing's existence</term> measured by **time**. This is the **sensible** <term>sensible: 'aisthēton', the world we can see and touch</term>, which is "apprehended by opinion with sensation." It has been said that 

the **intelligible** <term>intelligible: 'noēton', the higher realm of pure forms and divine intellects</term> is **self-subsistent** <note>existing by its own power rather than being created by another</note> and eternal, while the sensible is produced by another cause and exists alongside time. For the "eternal" is one kind of number, and the "temporal" is another; the one *is* in number, while the other *becomes* in number. **Eternity** is paired with the former, and **Time** with the latter. Thus, even if the **generated** ⁶) <term>generated: 'genēton', something that has come into being</term> is called "everlasting," it has a subsistence that extends along with the whole of time, always becoming and always being perfected by the cause that produces it. If, then, "always being" refers to the eternal, and that which "has a beginning of generation" refers to that which is produced by another cause (for such is the nature of that which is "always becoming"), then **Plato** asks ⁷) whether the world is "always being" or 

<margin>F</margin>
has a beginning from some kind of generation. This inquiry is the same as asking: is the world among the **eternals**, or among those things produced throughout the whole of time? Is it one of the self-subsistent beings, or one of those things given order by another cause? ⁹) Furthermore, the term **"generated"** ¹⁰) is used in many different ways. For that which has a **beginning in time** is called generated, whether it reaches that state through a process of birth ¹¹) or without such a process (as Aristotle says). Also, everything that 

<margin>86</margin>
**proceeds** ¹²) from a cause is called generated; and that which is **composite** in its essence is called generated; and that which has a **generated nature** even if it has not [yet] come into being—just as we call something "visible" even if it is not currently being seen. Since "generated" is said in so many ways ¹³), that which is generated according to time possesses all the other types of generation: it proceeds from a cause, it is composite, and it has a generated nature. However, it is not necessarily true that something generated in another way possesses all these types. We must ask ¹⁵), therefore, whether [the world] is "generated" according to time, or whether it does not have this kind of generation...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the "beginning" of the universe as described in Plato's Timaeus. On the previous page, Proclus distinguished between the eternal existence of the divine "Paradigm" and the flowing, temporal existence of the physical world. Here, he examines whether the universe had a "temporal" starting point or if its "beginning" refers to its causal dependence on a higher power.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II

...temporal beginning of generation. Since he [Plato] did not state this contradiction, but rather that one: "whether it has no beginning of generation, or some beginning," he makes it clear to those who are capable of understanding even a little, that he is not inquiring about a temporal beginning. Rather, he asks if, among the many types of generation that exist, the Universe has a specific "beginning of generation." For if it had no beginning at all, it would be among the **eternal** and the **self-constituted** <term>self-constituted: 'authypostatos', a being that causes its own existence and does not depend on an external creator</term> beings, in which there is no generation because there is not even time. For even if we sometimes speak of the "generations of the gods," we say this 

<margin>B</margin>
to indicate their **ineffable procession** | <term>procession: 'proodos', the way divine reality flows outward from its source into more complex forms</term> and the distinction between secondary beings and their causes. But the "theologists" <note>original: 'theologoi'; Proclus likely refers to Orphic or Chaldean sources who used mythological language to describe philosophical truths</note>, removing all such difficulties in advance so that the "generations" of the gods might be fashioned according to reason, gave the name "**Time**" to the first principle. They did this because wherever there is generation, Time must lead the way—the time through which and because of which generation occurs. For these thinkers, then, the cause and Time converge into the same thing, just as procession and generation do. 

But that which "truly becomes" [the physical world] is that which does not give birth to itself, but is produced by another. It is an image of something else, composed of many unlike parts, and it always receives its **subsistence** <term>subsistence: 'hypostasis', the underlying reality or foundation of a thing's existence</term> as something **added onto** or **repaired** <note>original: 'episkeuastēn'; implying the physical world is not self-sustaining but needs constant maintenance from its source</note>. Time is the partner of such a thing; it possesses a generation that is **inexhaustible** <term>inexhaustible: 'anekleiptos', never-failing or continuous</term> because it stretches along with the infinity of time. Such a thing remains numerically "one" by always *becoming* one, but not by always *being* one <note>Proclus is explaining that the world stays the same only through a constant process of change and renewal, unlike the static perfection of the divine</note>. 

You might say that what is "generated" in this way proceeds from "non-being." For the self-constituted being, which is born from itself, does not proceed from non-being. Even if you divide it in thought into 

<margin>C</margin>
cause and effect, it proceeds from "being." | For the maker and the made were one; thus it proceeds from its own "being" and is therefore eternal, never leaving itself. But that which comes from another alone exists by subsisting from "non-being" <note>meaning it has no existence of its own; if the external cause stopped, the object would vanish into nothingness</note>, because if it were separated from its cause, it would no longer exist. 

In this way, the physical axiom must be applied to this type of generated thing according to proportion. That which is always "becoming" is always in time and is always **illuminated** by True Being. This is clear: if you remove the "maker," the whole [universe] immediately becomes incomplete—which is the case for all things still in the process of becoming. Yet it is not for this reason both incomplete and complete at once; it always "becomes," and therefore its "always" and its "perfection" exist throughout the whole of time. For **Time was created along with the Heavens** <note>Plato, Timaeus 38b</note>—not just a part of time, but all of time. Thus, the Heavens "become" within infinite time and are inexhaustible...

<summary>Proclus argues that the universe's "beginning" is not a point in time, but rather its constant causal dependence on a divine creator. He distinguishes between self-caused eternal beings and the physical world, which exists as a continuous flow of "becoming" sustained by the light of True Being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s investigation into the "beginning" of the universe. Having established on the previous page that the "beginning" mentioned by Plato is not necessarily a point in time, Proclus now argues that the universe is "becoming" and "has become" simultaneously because it exists through the entirety of time, rather than just a segment of it.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II. 203

on both sides, just as time is. Thus, it is said both to have a "beginning of generation" <note>original: 'genesis'; refers to the process of coming-into-being or the world of change</note> and to have started from something else. First, it starts from the most authoritative beginning, as he [Plato] will say, the **final cause** <term>final cause: the 'telos' or ultimate purpose for which something is created</term>. For it was from this purpose that the Father who generated the world began its production. Secondly, it has a beginning in relation to this, | as it is always "becoming" throughout the whole of 
<margin>D</margin> 
time, having both "begun to become" and "having its end." For in the case of the world, "it has become" is not one thing and "it is becoming" another; consequently, the beginning is not one thing and the end another. While something that comes to be in a *portion* of time begins at one moment and is finished at another, that which comes to be throughout *all* time is always beginning and is always complete. It possesses a "beginning of generation" that is perfected by another [cause], but it possesses no beginning in the sense of a specific starting point in partial time. Since "generation" is meant in many ways, the "beginning of generation" is also meant in many ways. Thus, the generation that subsists for the whole [of time] is a specific kind of generation, and its beginning is a beginning of *that* generation, not of all generation in general. What kind of beginning is this? It is the one that holds the end gathered together in union with it. Therefore, because it is a body, it is "becoming" and has a "beginning of generation"; but because the Intellect is its maker, it "has become" and possesses the "end" of its generation. Because of both, it is both beginning and complete in its generation—it "has become" and "is becoming" as if it were already finished. These states are separated in things that come to be in a part of time, but for things that come to be throughout all time, they subsist together | just as the motion of the heavens does: it is "always at its goal," as Aristotle says, which is not the case for motions here on earth.
<margin>E</margin>

**It has come into being; for it is visible and tangible and possesses a body. All such things are sensible. And sensible things, being graspable by opinion with sensation, appeared to be becoming and generated. (Page 28 C.)**

Just as the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: the 'Craftsman' or divine mind that fashions the physical universe according to an eternal model</term> of the whole looks toward himself, and by remaining always in his own customary character, produces the whole world universally, all at once, and always in the same way (for he does not act at one time and not at another, lest he fall out of eternity), in the same way, Timaeus, having turned toward himself, reveals the entire contemplation. He runs up to **Intellect** <note>original: 'nous'</note> from **discursive thought** <note>original: 'dianoia'</note> and proceeds to **reasoning** from Intellect. In his state of wondering and questioning himself, he acted according to the **self-moving** <term>self-moving: 'autokinēton', the characteristic of the soul to initiate its own activity and thoughts</term> power of the soul; but in answering, he imitates the direct intuition of the Intellect, first with a single voice...

--- Page 229 ---
<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the "becoming" of the cosmos. On the previous page, he explained that the universe is "always beginning" and "always complete" because it exists through the entirety of time. Here, he examines the specific wording Plato uses—"it has become"—and defends this description against literalist interpretations like those of the philosopher Atticus.</meta>

# PROCLUS

<margin>F</margin> Having grasped the doctrine—**"it has become"** <note>original: γέγονε (gegone)</note>—and having proclaimed the conclusion before the proof, he acts exactly like those who are divinely inspired. Such people see the whole all at once; they have already grasped the end before the outcome by seeing everything together in the mind. But when he reasons, he descends from the Mind into logical discourses <note>original: διεξόδους (diexodous); refers to step-by-step reasoning</note> and the hunt for the nature of the world through demonstration. Indeed, he demonstrates the entire form of the universe from his initial assumptions in a truly marvelous way. For if the world is visible and tangible and possesses a body, and that which is visible, tangible, and possessing a body is sensible <term>sensible: that which can be perceived by the five senses</term>, and that which is sensible is an object of opinion <note>original: δοξαστὸν (doxaston); something believed rather than known through pure reason</note> paired with sensation and is therefore **generated**, it follows that the world is generated. This has been shown demonstratively from the definition through the conversion of the terms, since even geometers 
<margin>87</margin> use such proofs. So much, then, for the form of these arguments. But since, as we said, he [Plato] asked whether the universe is eternal or has some beginning of generation, he followed this with the phrase "it has become," imitating the Mind <note>original: νοῦν (noun); some manuscripts read "now"</note>. It is clear, then, that he assigns a certain kind of "generation" <term>generation: the process of coming-into-being or existing in the realm of change</term> to the world. For this was the other side of the contradiction we mentioned. But if this is so, he establishes that the universe is far removed from a "beginning in time." For if the world has a "beginning of generation" but not *every* kind of beginning, while that which has come to be starting from a point in time has *every* kind of beginning of generation, it follows that the world has not come to be starting from a point in time. 

Furthermore, let us follow the wondrous hypotheses of Atticus <note>Atticus was a 2nd-century Platonist who argued for a literal beginning of the world in time, a view Proclus and other Neoplatonists rejected</note>, who says that while that which moves in a discordant and disorderly way is "ungenerated," the world is "generated from a point in time." Let us speak regarding this phrase: "it has become." Since he himself has provided the cause of this generation, let us see what kind of cause he says it is. For he says the world is **visible and tangible**. Is it the case, then, that *everything* sensible 
<margin>B</margin> is "generated from a point in time," or is it not? If everything is, then even that which moves in a discordant and disorderly way will be "generated from a point in time"—for he [Plato] says that [chaos] was also visible. But if not everything is, then the argument of Atticus is un-syllogistic and proves nothing. Perhaps he will say that the world is visible and tangible *now*, whereas that which moved discordantly and disorderly was not visible *now*, but only *before* the making of the world. For Plato says it this way: "all that was visible, moving discordantly and disorderly." But in this passage, he says the world "is" visible, tangible, and possessing a body. Thus, everything that **is** visible and tangible is shown to be "generated," but not necessarily that which **was** [visible]. Even if Atticus says these things—for the man is clever at seizing upon words—we must say that in the definition of "the generated," there is no such distinction. Rather, it is simply stated that everything generated is "perceived by opinion with irrational sensation."

<summary>Proclus analyzes Plato's syllogism that the world is "generated" because it is sensible (visible and tangible). He argues against Atticus's literal view that the world had a beginning in time, pointing out logical inconsistencies in how Atticus treats the "disorderly chaos" that preceded the world.</summary>
<keywords>Proclus, Plato, Timaeus, Atticus the Platonist, generation, sensible, visible, tangible, logic, syllogism, chaos, cosmology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s rebuttal of literalist interpretations of Plato's creation narrative. Specifically, he challenges the philosopher Atticus, who believed the world had a beginning in time. Proclus argues that "generation" refers to causal dependence on a higher principle, not a chronological start date.</meta>

### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 2

...it follows that if something is sensible, such a thing would entirely be **generated**. All that is visible is sensible; therefore, that which moves in a discordant and disorderly fashion <note>Proclus refers here to the "pre-cosmic" state of chaos described in Plato's Timaeus 30a</note> is generated, especially since Plato clearly calls that state **generated**. For he says that before the heaven 
<margin>C</margin> came to be, there were three things: **Being**, **Space**, and **Generation** <note>original: τὸ ὄν, τὴν χώραν, τὴν γένεσιν; see Timaeus 52d</note>, the latter existing as a mere <column-break/> trace of forms. Consequently, that discordant state is generated just as it is visible. 

Therefore, one must not say that the former [disorder] is ungenerated in time while the whole [the cosmos] is generated; rather, either both are generated according to him, or both are ungenerated. Indeed, both are similarly called "visible" and "generation" by Plato. But if both were generated <note>in a literal temporal sense</note>, then before that world, another cosmos would have had to change into that discordant state. For generation always proceeds from an opposite to an opposite. And if the one who made that world was good, how did he either fail to harmonize it simply, or destroy it after harmonizing it well? If he was not good, how could he produce something ordered and beautified while not being good? For it belongs to the Good to beautify and order other things. Moreover, if that which is both visible and generated is not generated in terms of time, then of necessity the whole—being visible and generated—must also not be made generated in terms of time.

So much, then, for the arguments against **Atticus** <term>Atticus: A 2nd-century AD philosopher who interpreted Plato's creation story literally, believing the world had a beginning in time</term>. Let us return to our own principles and speak thus: Was the cosmos always existing as **eternal**, or was it not eternal, but rather co-existent with **time**? And is it self-subsisting, or produced by another? 
<margin>D</margin> This is the question, and the answer is this: it is produced by another and it co-exists with time; such a thing is **generated**. For if it possesses a composite form, it has "generation" according to its composition; and if it subsists from another cause alone, it is **generated** in the sense that it does not produce itself; and if it is not something eternal <term>eternal: in this context, "aionion" refers to being outside of time altogether, like a mathematical truth</term>, it has its whole existence according to time. Indeed, it has been fashioned in relation to another and has become an **image** <note>original: εἴδωλον (eidolon)</note> modeled after true Being. 

Therefore, as the composite is to the simple, and as time is to eternity, so is **generation** to **essence** <note>original: οὐσία (ousia)</note>. If, then, simple and uniform essence is eternal, then composite and multiform essence, which is yoked to time, is "generation," since it is also said to have begun from a certain **beginning** <note>original: ἀρχή (arche); can mean both a starting point in time and a ruling principle/cause</note> in a harmonious way. For that which has become at some point began from a temporal beginning, a productive beginning, a final beginning, a material beginning, and a formal beginning. Since "beginning" is spoken of in many ways, such a thing began its generation according to all of them. But the cosmos began from *some* beginning, but not all of them. Which one, then? 
<margin>E</margin> Not the temporal one, he would say; for that which begins from a temporal start would participate in all the other types of beginnings of generation. Rather, it begins from that which he himself will teach as he proceeds—the most sovereign beginning, I mean the **final cause** <term>final cause: the "telos" or the goal/purpose for which something is made</term>. For the world has become because of the **Good**, and this is the "beginning" of generation from which it started. At any rate, he himself calls this the most sovereign beginning of the generation of the cosmos, so that he would be speaking of this one. First...

<summary>Proclus argues that the "beginning" of the cosmos is not a point in time, but rather its causal dependence on the Good. He refutes Atticus by showing that if the world had a literal temporal beginning, it would lead to an infinite regress of previous worlds and disorders.</summary>

<keywords>Proclus, Atticus, Timaeus, generation, eternal, final cause, the Good, sensible vs. intelligible, cosmic order, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the Timaeus, specifically analyzing the logical structure of Plato's argument for the creation of the universe. Proclus is contrasting a literal, temporal "birth" of the world (as argued by the philosopher Atticus) with a philosophical "generation" based on causal dependence.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...embracing the doctrine: **"it has come to be"**; and having proclaimed the conclusion before the proof, quite like those who are divinely inspired, who have grasped the whole all at once—
<margin>F</margin> seeing the end before the outcome with the mind, seeing all things together at once—
but then he descends from the mind into logical paths and the hunt for the nature of the world through proof. Indeed, in a quite extraordinary way, he demonstrates the entire form of the whole from these hypotheses. For if the world is visible and tangible and possesses a body, and that which is visible and tangible and possessing a body is sensible, and that which is sensible is graspable by opinion along with sensation <note>original: περιληπτὸν μετ᾿ αἰσθήσεως</note>, it is then **generated** <note>Proclus uses the term "generated" (γενητόν) to mean something that has a cause for its existence, rather than necessarily having a starting point in time</note>. Therefore, the world is generated, having been demonstrated by the proof according to the definition, through the conversion of the term; for even
<margin>87</margin> geometricians use such proofs. This, then, is the character of his words. But since, as we said, he asked whether the whole is eternal or has a beginning of generation, he then introduced this statement: **"it has come to be,"** imitating the Mind <note>original: νοῦν; the Divine Intellect</note>, in that he assigns a certain "generation" to the world. For this was the other part of the initial contradiction. But if this is so, he establishes the whole far away from a temporal generation. For if the world has a *certain* beginning of generation but not *every* kind, whereas that which is born of time has *every* kind of beginning of generation, then the world has not come to be from time. But even if we follow the "admirable" hypotheses of **Atticus** <note>Atticus was a 2nd-century Platonist who argued for a literal, temporal beginning of the world, a view Proclus rejects</note>, who says that that which moves discordantly and in a disorderly fashion is **ungenerated**, but the world is **generated from time**, let us speak about this "it has come to be." Let us see what kind of nature he says it has, just as he himself has rendered the cause of its generation. For he says it is **"visible and tangible."** Is everything
<margin>B</margin> that is visible "generated from time," or is it not all? If indeed it is all, then even that which moves discordantly and in a disorderly fashion <note>The pre-cosmic chaos described in Plato's Timaeus 30a</note> will be generated from time; for he says that state, too, is visible. But if it is not all, the argument according to Atticus is logically flawed and concludes nothing. Does he then say that the world **is** visible and tangible, but that which moves discordantly and in a disorderly fashion is not visible **now**, but was so **before** the making of the world? But Plato says it thus: "all that **was** visible, moving discordantly and in a disorderly fashion." But in this passage he says, "for it **is** visible and tangible and possesses a body." Everything, therefore, which **is** visible and tangible, is also generated—but not that which **was**. Even if he says these things (for the man is clever at clinging to words), it must be said that in the definition of the "generated" there is no such distinction; rather, it is stated simply that everything generated is graspable by opinion with sensation.

<summary>Proclus analyzes Plato's syllogism that the world is "generated" because it is sensible, visible, and tangible. He critiques the philosopher Atticus for arguing that the world had a literal beginning in time, pointing out logical inconsistencies in how Atticus defines "visible" things.</summary>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II

So that if anything is sensible, such a thing would entirely be **generated**. Everything that is sensible [is such]; therefore, that which moves out of tune and in a disorderly fashion is generated, and Plato clearly <note>original: "σαφῶς"; some manuscripts read "let us say" (φῶμεν)</note> says that it is generated. For before the heaven existed, he says there are three things: **Being**, **Space**, and **Generation**, existing in "traces" <note>referring to Plato, *Timaeus* 52d, describing the state of the universe before order was imposed</note>; <margin>C</margin> so that this disorderly state is also generated, just as it is also visible. If, then, someone were to say that the former [disorder] is ungenerated in time, while the whole [ordered world] is generated, then both are generated according to him, or both are ungenerated. For both are called "visible" and "generation" by Plato. But if both are generated, then the world would have changed back from that [ordered state] into the disorderly. For generation always arises from its opposite. And if the one who made that world was good, how did he either fail to harmonize it, or—having harmonized it well—did he then destroy it? But if he was not good, how could he produce something ordered and adorned without being good? For to adorn and to order is the work of a good being. But if, being both visible and generated, it is not generated in time, then it is right to make the whole world immediately generated [in a causal sense] rather than generated in time, on account of it being visible and generated. So much, then, for the arguments against <term>Atticus</term> <note>A 2nd-century Platonist who argued the world had a beginning in time</note>; let us return to our own views and speak as follows: Was the world always existing as something <term>eternal</term> <note>original: αἰώνιος (aionios); existing outside of time</note>, or was it not eternal, but co-existing within time? And is it <term>self-constituted</term> <note>original: αὐθυπόστατον (authypostaton); having the cause of its existence within itself</note>, or produced by another? <margin>D</margin> This is the question, and here is the answer: it has been produced by another and it co-exists with time; and such a thing is "generated." For if it has a composite being, it has its "generation" according to that composition; and if it subsists from another cause alone, it is generated in the sense that it is not the producer of itself; and if it is not eternal but has its entire existence in time [it is generated]. For it has been fashioned in relation to something else and is "generated" as an image derived from Being. Therefore, as <term>the Intelligible</term> is to the simple, and as time is to eternity, so is **generation** to **essence**. Thus, simple and uniform essence is eternal, while composite and multiform essence, coupled with time, is "generation," since it is also said to have started from a certain beginning. For that which has come to be at some time starts from a temporal beginning, and from a productive, a final, a material, and a formal beginning. For since "beginning" is spoken of in many ways, it began its generation according to all of them; but the world began from a certain beginning, and not from every kind. Which one then? The "productive" beginning, one might say; for that which begins from this also begins from the other <margin>E</margin> forms of the beginning of generation. But it starts from that one which he himself will teach as he proceeds—the most powerful one—I mean the "final" beginning <note>the 'telos' or purpose</note>. For it came to be because of the Good, and the beginning of its generation, from which it started, is this. At any rate, he himself will call this the most authoritative beginning of the generation of the world, so he would be speaking of this one. First—

Therefore, from its composition, he shows that this [world] is **generated**. For it is tangible and <unclear>visible</unclear>. These, then, are the extremities of the whole; for the heaven is visible, while the <unclear>earth is</unclear> tangible. Indeed, even in earth there is visibility insofar as it participates in light, and in heaven there is <unclear>tangibility</unclear> insofar as the "earthy" quality is pre-contained within it according to its cause. But it is simply <unclear>a</unclear> body <note>original: "σῶμα"; Proclus argues that being a "body" implies being sensible and therefore "generated" in a metaphysical sense</note> possessing <note>The scholar Taylor suspects the words "visible and tangible" fell out of the text here, though others disagree.</note>, so that you may also grasp the intermediary fulfillments of the cosmos. Insofar, then, as it possesses something bodily, the whole is **generated**. For according to this, it is both visible and tangible; and everything visible and tangible is <unclear>sensible</unclear>. For touch and sight are [forms of] sensation; and the sensible is "subject to opinion" <note>In Platonic thought, "opinion" (doxa) is the type of knowledge we have of the changing physical world, as opposed to the certain "intellectual" knowledge of eternal truths.</note>, being <margin>F</margin> constructed from <unclear>dissimilar</unclear> parts and not <unclear>receiving</unclear> the power to maintain the purity of the **intelligible forms**. Everything of this kind is **generated** because its <unclear>essence</unclear> is composite.

Therefore, Plato does not destroy the eternity of the universe, as <unclear>some</unclear> think who have followed **Aristotelian** hypotheses. That this is true is <unclear>easy</unclear> to learn from the following: he says that **Time** came into being along with the heaven. <note>referring to *Timaeus* 38b</note> <unclear>If</unclear>, then, Time is eternal, the heaven is also eternal. But if [Time] has a <unclear>temporal</unclear> beginning, then the heaven will also have a temporal beginning—which is the most impossible thing of all. <margin>88</margin> For they say that Time is twofold: one kind is disorderly, <unclear>while</unclear> the other proceeds according to number; just as motion is twofold, one kind being disorderly and out of tune, the other ordered and <unclear>harmonious</unclear>. Time is coordinate with each type of motion. However, while it is possible for a body to be moved <unclear>smoothly</unclear> or unevenly, it is <unclear>impossible</unclear> to conceive of Time itself as being "smooth" or "uneven"; for in that way, the essence of Time would be composite. And why do I say this? <unclear>Even</unclear> when motion is uneven, Time is smooth. For example, <unclear>there are</unclear> many motions now, some faster and some slower, and one is [more] <unclear>violent</unclear> than another, yet there is one Time for all of them, continuous and proceeding according to number. <unclear>Therefore</unclear>, it is not correct to make Time twofold in this way.

But if Time is one and continuous, if it is ungenerated, then the heaven is also ungenerated, having <unclear>co-existed</unclear> with Time. But if it is generated, it is absurd; for if Time were to be "generated," it would require [a prior] Time <unclear>for</unclear> this to happen when it did not yet exist. For at the moment Time was being "born," Time did not yet exist. Furthermore, he [Plato] joined the <unclear>Soul</unclear> of the universe to the Body immediately upon its being born, and he did not give it a life <unclear>prior</unclear> <margin>B</margin> to the bodily state, but from the moment it stood firm, he bound it together with the Body. # PROCLUS
## ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.

[It] co-exists with it; for the soul is "always being," and according to him, the body is also eternal. For that which co-exists [with] the eternal is itself unborn <note>original: "ἀγέννητον" (agennēton); Proclus argues that if the soul is eternal and the body is its necessary companion, the body must also be eternal in its own way.</note>. Furthermore, in these passages, [the] Timaeus calls the soul "generated," but Socrates in the *Phaedrus* calls it "unborn." It is clear, then, that he calls that which is clearly unborn "generated" in a different sense. Further, he will say [the] world... <note>original: "ἐρεῖ"; likely a reference to a forthcoming argument about the world's status.</note> just as even the heterodox <note>original: "ἑτερόδοξοι"; referring to philosophers with differing schools of thought, perhaps those who interpret Plato literally.</note> have conceded this point, he clearly defined it in the *Republic*, or rather not he himself but the Muses: that for every [gen]erated thing, destruction is a necessity. Understand from [these] points what I am saying: for it is shown that the cosmos is unborn. For if the cosmos is [perish]able, and nothing generated according to time is imperishable, then the cosmos is not [generated] according to time.

But what need is there for such syllogisms? For [he] himself expressly stated in the *Laws* that time is infinite in the past, and that in this [change] there have been tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of prosperities and famines of men. | **C**
For as if seeking a beginning from which [man]kind changes toward virtue and vice, he added: "From what point do you say?" "I think from a great [length] and infinity of time and the changes occurring within such a thing." [Ra]ther, so that we may remind ourselves from the matters at hand, we heard [him] saying a little before that where there is no extraordinary winter or heat, there the [race] of men is always more or less present. And if there is [al]ways a race of [men], it is necessary that the whole exists as eternal.

Furthermore, if he is the creator of [all] things, he does not create at one time and then at another let go of the rudders; for he would not [possess] his character in the same way, nor would he possess immutability. But if he is always creating, then that which is [being created] is [al]ways as well. For what would he want, being idle for an infinite time, to then turn to [creation]? Did he take this up because he considered it "better"? But was this very thing "better" | **D**
previously, or not? For if the Intellect was [igno]rant of it, that would be absurd; for there would be [igno]rance and knowledge within him. But if he knew it, why did he [not] previously begin to beget and make the [world]? But if this [creating] was not better, why then did he not remain in [idleness], [as one] might say? For to imagine a being who is Intellect and God pursuing the less beautiful instead of the more beautiful is not even pious to conceive. 

Indeed, it is necessary to concede these points if the world is "generated" [according to] time; but [rather], it co-exists with the infinity of time. They [seem] to me to also offend the creator of the world himself in another way by saying that [the] world at one time did not exist. For if this world once was not, then that creator [at that time] was not creating. For the thing being made and the maker exist together. And if he once was not creating, <unclear>then...</unclear>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s defense of the universe’s eternity by addressing the nature of the Creator (the Demiurge). Proclus argues against the idea that the world had a beginning in time, as this would imply a change in the Creator’s nature from "not creating" to "creating," which suggests imperfection.</meta>

# 208 PROCLUS
## ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.

[The Demiurge] was then creating potentially. But if he was creating potentially, he was imperfect, and only later became perfect when he began to create. If "before" and "after" exist regarding him, it is clear that he is not among those who act eternally, but rather someone who shifted from not-creating to creating according to time. But indeed, he himself produces time. How then can he possess an activity that requires time, when that very activity is what produces time? For *when* <note>original: "πότε" (pote)</note> does he make time? Was there a time when he was not making it, so that he might then produce the very time which he brought forth? This certainly could not be otherwise. 

After this opinion, let us examine Severus, who says that there are simply <margin>E</margin> two revolutions <note>original: "ἀνακυκλήσεις" (anakyklēseis); a term for the periodic cycles or "recycling" of the universe's motion.</note>, as the Eleatic Stranger <note>A character in Plato's dialogue, the *Statesman* (Politicus), who discusses the reversal of the universe's rotation.</note> showed: one in which the universe currently travels, and another that is the opposite. He claims the world is "generated" because the one who performs this specific revolution started from a certain beginning, but the world is not "generated" in an absolute sense. 

We shall meet this explanation by saying that one ought not to transfer mythical tales <note>The OCR reads "αἱματα" (bloods), but context suggests "ᾄσματα" (songs/tales) or "αἰνίγματα" (riddles).</note> into the study of nature. For where could the soul that moves the world grow weary and change its ancient circuit? And how is the "Whole" perfect and self-sufficient if it desires change? Moreover, if both the moved and the mover preserve their proper condition, how is there any place for the reversal of the revolutions? And how does Timaeus say that the "revolution of the Same" moves to the right according to the will of the Creator, while the "revolution of the Other" moves to the left? For if the works of the Creator must remain the same and exist forever, then the revolutions must also always be the same, and the circuit of the Same must always move in a motion to the right. For as soon as it proceeded from the Creator, <margin>F</margin> it received this specific rotation. 

Furthermore, how is it not necessary that an irregularity would overtake the motion of the heavens? For everything that is about to cease from its former motion and transition to another opposite one must hasten toward a standstill, which withers away the preceding motion. If the cause of the second revolution remains fixed in the same activity, what is the cause of the reversal? <note>Proclus argues that a change in the universe's direction would require a change in the divine cause, which is impossible.</note> These explanations, not being based on the laws of nature, must be rejected. Nor do those views hold weight which are offered in a more conceptual manner—for instance, that "generation" is applied to the world only as a matter of thought <note>original: "κατ’ ἐπίνοιαν" (kat’ epinoian); the idea that the world didn't actually start, but we "think" of it as having a beginning to understand its structure.</note>.

For the "always being" <note>original: "τὸ ἀεὶ ὄν" (to aei on)</note>, as **Iamblichus** <note>A highly influential Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized ritual and the hierarchy of being.</note> says, is what is proper to scientific knowledge. For even the <term>Intellect</term> <note>The "Nous," the first level of being after the "One."</note> comes from the first cause, and all things after the first cause are from it, yet not all things are "generated." For where would the eternal be, if all things were generated? For there is one thing even before eternity <note>original: "αἰῶνος" (aiōnos)</note>. 

How then is the whole "generated"? One might say: as <margin>B</margin> **always becoming** and **having been generated** at the same time. For it is not like a partial thing. A partial body does not just exist, but there is a time when it also "became." But the entire heaven subsists in "becoming," yet it has not also "become" all at once; rather, it is always at its completion, according to **Aristotle**, since it is "always in time" according to temporal infinity. Just as the sun-like light always proceeds from its own source, so too the world is always becoming, always being produced, and is always "becoming" and "having been generated" at the same time. And it is "generated" as something composite <note>original: "σύνθετος" (synthetos)</note>. For every composition is a "generation" <note>original: "γένεσις" (genesis)</note>. That which is composed has "always been generated"; "becoming" runs alongside it. This, it seems to me, Plato knew when he used "has been generated" <note>original: "γέγονεν" (gegonen)</note> instead of "is becoming," just as in the case of "being" he used "was" <note>original: "ἦν" (ēn)</note> instead of "is" when he asked "Was it always?". For in the case of the <term>Intelligible</term> <note>The realm of ideal forms, which is outside of time.</note>, "was" and "is" are the same. For all things there are "being," because all things are in the "Now," which is more indivisible than the "now" of time. In the same way, the terms "becomes" and "has been generated" coincide in the case of the entire sensible world. For it "has been generated" as something becoming, and it "is" as something generated. <margin>C</margin> For the term "generated," when taken according to a certain time, indicates the composite nature...

# 210 PROCLUS
## ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.

->PROCLUS<-

Simply put, this is clear from its opposite. For by this [term], he [Plato] distinguished the <term>Always Being</term> <note>original: "τὸ ἀεὶ ὄν" (to aei on). In Platonic thought, this refers to reality that exists eternally without change.</note>. If the "Always Being" indicated that which is simple, we would say that only the composite is <term>Generated</term> <note>original: "γενητόν" (genēton). While it often means "created," Proclus uses it here to mean "having a cause" or "dependent."</note>. But if the "Always Being" signaled that which exists according to all time, then "coming into being" would refer only to that which started at a specific moment. For it is not the thing existing in a part of time that is the opposite of the eternal, but rather the thing existing through all time. Yet, in this passage, he has contrasted the "generated" with the "eternal." Therefore, as something that has participated in time, this is the opposite of that, and for this reason, it is called "generated."

If the "Always Being" refers to the eternal, it is clear—since the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The divine "Craftsman" who orders the universe.</note> who produces time is called "Always Being," as is his model—that he signifies an eternal substance and not one that merely participates in temporal eternity. 

However, one might ask, while agreeing with these points: why did he call the world "generated" based on its body? For since there is in it a body (which is "generated" in the strict sense) and a divine soul, and even a divine <term>Mind</term> <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous). The highest form of intelligence in the Neoplatonic hierarchy.</note> prior to that soul, what have we learned that makes us call the whole "generated"
<margin>1)</margin> because of the body, rather than "ungenerated" because of the soul or the mind? 

| Some say that the whole world is characterized by its form | but not by its underlying nature. |
| :--- | :--- |
| Or we might say that we call Socrates "mortal," | even though he has an immortal soul, |
| because the living being within him is mortal. | |

If you should also say this: that we are now considering the "body-like" aspect of the universe before it has been coordinated with the soul, you would be speaking of its visible appearance. But when you see it as ensouled and possessing mind, you will call it a god; for Plato in the *Republic* <note>Book VIII, 546b.</note> saw fit to call it a "divine generated [being]," and here <note>Timaeus 34b.</note> a "happy god." 

Who could have praised the "Whole" more greatly than he? Since he was going to call it "generated," assigning the "ungenerated" to eternal things, he thus named the world "generated"—for it is not diminished by being called "generated" in comparison to the eternal—and he wove together "that which is coming into being" with "that which has become" <note>original: "τὸ γιγνόμενον ἐν τῷ γέγονε" (to gignomenon en tō gegone). A linguistic reconciliation of the world's ongoing process and its completed existence.</note>. He did this so that it might be revealed as a perfect "Whole" and a "Being," yet as something that has its essence in time and is thus "generated." He gave it a "beginning of generation" of a certain kind, but not of every kind, and he named its generation according to its "body-like" nature, while demonstrating 
<margin>B</margin> the divine powers within it, because of which it is "happy" and is called a "god." 

Furthermore, the demonstration itself is worthy of wonder: how scientifically he proceeded from the definition and reversed the order. For in the initial propositions, he defined the "generated" as the "object of opinion" <note>Knowledge based on appearance or belief rather than certain truth.</note>, but in the proof of the "generated," he has taken up the reverse, and he will make the definition the "middle term," just as is absolutely necessary in demonstrations. For these things were intended to make the argument a true demonstration. For opinion...

## ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.
### 14*

<warning>The left edge of the main text and the bottom left corner of the footnotes are partially obscured or cut off.</warning>

<unclear>...ing</unclear> of things <term>generated</term> <note>original: "γενητῶν" (genētōn). In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to things that depend on a higher cause for their existence, rather than things that simply "started" at a point in time.</note> he refers back to that very order. Therefore, it seems to me that he was not satisfied with using the <term>sensible</term> <note>That which can be perceived by the five senses.</note> to demonstrate what is generated, but added that it is an <term>object of opinion</term> <note>original: "δοξαστόν" (doxaston). Plato distinguishes between "knowledge" (of eternal things) and "opinion" (of changing, physical things).</note>, since sense-perception knows the activities of <unclear>generated things</unclear> by being affected by them, whereas opinion knows their essences as well, because it has already grasped their rational principles. In order, then, to declare that the very essence of sensible things is generated, he constructed his argument from the "object of opinion." Furthermore, his failure to add "that which perishes" to the "generated" demonstrates the reverence he holds for the world. And this is true in a certain respect, as we said before; nevertheless, this also shows the <margin>F</margin> caution of <term>Plato</term> <note>The text uses "the philosopher" or refers to his caution (eulabeia).</note>. For even though it follows [logically], he nevertheless avoids the <unclear>expression</unclear>. One might wonder at those who think that, according to Plato, "generated" means "existing according to time." For this "thing that comes to be," which he indeed calls "object of opinion," is also "that which perishes," but the world is not both at the same time. The world is at once "perishing" and "indestructible," but surely it is not perishing and <unclear>indestructible</unclear> in the same respect, <margin>90</margin> even though the philosopher calls it both; for that would be ridiculous. Rather, it is indestructible in one way, just as it is also "un-generated." For if that which is generated according to time is destructible, as is written in the <term>Republic</term> <note>original: "Πολιτείᾳ" (Politeia). Refers to Plato’s famous work; specifically the passage in Book VIII (though the footnote notes Book VII) regarding the "nuptial number" and the inevitability of decay for all things born.</note>, then the indestructible is "un-generated." It is "perishing," however, insofar as it is unable <unclear>to sustain</unclear> itself. For just as the <term>corporeal</term> <note>The "body-like" or physical nature of the world.</note>, as far as it depends on itself, is moved by another, <unclear>likewise</unclear> as far as it depends on itself, it is perishing, insofar as it is held together by another. No <unclear>body</unclear> is capable of generating or sustaining itself. For everything that generates is "active," and every "active" thing is <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: "ἀσώματον" (asōmaton). Proclus argues that only a non-physical power (like a soul or god) can truly hold a physical body together.</note>. Even if it is a body, it acts through incorporeal powers. <unclear>Therefore</unclear>, the generator is incorporeal, and every sustaining thing is productive of something (namely, of union and of the lack of dispersion). Everything productive is partless; therefore, the sustaining power is partless. Thus, it is <unclear>impossible</unclear> for a body to be the sustainer of itself. For "sustaining" is not a property of a body. For a body is divisible, as <unclear>Plato said</unclear> also in the <term>Sophist</term> <note>A Platonic dialogue where the nature of being and the physical world is discussed.</note> against those who say that all things are bodies. But the sustainer is <margin>B</margin> <unclear>partless</unclear>. If the thing sustained is a body, and the sustainer is incorporeal, the body is not its own sustainer. It is necessary, then, that the thing sustained by itself be partless. <unclear>Insofar</unclear> as the body has a finite power according to its own nature, so too according to <unclear>its own</unclear> nature it is "perishing"—not as if it were prone to destruction, but as <unclear>one</unclear> not naturally suited to preserve itself, nor as if it were "potentially destructible" (so that you would look for it to be destroyed in actuality), but as that which is unable to provide indestructibility for itself. From where, then, does it possess eternity <unclear>and</unclear> receive infinite power? From the <term>productive cause</term> <note>The Demiurge or Creator.</note>, I would say. For just as it is moved from that source, so it also "comes to be" from there, and is always "coming to be." For that which comes to be from an unmoved cause has obtained an unfailing nature, just as...

# 212
## PROCLUS

...as the divine <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Ἀριστοτέλης" (Aristotelēs). Proclus often calls him "divine" despite their philosophical differences, recognizing his authority in logic and physics.</note> also says ¹). Thus, according to this argument ²), the world would possess eternity as it proceeds from an unmoved <term>demiurgy</term> <note>original: "δημιουργίας" (dēmiourgias). The act of divine "crafting" or creation by the Demiurge.</note>. But since, according to its own nature, it is <term>generated</term> <note>original: "γενητόν" (genēton). Meaning it depends on a cause for its existence.</note>, it is always being generated by the Father. Because the world is a complete being and a whole, it is not incomplete; it has always "become" in the very act of "becoming," just as [even] its motion is always "at its end" <note>Meaning its motion is perfect and complete at every moment.</note>, as that man [Aristotle] says. Therefore, much ⁴) more so is its <margin>C</margin> | generation in respect to its <term>essence</term> <note>original: "οὐσίαν" (ousian). Its fundamental being or "substance."</note> always at its end, imitating the perfection of its Maker. Thus, it is always "becoming" and has always "become" because it is always "becoming" ⁵), as the whole infinity of its generative ⁶) power exists all at once. Yet, it is always being empowered toward <term>existence</term> <note>original: "εἶναι" (einai).</note> by that power in the "now," through its "now" contact ⁷) with the infinite. It receives something from that power that is the same (because the power gives it) and yet not the same (because of itself), since it is not able to grasp the infinite all at once.

And in this way, the eternity of the world remains, and its "generation" finds its place. In this regard, these men [Plato and Aristotle] do not fight, yet they differ nonetheless: Plato says the essence of the heaven is stretched out alongside all of time, whereas Aristotle assumes it is simply eternal. Yet Aristotle is himself compelled by many arguments to lead it back to a temporal infinity, calling <term>Eternity</term> <note>original: "αἰῶνα" (aiōna). Often translated as "Aeon," referring to a timeless, infinite state of being.</note> a standing infinite power. He demonstrates that no infinite power can exist within a finite body. It follows, then, ⁸) that the world—being corporeal—is always receiving infinite power but never possesses the whole of it at once, because it is finite. Therefore, it is only true to say <margin>D</margin> | of the world ¹⁰) that it *becomes* infinite in power, but it *is* not so. And if it "becomes," it is clear that it is made infinite through infinite time. For to be infinite belongs only to the eternal, but to that which is "becoming," it belongs to be "infinitized" ¹²); for <term>generation</term> <note>The process of coming-into-being.</note> is analogous to time. Thus, even Aristotle would be forced to admit that the world is, in a certain way, "becoming."

And indeed, both say it is "the same in number" ¹³), but one [Aristotle] says it *is* the same, while the other [Plato] says it *becomes* the same, following their respective principles. For the one [Plato] placed a <term>productive cause</term> <note>original: "αἰτίαν ποιητικήν" (aitian poiētikēn). A "Demiurge" or Creator.</note> before the universe, from which he brings the whole into existence, while the other [Aristotle] hands down no productive cause for any of the eternal things. And one [Plato] brought forth Time along with the essence of the heaven, while the other [Aristotle] brought it forth along with motion; for he says time is the "number of motion." Aristotle is also accustomed to doing this in other matters. For whatever qualities Plato attributes to "the One," Aristotle assigns to "the Whole"—such as being unmultiplied, being the object of desire, and thinking of nothing secondary. And whatever Plato assigns to the <term>Demiurgic Mind</term> <note>The divine intellect that crafts the world.</note>, Aristotle assigns to the heaven and the celestial gods; for he says that craftsmanship and <term>providence</term> <note>original: "πρόνοια" (pronoia). Divine care or foresight.</note> come from these. And what Plato assigns to the essence of the heaven, Aristotle assigns to circular motion; thus he departs from <margin>E</margin> | theological principles and gives in more than is necessary to physical arguments.

Since the divine <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: "Ἀριστοτέλης" (Aristotelēs). Proclus frequently calls him "divine" despite their disagreements.</note> is often talking up and down about the relationship of the <term>generated</term> <note>original: "γενητοῦ" (genētou). Something that has a cause for its existence.</note> to the corruptible and of the ungenerated to the <unclear>eternal</unclear>, he must be reminded that much earlier Plato also used these axioms. In the *Republic* ¹) he writes that "for everything that has been generated, <unclear>corruption</unclear> <note>original: "φθορά" (phthora). Destruction or ceasing to be.</note> exists," and in the *Phaedrus* ³) he says that "the ungenerated is also incorruptible." How then <unclear>can</unclear> he, while granting a "generation" to the universe, not also introduce corruption? Or <unclear>how</unclear> can that which moves "discordantly and out of order" <note>A reference to the pre-cosmic state described in Timaeus 30a.</note> not also have a "generation" <unclear>be</unclear>fore its corruption? The argument <unclear>ser</unclear>ves the hypotheses—or rather, it follows the very order of things, for which the hypotheses were taken. Just as the <term>Form</term> <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos).</note> everywhere depends on the <term>productive cause</term> <note>original: "ποιητικῆς αἰτίας" (poiētikēs aitias). For if the world is a thing that "becomes," and everything that "becomes" <unclear>necessar</unclear>ily becomes by some cause, then the world has of necessity come to be by some cause. Therefore, that which completes is always something else existing in accordance with that Form. But that which is becoming <unclear>is</unclear> ¹³) becoming because it is incomplete. Therefore, that which becomes, insofar as it is becoming, is not able to complete another. And if it cannot complete another, it is much more impossible for it to complete itself. This latter is certainly greater than the former; for that which can complete itself can also <unclear>com</unclear>plete others. But it is not possible for that which is becoming to complete another, being itself incomplete. Nor...
