<meta>This page continues the logical proof that the world must have an external cause. Having established that the world is "generated" (in the sense of being dependent), Proclus now explores whether the world could be its own cause or if it requires a superior, external Creator (the Demiurge).</meta>

# 214
## PROCLUS

...is it <note>original: "ἆρά" (ara)</note> its own perfecting principle? If it is not perfected by itself, it is clear that it is by another. For how can something have come into being without being perfected? Again, then, it must be said: the world is <note>Proclus is using a logical syllogism here.</note> everything that becomes is incomplete. Everything incomplete is perfected either by another or by itself. Everything that becomes, therefore, is perfected either by another or by itself. 
<margin>B</margin> But the world is | not perfected by itself; therefore it is by another; so that it comes into being from some cause. Furthermore, the world is composite and holds its existence from dissimilar parts. If it is composite, it was put together either by itself or by another. For there must be a cause for the composition, if we are not to make it accidental and spontaneous. If it were composed by itself, it would again be perfecting itself and giving itself existence, and we would find ourselves shifting it into the category of <term>incorporeal substance</term> <note>original: "ἀσώματον οὐσίαν" (asōmaton ousian). In Neoplatonism, only non-physical things can truly cause or move themselves.</note>. How then does a body compose itself? Is it by the parts arranging themselves? But then we would be making bodies <term>self-moving</term> <note>original: "αὐτοκίνητα" (autokinēta).</note>. Or is it by the parts pushing one another? And what would be the first thing to move them? It is not holy to entrust the universe to such pushings and leverings. And how shall order come from the disordered, and a "cosmos" <note>The Greek word "Kosmos" implies beautiful order.</note> from the unadorned? Everywhere the maker is better than the result, and the parent better than the offspring. If the material parts are the causes of the world’s composition, what is it that <unclear>limits</unclear> <note>original: "πε[ριορίζον]" (periorizon)</note> them? For this is what we are seeking. If the parts are the productive causes, how can disordered things be productive of 
<margin>C</margin> ordered things, | and chaotic things of the arranged? If, therefore, the world was not composed by itself, it clearly received this composition from another. If, then, the world is composite, and the composite is put together from some cause, the world therefore holds its birth from a cause. That what becomes, then, happens by some cause, is evident. If Plato called it "some cause" <note>original: "τὶ αἴτιον" (ti aition).</note>, meaning the cause of everything that becomes, it is no wonder; for the "absolute cause" <note>original: "ἁπλῶς αἴτιον" (haplōs aition).</note> and not merely "some cause" is the cause of all things, about which he himself said: "that is the cause of all beautiful things." For that is also God in the highest sense. But what follows after that is "a certain god," such as the <term>Demiurgic</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator god of the Timaeus.</note> or the Life-giving. What then is the cause of generated things, as distinct from the cause of the whole? It is for this reason that he says "by some cause" the thing becoming must become. And he does well to say that the cause of the whole of generation is one; for he says that the One is prior to all things. For even plurality is arranged around the one principle, 
<margin>D</margin> and many monads <note>original: "ἑνάδες" (henades). Divine units or ones.</note> around the One. Among others, some assigned the cause to <term>co-causes</term> <note>original: "συναιτίοις" (sunaitiois). Instrumental or secondary causes like heat or cold.</note>, others went back to natural forces, others to scattered infinite principles <note>Likely a reference to the Atomists like Democritus.</note>, others to this very nature, others to the Soul. Plato set aside these causes and established, as the first of all, the One Cause. For the rank of the Soul works with this cause, and nature serves it, and all the co-causes are enslaved to it and move according to its will.

# 215
## ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.

<note>The following lines are reconstructed where the left margin was damaged.</note>

...The creative monad <note>original: "δημιουργικὴ μονὰς" (dēmiourgikē monas). In Neoplatonism, the "monad" is the single source or head of a specific level of reality.</note> precedes the multitude, and [Plato] addressed it as "this cause," for this [term] is indicative of its singularity. But because it does not [hold] the first rank among the causes, nor is it unparticipated <note>original: "ἀμέθεκτος" (amethektos); an "unparticipated" cause would be the absolute One, whereas the Demiurge interacts with the world.</note>, he added the word "certain." For "from a certain cause" is the same as saying it comes from a single cause, yet not from the [absolute First]. Therefore, it is not logical to produce that which is generated directly from the One; [rather, there must be a medium], so that from the One, which is before Eternity, comes the entire eternal nature, and from this [eternal nature] comes the generated and temporal nature. Thus, from the highest of all things come the self-subsisting <term>self-subsisting</term> <note>original: "αὐθυπόστατα" (authupostata). Entities that have their cause of existence within themselves.</note> beings, and from these come the things produced by others. For there is a chain and an order of things proceeding from the One, and those things closer to the Source become the sustaining causes of those further away.

<margin>E</margin>
->Now, the maker and father of this universe it is a hard<-
<margin>A.)</margin>
->task to find, and having found him, it is impossible to tell him to all.<-

Those before us rightly said that once Plato showed the world was produced from a cause, he immediately ascended—in a manner worthy of his own intellect—to the God who is the Craftsman <note>original: "δημιουργόν" (dēmiourgon); often translated as "Demiurge."</note>. For it would not be fitting for a creator to introduce a calculated and divine cause for his offspring and then introduce "Chance" or "Spontaneity"—things which are neither causes, nor possess any power of existence, nor can they sustain the well-ordered procession of beings at all. It is proper that we first examine the phrasing itself and then run through the entire theory. 

"Father" and "Maker" <note>original: "πατὴρ καὶ ποιητὴς" (patēr kai poiētēs).</note> differ from one another in that the "Father" is the cause of the matter, while the "Maker" is the cause of the world, its order, and its formal cause in general. Furthermore, the Father is the provider of "being" and "substance," while the Maker provides "powers" and "multi-formed essence." The Father holds all things together within himself in a state of permanence, while the Maker is the cause of their "procession" <note>original: "προόδου" (proodou); the unfolding of reality into lower levels.</note> and birth. And while "Father" signifies an ineffable and divine providence, "Maker" signifies the manifestation and distribution of the <term>Logoi</term> <note>original: "λόγων" (logōn); here referring to the rational formative principles or blueprints of the world.</note>. 

<margin>F</margin>
Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> says that a "Father" is one who generates the whole, while a "Maker" is one who receives the matter from another. Hence, Ariston is called the "father" of Plato as the cause of the whole man, but a builder is the "maker" of a house, as he does not generate the matter himself. If this were true, it would follow that one could not call the Demiurge both at once, since according to the *Timaeus*, he does not bring matter into existence. And yet, does [Plato] not say this clearly? Perhaps, then, he is a "Maker" insofar as he is more of a "form-giver" (for we say everyone who leads things from non-being into being is "making" something); but he is a "Father" insofar as he produces what he produces with life; for Fathers are the causes of living things.

He also addresses Porphyry's view on the origin of matter in the creative process.</summary>

<meta>The previous page discussed the Demiurge as a "certain cause" that is not the absolute One but the singular source of the generated world. It introduced the famous Platonic quote about the difficulty of finding the "Maker and Father of this universe." This page analyzes the specific terms of that quote, particularly what is meant by "this universe" and why the "finding" is so difficult.</meta>

# 216
### PROCLUS

...fathers are the causes of certain living beings and are the providers of seeds accompanied by life. This, then, is the nature of a father. Regarding "this universe" <note>original: "τὸ πᾶν τόδε" (to pan tode)</note>, it signifies the physical masses—the entire spheres and the contents of each—but it also signifies the vital and intellectual powers that "ride" upon these masses. Indeed, it encompasses all the worldly gods and the entire divinity of the cosmos, around which the multitude of worldly gods proceeds. Let "the universe" be understood as the one divinity, the one intellect, the divine soul, and the entire physical mass, along with the associated divine, intellectual, psychic, and body-like numbers (for every unity <term>monad</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, a "monad" is a leading unit that heads a specific rank of reality.</note> possesses a multitude corresponding to itself). For "the universe" signifies all these things. Perhaps the addition of the word "this" also indicates that it is sensible and somehow particular. For the "intelligible universe" <note>The realm of pure ideas/forms before they are physicalized.</note> is not "this," because it contains all the encompassing limits and forms; but to this physical universe, the term "this" is appropriate, as it has received a sensible and material nature. To find the creator of "this universe," then, is a "task," as he says. For since "finding" <note>original: "εὕρεσις" (heuresis)</note> is of two kinds—one proceeding from first principles through scientific knowledge, and the other traveling from secondary effects through recollection <term>reminiscence</term> <note>The Platonic idea that "learning" is actually the soul remembering truths it knew before birth.</note>—you might say that finding him from first principles is difficult because the discovery of the intermediate powers requires the highest level of contemplation. But let me say that the path from secondary effects is even more difficult than that. For if we are to see the way to the Demiurge and his other powers from these [material] things, we must contemplate the entire nature of these things generated by him: all the visible parts of the world and the invisible natural powers within it, according to which the sympathy and antipathy <note>The hidden "magnetic" connections between different parts of the universe.</note> of the parts of the world are established; and before these, the stable "natural reasons" <term>logoi</term> <note>The divine blueprints or formative principles inherent in nature.</note> and the natures themselves—both the more universal, immaterial ones and the material ones—the divine, the demonic, and those of mortal animals. Furthermore, [one must understand] the ranks proceeding from life,

<margin>C</margin> some | eternal and others mortal, some pure and others material, some whole and others parts, some rational and others irrational, and the "fullnesses" <term>pleromas</term> <note>The collective groupings of divine or spiritual beings that "fill" the ranks of existence.</note> greater than us, through which the entire interval between the gods and mortal nature is bound together. One must also understand souls of every kind, and the various numbers of gods in different parts of the universe, and both the "ineffable" and "effable" tokens <term>symbols</term> <note>original: "συνθήματα" (sunthēmata). Mystical signatures or passwords placed in the world by the Creator to lead the soul back to him.</note> of the cosmos through which it is joined to the Father. For the one who rushes toward the contemplation of the Demiurge without these is too imperfect for the intellection of the Father; and it is not lawful for anything imperfect to be joined to the All-Perfect. Rather, the soul itself must first become an "intellectual world"...

# 212
### PROCLUS

...of names and verbs to announce what has been seen and to bring it out to others; for a discourse that proceeds through composition <note>Logical or grammatical construction</note> is unable to express that unified and simple nature. What then? Someone might say: "Do we not say many things <note>original: "polla"</note> ¹) both about the Creator <term>Demiurge</term> of the other gods and concerning the One Himself?" We speak indeed *about* them, but we do not speak of each thing *itself*; and while we are able to speak scientifically, <margin>93</margin> we cannot speak of the thing itself. For this is what "finding" is, as we said before. But if the "finding" is a matter of the soul's silence, how could a spoken word flowing from the mouth be sufficient to bring what was found into the light just as it is? Come then, let us also look upon this very thing we are discussing by following the light of science: who is this <margin>B</margin> Creator and in what rank of beings is He stationed? For different men among the ancients were carried toward different opinions. Numenius <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who bridged Pythagoreanism and Platonism; he famously influenced later Neoplatonists like Plotinus.</note>, for instance, celebrated three gods: he calls the first "Father," the second "Maker," and the third "Poem" <note>original: "poiēma" (work or creation)</note>; for according to him, the world is the third god. Thus, according to him ³), the Creator is twofold: both the first god and the second ²), while that which is created is the third. For it is better to say this than to speak as he ⁴) does in his dramatic style, calling them "Grandfather, Son, and Descendant."

The person saying these things, however, first of all does not correctly associate the Good <note>The "Good" (to agathon) is Plato's term for the ultimate First Principle, synonymous with "the One" in Proclus' thought.</note> with these causes. For it is not the nature of the Good ⁵) to be yoked to anything nor to hold the rank of another; yet the "Father" in Plato is stationed second to the "Maker." Furthermore, Numenius coordinates that which is exempt from all relation ⁶) with the things that come after it; but one must refer these things back to the First, while removing all relation from Him. Therefore, not even the "Father of the whole" ⁷) will apply to the First. For the "paternal" <note>The "paternal" function refers to the generative power of a deity.</note> rank appeared among the gods in the orders following the First. Thirdly, in addition to these points, it is not correct to separate the "Father" and "Maker" of Plato, since Plato celebrates Him as one and the same by both names. For divine creation <term>demiurgia</term> is one, and the Maker is one. The "Father" is everywhere handed down by Plato as one, and to tear apart this unity by following names is just as if someone, seeing Plato naming the whole "All" and "World" <term>kosmos</term>, were to say there were two creations—one the "Heaven" and the other the "World"—just as here he says ⁸) the creative power is twofold: one the "Father" and the other the "Maker."

I would also be surprised at Harpocration <note>A Middle Platonist who wrote a commentary on Plato; his views often aligned with Numenius.</note> if he too were satisfied with such arrangements concerning the Creator. For he follows Porphyry <margin>C</margin> according to the tradition of the three gods, and insofar as | he makes the Creator twofold, calling the first god "Ouranos" <note>Uranus (Heaven)</note> and "Kronos," the second "Zeus" and "Zên," and the third the "heaven" and "world." Then again ¹⁰), he addresses the first as "Zeus" and "King of the Intelligible," and the second...

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Proclus is critiquing the views of earlier philosophers regarding the nature of the Creator (the Demiurge). He had just mentioned Numenius, who proposed a hierarchy of three gods. He now moves through the interpretations of Atticus, Plotinus, and Amelius, contrasting their views with the teachings of Plato’s "Republic" and Orphic theology.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II.

...and the same being becomes for himself <note>original: "autos hautō"</note> Zeus, Cronus, and Uranus. At any rate, all these things are said of the First, from whom Parmenides removed everything—every name and every discourse. We, however, did not even allow the First to be called "Father," yet he <note>Referring to Numenius</note> declared the same being to be Father, Offspring, and Descendant. Atticus, the teacher of this man, immediately identifies the Creator with "the Good" itself; for while he is called "good" <note>original: "agathos"</note> in Plato, he is never called "The Good" <note>original: "tagathon"</note> itself. Furthermore, the Creator is addressed as "Intellect" <term>Nous: the divine mind or principle of reason</term>, whereas the Good is the cause of all essence and is "beyond being," as we have learned in the *Republic* <note>original: "Politeia," referring to Book VI, 509b</note>. What then would he say about the Paradigm <note>The eternal model used by the Creator to shape the world.</note>? Either it exists before the Creator, in which case something would be older than the Good; or it exists within the Creator, and thus the First would be many; or it exists after the Creator, | and <margin>D</margin> then—which is not even lawful to say—the First would turn toward things after it, and those things...

After these men, Plotinus the philosopher posits a twofold Creator: one within the intelligible realm <note>The realm of pure forms and ideas</note>, and the other as the ruling element of the cosmos. And he speaks correctly; for the world-dwelling Intellect is also, in a way, the creator of the whole world. Even Aristotle <note>The famous student of Plato and founder of the Lyceum</note> declared this to be the "First," calling it "Fate" and addressing it by the name of Zeus. But there is also an exalted Father and Maker whom Plotinus places in the intelligible realm, calling everything between the One and the world "intelligible." For there, according to him, is the true God, the Kingdom of Cronus, and the Intellect of Zeus. This is as if one were to say that within the heavens, there is the sphere of Cronus, the sphere of Zeus, and the sphere of Ares. For the whole intelligible realm is "one-many," and one Intellect composed of many intelligibles. These are the philosophical views of Plotinus.

Amelius, however, makes the Creator threefold, positing three Intellects and three Kings: "The One Who Is," "The One Who Has," and "The One Who Sees" <note>original: "ton onta, ton echonta, ton horōnta"</note>. These differ from one another because the first Intellect truly is what <margin>E</margin> it is; the second is the intelligible within itself, but "has" the one before it and participates in it, and for this reason is second; while the third is the intelligible within itself—for every Intellect is identical to its paired intelligible—but "has" the one within the second and "sees" the first. For the greater the distance, the more dim the "having" becomes. These three Intellects and Creators he identifies with the three Kings in Plato <note>Referring to the pseudo-Platonic Second Letter</note> and the Orphic triad of Phanes, Uranus, and Cronus; and according to him, the most specific Creator is the "One Who Sees." It is therefore worth saying to him what we said before: that everywhere Plato...

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Proclus has been examining various interpretations of Plato's Creator (the Demiurge). He has just concluded his critique of Amelius, who proposed a triad of creators, and is now arguing for the necessity of a single, unified principle—a "monad"—at the head of the divine order.</meta>

-># PROCLUS<-

...it is accustomed to return from the multitude to the henads <term>Henad: a divine unit or "one," the highest principle of unity in a specific order</term>, from which the order existing among the many has also proceeded. Rather, even before Plato, according to the very order of things, the monad <term>Monad: a single, indivisible mathematical and metaphysical unit</term> exists before the multitude, and every divine order begins from a monad. For while it is necessary for the divine number to proceed from a triad <note>original: "triados"</note>, the monad must exist before the triad. Where then is the <margin>F</margin> demiurgic monad, so that the | triad may come from it? And how could the world be "one" if it were not created by a single cause? For it is necessary that the cause itself be unified and monadic long before the effect, so that the world may also become "only-begotten" <note>original: "monogenēs," meaning unique or one-of-a-kind</note>. Let it be granted, then, that the creators are three; but who is the "One" before the three? For none of the divine orders begins from a multitude. Furthermore, if the paradigm <note>The eternal model of the universe</note> is one and the world is one, how shall the Creator not also be one before the many—looking as he does toward the one paradigm and making the world only-begotten? Therefore, the demiurgic number must not begin from a triad, but from a monad.

<margin>94</margin> After Amelius, Porphyry |—thinking he was in harmony with Plotinus—calls the "supercosmic soul" the Creator. He calls its Intellect <note>original: "noun"</note>, toward which this soul is turned, the "Animal-itself" <term>Animal-itself: the "Autozōon," the living model containing all intelligible life</term>, so that according to him, the paradigm is superior to the Creator. It is worth asking him: in which works does Plotinus make the soul the Creator? And how is this consistent with Plato, who constantly names the Creator "God" and "Intellect," but never "Soul"? How can he call the world a "god"? And how does the Creator pervade all things within the world? For while not all things participate in Soul, all things have received a share of demiurgic providence. Furthermore, divine intellection is capable of generating both intellects and gods, whereas the soul is not by nature suited to produce anything in an order higher than itself. I will refrain from mentioning that this itself requires much evidence—namely, whether Plato recognizes any such "unparticipated" soul.

But indeed, after this man, the divine Iamblichus—having written much in opposition to Porphyry's opinion and having rejected it as being un-Plotinian—himself | <margin>B</margin> hands down his own theology. He calls the entire "intelligible world" the Creator, as is clear from his own words, where he speaks in agreement with Plotinus. At any rate, he says the following in his *Commentaries*:

> We call the truly real cause, the source of things that come into being, and the intelligible paradigms of the world, the **Intelligible World**. And as many causes as we posit to pre-exist all things in nature, all these the God now under investigation—the Creator—contains, having gathered them into one under himself.

In saying these things, if he means that all things exist "creator-wise" within the Creator—including Being-itself and the Intelligible World—he will be in harmony with himself and with Orpheus, who says: "All things..." <note>Proclus is likely referring to the Orphic fragment where Zeus swallows the universe to contain all things within himself.</note>

<summary>Proclus argues that the Creator must be a single "monad" rather than a "triad" to ensure the world is unique. He critiques Porphyry's identification of the Soul as Creator and introduces Iamblichus' view that the Creator encompasses the entire Intelligible World.</summary>
<keywords>Monad, Triad, Demiurge, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Intelligible World, Only-begotten, Plotinus, Orpheus</keywords>

-># ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 2<-

"...'these things lie in the house of great Zeus' <note>original: "Zēnos megalou tade dōmati." A fragment from Orpheus, the legendary poet-prophet whose verses Proclus considered divinely inspired.</note> and 'within the [unclear] of Zeus they grew' <note>The Greek "sybra" is obscure; it may refer to a divine enclosure or "the heart."</note> and all such things. It is not at all surprising that each of the gods is 'the All,' though one is so in one way and another in another: one creatively <term>Demiurgically: in the manner of a craftsman or creator</term>, another intellectually, another immutably, another in a manner that admits change, and another according to some other divine characteristic. 

But if it is suggested that the Creator is the entire breadth of the reality between the world and the One, <margin>C</margin> | this is indeed a point worth questioning. We shall address this based on what he himself <note>Referring to Plato</note> taught us. For where are the kings who existed before Zeus—the fathers of Zeus? And where are the kings mentioned in Plato <note>Likely a reference to the "Second Letter" attributed to Plato, which discusses three kings of the universe.</note>, whom he himself sees fit to rank above the Creator, after the One? Furthermore, how could we say that the 'Always-Being' <note>The eternal realm of Forms</note> is the same as the 'Now-Being,' and yet call the Creator the entire 'Intellectual Order'—which is the Eternal Being, just as the 'Living-Being-Itself' is? For if we do that, we might be forced to conclude <margin>D</margin> | that the Creator is *not* an 'Always-Being,' unless he happens to encompass this along with the other eternal beings. 

Even Iamblichus himself <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a hugely influential philosopher who refined the Neoplatonic hierarchy.</note>, though he may be more general here, celebrated the demiurgic rank more accurately in other works, from which we should take our lead. Writing about the 'Speech of Zeus' <note>In Plato's Timaeus (41a), Zeus delivers a speech to the lesser gods.</note> in the *Timaeus*, and following the 'Intelligible Triads' <term>Triad: a group of three divine principles</term> and the three triads of the 'Intellectual' <term>Noeric: relating to the divine intellect</term> gods, he assigns the Creator the third position among the 'Fathers' in the third 'Heptad' <term>Heptad: a group of seven</term>. 

For he says that these are three gods celebrated even among the Pythagoreans. Regarding the first Mind, he says it contains the entire Monads within itself; it is | undivided, good-form, remaining within itself, and unified. They have handed down such hallmarks of its excellence. The second Mind, he says, gathers together the completion of such things; it is characterized by being 'fecund,' 'gathering,' and 'completing activity.' It is the generator of divine life, proceeding to all things and acting with the greatest goodness. Of the third Mind, which is the 'Creator of the Whole,' they say the hallmarks are the 'generative processions,' the 'creations of the whole causes,' and the 'connections'—both those causes that are distinct in their forms and all the demiurgic activities that proceed into the world...

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Proclus critiqued the views of Amelius and Porphyry regarding the nature of the Demiurge (the divine Creator). He moves now to the interpretations of Iamblichus and Theodore of Asine before presenting the definitive view of his own teacher, Syrianus.</meta>

# PROCLUS

Similar proofs to these teach us most excellently that we should judge the Iamblichean **theurgy** <term>theurgy: from 'theos' (god) and 'ergon' (work); the practice of divine rituals intended to achieve union with the divine</term> based on these points: what kind of being it considers the Demiurge to be. For how could the "Always-Being" as a whole be the Demiurge, if he <note>Plato</note> restricted the "Always-Being" through a defining explanation, but says that to find the Demiurge is a great task, and having found him, it is impossible to speak of him to all? How indeed could these things be said <margin>E</margin> | about that which has been defined and brought into the light for all who see?

But **Theodore**, following **Amelius**, posits three creators. He does not place them immediately after "the One," but at the level of the Intelligible and Intellectual gods <note>In the Neoplatonic hierarchy, the "Intelligible" gods are pure Being, while "Intellectual" gods represent Mind or Intellect; Theodore places the creators in the transitional space between them.</note>. He calls the first "Essential Mind," the second "Essence," and the third the "Spring of Souls." He describes the first as undivided, the second as divided into wholes, and the third as having produced the division into particulars. Again, one must say the same things to him that were said to the noble Amelius: that while we agree there are three gods here, or three levels analogous to these, we do not agree there are three creators. Rather, one is the *Intelligible* aspect of the Demiurge, the second is his *Life-giving power*, and the third is the *Truly Demiurgic Mind*. 

One must take care: the "Spring of Souls" should be ranked third. For the power of the middle realm—as he <note>Theodore</note> says somewhere—should be named partially in this way, but more universally it should be called **Life**. For the "Spring of Souls" is but one of the springs contained within Life. Since life is found <margin>F</margin> | not only in souls or in ensouled beings, but there is also a divine | and intellectual life prior to the psychic life, which they say proceeds from that source, one after another, through divided channels.

Such, then, to speak briefly, are the doctrines of the ancient interpreters concerning the Demiurge. But come, let us summarize and write down what has been contemplated by **our own leader** <note>Proclus refers here to his teacher, Syrianus, whose interpretations he considered the pinnacle of Platonic philosophy.</note> regarding this subject—views which we believe most accurately hit the mark of Plato's own thought.

According to him, the **Demiurge is the One** <margin>95</margin> who stands at the limit of the intellectual | monads <term>monad: a primary, unified divine principle from which a series of lower beings originates</term> and the springs of life. While he sends forth the entire creation from himself and establishes the more particular "fathers" of the whole, he remains himself unmoved, eternally established upon the "summit of Olympus" <note>original: "koryphē tou Olympou." Proclus uses the Homeric image of Mount Olympus to describe the highest, most stable point of the intellectual realm.</note>, reigning over both the hyper-cosmic and the cosmic worlds, encompassing the beginning, middle, and end of all things. For how could it be otherwise? In the whole of the creative rank, one cause is the universal creator of wholes, while another is the creator of particulars...

# ON THE TIMAEUS II

...of the wholes in a partial manner, and that of the parts in a partial manner. The **Demiurgic Monad** <term>Monad: from 'monas' (unity); the primary, single principle from which a hierarchy begins</term> has bound to itself the universal creation of all things in a fourfold way, and from it is suspended the **Demiurgic Triad**, which governs the universe as a whole <margin>1) Perhaps "of the monad," according to Taylor <note>Thomas Taylor (1758–1835) was a prolific translator of Neoplatonic texts.</note></margin> [having] divided the power of the triad <margin>2) 95, 6 "divided": Perhaps "having divided"</margin>. Just as, conversely, in the case of the other <column-break/> partial creation, the Monad leads the Triad that organizes the whole in a partial way and the parts in a partial way; and from the Triad <margin>3) "from the Triad": namely, "is suspended"</margin> is suspended the entire multitude, which is both distributed around it and divided around it, receiving its productions from it. 

Just as the One leads the many paradigms <term>Paradigm: the eternal blueprint or model that the creator looks upon to build the world</term>, so too the **One Demiurge** leads the many <margin>4) 95, 9 "of paradigms — many": omitted in Manuscript B. (Note: Of many Demiurges, therefore, there is one Demiurge who is the monad of the rest, in order that all things etc. Taylor writes as if he had read "there is therefore," not "the one," although even if this is admitted, the sentence remains hanging and incomplete.)</margin> demiurges, so that all things may follow one another: the One Paradigm of the Intelligibles, the one Intellectual <margin>5) 95, 10 "Intellectual": "Intelligible" in Manuscript B</margin> Demiurge, and the one unique <note>original: "monogenēs," meaning only-begotten or one-of-a-kind</note> sensible <margin>6) 95, 10 "sensible": omitted in Manuscript B</margin> world.

If these things are said correctly, the **Demiurge of the universe** is the limit <note>The "limit" (peras) marks the boundary between the Intellectual realm of active thought and the Intelligible realm of pure Being</note> of the Intellectual gods, established in the Intelligible realm, but full of power, by which he produces all things and turns all things back toward himself. For these reasons, **Timaeus** <note>The narrator of Plato's dialogue</note> says that he sees the Intellect and is the "best of causes" <margin>7) 95, 12 "best of causes": Reference to Plato's Timaeus, Page 28A. Therefore, he is an **Intellectual God**, set apart from all demiurges. Nor is he [simply] the "Soul-maker," for he generates the Soul along with the Crater, but he alone both establishes and distributes the Mind in the universe. Since he is the Mind-maker, he naturally holds an Intellectual rank. <meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Proclus discussed the hierarchy of the Demiurge and the Triad. Here, he shifts to a comparison between Plato and Aristotle regarding the eternity of the world, arguing that both ultimately agree that the cosmos is "becoming" in relation to its infinite source of power.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...as the divine Aristotle also says. <note>original: "φησὶ καὶ ὁ δαιμόνιος Ἀριστοτέλης"</note> 1) Thus, according to this 2) reasoning, the **cosmos** <term>cosmos: the ordered universe</term> would possess eternity by proceeding from an unmoved **demiurgy** <term>demiurgy: the act of divine creation or "crafting" by a higher intellect</term>. However, since it is by its own nature "generated," it is always "becoming" from the Father; and because the cosmos is a "whole" being and not incomplete, it has always been in a state of having been "made" in relation to its "becoming"—just as its motion is always "in its end" (complete), as that man [Aristotle] says. 

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, its generation according to **essence** <term>essence: 'ousia', the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</term> 4) is much more always complete, imitating the perfection of its maker. Consequently, it both is always "becoming" and has always "been" that which is always "becoming" 5); the infinity of its generative 6) power is present all at once as a whole, yet it is always being empowered toward "being" by that power in the "now," through its contact 7) with the infinite "now." It receives something from that power—something identical because of the giving, yet not identical because of its own nature, since it lacks the strength to grasp the infinite all at once. In this way, both the eternity of the cosmos remains, and its "becoming" finds its place. 

In this regard, these men [Plato and Aristotle] do not actually fight, though they differ nonetheless: Plato says the essence of the heavens is extended along with all of time, while Aristotle assumes it is simply "always being." Yet, through many arguments, Aristotle himself is forced to lead essence back to temporal infinity, calling the **Aeon** <term>Aeon: 'Aion', eternity or a divine, timeless duration</term> an "infinite standing power." He demonstrates, however, that no infinite power can exist within a finite body. It follows then 8) that the cosmos—being corporeal—always receives infinite power but never possesses it as a whole, because it is finite. 

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, it is only 9) true to say of it 10) that it *becomes* infinitely powerful, but it *is* not so [in itself]. If it "becomes," then it is clear that it is made infinite through infinite time. For "being infinitely" belongs to the eternal alone 11), while to that which is becoming belongs "being made infinite" 12); for "becoming" is the partner of time. Thus, even Aristotle himself would be forced to admit that the cosmos is, in a certain way, "becoming." 

Both men say the cosmos is "the same in number," 13) but one says it "is" the same, while the other says it "becomes" the same, following their own principles. For Plato placed an efficient (productive) cause before the universe, from which he establishes the whole; but Aristotle provides no efficient cause for eternal things. Furthermore, Plato gave birth to Time alongside the essence of the heavens, while Aristotle did so alongside motion—for time, he says, is the "number of motion." 14) 

Aristotle is also 15) accustomed to doing this in other matters. Whatever Plato attributes to the **One**, Aristotle assigns to the **Intellect**—such as being unmultiplied, being the object of desire, and not thinking of secondary things. Whatever Plato attributes to the **Demiurgic Intellect**, Aristotle assigns to the heavens and the celestial gods—for he claims that "demiurgy" and **providence** <term>providence: 'pronoia', the divine care and forethought for the world</term> come from them. And where Plato speaks of the essence of the heavens, Aristotle speaks of its circular motion—

<margin>E</margin> thus departing from theological principles and giving in to physical arguments more than is necessary.

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.

...practiced. Since the divine Aristotle <note>original: "δαιμόνιος Ἀριστοτέλης"</note> is frequently talking about the correlations between that which is "generated" and that which is "corruptible," and between that which is "ungenerated" and that which is "incorruptible," we should remind him that much earlier, Plato also agreed with these axioms. In the *Republic*, 1) he writes that **"everything that has come into being is followed by decay,"** 2) and in the *Phaedrus*, 3) he states that **"the ungenerated is also incorruptible."** How then is it possible for Plato, while granting a "generation" <term>generation: 'genesis', the process of coming into being</term> to the universe, not to also introduce "decay"? Or, if he describes the destruction of that which was moving "discordantly and without order" <note>This refers to the pre-cosmic state described in the Timaeus</note>, how could he not also grant it a generation prior to its destruction? It must be, then, that the generation of the universe was devised by him in a different way, 4) and that an eternity appropriate to that mode of generation has been harmonized with it. 5)

->Everything that comes into being, we say, must of necessity come into being by some cause. (Page 28 C.)<- 6)

The argument follows the hypotheses—or rather, the order of things from which the hypotheses were taken. For just as form is everywhere dependent on a **productive cause** <term>productive cause: 'poietikon aition', the agent or maker that brings something into existence</term>, so too the first hypotheses are continuous with the second. <margin>F</margin> They provide a starting point <unclear>for</unclear> the proofs that follow them. For since it <unclear>follows</unclear> from the first hypothesis that the world is "generated" (by way of a middle doctrine), he next demonstrates the consequence of this: that it was made by a cause, according to the <unclear>second</unclear> hypothesis. For if the world is a thing that "becomes," and everything that becomes comes into being <unclear>by</unclear> some cause, then the world has necessarily come into being by some cause. <unclear>How</unclear> then should we understand the productive cause of the universe, from which the world receives its "becoming"? <unclear>It</unclear> is necessary to investigate this next, following the proof. We <unclear>shall see</unclear> 7) what <margin>91</margin> <unclear>sort</unclear> of arguments 8) he will use regarding this as he proceeds. For now, let us briefly remind 10) ourselves why everything that <unclear>becomes</unclear> necessarily becomes by some cause. 9) Now, everything that becomes is, by its own nature, incomplete. Being <unclear>incomplete</unclear>, it is not naturally suited to complete itself, just as 11) it cannot complete anything else. For everything that is <unclear>being completed</unclear> is made complete by that which exists "in actuality" <term>actuality: 'energeia', the state of being fully realized or active</term>; and that which exists in actuality is "complete" (perfect). <unclear>Thus</unclear>, every "completer" is always something else 12) that already possesses that specific form. But that which is <unclear>becoming</unclear>, insofar 13) as it is becoming, is incomplete. Therefore, that which is becoming, in the very respect that it becomes, is <unclear>not naturally</unclear> suited to complete another. And if it cannot complete another, it is even more impossible for it to complete itself. This latter is a greater feat than the former; for that which can complete itself can also complete another. But it is impossible for a thing that is becoming to complete another, since it is incomplete. Nor...

# PROCLUS

...having suspended the harvest, in the manner of the **Homeric Golden Chain** <note>The 'Golden Chain' (seira) refers to the succession of divine powers connecting the highest reality to the physical world.</note> of divine actions called "worldly" ¹). <margin>B</margin> the whole and the "younger gods," | through whom he also ordered the specific parts. He holds the rank of King among kings, as has also been divinely demonstrated by our Leader <note>This refers to Proclus' teacher, Syrianus.</note> in his Orphic lectures. He is the counterpart to Phanes, which is why he is both **"Poet" and "Father,"** and each of these in a universal sense. 

Plato also holds these same conceptions regarding the Great Zeus. In the *Cratylus* ⁵), he shows through the analysis of names that Zeus is the **cause and granter of life**; for it is because of him that "living" <note>original: "to zēn"</note> exists for all beings, and for this reason he is named "Zeus" ⁶) by us. In the *Gorgias* ⁷), Plato ranks him with the sons of Cronus while also setting him apart ⁸) from them, so that he may exist both before the Triad and be shared by them. He also establishes the Law alongside him ⁹), just as Orpheus did; for 
<margin>C</margin> according to the instructions of Night | and from her ¹⁰), he makes Law his assistant <note>original: "paredros"</note>. Furthermore, in the *Laws* ¹³), he places **Justice** <note>original: "dikē"</note> as his constant follower ¹²), just as the theologian <note>Proclus often calls Orpheus "the theologian."</note> does. In the *Philebus* ¹⁴), he declares that a **kingly soul and a kingly intellect** exist pre-eminently in Zeus as the principle of Cause. 

Following these points, Plato will hand down the teaching ¹⁵) that Zeus establishes both intellect and soul, reveals the "laws of fate," and establishes all the ranks of the worldly gods down to the very last things—some things produced by him alone, and others through the mediation of the celestial gods. Indeed, in the *Politicus* ¹⁶), he calls Zeus the **Demiurge and Father of the universe**, just as he says of himself in these passages: *"Of these works, I am the Demiurge and Father."* He states that the current orderly arrangement of the world exists under Zeus, and that the world [moves] according to fate...

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II

...to move. Thus, the world, being alive, possesses the life of Zeus; it has Zeus as the creator and father of its own life. If Plato introduces the Creator as a public speaker <note>original: "demegorounta." Footnote 1 indicates a correction from 'creating' to 'speaking as an orator,' suggesting the Creator communicates the laws of the universe to the other gods.</note>, 
<margin>D</margin> this is also entirely characteristic of Zeus. Indeed, in the *Minos* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato concerning the nature of Law.</note>, for this reason, he called him a "sophist," in the sense that he fills the gods who come after him with all kinds of divine discourse. The divine poet [Homer] also demonstrates this, presenting him speaking as an orator from the highest peak of Olympus:

-> "Hearken to me, all you gods and all you goddesses;" <-

And he turns the double coordinations <term>Coordinations: 'sustoichias', referring to the Pythagorean table of opposites (like Light/Dark, Limit/Unlimited) which Zeus harmonizes.</term> toward himself. Throughout all his poetry, Homer hymns him as the "highest of rulers" and the "father of men and gods," and praises him with all the names of a creator. 

Since we have shown that the entirety of Greek theology assigns the whole work of creation to Zeus, what should we think of this passage from Plato? We should think that the same god is celebrated by him as both "Poet" and "Father"—namely, King Zeus—and not as Father alone, nor as Father and Poet separately. For the "Father" was a <term>Monad</term> <note>The Monad (1) represents the primary, unified source of all things.</note>, as the **Pythagoreans** say, while this rank of the gods is a <term>Decad</term> <note>The Decad (10) represents the completed, organized structure of the universe.</note>. As the divine number proceeds from the sanctuary of the **Monad**, it reaches the "all-receiving, venerable limit
<margin>E</margin> placed around all things," the "unturning" [Atropos], the "tireless **Decad**," | which they celebrate as holy. 

Thus, after the paternal **Monad** and the simultaneously paternal and poetic **Tetrad** <note>The Tetrad (4) was considered the 'root' of all creation by Pythagoreans.</note>, the **demiurgic Decad** has come forth. It is "unturning" because divinity is present within it without change; it "sets a limit for all" because it provides order to the disordered and arrangement to the unarranged. It illuminates intellect within souls, being itself intellect in a universal sense; it places soul within body, because it possesses and encompasses the cause of the soul. It generates the types of being—both the intermediate and the lowest—as if it had pre-contained the power of creation within itself. 

Furthermore, from what is written in the *Protagoras* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning virtue and the origins of society.</note>, one can deduce the rank of the Creator. In that work, Zeus is the cause of the entire political life and of the rational principles sown substantially into souls. This is what it means to take up the whole work of creation and to hold all things together by his own unchanging powers.

# PROCLUS

<note>The right margin of this page is damaged in the original manuscript, resulting in the loss of characters. These have been reconstructed by scholars (noted in the following text) based on the context of Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>

Just as the theologian [Orpheus] stations the Curetic order <note>The Curetes were mythical guardians who protected the infant Zeus; Proclus views them as a "unpolluted" protective rank of gods.</note> around him, so Plato says there are fearsome guards around him. And as Orpheus establishes him on the peak of
<margin>F</margin> Olympus, so too does Plato attach him to the "acropolis" [the highest point of the divine city] where, eternally established, he organizes all things through the middle ranks of being. Who the 
Demiurge <term>Demiurge: From the Greek 'demiourgos' (craftsman). In this context, it refers to the divine Mind that shapes the universe.</term> is, and that he is a divine Mind, the cause of the whole of creation, has been discussed. How the same 
Zeus is hymned by both Orpheus and Plato as the Creator should be remembered from those previous points. However, whether we should say he is "Source-like" <note>original: 'pegaios'. Referring to a 'Fountain' or primary source of reality.</note> or "Principle-like" <note>original: 'archikos'. Referring to a ruling authority.</note>, or of some other rank among the creative powers, is worth considering rather than passing over in silence.
<margin>97</margin> It seems, then, that the Theurgist <note>A reference to the author of the 'Chaldean Oracles', a mystical text Proclus considered divinely inspired.</note> attributes to the third of the "Principle-like" gods the act of giving these things to the world: the creation of the heavens, enclosing them in a curved vault, the fixing of the vast multitude of fixed stars, the establishment of the seven wandering spheres [the planets], and the placement of the earth in the center, with water in the hollows of the earth and air above them. Yet, if we look accurately, we find that the third of the cosmic "Principles" divides the universe into parts, the second is the creative cause of wholes and follows movement, but the first establishes all things by will alone and brings the entire world into existence. This first one is the one spoken of by Timaeus as the Demiurge, who brings all things forth by his will, producing both the division into wholes and the division into the parts that complete those wholes. For he does not only make the whole out of wholes, but also each whole...
<margin>B</margin> For all these reasons, we deem him to be beyond the triad of the "Principle-like Fathers" and to be a single "Source-cause" <note>original: 'pegaias aitia'.</note>. This is the one whom the Oracles present as "rooting out" <note>The scholar Taylor suggests this might mean 'flowing out' (original: 'ekroein').</note> the multitude of Ideas, and from Mind, Soul, and Body establishing the world, generating our souls and sending them into generation. About him, the Oracles say the same things as Timaeus:

-> He placed Mind in Soul, and in our [bodies] he placed us, <-
-> both of men and of gods. <-

This "marvel" is a doctrine celebrated among the Greeks regarding the Demiurge. If these things are said in harmony <note>original: 'homophylos' (of the same race/kind) or 'homophonos' (in one voice).</note> by Timaeus and the Oracles, then this Demiurge is a "Source-like" creator, as those who start from the god-given theology would say, and he too creates according to the Ideas.

## ON THE TIMAEUS II

...the whole world as both one and many, and as divided into wholes<sup>1)</sup> and parts; and one creator and father of the whole is celebrated by Plato, Orpheus, and the Oracles <note>The "Oracles" refers to the Chaldean Oracles, a sacred text for Neoplatonists.</note>, as "father of men and gods," begetting<sup>2)</sup> the multitudes of gods while sending souls into the births of men, as Timaeus also says. For if he is the "best of causes," as he himself says<sup>3)</sup>, what device could place him in the secondary ranks<sup>4)</sup> of the demiurges <term>Demiurges: Divine craftsmen or creators who shape the material world.</term>? For the "best" among creators indicates a supreme excellence at the very summit of the demiurgic series. Now, the summit of every series is "source-like" <note>original: 'pegaios'. In Neoplatonism, a 'Source' is the highest origin of a specific quality or power.</note>, so it is necessary that this creator be source-like, rather than "principle-like" <note>original: 'archikos'. A secondary ruling power.</note>, since principles are everywhere secondary<sup>5)</sup> to their own source. 

Therefore, he himself brings the worldly gods to completion as creators, being himself a kind of demiurgic source. But since there are many source-like creators, where we shall rank him in the divine choir requires more careful consideration. However, from what has been said, it is clear in what rank of gods we should seek him. From this it remains clear in what way it is "a task to find him and, having found him, to speak of him to all,"<sup>6)</sup> and how he is both "maker and father," and what the "making" power is—and not as some say<sup>7)</sup>, that "maker" refers to the creation of soulless things while "father" refers to the creation of soulful things. For he is the same maker and father<sup>8)</sup> of all things; indeed, he is called "father of works," as he says in the speech to the gods<sup>10)</sup>. Rather, he is father as the cause of their union and essence, and the provider of their subsistence and providence for all things<sup>11)</sup>.

<margin>D</margin> **This, however, we must again consider concerning him: towards which of the models did the one who crafted it work it out? Was it towards that which is the same and uniform, or towards that which has come into being? (Page 29 A.)**

Having stated the form of the cosmic system—that it is "generated"—and the "how" of its generation, namely that<sup>13)</sup> it is "sensible" (for he has made no mention of time yet, because time does not yet exist), and what the demiurgic cause is—that it is both "making" and "fatherly" (this being an intellectual, unparticipated, and universal cause)—he now moves to the third point, seeking what kind of model <term>Paradigm/Model: The eternal blueprint or ideal form that the creator looks toward when making the physical world.</term> the whole has: whether it is generated or eternal. For it is a rule that every creator either takes the model of what he creates from the outside, or he himself brings it forth<sup>16)</sup> from within himself. Just as among the creators here on earth, some are able to imitate other things accurately, while others have a creative<sup>17)</sup> power...

<summary>This page discusses the rank of the Demiurge as the "Source" of all creation, arguing that he is both the father and maker of all things, regardless of whether they have souls. It also begins an inquiry into the "Paradigm" or model used by the creator to shape the universe.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Proclus established the Demiurge as a "source-like" (pegaios) creator rather than a secondary principle. He now moves to explain why such a creator must work from a mental blueprint or "Paradigm" to ensure the world is orderly and purposeful.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...they possess the forms of wonderful works that are necessary for their 
<margin>E</margin> uses. For the person who first built a ship did so by having the model <note>original: 'paradeigma'. In Platonic thought, this is the eternal "blueprint" used by the Creator.</note> of the ship within himself in an internally formative way. Furthermore, he also perceived this: that everything acting in an orderly fashion also possesses a measure of its work. For if it does not, it will wander in its acting; if it reaches the end, it will not even know it. For how could it know if this is the intended end? Perhaps something is lacking or there is an excess, and it is necessary to take something away or add to it. This is why physical bodies act irrationally and mindlessly—because they possess nothing that contains the cause of what is being produced. For example, a medicine must be heated to a specific degree; if the art of medicine and the medical mind are not present to define the measure for the fire to produce health, the fire works the opposite effect and destroys the whole thing, which was meant to be beneficial to the patient's recovery. For the fire did not possess the form <note>original: 'eidos'. The specific "essence" or "type" of the thing being made.</note> of the thing being generated. That which acts must possess the rational principle <note>original: 'logos'. Here meaning the structured plan or logic of the object.</note> of what is being made, if it is to act in an orderly way. 

Plato, having observed these things, left the paradigm of the universe alongside the creative cause, whereas Aristotle, by doing away with the paradigm, also does away with the creative cause. Plato, having established that there is a paradigm 
<margin>F</margin> for these things, and having defined what sort of thing the paradigm is through the three hypotheses mentioned above, discovers the object of his inquiry. How he himself makes this discovery and through what kind of demonstration, we shall see later. For us, we must first show this very thing: that the world has come into being according to a certain paradigm; and then, we must seek what this paradigm is and in what rank of beings it is located. If the craftsmanship <term>Demiurgy: The act of divine creation or "crafting" the cosmos.</term> of the whole is indefinite and aimless, there would be no 
<margin>98</margin> paradigmatic cause of the universe. But if it is not even lawful | to think this, then the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: The divine "Craftsman" or Creator in Plato's philosophy.</term> knows what he makes. And knowing it, he thus brings forth the making of the world; he possesses within himself the causes of the things generated within it. It is necessary that these causes are either primary within him, or that they descend into him from more ancient principles. Whichever way we say it, the paradigmatic cause exists before the world. Furthermore, since there is a Demiurge, if he creates by his very being, then that which he makes is most like himself; and this is to make an image of himself. But if he creates by deliberating, this is entirely and in every way unworthy of the creative cause. But even if one were to suppose this, it still follows that the form of the work must pre-exist within him. For everyone who deliberates has already grasped within himself the thing to be made, about which he is deliberating. This, then, is demonstrated through many other arguments: that the paradigm of the world pre-exists, especially since the creative cause is 
<margin>B</margin> presupposed. For it is necessary that the creative power |—being intellectual—is either ignorant of the order of what is being generated, or knows it. But if he is ignorant, how does he create? How does he bring order to the whole? But if he knows it, how can he not contain within himself the thing being made?

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Proclus discussed why a creator needs an internal rational principle (logos) to act purposefully. # ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II

<note>Translator's warning: The left margin of the original manuscript is dark and faded, resulting in the loss of several initial letters on each line.</note>

...will he create according to a single cause? After this, we must examine what this **Paradigm** <note>original: 'paradeigma'. The eternal "model" or "blueprint" of the universe in Plato's thought.</note> is and what rank it holds among beings; for different thinkers have placed it in different ranks. 

The divine Iamblichus <note>A highly influential 4th-century Neoplatonist who expanded the hierarchy of the divine.</note> defined the **Paradigm of the universe** as "Being Itself" <note>original: 'hoper on'. Pure existence before it is divided into specific things.</note>, which is indeed grasped by Intellect. He placed this at the level of the Paradigm, identifying "Being Itself" as running alongside it, and calling both "graspable by Intellect." 

The philosopher Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus; he often argued that the levels of reality were more closely unified than later philosophers did.</note>, however, supposed the **Soul** to be the Demiurge <note>The "Craftsman" or creator god.</note>, as has been said before, and the **Intellect** to be the Paradigm, acting upon the things in the lower ranks through the things in the higher ranks. For while Plato called the Intellect the "Demiurge" and the "Paradigm," this commentator <insert>Porphyry</insert>, by taking the Soul as the Demiurge, has called the Intellect the "Paradigm."

Thirdly, the wondrous Theodore <note>Theodore of Asine, a student of Iamblichus known for his complex mathematical and triadic theories of the soul.</note>, by establishing a **Demiurgic Triad** <margin>C</margin> and seeing a first, middle, and final part within each unity, called the final part of each "Living-Being-Itself" <note>original: 'autozōon'. The Platonic Form that contains all living creatures.</note>. He stated that the Demiurge looks toward this "Living-Being-Itself," for he is suspended from the "Essential Living Being" in a primary way. 

According to this view, the "Essential Demiurge" does not create by looking toward something external, or there are not many paradigmatic causes, or the Demiurge is not projected toward his own creation according to some paradigm—lest he be seen to act by looking at things *after* himself, thereby falling into the state of a "partial soul" <note>A "partial soul" (like a human soul) is one that is distracted by external things, whereas a divine mind should be self-contained.</note>. 

But our leader <note>Syrianus, who was Proclus’s teacher and the head of the Academy in Athens.</note>, following a divinely inspired understanding, has granted this matter the proper distinction. For some made the Demiurge possess the Paradigms within himself—such as Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism, who taught that "the Intelligibles are not outside the Intellect."</note>. Others said they are not in him, but either *before* him or *after* him. Porphyry says the Paradigm is *before* him, while Theodore <note>Likely referring to Theodore of Asine again.</note>, whom he used to ask: "Is the Demiurge immediately after the **One**, or are there intelligible ranks between the Demiurge and the One?" <margin>D</margin> 

If the Demiurge is the **One**, it would be absurd for the entire multitude of Intelligibles to exist after the One as a non-multiplied thing. For the progression toward number and the entire multitude happens through the numbers closest to the One. But if there are other ranks between the One and the Demiurge, we must ask: Does the Paradigm of the universe exist primarily in the Demiurge, or after him, or before him? For if it exists primarily in him, then every...

# PROCLUS

<margin>C</margin> An inquiry: Is it perhaps impossible to establish <note>original: 'hypostēsai'—to give substantial existence to</note> anything other than the "Whole" [the Universe] as a generated pattern for that which is becoming? We shall resolve this difficulty by being mindful of what has often been said: that even the Soul is called "generated" because it participates in time. The argument questions what the paradigm is: is it Soul, or Intellect, or the Intelligible? For these are the only options. For this reason, he [Plato] inquired whether the world was made according to a generated pattern or an eternal one. Let us speak then as it seemed fit to some, and in this way: perhaps we said that a "perfection" <note>completeness or fulfillment</note> is able to meet this difficulty, by which it is clear why we must not say that the "discordance" <term>plēmmeles</term> (the out-of-tune or disorderly state of matter) of the cosmos exists in the way that Atticus and P[lutarch] <note>Middle Platonist philosophers who believed the world had a literal beginning in time.</note> supposed—namely, as something ungenerated. For if nothing existed before the heavens came into being, it would be foolish to ask whether the world was made according to an eternal being or a generated one. But he [Plato] does inquire about this now. Therefore, there was indeed something "generated" even before the world. And since space <note>original: 'chōra'—the "receptacle" or place where things come to be</note> was not yet [ordered], and yet three things existed even before the heavens came into being—which he also calls space—it is clear that the famous "discordance" was such a thing.

<margin>D</margin> For not only the "Whole," but also this "discordant and disorderly" state exists, as we said, and is prior. Therefore, since the world has this discordance as its matter <term>hylē</term>, but has the Intelligible as its superior pre-existing cause, which of the two does it resemble? Does it resemble the material within itself, or the more divine reality according to its essence? Being in the middle, it is necessarily made like one of the two extremes. For the Demiurge <note>The Divine Craftsman</note> is assumed to have taken the one [the disorder] and to look upon the **Living Being-Itself** <term>Autozoon</term> (the eternal Model). Thus, he reasonably asks to which of the two it is assimilated: to that which he "took," or to that which he "beholds"? It follows from these points that, being beautiful, it must have been made like the Intelligible and not like the discordant and disorderly motion; for that which is made like the latter would be ugly. Or, as some of the interpreters say, Plato is not speaking here about the Demiurge—as if the Creator were uncertain which of the paradigms he used—but rather he is speaking about us: that since the paradigms are twofold, which of the two shall we say the "Whole" has become like? In a certain way, this too has reason. For it is we who look toward both.

<margin>E</margin> It is not lawful <note>original: 'themis'—divinely permitted</note> for the Demiurge to look toward the worse; rather, <unclear>we</unclear>, looking at those things before him and after him, ask ourselves to which of the two it is proper to assign the paradigm. Others say that he proposed the "generated" as part of the division so that he would not seem to be snatching the conclusion in advance—namely, that the cosmic paradigm is eternal. For by assuming the opposite, he showed that an absurdity follows. Others say that, since among the objects of sense...

# PROCLUS
## ON THE TIMAEUS II

->ON THE TIMAEUS II<-

...contrary to nature, while others are according to nature; and of these, some possess images of certain classes <note>original: 'genōn'—kinds or species</note>, while others are likenesses of ungenerated <note>original: 'agenētōn'—eternal or uncreated</note> things. Wishing to demonstrate that the world was brought into being in relation to an eternal paradigm, he [Plato] has constructed the refutation of other possibilities by means of the principle that the "Whole" is the most beautiful of things. For that which is "most beautiful" is neither contrary to nature, nor is it derived from an essence that is merely a generated model. For that which is produced from such a model would not be the "most beautiful." Furthermore, because it is beautiful, it is not contrary to nature. Such, then, is the solution to this difficulty; but we must also grasp the precision of the words used through rational analysis. For the word **again** <note>original: 'palin'</note> indicates the order of the problem, showing that this follows continuously from what was said before and proceeds next in the sequence of those inquiries.

<margin>F</margin> The word **also** <note>original: 'au'</note> gathers all the inquiries together toward the single theory concerning the world. For both the discourse concerning the Demiurge <note>The Creator</note> and the discourse concerning the Paradigm are taken up for the sake of the theory of the "Whole" [the Universe]. The phrase **toward which of the paradigms** distinguishes the "Intelligible" and the "Generated" as extremes and as different from one another—the one being among the very first of beings, the other among the last.

<margin>100</margin> The phrase **having gazed** <note>original: 'theasamenos'</note> shows the craftsman-like art that descends from the Cause and proceeds into the world. For as the Theologian <note>Proclus usually refers to Orpheus by this title</note> says, the first "craftsman-handed ones" gave to Zeus the demiurgic powers of all worldly creation:

*Who for Zeus fashioned the thunder and the lightning-bolt,*
*The first craftsman-handed ones, who Hephaestus and*
*Athena taught all the intricate works, as many as the heaven holds within.*

Thus, Plato also, following this, continuously uses the terms **having fashioned** and **did fashion** in relation to the demiurgic production. That which is **according to the same and in the same way** <note>original: 'kata tauta kai hōsautōs'—a standard Platonic description of eternal Being</note> is the eternal paradigm of the Whole, which is indeed the very first of eternal things, established at the limit of the highest Intelligibles. But the **generated** <note>original: 'gegonos'</note> is that which is moved discordantly and without order. For this too is composite, much-mixed, and moved by another—which are indeed the elements of a generated nature.

<margin>B</margin> He [Plato] does not, therefore, say that the one [the paradigm] is ungenerated and incorruptible while the world is generated and corruptible, but rather that even that [pre-cosmic state] is "generated" in the sense of being moved by another and mixed. For throughout his work, Plato will say that these things existed even before the generation of the heaven: Space, Generation, and Being—clearly calling the "discordant state" by the name "Generation." Therefore, this too is a "kind" <note>original: 'genos'</note>, and the world is "ungenerated" according to the sense of temporal generation <note>Proclus argues the world has no beginning in time, though it depends on a cause</note>. These points are more in harmony with Plato and with our natural and undistorted conceptions regarding the "Whole."

<summary>Proclus analyzes Plato's terminology to argue that the world's beauty proves it was modeled on an eternal paradigm. He uses Orphic poetry to illustrate the divine nature of craftsmanship and explains that "generation" can refer to the disorderly state of matter preceding the world's ordered existence.</summary>

# PROCLUS
## ON THE TIMAEUS II

->PROCLUS<-

**If indeed this world is beautiful¹), and the Creator is good, it is clear that he looked toward the eternal; but if—what it is not even lawful for anyone to say—he looked toward that which has come into being.** (Page 29 A.)

First, let us consider the logical approach of Plato, how he has proceeded in a demonstrative manner. From the hypotheses, he held these two sets of axioms: first, that which is produced toward an eternal paradigm is beautiful; and second, that which is produced toward a generated model is not beautiful. From these, the following are the contrapositives: that which is beautiful was produced toward an eternal paradigm; and that which is not beautiful was not produced toward an eternal paradigm. For if to the 
<margin>C</margin> subject of the antecedent there follows the opposite of the consequent, these things convert into one another, and the original²) point is demonstrated | through a reduction to the impossible³) <note>original: 'eis adynaton apagōgēs' — a logical proof where you show that the opposite of your claim leads to a contradiction.</note>. For if the beautiful were produced toward a generated model⁴), and that which is produced toward a generated model is not beautiful, then because of the other axiom, the beautiful would be not beautiful. And again, if that which is not beautiful were produced toward the eternal⁵), and that same thing were beautiful, then the not-beautiful would be beautiful. Why then did he not adopt these axioms directly in the hypotheses—namely, "the beautiful was produced toward the eternal" and "the not-beautiful was not produced toward the eternal"—but instead used those from which these are converted, even though he intended to use these latter ones in his proof and not the former? It must be said that the former, starting from the causes, are more appropriate for the hypotheses, whereas the latter, starting from the effects, are more appropriate for the arguments following the hypotheses. For when he says, "that which is produced toward the eternal is beautiful,"⁷) he begins from the cause and ends with the effect. But the reverse—"the beautiful was produced toward the eternal"⁸)—makes the effect the leading term and the cause the following term⁹). Therefore, so that he might take axioms suitable for principles and effects for the hypotheses, he chose the former, but converted them in his proofs, selecting what was suitable for the points being demonstrated. Having established these four axioms, he then defines 
<margin>D</margin> concerning the "All" [the universe] with good reason |: either the world is beautiful, or it is not beautiful; but if it is beautiful, it was produced toward the eternal; if it is not beautiful, it was toward the generated. But indeed, that the world is beautiful is clear from sense-perception. Therefore, it was produced toward the eternal. And since the beauty in the world is reached from the paradigm through the mediation of the creative cause, he included in the leading premise, along with the world being beautiful, the fact that the Creator is good. For every good creator masters his own material and imposes the form he wishes upon the underlying subjects, and much more so the Universal Creator, who even brings into existence the underlying nature itself—as other accounts say¹⁰)—and brings it into existence in such a way as to be effective¹²) toward—

...the world proceeds from him and the craftsmanship <note>The Greek term is 'dēmiourgia', referring to the work of the Creator or 'Demiurge'.</note> proceeds from him. But since he added in the second conditional statement ¹), the opposite was passed over in silence; for even a disparaging word <note>original: 'dysphēmia' — speech that is ill-omened or impious.</note> about the world is harsh—since it is the most beautiful and blessed of things—but a disparaging word concerning the Creator is harsher still. Therefore, he preceded the discourse with **Themis** <note>Themis is the personification of divine law and order; Proclus sees her as the force that ensures the world remains linked to the goodness of its creator.</note>, who brings | <margin>E</margin> together toward the Creator even those things that [text lost] and does not allow them to be torn away from the goodness of the Father; this ensures that nothing transgressive or ill-omened against the Creator of all things is attributed to Themis herself. Since these conditionals are of such a nature, having taken their beginning from the process of division, let us see what sort of things ²) Plato brought forward next.

**[Instead of "indeed" ³)] it is clear that he looked toward the eternal; for the world is the most beautiful of generated things; and he is the best of causes. Thus, having been generated, it has been fashioned according to that which is grasped by reason and intelligence and which stays the same ⁴).** (Page 29 A.)

From these words, he first took up the conclusion, as is his habit, establishing the foundations of his proofs; then he brought forward a reminder of the vision, and upon this he added the concluding clause ⁵) ⁶). For the phrase "it is clear that he looked toward the eternal" is the conclusion, while "for the world is the most beautiful of generated things, and he is the best of causes" is the explanation of the [lost word] vision, as the causal conjunction "for" shows. The remainder is the inference regarding the whole. Such is the logical arrangement; but turning back again to the | <margin>F</margin> contemplation of the facts, let us first see for what reason he changed the word "beautiful" to "most beautiful" and "good" to "best," and then how these statements are true and what order they have toward one another. That the beautiful world was fashioned according to an eternal paradigm is obvious, and was stated previously. For where else would its beauty come from, if not from the imitation of that [eternal paradigm]? And if this is the case, it was modeled not simply toward "the eternal" in a general sense, but—if one must say so—toward the **highest** | <margin>101</margin> of eternal things ⁷) ⁸). For every image that participates more clearly in a Form <note>In Platonic philosophy, a 'Form' or 'Idea' is the perfect, eternal original of which physical things are mere copies.</note> is an image of a more primary paradigm. Just as in the products of the **telestic** <note>original: 'telestikē' — the ritual art or 'theurgy' used to draw divine presence into statues or symbols.</note> art ⁹), some things receive a dimmer presence of the divine because they partake of secondary or tertiary divine powers, while others receive a more vivid presence and participate in the first and highest of the divine activities; in the same way, surely, the God who perfected the world revealed it to be the most beautiful image of the first of eternal beings. For from that source comes the "most beautiful," and that which is most beautiful stretches upward through its own beauty toward a likeness of that source. Again, then...
