<meta>Continuity: Proclus continues his line-by-line commentary on Plato's Timaeus (29a), specifically examining the logic behind the "Demiurge" (the divine craftsman) choosing an eternal model for the universe. He is arguing that a "best" cause must produce a "most beautiful" effect.</meta>

# PROCLUS

Now, if the creative cause is good, he looked toward the eternal, or toward that which is generated <note>meaning something that has a beginning in time</note>, lest—by looking toward the inferior, which it is not lawful <note>original: 'themis' — referring to divine law or what is religiously permissible to say</note> to say—he fall away from goodness. But if this cause is not only good, but the best among causes, he looked toward the most eternal thing. | <margin>B</margin> For to the degree that the agent is more divine, so much higher is the object contemplated. For the same thing would not be contemplated by both a superior and an inferior being. Plato, demonstrating these things and subtly providing comfort through them, shows that the paradigm <note>the 'blueprint' or eternal model</note> of the universe is not merely one among many eternal things, but the most eternal of all; and he has called the world "most beautiful" and the creator "best" to show it is the primary and most excellent model. For it is necessary that the most beautiful world was made in relation to the most divine paradigm, and that the best creator looks toward the most supreme model. 

For if the most beautiful world did not come from the primary paradigm, then that paradigm would be a model of nothing, or of something inferior. But it is not the way of superior beings to make things that are inferior to the works of secondary beings. And if the best creator does not look toward the very first paradigm, either he creates without looking at a model at all, or he does not even intellect it. And how will that model hold the place of a paradigm if he does not grasp it with his mind? And how could that which is intelligible to an inferior being be incomprehensible to a superior one because of its excellence? 

Therefore, it is necessary that the | <margin>C</margin> most beautiful world came to be in relation to the most divine paradigm, and that the best creator looks toward the most eternal thing; and further, that the most beautiful world is produced by the best creator. For of what is the "best" a cause, if not of the "most beautiful" among things that are brought into being? For if it were not the cause of the most beautiful, it would be the cause of something inferior. If the best were the cause of an inferior thing, then the "not-best" would surely be the cause of the most beautiful, and in this way the entire order of things is completely overturned. 

Therefore, let these three things, demonstrated by "geometrical necessities" (as he says), be established; and through these, let us be reminded of how Plato has employed these names. Porphyry <note>A significant Neoplatonist philosopher and predecessor to Proclus</note> adds that if the creator is best, it follows that he looks toward the eternal, even if he were not creating beautiful things; or, if anyone creates beautiful things, it follows that they look toward the eternal—otherwise, one who is not the best of creators would be making beautiful things only by chance. Because of this, he linked [the concepts]...

He refutes the idea that an inferior model could result in the most beautiful world or that a superior creator would look to an inferior model.</summary>

...[and] that the <term>daimones</term> <note>original: 'daimones' — intermediary spirits or lesser divine beings who bridge the gap between gods and the material world</note> are the creators of mortal beings. Even if they are not $^1)$ simply the best, nothing prevents them, as craftsmen and sustainers of mortals, from being the best [for that task] and thus creators of beautiful images. These are the arguments of that man <note>likely referring to a previous commentator or Plato himself</note>. 

<margin>D</margin> But that the cosmos is rightly called "most beautiful" and its creator "best," is easy to learn. First, the visible appearance of the heavens, the order of their cycles, the measures of the seasons, the harmony of the elements, and the <term>analogy</term> <note>original: 'analogia' — the mathematical proportionality that binds the universe together</note> $^5)$ extending through all things shows—to those who are not completely blinded—that the whole is most beautiful. Next, the order of the invisible powers within it, by which the parts of the world are held together, and the order of the intellectual essence—how do these not reveal it as the most beautiful of generated things? For there is in it a $^6)$ harmonious dance, a participation in Mind, a gift of divine life, and an [ineffable] deity $^7)$ [and] a number of <term>henads</term> <note>original: 'henads' — 'units' or 'monads' of the highest divine unity</note> from which the whole becomes saturated with beauty. For where a soul, when it becomes orderly <note>original: 'kosmia' — a play on 'cosmos' (order/world)</note> by being likened to the whole, displays a marvelous $^8)$ beauty within itself, how does the whole not possess beauty in a far greater degree? For these reasons, the theologians <note>referring to Orphic or ancient mythologists</note> have wedded <term>Aphrodite</term> <note>goddess of beauty</note> to <term>Hephaestus</term> <note>god of craft/fire</note> $^9)$ and have said that the whole world prides itself on this. Again, from Hephaestus and <term>Aglaia</term> <note>one of the three Graces, representing Splendor</note> they give birth $^{10)}$ to <term>Eukleia</term> <note>Glory</note>, 

<margin>E</margin> [Euthenia] <note>Prosperity</note>, Euphēmē <note>Acclamation</note>, and Philophrosynē <note>Friendliness</note>, who $^{11)}$ make the bodily world excel in beauty. Indeed, not even those who have insulted the creator have dared to say that the world is not most beautiful; rather, they say the opposite: that souls are "lured" $^{12)}$ by the beauty of this world. 

How might we show that the creator is the "best" of causes? $^{13)}$ For some have submitted this "best" to mean [best among] generated things, so that he is not simply the best of all causes (for they say this would be false) but the best of causes that have been generated. For they say there is no cause of generated things $^{14)}$ above him. But I would be ashamed of these words if I needed such a trick, forgetting what was said a little while ago, where it was shown to us that the creator now handed down by Plato is the source and [father] of the entire creative order. Therefore, he is the best of causes because he has received the foremost rank among the creators of the whole. Here, Plato openly emulates Homer, 

<margin>F</margin> when he calls him "Father of all" and "Highest of rulers," even while Homer is mindful of the [ancient] $^{15)}$ gods all the way back to Night itself. However...

# PROCLUS: ON THE TIMAEUS
### BOOK II, PAGE 228

For just as the "theologian" <note>original: 'theologos' — Proclus uses this term to refer to Orpheus, the mythical poet-prophet</note> surrounds him with the <term>Curetic order</term> <note>the Curetes were minor deities who guarded the infant Zeus; here they represent protective, purifying powers</note>, so too Plato says that there are "terrible guards" $^1)$ around him. And just as Orpheus establishes him upon the 

<margin>F</margin> peak of Olympus, so also Plato assigns to him the "acropolis" <note>a reference to the 'high point' of the heavens or the soul</note>, in which he is eternally established, ordering all things through the middle orders of being. Who 

<margin>97</margin> the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>original: 'demiourgos' — the 'craftsman' or creator god of the world</note> is—that he is a divine Mind and the cause of all creation—has been established by these points. Let it also be remembered from this how the same Demiurge, Zeus, is hymned by both Orpheus and Plato. But whether we should say he is "fontal" $^2)$ <note>original: 'pēgaios' — acting as a primary fountain or source</note>, or "ruling" <note>original: 'archikos' — belonging to a specific rank of governing gods</note>, or of some other order of creative gods, is a question that deserves more than silence. 

It might seem that the things the <term>theurgist</term> <note>original: 'theourgos' — likely referring to Julian the Chaldean, author of the 'Chaldean Oracles'</note> attributes to the "third of the ruling fathers" are the same things that Plato's Demiurge $^3)$ gives to the world: namely, creating the heavens by enclosing them $^4)$ in a curved shape, fixing the vast multitude of the fixed stars, establishing the seven-fold wandering stars <note>the planets</note> $^5)$, and placing the earth in the center, with water in the hollows of the earth and air above these. 

However, if we look closely, we find that while the third $^6)$ of the cosmic rulers divides the whole into specific parts, and the second $^7)$ is hymned as the creative cause of motion for the whole, the first creates all things by his will alone and establishes the entire cosmos as a single state of being. But this $^8)$ Demiurge described by Timaeus $^9)$ produces all things through his "willing," providing both the division into "wholes" and the division into the "parts" that complete those wholes. For he does not only make the Universe a "whole of wholes," but also creates the multitudes within each whole. 

<margin>B</margin> For all these reasons, we consider it right to say he is *beyond* the triad of ruling fathers—a single "fontal" cause. He is the one whom the Oracles $^{10)}$ describe as "uprooting" $^{11)}$ <note>original: 'ekrizounta' — likely a corruption of 'ekrhoizounta,' meaning 'whizzing forth' or 'issuing'</note> the multitude of Ideas within the "Fontal Soul," establishing the world out of mind, soul, and body, and generating our souls and sending them into the world of "becoming." Concerning him, the Oracles say the same things as Timaeus: "For he placed 

Mind $^{12)}$ in Soul, and in the body $^{13)}$ of us he established [Soul], the Father of men and gods." This wonder is widely celebrated among the Greeks regarding their own $^{14)}$ Demiurge $^{15)}$. If these things are said in harmony $^{16)}$ with the *Timaeus* and the Oracles, then those who follow the god-given theology would say that this is the "Fontal Demiurge," creating according to the Ideas.

### It is a very great thing in every matter to begin from a natural beginning. (Pa[ssage from Timaeus 29b])

<margin>103</margin> Some read this by placing a punctuation mark at the word "all" <note>original: 'pantos'</note>; to whom it is indicated that it is the greatest of all things to set the [nature] which is the beginning as the start of the discourse; but others [place the mark] at "it is a very great thing," connecting "of every" to the following [clause]; to whom the phrase signifies that it is the greatest thing to begin from the [natural] beginning of the whole. And some say this for the sake of what went before [...] as being correctly concluded $^6)$ because the hypotheses were necessary; others [say it for the sake of] what will be said immediately after, as it is necessary, if we are to set the due beginning, to first determine what kind of discourses are appropriate for sensible things. [This relates to] those things which will be handed down later concerning the <term>final cause</term> <note>original: 'telikē aitia' — the 'purpose' or 'end' for which a thing exists</note>; for this [...] is the greatest and most natural, which one must especially contemplate, and from which it is fitting to render the subsequent explanations. But before making the discourse about this, [let us] say $^7)$ what the manner of physical discourses will be. But to me it seems that this axiom has been stated correctly concerning [the whole]. For it is universal and applies to [the things] <margin>B</margin> already stated, and to those following, and to those that will be said hereafter—[not] only to these, but also to the whole of creation <note>original: 'demiourgia'</note>. For just as starting from the [natural] beginning as if $^8)$ from a root, he renders [things] corresponding to it...

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 2

<unclear>...for</unclear> the accounts of the cause, and this science draws its own conclusions from its own appropriate hypotheses. It follows $^1)$, therefore, the order of things <unclear>as</unclear> a science, and through this, the pedagogical discourse. And this is the greatest thing: <unclear>firstly</unclear>, because it imitates the wholes and the procession of beings; secondly, because even the <unclear>slightest</unclear> error overlooked at the beginning multiplies as the work proceeds; and thirdly, the <unclear>beginning</unclear> is said to be "half of the whole." <note>This is a famous Greek proverb, often attributed to Hesiod or Pythagoras, suggesting that starting a task is the most significant part of completing it.</note> If this is so, it holds the greatest share of the matter; <unclear>but</unclear> if, as some say $^3)$, the beginning is even something more than the whole, the <unclear>term</unclear> "greatest" would properly belong to it. The poets also show this when they say <unclear>that</unclear> all things, if they receive beautiful beginnings, usually end beautifully <unclear>for</unclear> mortals. And indeed, the Athenian Stranger $^6)$ <note>The "Athenian Stranger" is the primary speaker in Plato's "Laws".</note> <unclear>calls</unclear> this $^7)$ beginning a "god," if it attains what is fitting. <margin>C</margin> | For the beginning, a god established among men, makes all things right, if it attains its proper allotted share.

But what is "according to nature"? It is either the whole having received what is owed to it, <unclear>proceeding</unclear> from the primary things according to essence $^8)$. For the beginning and the end are related to one another, but not to nature. This very point is appropriate to the subjects at hand—<note>Proclus is arguing that a "natural" beginning follows the actual order of how things are created in the universe, rather than just an arbitrary starting point for a book.</note> [namely] <unclear>nature</unclear>, in which the discourse about the whole of nature $^9)$ and the works of nature takes place, and the beginning of the proposed discourses. Therefore, the "beginning according to nature" in every matter is the final cause <term>final cause: the purpose or "that for the sake of which" something exists</term>; in demonstrations, it is the hypotheses; and in <unclear>discourses</unclear>, the definition regarding the form of teaching—whether one should assume it is fixed, unerring, and precise, or a "likely account" <note>original: 'eikotologia'</note>, which is not truth itself, but a belief made like unto $^{11)}$ the truth.

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Proclus discussed the importance of establishing a "natural beginning" for any philosophical inquiry, noting that a correct starting point is essential for the integrity of the entire work. # PROCLUS

...or from known things? From where does the difference in the accounts arise, if not from the things known? 

Some people say that it is a matter of **literary composition** $^1)$ <note>original: "logographia" — the art of writing or composing speeches.</note> to determine in advance what the nature of the discourse is and what kind of listener is required. They note that Aristotle emulated this practice, as did many of the more recent thinkers. But I would say that the discourse instead imitates **creation itself**. <note>original: "demiurgia" — the work of the Demiurge or Craftsman of the universe.</note> For just as creation brings forth the invisible lives of the world and establishes the visible realm, maintaining the boundary of the entire cosmos, so too Timaeus holds to the truth of the matters at hand. <margin>E</margin> He makes the form of his words appropriate to the things themselves, having pre-selected and pre-defined the manner of the discourse for the entire contemplation, so that he might direct the whole of his teaching toward that specific limit. 

Why then does he do this now, and not earlier? Because after the proof that the world must be "generated" <note>That is, having a cause or being part of the realm of change, rather than being an eternal, unchanging primary being.</note>, it is necessary to define what kind of account must be given concerning sensible things. This would have been impossible earlier, while the nature of the whole was still unknown. 

When he calls the whole world an **image**, we should not take "image" $^2)$ to mean the kind of image we consider the souls <unclear>of things</unclear> to be, nor is the **paradigm** <note>original: "paradeigma" — the eternal model or blueprint the Creator looks upon.</note> to be thought of as barren or weak. Instead, we must grant that there is an assimilation in this world toward the **intelligible** realm <note>The realm of pure thought and eternal forms.</note>. 

This happens in three ways: 
1. Firstly, according to the productive power of the paradigm; for by its very existence, it produces the image from itself. 
2. Secondly, according to the creative cause which completes the whole, making it as similar as possible to the model through its activities upon it. 
3. Thirdly, according to the world’s own turning back <note>original: "epistrophe" — the Neoplatonic concept of a created thing seeking to return to or align itself with its source.</note> and participation in the intelligible realities. 

<margin>F</margin> For the world assimilates itself to that model, as the **oracle** says $^7)$, "striving to wrap itself in the form of the images which the intelligible gods extend to it." <note>This likely refers to the "Chaldean Oracles," a text highly revered by Neoplatonists like Proclus.</note>

->As then the accounts are the interpreters of the very things they explain,<-
->so these accounts are also kindred to them. (Page 29 B.)<-

Just as the procession of beings originates from the One to the many, and the procession of worldly things goes from a "monad" <note>A single, unifying principle.</note> to its proper number, so too the discourse concerning the world—being made like the things that are—begins from the one and the universal, and then introduces division into the parts. 

<margin>104</margin> What then is the single axiom and the common principle in these matters? It is that the account must be **kindred** to the things of which it is the interpreter. It seems that from this starting point, the Platonists associated with **Albinus** and **Gaius** $^{13)}$ <note>Middle Platonist philosophers who lived in the 2nd century AD, known for categorizing Plato's doctrines.</note> began to distinguish how many ways Plato formulates his doctrines. They concluded he does so in two ways: either **scientifically** or through **likely accounts**. <note>original: "eikotologikos" — the famous "likely story" (eikos mythos) that Plato uses for physics and the material world.</note>

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Proclus discussed how Timaeus (the character in Plato's dialogue) defines the nature of his discourse only after establishing that the world is a generated image. This page continues that exploration, explaining why the "accuracy" of an account must change depending on whether it describes eternal being or the world of change.</meta>

->## ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II<-

...not in a single manner, nor as if there were one standard of precision for all kinds of accounts, whether they concern eternal beings or those things that subsist through **generation** <note>original: "genesis" — the process of coming-into-being or the physical world of change.</note>. Rather, just as the things themselves are, so too are the accounts divided alongside the things. They possess a certain state of precision and clarity relative to their underlying subjects, such that some accounts express the **precision** <note>original: "akribes" — exactitude or scientific certainty.</note> of the doctrines, while others express what is **likely** <note>original: "eikos" — a probable or "likely story," which is the standard Plato sets for physics.</note>. For the account must be akin to the things it describes; otherwise, it could not explain their nature unless it shared a kinship with them. Indeed, what the object is in a concentrated or "enfolded" state, the account must be in an "unfolded" state, so that it may both reveal the object and yet remain subordinate to its nature. For in this way, the divine causes of the account | <margin>B</margin> reveal the essences of the things that come before them and are naturally joined to them.

Among the gods, for instance, the **messenger of Zeus** <note>This refers to Hermes, acting as the "Logos" or expressive Word of the divine Mind.</note>, who is indeed the "account" or Word relative to the Intellect of the Father, announces his will to the secondary beings. Among essences, the **Soul**, being the "account" of the intelligible realities, reveals the unified cause of all things within them, having received its starting point from them. And among the orders of beings superior to us, the **angelic order**, having its subsistence from the gods, continually interprets and conveys the "unspoken" nature of the gods. It is reasonable, then, that here too the account of things should be akin to the things themselves. Let this be stated as a common axiom before we move to the specific divisions; for what follows divides the different types of accounts according to the quality of the things they describe.

**Concerning that which is permanent and stable, and made clear with the aid of intellect, it is fitting that the accounts should be permanent and unchangeable, and—so far as is possible—irrefutable and invincible; and in this, nothing should be lacking.** (Timaeus, page 29 B.)

Earlier, Plato called the **Model** <note>original: "paradeigma" — the eternal blueprint the Creator uses to make the world.</note> "that which always is" and "existing in the same state" and "comprehensible by intellect." Now, however, he calls it "permanent and stable"—the former instead of "always being" and "clear with the aid of intellect," and the latter instead of the remaining term, | <margin>C</margin> "comprehensible by intellect." He calls the accounts concerning it "permanent," so that through the identity of the name he might indicate their similarity to the things they describe; and "unchangeable," so that they might mirror the stability of the object; and "irrefutable," so that they might imitate that which is comprehensible by intellect and proceed in a **scientific** <note>original: "epistemonikos" — with the certainty of true knowledge or science.</note> manner. For if the accounts are to be appropriate to the intelligible realities, they must possess this refined precision.

He illustrates this through a hierarchy of "messengers"—from Hermes to the Soul to the angelic orders—who all translate higher realities into lower forms of expression.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Proclus explained that the precision of a description must match the nature of its subject—accounts of eternal things are stable, while accounts of the physical world are merely "likely." Here, he addresses a specific logical puzzle: if the world is a copy, what kind of model did the Creator use?</meta>

-># PROCLUS<-

<margin>C</margin> ...inquiry, lest it be impossible to establish the universe <note>original: "to pan" — the totality of all things.</note> relative to that which is **becoming** <sup>1)</sup> <note>original: "gignomenon" — the realm of change and physical existence.</note> <sup>2)</sup>. Is the rest of reality becoming, or only the universe? We shall resolve <sup>3)</sup> this difficulty by recalling what has often been stated: that Plato also calls the **Soul** "becoming," insofar as it participates in time. However, the argument faces a difficulty <sup>4)</sup>: what is the **model** <note>original: "paradeigma" — the perfect blueprint the Creator follows.</note> of the universe? Is it Soul, or Mind, or the Intelligible? For these alone are eternal. For this reason, he sought to know whether the world came to be according to a "becoming" model or an "eternal" one. Let it be explained, then, as it seemed to some, and in this way: perhaps it is possible to meet the difficulty with a more perfect approach <sup>6)</sup>, through which it will also be clear that one must not say the world is "disorderly" in the way that **Atticus** and **Plutarch** <sup>7)</sup> thought—namely, that it was **ungenerated** <note>original: "agenneton" — existing without a beginning or cause.</note>. For if nothing existed before the heavens came to be <sup>8)</sup>, it would be ridiculous to ask whether the world was created according to an "always-existing" model or a "generated" one. Yet, he is indeed asking <sup>9)</sup> this now. Therefore, there was something "generated" even before the world. And since it was not the whole universe nor "space"—for three things existed even before the heavens: being, space, and generation—it is clear that the thing so often spoken of, the **discordant** <note>original: "plemmele" — literally "out of tune," referring to the chaotic pre-cosmic state.</note>, was of such a nature. 

<margin>D</margin> Not only is the whole universe a "becoming" thing, but also that which is moved **discordantly and without order**, just as we said, and this exists prior to the world. Since the world possesses this "discordant" element as its **matter**, and the **Intelligible** <note>The realm of pure forms and ideas.</note> as its superior pre-existing cause, does it resemble the material within itself, or the one that is more divine in its essence? For being in the middle of these two extremes, it is necessarily made like one of them. For it is assumed that the **Craftsman** <note>original: "dēmiourgos" — the divine creator in Plato's Timaeus.</note> <unclear>and</unclear> taking over [the discordant] and looking toward the **Self-Animal** <note>original: "autozōon" — the perfect Living Being that contains the forms of all creatures.</note>; thus, he reasonably asks: to which of the two does the universe belong—to <sup>10)</sup> that which he took up <sup>11)</sup>, or to <sup>12)</sup> that which he looks upon? Following from this, it is clear that because the world is beautiful, it must be modeled after the Intelligible and not after that which is moved discordantly and without order; for that which is modeled after the latter would be ugly. Now <sup>13)</sup>, some of the interpreters say that Plato is not asking what kind of model the Craftsman used, but rather is speaking about *us*—we who know <sup>14)</sup> that models are twofold, and we are deciding which one we shall say the universe was modeled after. Yet this view also has some merit in a way. For it is we who look toward both, but not 

<margin>E</margin> the Craftsman. For it is not lawful for him to look toward the worse; but we, who exist both before him and after him, ask ourselves in which category it is proper to place the model itself. Others <sup>15)</sup> say that he proposed the "generated" model for the sake of a perfect logical division, so that he might not seem to jump to the conclusion that the cosmic model is eternal; for by hypothesizing the generated model, he showed that an absurd consequence follows. Still others <sup>16)</sup> say that since among sensible things...

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Proclus began discussing whether the world was modeled after something eternal or something created. # ON THE TIMAEUS II.

...contrary to nature, while others are according to nature; and of these, some possess images of certain **generated** <note>original: "genēton" — things that come into being and pass away.</note> things, while others are likenesses of **ungenerated** <sup>1)</sup> <note>original: "agenētōn" — eternal things without a beginning.</note> beings. Wishing to demonstrate that the world has become an eternal model for all other things, he has performed a "reduction to the impossible" by showing that the "Whole" <note>original: "to pan" — the totality of the universe.</note> is the most beautiful of things. For that which is most beautiful can neither be "contrary to nature," nor can it be separate from the "essential model." For that which comes from such a model would not be "most beautiful" [otherwise]. Because it is beautiful, it is not "contrary to nature." Such, then, is the solution to this puzzle.

We must also use our reasoning to grasp the precision of the words used. For the term **"again"** or the phrase **"to be examined"** indicates the order of the problem, <margin>**F**</margin> showing that it is continuous with what came before and that this inquiry proceeds in sequence following those investigations. The phrase **"concerning it"** gathers all the questions together toward the single inquiry concerning the world <sup>2)</sup>. For indeed, the discourse concerning the **Creator** <note>original: "dēmiourgos" — the divine craftsman.</note> and that concerning the **Model** <note>original: "paradeigma"</note> are taken up for the sake of the contemplation of the world. The phrase **"toward which of the two models"** distinguishes the **Intelligible** <note>original: "noēton" — the realm of pure thought and forms.</note> and the **Generated** as extremes and as different from one another—the one being among the very first of beings, the other among the last. The phrase **"the one who crafts"** <note>original: "ho tektainamenos"</note> points to the **form-giving** activity that descends from the Cause <margin>**100**</margin> and the creative art that proceeds into the world. For as the **Theologian** <note>Proclus refers to the legendary poet Orpheus as "the Theologian."</note> says, the first "master-hand-craftsmen" gave to Zeus the creative powers for all cosmic making:

*They for Zeus the thunder and the bolt did fashion,* <sup>4)</sup> <sup>5)</sup>
*The first master-hand-craftsmen, who Hephaestus and Athena* <sup>7)</sup>
*In all works of wonder taught, all that the heavens within contain.* <sup>8)</sup>

Thus, Plato, following this tradition, uses the terms **"crafting"** and **"did craft"** <sup>9)</sup> <sup>10)</sup> continually in reference to the creative making. The phrase **"according to the same and in the same way"** refers to the eternal model of the whole, which is indeed the very first of eternal things, established at the boundary of the primary Intelligibles. The **"generated"** is that which moves **discordantly and without order** <note>original: "plēmmelōs kai ataktōs" — a famous Platonic description of chaos.</note>. For this is also composite <sup>11)</sup> and highly mixed and moved by another—which are the very elements of "generated" nature. He does not say, therefore, <sup>12)</sup> that while the model is ungenerated and incorruptible, the world is generated and corruptible; rather, he says that even the model is "generated" in the sense of being "moved by another" and composite. For how else could Plato say <sup>13)</sup> that these things existed before the birth of heaven: **Space**, **Becoming**, and **Being**? He clearly calls the "discordant state" a form of **becoming**. Thus, this too "has become," <margin>**B**</margin> and the world is "ungenerated" according to a temporal beginning. These points are more in harmony with Plato and with our natural and undistorted conceptions regarding the "Whole."

# PROCLUS

**If this world is indeed beautiful, and its maker is good, it is clear that he looked toward the eternal; but if—which is not even lawful for anyone to say—he looked toward that which has come into being.** (Page 29 A.)

First, let us consider the **logical approach** <note>original: "logikēn ephodon" — the systematic method of reasoning</note> of Plato, and how he has proceeded by way of demonstration. From his initial assumptions, he held these two **axioms** <note>original: "axiōmata" — self-evident principles or starting points for an argument</note> as established:
1. That which is created according to an **eternal model** <note>original: "aidion paradeigma" — a perfect, unchanging template</note> is beautiful.
2. That which is created according to a **generated model** <note>original: "genēton" — something that itself had a beginning and is subject to change</note> is not beautiful.

These axioms also have their converses:
1. That which is beautiful was created according to an eternal model.
2. That which is not beautiful was not created according to an eternal model.

For if the opposite of the leading term follows the opposite of the resulting term, then these <margin>C</margin> terms are convertible with one another, and the original point is demonstrated | through a **reduction to the impossible** <note>original: "eis adynaton apagōgēs" — a logical proof (reductio ad absurdum) that shows a statement is true by showing its opposite leads to a contradiction.</note>. For if the beautiful were created according to a generated model, but that which is created according to a generated model is not beautiful (by the other axiom), then the beautiful would be "not beautiful." Conversely, if that which is not beautiful were created according to the eternal, but that which is created according to the eternal is beautiful, then the "not beautiful" would be beautiful.

Why then did he not simply adopt these axioms directly in his assumptions: "the beautiful is created according to the eternal" and "the not beautiful is not created according to the eternal"? Why did he use the first set, to which these are converse, even though he intended to use these latter ones in his proof? We must say that the first set is more appropriate for the initial assumptions because they begin from the **causes**, while the latter set is more appropriate for the arguments following the assumptions because they begin from the **effects**.

For when he says, "that which is created according to the eternal is beautiful," he begins from the cause and ends with the effect. But when he says the reverse, "the beautiful is created according to the eternal," he makes the "beautiful" (the effect) the leading term and the "cause" the result. Therefore, so that he might take principles suitable for beginnings and causes, he used the first set in his assumptions; but he converted them in his demonstrations, selecting what was suitable for the points being proven.

Having established these four axioms, he then <margin>D</margin> defines | the nature of the universe based on probability: either the world is beautiful, or it is not. But if it is beautiful, it was created according to the eternal; if it is not beautiful, then according to a generated model. However, it is clear from our own perception that the world is beautiful. Therefore, it was created according to the eternal.

Furthermore, since the beauty of the world descends from the model through the mediation of the **creative cause** <note>original: "dēmiourgikēs aitias" — the work of the divine craftsman</note>, he included in the premise—alongside the world being beautiful—the fact that the **Creator** <note>original: "dēmiourgos"</note> is good. For every good creator masters his own material and imposes the **form** <note>original: "eidos"</note> he wishes upon the subjects. This is even more true for the Universal Creator, who brought the very nature of matter into existence, as other accounts say, and established it in such a way that he might be **productive** <note>original: "euergos"</note> toward...

# PROCLUS

...of the creative [causes], he is celebrated as the highest of those who rule for the former <note>The Intelligible realm or the world of Forms</note> and the best <note>original: "aristos"</note> of causes for the latter <note>The physical, generated world</note>. Some people do not dare to blame the Demiurge <term>Demiurge: from the Greek 'dēmiourgos,' meaning a craftsman or artisan; in Platonism, the divine mind that shapes the universe</term>, yet they blame this universe and cite the sayings of the ancients who call it a "cave" <note>original: "spēlaion," a reference to the famous allegory in Plato's Republic</note>. Others, like Heraclitus, have said that even the Demiurge is "at play" while crafting the world. It is easy to answer these points:

<margin>102</margin> For the world, if it is a most beautiful and "happy god" as Plato says, is reasonably called a cave and a cavern <note>original: "antron" and "spēlaion"</note> only in comparison to the Intelligible realm <term>Intelligible: the higher reality of perfect Forms that can only be understood by the intellect, not seen by the eyes</term> and that [divine] place, especially for individual souls who have fallen into bodies and into the realm of generation. Even if the Demiurge is the "best of causes," one might call his entire providence <note>The divine care or 'pronoia' he exerts over the world</note> regarding these recent creations "play" <note>original: "paidia"</note> when compared to his activities that are entirely elevated above the world of the senses. For these reasons, the Demiurge received such praise from Plato in the present passage. One must also consider the arrangement of the "most beautiful" alongside the "best," and how this is suspended from the primary origins. For just as Beauty in those higher realms is attached to the Good—and the power that makes things beautiful is attached to the fountain of all goods—so it is here: for the world is called "most beautiful" and the Demiurge "best," and the most beautiful is dependent upon the best. Furthermore, [one should note] how the discourse about the creation imitates the creation itself.

<margin>B</margin> For just as the world itself is led from discordance toward order and toward a likeness of the Intelligible through the act of creation, so too the discourse concerning it previously used names that were somewhat unseemly—calling the world "that which becomes and perishes"—but now uses the most venerable names: calling it the "most beautiful of things that have come to be," the "offspring of the best father," and the "divine statue of an eternal model." A little later, he [Plato] will even celebrate it with the most holy of names.

->**“These things being so, it is an absolute necessity that this world be an image of something.” (Timaeus 29B)**<-

To simpler readers, this might seem to be the same as what was said before. Someone not looking closely might say: what difference does it make to say that the world was crafted according to a model, or that it is an "image" of something? In truth, however, each statement is distinct from the other. For although it is possible for a creator to work toward a model, it is possible for the thing being created to fail to become a true image of that model if it is not fully mastered by the creative cause. Lest you

<margin>C</margin> should think this is the case regarding the world, [Plato] has shown through what he said previously that the Demiurge looked toward a model because, being the "best," he looked toward the most divine thing; he showed it through the Intelligible...

### BOOK II OF THE COMMENTARY ON THE TIMAEUS

...the whole. He has shown through this very statement that this universe is also governed by the Form <note>original: "eidos"</note> and is truly a [modeled] paradigm. For if it is an image, it has been made like the Intelligible Whole. For that which is not unlike, but like, is an image. You have, therefore, the sensible universe as the most beautiful of images, the intellectual realm as its cause, and the intelligible as the most divine of paradigms. All things are in all things, but in a manner appropriate to each; since even the sensible world partakes of Intellect and of Being, and the intellectual realm contains the sensible within itself [conceptually], while possessing the intelligible in a secondary degree. The intelligible realm has embraced both the intellectual and the sensible within itself in a unified way, but the whole universe will possess these traits in its own way. The sensible world is set forth as a work of craftsmanship (a product of the Demiurge), the [intellectual] as the source of that craftsmanship, and the [intelligible] as the model or paradigm. 

And yet, the "paradigmatic" quality is also found within the [creative realm]; for in looking into itself, the divine mind acts. Every [intellect] sees what is in itself and is the same as the "intelligible" that exists within it. And conversely, within the 
<margin>D</margin> 
[paradigmatic realm] | exists the "creative" quality. For that Intelligible Model also "makes" the thing being born. This is not like a physical mold or an impression, nor is it like the portrait of Socrates which is merely a copy of another person; rather, by its very existence, the paradigmatic cause makes things similar to itself. 

However, there is still a difference between "creating in the manner of a model" and "being a model in the manner of a creator." The first is to act according to one's essence, while the other is to act [intellectually]. One is to think in an intelligible way, the other is to be an "intelligible" in an intellectual way. It is characteristic of the Paradigm to act by its very being, while it is characteristic of the Demiurge to act through his activity. Yet [for the Demiurge], acting by being and knowing/acting through knowledge are the same; just as the soul makes life happen simply by being present, but it acts with skill by knowing. The first belongs to the soul's essence, the second to its activity. 

And why must one speak of this only in the language of philosophers? For long ago the Theologian <note>Proclus refers to the mythical poet Orpheus as "The Theologian"</note> established the creative power within Phanes <term>Phanes: the Orphic "Protogonos" or first-born deity, representing the Intelligible Paradigm from which the universe is modeled</term>. For there was, and pre-existed within him—as he himself said—Bromios <note>A title for Dionysus</note> and all-seeing Zeus, so that Phanes might possess the 
<margin>E</margin> 
sources | of the double creation. Conversely, the Theologian placed the paradigmatic power within Zeus. For he says that Metis <note>The goddess of wisdom/counsel</note> is within him, and says: "And Metis, the first progenitor, and much-delighting Love <note>original: "Eros"</note>..." and Dionysus, Phanes, and Erikepaios <note>A mystical Orphic name for the creator-god</note> are named continuously. The causes have partaken of one another and exist within one another, so that one may say that the Demiurge contains the paradigm within himself (as the divine Iamblichus <note>A highly influential Neoplatonist philosopher, c. 245–325 AD</note> teaches), or that the Paradigm is himself a creator (as the noble Amelius <note>A student of Plotinus who argued for a threefold Demiurge</note> suggests). For the former saw...

<summary>Proclus explains the relationship between the Intelligible Paradigm (the model) and the Demiurge (the creator), arguing that they are distinct yet exist within one another. He supports this Neoplatonic theory by citing Orphic theology, where gods like Phanes and Zeus contain each other's powers.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page follows the discussion of the Demiurge (the Creator) as the "best of causes." Proclus now transitions into explaining how the physical universe, or "the Whole," is a perfect image modeled after an "Intelligible Paradigm" (a divine blueprint), and how these divine causes—the Model and the Maker—interpenetrate each other.</meta>

### PROCLUS

...paradigm. The demiurgic <note>creative or craftsman-like</note> characteristic pre-exists there; for in that realm exists the foremost Zeus, and for this reason, he made Phanes <note>a primeval deity in Orphic cosmogony representing the Paradigm</note> the creator; yet the paradigm also exists within the Demiurge. For Metis <note>Wisdom or Counsel</note> was also swallowed within him; and for this reason, he brought the paradigmatic cause into a unity with the demiurgic cause. This is enough regarding these matters. If Plato called the cosmos an "image," one should not be surprised. For even though it is the most beautiful thing, it is nonetheless an image of the intelligible <note>perceivable only by the mind</note> beauty; and through this likeness, it reveals <margin>F</margin> the elements that govern generation <note>original: "epityropeuonta." Thomas Taylor suggested "epipreponta," meaning "those things that adorn generation."</note> and those that have received the Form <note>original: "eidos"</note> of the paradigm as a whole | within themselves. Thus the philosopher also called the cosmos an "image" of the intelligible, as it is like its own paradigm. And the addition of the word "necessity" reveals a wonderful, unspoken, and truly ineffable <note>beyond words</note> likeness of the former to the latter. After this, he testifies to the demonstration as having an irrefutable and fixed character. For it has proceeded from the very first principles.

-> **In every matter, it is most important to begin at the natural beginning. (Page 29 B.)** <-

<margin>103</margin> Some read this by placing a punctuation mark after the word "all" <note>original: "pantos"</note>; for these readers, the phrasing indicates that the greatest thing of all is to establish the natural beginning of the arguments. Others, however, join "of all" to the words that follow "the greatest indeed"; for these readers, the clause signifies that it is most important to begin from the natural beginning of the whole [universe]. Some say this was stated for the sake of what preceded it, as those points were correctly concluded because the initial premises were necessary; others say it refers to what is about to be said—that if we intend to establish the proper beginning, we must first define what kind of arguments are appropriate for sensible <note>perceived by the senses</note> things. Still others say it refers to what will be handed down later regarding the final cause <term>telikē aitia: the ultimate "why" or purpose of a thing's existence</term>; for this is the greatest and most natural beginning, which must be observed above all, and starting from which one must provide the subsequent explanations. But before making the argument about this cause, we have stated <note>some manuscripts read "let us state"</note> what the manner of physical arguments will be. To me, however, it seems that this axiom is stated correctly regarding all things. For it is universal and applies both to <margin>B</margin> what has been said | and to what follows, and to what will be said hereafter—or rather, not only to these, but to the entire work of creation <note>original: "demiurgia"</note>. For just as if proceeding from a natural beginning as if from a root, he provides the subsequent details in harmony with it...

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically focusing on the methodological transition where Plato moves from discussing the nature of the Creator (the Demiurge) to the nature of the physical world as an "image." Proclus is currently explaining the importance of starting from the "natural beginning" and the relationship between reality, thought, and language.</meta>

### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II

...these as accounts of the cause, and this science <note>referring here to the study of nature or dialectic</note> draws its proper conclusions from its proper hypotheses. It follows, then, that science corresponds to the order of things, and the instructional discourse follows science. This is of the greatest importance: first, because it mimics the whole and the progression of beings; second, because even the smallest error overlooked at the beginning multiplies as the argument proceeds; and third, it is said that "the beginning is half of the whole" <note>a Greek proverb attributed to the poet Hesiod</note>. If this is so, the beginning holds the largest portion of the matter; and if, as some say, the beginning is even something *more* than the whole, then the greatest importance would wonderfully attach to it. Even the poets show this when they say that if all things receive a beautiful beginning, they tend to end and reach their middle beautifully for mortals. Furthermore, the "Athenian Stranger" <note>the primary speaker in Plato's Laws, whom Proclus identifies here</note> for this reason calls the beginning a "god," if it happens to be appropriate. <margin>C</margin> | For a beginning, he says, is a god established among men that makes all things right, if it attains its proper lot. 

But what does "according to nature" <term>kata physin</term> mean? It is either that which has received everything owed to it, or that which proceeds first from those things that exist according to essence <term>ousia</term>. For the "beginning" can also be the last point relative to us <note>i.e., the first thing we notice in the physical world</note>, but not in relation to nature itself. This very concept of "according to nature" is particularly suited to the present subjects, where the discourse concerns the whole of nature and its works, as well as to the starting point of these arguments. Therefore, the "natural beginning" of the whole is the final cause <note>the purpose or 'End' for which things are made</note>; of demonstrations, it is the hypotheses; and of discourses, it is the precise determination regarding the style of instruction—whether it should be assumed to be fixed, unchangeable, and accurate, or a "probable account" <note>original: "eikotologia"</note>, which is not the Truth itself, but a faith <note>original: "pistin"</note> made in the likeness of Truth.

->So here we must distinguish concerning the image and its paradigm. (Page 29 B.)<-

These three things are naturally joined to one another: things, thoughts, and words. Regarding things and thoughts, Plato has already laid down the first hypotheses; but regarding words, he will now make this definition. For when he distinguished "that which becomes" <note>the physical world</note> from | "that which is" <note>eternal reality</note>, he held fast to the contemplation <margin>D</margin> of things. When he defines our ways of knowing these things, he holds to the contemplation of thoughts. Now, by dividing the words according to the different types of knowledge, he will show us the specific nature of the words. Thus, these categories are in agreement with one another: 

| Things (Two-fold) | Knowledge (Two-fold) | Words (Two-fold) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Being** <note>the eternal</note> | Intellection <note>reasoned understanding</note> | Stable / Permanent |
| **Becoming** <note>the physical</note> | Opinion <note>sensory belief</note> | Probable / Likely |

For from where else does knowledge arise...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the methodological prologue of Plato’s Timaeus. Having just discussed the importance of the "beginning" (archē), Proclus now explores why Plato chooses a specific style of discourse—one that is "akin" to the subject matter—and how this mirrors the way the divine Creator (the Demiurge) brings the world into being.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...or from things known? And whence comes the difference in arguments, if not from the types of knowledge? Some say that it belongs to the art of writing <term>logographia</term> <note>original: "λογογραφίας"; the technical skill of composing speeches or prose</note> to define in advance what the style of the arguments should be and what kind of listener is required, and that Aristotle and many of the more recent writers emulated this practice. But I would say that the discourse mimics creation <term>demiurgia</term> itself. For just as creation brings forth the hidden lives of the cosmos and establishes that which is manifest, holding the definition of the latter before the entire cosmos, so too Timaeus holds fast to the contemplation of things, 
<margin>E</margin> while also making the form of his arguments appropriate to those things; he has grasped in advance and pre-defined the style of the arguments for the whole investigation, so that he might direct the entire teaching toward this standard. Why then does he do this now, and not earlier? Because, after the proof that the cosmos must be generated, it is then necessary to define what kind of discourse is required concerning sensible things—but not before, while the nature of the universe was still unknown. And when he calls the universe an "image," we must take "image" to be the kind we consider souls to be; just as the model <term>paradeigma</term> <note>the divine Blueprint or World of Ideas</note> is not barren or powerless, we must grant that this cosmos is assimilated to the Intelligible realm. This happens first according to the productive power of the model—for by its very being, it produces the image from itself; second, according to the creative cause which completes the universe as most similar to the Intelligible through its own activities; and third, according to the "reversion" <term>epistrophe</term> <note>the Neoplatonic concept of an effect turning back toward its cause to achieve perfection</note> of the cosmos itself toward the formal structure and participation in the Intelligible. For the cosmos also 
<margin>F</margin> assimilates itself, as the oracle <note>referring to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a sacred text for Neoplatonists</note> says, "hasting to clothe itself in the form of the images" offered to it by the Intelligible Gods.

->**So then, the arguments are akin to the very things of which they are the interpreters. (Page 29 B)**<-

Just as the procession of beings occurs from the One to the many, and the procession of worldly things from a unity to their proper number, so also the discourse of Timaeus—being made like the things that exist, as he himself says—begins from a single axiom and a universal principle, and then introduces the division into the arguments. What, then, is this one and common axiom among these? That the argument must be akin to the 
<margin>104</margin> things of which it is the interpreter. And it seems that the Platonists around Albinus and Gaius <note>influential Middle Platonist philosophers of the 2nd century AD</note>, taking their starting points from here, defined the ways in which Plato delivers his doctrines—namely that he does so in two ways: either scientifically <term>epistemonikos</term> or through likely accounts <term>eikotologikos</term>. And...

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.

<warning>Dark ink blobs and shadows on the left margin obscure the beginning characters of almost every line in both the main text and the scholarly notes.</warning>

<margin>D</margin>
...and that the spirits <term>daimones</term> <note>original: "δαίμονες"; intermediary divine beings who carry out the work of the higher gods</note> are the creators of mortal beings. And even if they are not simply the "best" in an absolute sense, nothing prevents them from being the best craftsmen and sustainers of mortal things, and for this reason, they are creators of beautiful images. These then were the thoughts of that philosopher <note>likely referring to a previous commentator or opponent</note>. But that the cosmos is rightly called "most beautiful" and its creator "best," is easy to perceive. First, the visible beauty of the heavens, the order of the orbital periods, the measures of the seasons, the harmony of the elements, and the analogy <term>analogia</term> <note>original: "αναλογία"; the mathematical proportion that binds the universe together</note> pervading all things shows to those who are not entirely in the dark that the whole is most beautiful. Next, the order of the invisible powers within it, by which the parts of the cosmos are held together, and the preservation of the intellectual <term>noera</term> <note>original: "νοεράς"; relating to the higher divine Intellect</note> essence—how does this not prove it to be the most beautiful of generated things? For in it there is a harmonious dance, a participation in Intellect, a bestowal of divine life, a union of godhead, and a number of unities <term>henads</term> <note>original: "ενάδων"; the primary units of divine reality in Proclus's system</note>, from which the whole becomes saturated with beauty. If the soul, becoming orderly by likening itself to the whole, displays a wonderful beauty in itself, how much more so must the whole possess beauty? For this reason, the theologians <note>Proclus refers to the Orphic and traditional Greek poets as "theologians"</note> have coupled Aphrodite <note>The Goddess of Beauty</note> with Hephaestus <note>The God of Craftsmanship</note>, saying that he thus crafts the whole himself; and again, from Hephaestus and Aglaia <note>"Splendor"</note> 
<margin>E</margin> 
they say Eukleia <note>"Good Fame"</note>, Euthenia <note>"Prosperity"</note>, Eupheme <note>"Praise"</note>, and Philophrosyne <note>"Kindness"</note> are born, who make the entire bodily realm stand out for its beauty. Even those who have slandered the Demiurge <note>Likely the Gnostics, who viewed the physical world as an evil prison</note> have not dared to say that the cosmos is not most beautiful; on the contrary, they say the souls are "enticed" by the beauty of this world. But how might we show that the creator of these causes is the best? For some have limited this "best" to the realm of things that have come into being, so that he is not simply the "best" of all causes (which they say would be false), but rather the "best of the causes of generated things"; for they argue that the principle above him <note>The One, the ultimate source of all existence</note> is not a "cause of generated things" <note>meaning the One is too transcendent to be the direct cause of physical matter</note>. But I would be ashamed of myself if I needed such a contrivance, forgetting what was shown just a little while ago: that the Creator now delivered to us by Plato is the source <term>pēgē</term> and the monad of the entire creative order. For this reason, he is the best of causes, because he has received the primary rank among the creators of the whole. In this, Plato clearly emulates Homer, 
<margin>F</margin> 
who calls him the "father of all" and "highest of rulers," even while remembering the gods alongside him, down to Night herself. But since...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Book II of Plato’s *Timaeus*. Proclus is currently defending Plato’s claim that the physical world is the "most beautiful" of things that have come into being and that its creator, the Demiurge, is the "best of causes."</meta>

# PROCLUS

...the oldest of the creative powers; among them he is celebrated as the highest of rulers and the "best of causes" <note>original: "ἄριστος"; Proclus refers here to the Demiurge or divine craftsman</note>. Some people, however, do not blame the Demiurge at all, but they do blame this entire universe, bringing up the descriptions of the ancients who call it a "cave" <note>original: "σπήλαιον"; a reference to the Allegory of the Cave in Plato's *Republic*, often used by Neoplatonists to symbolize the darkness of the material world</note>. Others have said that the Demiurge actually lives within the cosmos, as Heraclitus did. To these points, it is easy to respond.

<margin>102</margin> For if the cosmos is the "most beautiful" and a "happy god," as Plato says, then compared to the Intelligible realm <term>noetos</term> <note>the world of eternal Forms/Ideas that exists beyond physical perception</note> and that higher region, the cosmos is rightly called a cave or a grotto, especially for "partial souls" <note>individual human souls as opposed to the World Soul</note> who fall into bodies and the realms of generation. And even though the Demiurge is the "best of causes," one might call his providence over these "new" <note>mortal or physical</note> creations "child's play" <note>original: "παιδιὰν"; Proclus suggests that compared to the Demiurge's higher, purely intellectual activities, the act of physical creation is a secondary, effortless overflow</note> insofar as these activities are distinct from his transcendent essence.

For these reasons, the Demiurge received high praise from Plato in this passage; Plato observed the alignment of the "most beautiful" with the "best," and how it depends on the primary principles. For just as in those higher realms, Beauty is attached to the Good—and Beauty itself flows from the Fountain of all Good—so it is here: the cosmos is called "most beautiful," and the Demiurge "best," and the former depends on the latter. Furthermore, the very discourse <term>logos</term> about the cosmos imitates the act of creation itself.

<margin>B</margin> For just as the cosmos itself is led from disorder <note>original: "πλημμελοῦς"; literally "out of tune" or discordant</note> toward order and toward a likeness of the Intelligible through the act of creation, so too does the text first use terms that are somewhat dissonant—calling the cosmos "becoming and perishing"—but now it uses the most venerable names, calling it the "most beautiful of things that have come into being," the "offspring of the best father," and the "statue <term>agalma</term> <note>original: "ἄγαλμα"; an object of worship or a divine representation</note> of the paradigm." A little later, he will even use the most holy of names for it.

> **These things being so, it is a total necessity that this cosmos is an image of something.** (Plato, *Timaeus* 29B)

To simpler readers, this might seem to be the same as what was said before. A person not looking closely might say there is no difference between saying the cosmos was "crafted in relation to an eternal model" and saying it "is an image of something." In truth, however, each statement is distinct from the other. For it is possible for a craftsman to work in relation to a model, yet the thing being created might not successfully become an "image" of that model because the creative cause did not fully master the material. 

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, to prevent you from thinking this about the cosmos, Plato first showed that the Demiurge looked toward a model, and that because he is the "best," he looked toward the most divine model. He proved this from what he said regarding the Intelligible...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, specifically the section where Plato argues that the universe is modeled after an eternal, intelligible pattern. Proclus is discussing the relationship between the Creator (the Demiurge) and the Model (the Paradigm).</meta>

# ON TIMAEUS, BOOK 2

...the universe has been crafted <note>original: "δεδημιουργῆσθαι"</note>. But that this universe is also ruled by the Form and truly exists according to a Model <note>original: "παράδειγμα"; the eternal blueprint used by the Creator</note>, he has shown through this very speech. For if it is an "image," it has been made like the whole of the Intelligible realm <term>noeton</term> <note>the highest level of reality containing the eternal Ideas</note>. For that which is not dissimilar, but similar, is an image. Thus, you have the sensible universe as the "most beautiful" of images, the intellectual realm <term>noeron</term> <note>the level of pure, active Mind or the Demiurge</note> as the "best" of causes, and the Intelligible realm as the "most divine" of models.

Each of these exists everywhere throughout the others. For the sensible world participates in Intellect and Being; the intellectual realm possesses the Intelligibles secondarily; and the Intelligible realm has pre-contained both the intellectual and sensible worlds in a unified and causal way. However, each is named according to its own place in the hierarchy. The sensible world is presented as a "work of craftsmanship" <term>demiurgema</term>, while of the higher principles, one is "creative" <term>demiurgikon</term> and the other is "paradigmatic" <term>paradeigmatikon</term>. 

And yet, the paradigmatic is also within the creative; for the Creator looks into himself when he acts. Every Mind sees itself and is identical to the Intelligible that exists within it. Conversely, <margin>102D</margin> the creative is also within the paradigmatic. For that [the Model] also "makes" that which comes into being. A divine Model is not like a clay mold made by hand, nor is it like a portrait of Socrates. Rather, by its very existence, the paradigmatic is a cause of things that are similar to itself. 

Nevertheless, there is a difference between "creating in a paradigmatic way" and "being a model in a creative way." The former is to act through one's very essence; the latter is to act as a craftsman. To "think" is the mode of the Intelligible, but "to be Intelligible" is the mode of the Intellectual. It is characteristic of a Model to create by its "being" <term>to einai</term>, while it is characteristic of a Creator to create by "acting" <term>to energein</term>. This is not to say that creating by "being" excludes knowing or acting through knowledge. For example, the soul makes things live by its very being, but it also creates through art and knowledge; the former it possesses by its essence, the latter by its activity.

And why is it necessary to explain this only through philosophy? Long ago, "the Theologian" <note>Proclus's standard title for Orpheus, the legendary founder of the Orphic mysteries</note> celebrated the creative power within Phanes <note>the first-born Orphic god of light and creation</note>. For there, as Orpheus himself said, resided "Bromius and all-seeing Zeus," so that Phanes might contain the sources of the twofold creation. Conversely, he placed the paradigmatic power within Zeus. <margin>102E</margin> For Metis <note>Wisdom</note> and Ouranos <note>Heaven</note> are there as well. Orpheus says: "And Metis, the first progenitor, and delightful Eros," and "Dionysus and Phanes and Ericepaeus" are named in succession. 

Therefore, these causes have shared in one another and exist within one another. So, when one says the Creator contains the Model within himself, he speaks truly in a certain sense, just as the divine Iamblichus <note>a hugely influential Neoplatonist philosopher from the 4th century AD</note> teaches. And one who sees the Model as "appearing as a creator"—as the noble Amelius <note>a student of Plotinus</note> did—is also looking at the truth. For the one [Iamblichus] saw the model in the...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus. Proclus is discussing how the "Paradigm" (the eternal Model) and the "Demiurge" (the Creator) are distinct yet fundamentally united. The text then transitions to a famous Platonic maxim about the importance of finding a proper starting point for any explanation.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...a creative property pre-existing in the model; for there is the first Zeus, and because of this ^1)) he made Phanes the creator. But he who is in the [Demiurge] is the model. For Metis <note>The goddess of Wisdom; in Orphic myth, Zeus swallowed her to gain her power. Proclus interprets this as the Creator containing all Intellectual wisdom.</note> was also swallowed up in this one; and because of this ^2)) <margin>F</margin> he led the paradigmatic cause to the same point as the creative cause. These things also apply to the "image" <note>original: "eikon"</note>. If Plato has called the world an image, one should not wonder. And yet—being most beautiful, it is indeed an image of intelligible beauty, and through this likeness, the things governing generation ^2)) and those that have received the form as a whole | [receive the likeness] of the paradigm. Thus the philosopher also calls the world an "image of the intelligible," as it resembles its own paradigm. And the addition of the word "necessity" reveals that the assimilation to this [model] is truly ineffable and unspeakable ^4)). After this, he testifies to the demonstration as having ^5)) that which is fixed and inevitable. For it has proceeded from the hypotheses themselves.

->**It is most important to begin every matter from its natural beginning.**<-

Some read this by placing a stop after "every" <note>Changing the meaning to: "It is the greatest thing of all to begin..."</note>; to these <margin>103</margin> it indicates that the greatest of all things is to establish the beginning of the discourse as that which is the beginning by nature. Others connect "of every" to the words that follow <note>Changing the meaning to: "It is most important to begin from the beginning of the whole..."</note>, after "It is most important indeed"; to these, the clause signifies that it is most important to start from the natural beginning of the whole [universe]. 

Some say this was said for the sake of the preceding points, as they were correctly concluded through the necessary hypotheses. Others say it refers to the things about to be said immediately, as it is necessary—if we are to establish the beginning as it should be—to define beforehand what kind of discourse about sensible things <note>Things perceived by the senses, like the physical world.</note> is appropriate. Still others say it refers to the things to be handed down later concerning the final cause <term>telike aitia</term> <note>The "purpose" or "goal" for which something is made; for Proclus, this is the highest form of explanation.</note>; for this is the greatest and according to nature, which one must especially observe, and from which it is appropriate to give the following explanations. But before making the discourse about this, let us say ^7) what the manner of physical discourses will be. 

It seems to me that this axiom has been stated correctly concerning all [these possibilities]. For it is universal and fits both the things already said <margin>B</margin> and those that follow and those that will be said hereafter—or rather, it fits not only these, but the whole of creation <term>demiurgia</term>. For just as if starting from the natural beginning as if from a root ^8)), he gives back [results] in harmony with it ^9)).

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the opening of Plato’s *Timaeus*. Having established that every discourse must start from a natural beginning, Proclus now explores why the "beginning" (archē) is so powerful and defines what "according to nature" means in the context of scientific and philosophical inquiry.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II

...these things provide the justifications for the cause, and this science draws its own appropriate conclusions from its own appropriate hypotheses. It follows ^1) then that science follows the order of things, and the instructional discourse follows science. This is of the greatest importance: first, because it imitates the whole of reality and the progression of all beings; second, because even the smallest detail overlooked at the beginning is multiplied as the work proceeds; and third, it is said that "the beginning is half of the whole." <note>original: "archē hēmisy legeitai tou pantos"; a famous Greek proverb emphasizing that starting a task is the most difficult and significant part.</note> If this is true, the beginning holds the greatest share ^2) of the matter; and if, as some ^3) say, the beginning is even something more than the whole, the highest importance would wonderfully attach ^4) to it. Even the poets show this when they say that all things, if they receive "beautiful beginnings," tend to end and reach their middle point well for mortals. Indeed, the "Athenian Stranger" <note>The unnamed protagonist of Plato's *Laws* (Book VI, 775e), often identified with Plato himself.</note> for this reason ^7) calls the beginning a "god," if it happens to be fitting. <margin>C</margin> | For a beginning, he says, established as a god among men, makes all things right, if it meets its proper destiny. 

But what is that which is "according to nature"? <note>original: "kata physin"</note> It is either that which has received the full amount owed to it, or that which proceeds first from the essential parts ^8). For the "beginning" can also be the "last" in relation to us <note>Proclus means that what we discover last (the cause) is actually what nature created first.</note>, but not in relation to nature; this very concept of being "according to nature" is fitting ^9) for the present subject, in which the discourse concerns the whole of nature and the works of nature, as well as the beginning of the proposed arguments. Thus, the beginning according to nature for the universe is the "final cause," for demonstrations it is the "hypotheses," and for discourses it is the "definition" <note>original: "diorismos"</note> regarding the style of teaching—whether we should assume it is stable, unchanging, and precise, or a "likely account," <note>original: "eikotologia"; a central concept in the *Timaeus* suggesting that our physical science is a likely story rather than absolute truth.</note> not being truth itself, but a conviction made to resemble the truth ^11).

->**Thus, one must distinguish concerning both the image and its model.** (Page 29 B.)<-

These three things are naturally connected to one another: the objects, the thoughts, and the words. Regarding the objects and the thoughts, he [Plato] took up the first hypotheses; but regarding the words, he will now make this definition. For when he distinguished "that which becomes" from "that which is," he was adhering to the theory of objects; <margin>D</margin> when he distinguished our types of knowledge based on the objects ^12), he adhered to the theory of thoughts; but now, by dividing the words according to the different types of knowledge, he will demonstrate to us the distinct nature of the words. Thus, these are in agreement with each other: two-fold objects (the Being and the Becoming), two-fold knowledges (Intellection and Opinion), and two-fold words (Permanent and Likely). For from what other source could the knowledges come...

He introduces a tripartite division of reality into objects, thoughts, and words, which must all correspond to each other in philosophical discourse.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the opening of Plato’s *Timaeus*. Proclus is transitioning from the general necessity of a "good beginning" to the specific requirement that a philosophical discourse must be "akin" to the nature of the reality it describes.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...or from the things known? And from where does the diversity of discourses arise, if not from the different types of knowledge? Now, some say that it is a task of "logography" <note>original: "logographias"; refers here to the formal art of writing or composing speeches</note> to determine beforehand what the style of the discourse should be and what kind of listener is required—and they claim that Aristotle and many of the more recent thinkers followed this practice. But I would say that the discourse imitates the very act of Divine Creation <note>original: "demiurgian"; the work of the Craftsman who built the universe</note> itself. For just as that Power brings forth the invisible lives of the cosmos, establishes the visible world, and holds the definition of this world even before the whole cosmos existed, so too does Timaeus hold fast to the contemplation of reality. He makes the form of his words appropriate to the things themselves, and he has already grasped and pre-defined the style of the entire contemplation, so that he may direct the whole of his teaching toward this standard. 

Why then does he do this now, and not earlier? Because after the proof that the world must be generated <note>meaning the world has a cause and a beginning in principle, rather than being an eternal, uncaused primary thing</note>, it is necessary to define what kind of discourse is appropriate for sensible things; it could not have been done before, while the nature of the whole was still unknown. 

<margin>E</margin> When he calls the "Whole" an "image," | we must take this "image" to be the kind that we consider the nature of souls to be. Just as the Model <note>original: "paradeigma"; the eternal Blueprint of the Forms that the Creator looks upon</note> is not barren or inactive, we must grant that this world is assimilated to the Intelligible <note>The realm of eternal, unchanging truth</note>—first, according to the generative power of the Model (for by its very existence it produces the image from itself); second, according to the Creating Cause which perfects the whole to be as similar as possible to the Intelligible through its activities upon it; and third, according to the "turning back" <note>original: "epistrophē"; the Neo-Platonic concept of a created thing seeking and returning to its source</note> of the world itself toward its own formation and its participation in the Intelligibles. For the world also assimilates 

<margin>F</margin> itself, as the Oracle <note>original: "logion"; likely referring to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a sacred text for later Platonists</note> says, | "hastening to clothe itself in the imprint of the images" which the Intelligible Gods hold out to it.

**"As therefore the words are interpreters of those very things, they are also akin to them." (Page 29 B)**

Just as the progression of all beings begins from the One and goes toward the many, and the progression of worldly things goes from a "monad" <note>a single, unifying principle</note> to its appropriate number, so too does the discourse of Timaeus. By making itself like reality—as he himself says—it begins from a single axiom and a universal principle, and only then introduces division into the discussion. What then is the one and common axiom in these matters? It is that the word must be akin to the 

<margin>104</margin> things | of which it is an interpreter. It seems that, taking their starting points from here, the Platonists around Albinus and Gaius <note>Influential Middle Platonist philosophers who lived in the 2nd century AD</note> defined the ways in which Plato teaches his doctrines: namely, in two ways—either scientifically <note>original: "epistēmonikōs"; providing certain, unchanging knowledge</note> or through likely accounts <note>original: "eikotologikōs"; providing "likely stories" or probabilities suited to the changing physical world</note>, and...

<summary>Proclus argues that Timaeus's discourse must mirror the act of divine creation, where the physical world (the image) is shaped to resemble the eternal Forms (the model). He introduces the principle that philosophical language must be "akin" to its subject matter, distinguishing between certain science and "likely accounts."</summary>
