# ON THE TIMAEUS II. 245

<warning>Staining and fading on the bottom left corner, particularly affecting the first few footnotes. Some text is obscured.</warning>

...not in a single manner, nor as if there were one kind of precision for all various subjects, <note>original: "pantoiōn"</note> whether they concern true Beings or those things that subsist through the process of generation. <note>original: "genesis"; the world of change and physical birth</note> Rather, just as the objects themselves are, so too are the discourses divided according to those objects; and just as precision and clarity exist in the underlying subjects, so the discourses express the "accurate" <note>original: "akribes"</note> for dogmas, and the "likely" <note>original: "eikos"</note> for others. For the discourse must be similar to the things it describes; otherwise, it could not explain their nature unless it were akin to them. For what the object is in a folded, unified state, the discourse must be in an unfolded state, so that it may both reveal the object and yet remain subordinate to its nature. In this way, the divine causes of discourse | <margin>B</margin> reveal the essences of the things that come before them and are naturally united with them. Among the gods, then, the messenger of Zeus—who is the Word <note>original: "logos"</note> relative to the Intellect of the Father—reports his will to the secondary powers. Among the Essences, the Soul, being the "rationality" of the Intelligible realm, reveals the unified cause of all things within itself, having received its starting point <note>original: "hypothesin"</note> from them. And among the ranks superior to us, the Angelic order, having been established continuously from the gods, interprets and conveys the ineffable nature of the gods. It is reasonable, then, that here too the discourse concerning things is akin to the things themselves. Let this be stated as a common principle before we address the specific divisions; what follows divides the different modes of discourse according to the quality of the objects.

->As for the abiding and stable, and manifest with the aid of reason, it is proper that the accounts be abiding and unchangeable, as far as possible irrefutable and invincible; and in this, nothing should be lacking. (Page 29 B.)<-

The Model <note>The "Paradeigma," the eternal blueprint used by the Creator to build the world</note> was previously called "always being," "consistent," and "graspable by intellection," but now he calls it "abiding and stable"—the former instead of "always being" and "manifest with the aid of reason," and the latter instead of | <margin>C</margin> the remaining term, "graspable by intellection." He calls the accounts about it "abiding" so that, through the identity of the name, he might show their similarity to the objects; and "unchangeable," so that they may mirror the stability of the object; and "irrefutable," so that they may imitate that which is graspable by intellection and proceed in a scientifically certain manner. For if the accounts are to be appropriate to the Intelligible realities, they must possess extreme precision.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus (specifically section 29C). Having established that discourses must be akin to the things they describe, Proclus now explores the specific relationship between "intellect" and "scientific knowledge," and why discourses about the physical world are merely "likely."</meta>

### PROCLUS

...them and that which is fixed, <note>original: "araros"; meaning stable or firmly joined</note> as they concern such matters. For just as the knowledge of eternal things is unchangeable, so too is the discourse; for it is an **unfolded knowledge**. <note>original: "aneiligmenē gnōsis"; the idea that discourse explains in sequence what the mind sees all at once</note> But since this discourse proceeds into a multitude and has obtained a **composite nature**, and for this reason falls short of the union and indivisibility of the object, he <note>Plato</note> called the object "singularly stable and certain and manifest to the intellect," while he called the discourse "pluralistically stable, unchangeable, and irrefutable." And since in the discourse there is a certain similarity to the paradigm, but also a certain dissimilarity—and the latter is greater—he used one common name, "the stable," while the other <margin>D</margin> attributes differ. And since | scientific discourse <note>original: "epistēmonikos logos"</note> is irrefutable regarding our own knowledge (for there is nothing in us superior to science), yet it is "refuted" by the object itself, as it is unable to grasp its nature exactly as it is and falls short of its indivisibility, he added the phrase: **"as far as is possible."** For indeed, science itself is irrefutable as it exists in souls, but it is "refuted" by the intellect <note>original: "nous"</note> because science unfolds what is indivisible and grasps the simple in a composite way. For even **imagination** refutes **sensation**, because sensation knows through an "affection" <note>original: "pathos"; a physical impression</note> based on combination or division, from which imagination is pure; **opinion** <note>original: "doxa"</note> refutes imagination because the latter works with types and forms, while opinion is superior to these; **science** <note>original: "epistēmē"</note> refutes opinion because the latter knows without an account of the cause, which science especially requires; and **intellect**, as has been said, refutes science, because science divides the known in a transitional <note>step-by-step</note> way, whereas the intellect knows everything together along with the cause. Thus, the intellect alone is undefeated. Science and scientific discourse are mastered by the intellect in the knowledge of true Being.

->**But as for those discourses that have been likened to that which is itself an image, but are themselves likely. (Page 29 C.)**<-

<margin>E</margin> It is manifest that | the discourse concerning generated things <note>physical things that are born and die</note> is about an image, and that for this reason the discourse itself must be called **likely**. <note>original: "eikōs"; meaning probable or resembling the truth</note> Perhaps, however, one might ask what kind of discourses are left for things that are not likened to the Intelligible realm, yet are still in the universe—such as things we call "imitations" and "artificial objects." Either **imitative** <note>original: "eikastikoi"</note> discourses are appropriate for these, being distinct from "likely" discourses. For "to imitate" is one thing (as this is more obscure than even sensation), but "to be like" is another; for the latter belongs to the discourses that explain the images of true Being. Therefore, both artificial things and imitations are interpreted through imitative discourses. Unless, perhaps...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the Timaeus 29C. The previous page discussed how scientific discourse must be "irrefutable" yet acknowledges that human language often falls short of the simple, indivisible nature of the Divine Intellect.</meta>

### ON THE TIMAEUS II.

...to those things which are truly likenesses, as we have said, <note>namely: "must be assigned"</note> others of such a kind; but of artificial things, <note>original: "technēta"; things made by human craft</note> to those which are primary, likenesses derived from the Forms; <note>original: "eidē"; the eternal Blueprints or Ideas</note> but to those which have a secondary existence—which are indeed "third from the truth"—likenesses of the same kind as those which are natural likenesses. For indeed, the likenesses of sensible things are images, just as those things are images of the Intelligible things; <note>original: "noēta"; things known only by the mind, not the senses</note> for example, the painted bed is an image of the one made by the carpenter. Furthermore, one must also consider that now Plato is discussing natural images, and for this reason <margin>F</margin> | he also divided the discourses into two parts. For things Likened to the Intelligible are those that exist by nature, but not artificial things. For the craftsman does not create what he creates according to certain Ideas, even if Socrates in the **Republic** <note>Book 10, Page 596 B</note> seems to say this; but in that passage, what was said was for the sake of an example and not concerning the Ideas themselves. For he calls God the "poet" and "craftsman" of the Ideas, yet God is not a craftsman of the Ideas; <note>rather: "of the Ideas he is not the craftsman"</note> and in the **Protagoras**, it has been clearly shown according to Plato that neither do the principles of the crafts exist within us, and much less <margin>105</margin> | do the paradigms of artificial things stand among the gods. These things, therefore, did not come into being according to the Intelligible. But now Plato has divided the discourses into those concerning the Intelligible and those concerning the image of the Intelligible. Indicating this, he said that "the discourses of that which has been Likened to that [the Intelligible], but which is an image, are likely." For the works of nature have been Likened to the Intelligible, but not the works of craft, nor are they distinguished as individuals, but rather as the commonalities found within them. These matters have been discussed elsewhere.

->**And being analogous to them: that which Being is to Generation, Truth is to Belief.** <note>Plato, Timaeus Page 29 C</note><-

Previously, he established two leading terms: the Intelligible and the Generated <note>original: "genēton"; the realm of change and physical birth</note> (or Paradigm and Image), and he took two things analogous to these: Science and Likely-discourse (or Truth and Belief). Just as Truth is to the Intelligible Paradigm, so is Belief to the Generated Image. But now, in a geometrical fashion, <note>referring to a mathematical proportion</note> he has added the "alternated" proportion. For if as Truth is to the Intelligible, so Belief is to the Generated, then <margin>B</margin> by alternation, as Truth is to Belief, | so the Intelligible is to the Generated. <note>original: "enallax"; a mathematical term for switching the middle terms of a proportion (A:B :: C:D becomes A:C :: B:D)</note> and very beautifully did he make the Intelligible and Truth the leading terms, yet he began nevertheless from the Generated and from Belief, so that he might mix the order "relative to us" with the order "according to nature," and preserve the dignity of the things themselves, while making his attempt from things familiar to us. Plato, therefore, explicitly connects both discourses and modes of knowledge to the things known...

# PROCLUS

...divided along with them <gloss>1)</gloss>. But Parmenides, although he is obscure because of his poetic style, nevertheless points these things out himself when he says: 'Both the unshaken heart of well-rounded <gloss>2)</gloss> **Truth**, and the **opinions** of mortals <gloss>3)</gloss>, in which there is no true reliability.' 

And again: 'Come now, I will tell you—and you, listen and preserve my story <gloss>4)</gloss>—which are the only <gloss>5)</gloss> ways of inquiry for thinking. The one <gloss>6)</gloss>, that it **is** <gloss>7)</gloss> and that it is not possible for it **not to be** <gloss>8)</gloss>, is the path of **Persuasion** <gloss>9)</gloss>, for Truth follows <gloss>10)</gloss> it. The other <gloss>11)</gloss>, that it **is not** <gloss>12)</gloss> and that it is necessary for it **not to be**, this I tell you is a path <gloss>15)</gloss> utterly beyond conviction <gloss>13)</gloss>. For <gloss>16)</gloss> you could neither know that which <gloss>17)</gloss> is not—for it is not reachable—nor could you speak of it.' 

Indeed, the philosopher <note>referring to Parmenides</note> speaks of two types of things—those that are <gloss>18)</gloss> and those that are not—and says there are two types of knowledge: **truth**, which he also called 'well-shining' <margin>C</margin> because it shines forth | with intellectual light <gloss>19)</gloss>, and **faith** <note>original: "pistis"; here meaning a conviction or belief less certain than scientific knowledge</note>, which he stripped of stable knowledge. 

It seems, however, that the 'faith' which Plato has now taken up is different from the one mentioned in the **Republic** <gloss>20)</gloss> in the 'sectioning of the line.' For that 'faith' is an irrational kind of knowledge—which is why it is separated from true **essence** <note>original: "ousia"</note> and ranked alongside sensation—but this 'faith' <note>in the Timaeus</note> is rational, yet it is mixed with irrational kinds of knowledge, making use of sensation and conjecture. Because of this, it is filled with much <gloss>21)</gloss> instability. For by receiving the 'fact' <note>original: "to hoti"; the observation that something is the case without knowing why</note> from sensation and conjecture, it then provides the explanations; but these types of knowledge possess much confusion and instability. 

For this reason <gloss>22)</gloss>, Socrates in the **Phaedo** <gloss>23)</gloss> also accuses sensation: 'We neither hear nor see anything accurately.' How then could knowledge that begins from sensation possess accuracy and infallibility? For while science <note>original: "episteme"</note> alone, using accuracy <gloss>24)</gloss>, gathers together the whole of the object of knowledge, the knowledge associated with sensation is deceived and falls away from accuracy because of the nature of sensation and <margin>D</margin> because the object of knowledge itself is unstable. | For if one speaks of material things, which are always changing and flowing, how could they remain the same for even a moment <gloss>25)</gloss>? As for the heavenly realm, because it is far away from us, it is not easily known nor even graspable by science, but we must be content <note>the text cuts off; likely "content with a likely account"</note>

<unclear>The one</unclear> who is near in the contemplation of it also possesses probability; for everything that exists in a place <unclear>o</unclear>f that which is to come into being there must be known entirely for what kind of thing it is. For through <unclear>geo</unclear>metrical demonstrations, which are universal, if it is necessary to conclude anything about it, it is <unclear>possible</unclear> only in this way <gloss>3)</gloss>. <meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus (29C). Having established that our words must reflect the nature of what they describe, Proclus now focuses on why descriptions of the physical world can only be "likely" stories rather than absolute truths, while also distinguishing between different types of "faith" or conviction.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...is filled by the intelligible <note>original: "noētou" — referring to the realm of pure, eternal forms</note>, and the psychic <note>the level of the Soul</note> in turn is filled by the intellectual <note>original: "noerou" — the level of active divine mind</note>.
<margin>106</margin> Therefore, we must grasp the truth within souls in this way now, since we also hold this to be faith <note>original: "pistin" — here meaning a form of certain conviction or foundational belief</note>, but not the irrational faith that is cast aside <gloss>2)</gloss> from all rational understanding. We must connect the one kind of faith to the intelligibles, and the other to sensible things <note>objects perceived by the senses</note>.

> If then, O Socrates, after many people have said many things about the gods and the generation of the universe, we are unable to provide accounts that are in all respects consistent with themselves and perfectly accurate <gloss>5)</gloss>, do not be surprised. ->(Page 29 C.)<-

First, he <note>Plato</note> provided the hypotheses for the whole study of nature and gathered the conclusions that are necessary for this theory—these being three in number, though they are unfolded into five. Second, he defined the manner of the discourses. Third, he prepared the listener, showing how it is proper for those who are about to receive these accounts to behave. Fourth, he tells them not to listen as if the accounts spoken about physical things were perfectly accurate, nor as if they were truly scientific, but as being "likely" <note>or "probable"</note> like the truths they represent. Furthermore, he suggests that just as the world is a mixture of physical powers and an intellectual and divine essence—for physical works subsist together with the intellectual light <gloss>7)</gloss>
<margin>B</margin> of the Father, as the oracle says—so too the account of the world is composed | of both faith and truth. For those things taken from sense-perception participate in "likely-talk" <term>eikotologia</term>, while those proceeding from the intelligibles possess that which is irrefutable and unerring. For whenever we speak even about the Creator <term>Demiurge</term> himself, saying that he "deliberates" or "reasons" or that "he makes these things before those," we fall away from the truth of the actual realities. Thus, if when speaking about eternal beings and how they provide for the whole, we are forced to divide the indivisible and make the eternal into something temporal <note>subject to time</note>, then much more would the accounts concerning sensible things themselves fall short of accuracy. 

What then? someone might say: do we not provide certain accurate accounts about the heavens, such as that the circles within it bisect one another? Or is it that whenever we are content with what is "close enough" rather than what is perfectly accurate, we fall away from accuracy because of our own weakness rather than the nature of the thing? And what when we do not <gloss>10)</gloss> take our principles from sense-perception, but from universal reasons? Insofar as they are among the intelligibles, the accounts concerning the heavens demonstrate accuracy
<margin>C</margin> and are irrefutable; but insofar as they are among sensible things, | even these are refuted by the physical forms. For consider this very thing just stated: the "greatest circles," they say, bisect one another. Therefore, it is necessary that this occurs at specific points...

# ON THE TIMAEUS II

251

<warning>The left margin is obscured by a dark shadow, making the starts of several lines partially illegible.</warning>

...and this is indivisible. What then is such a thing in the divisible? What is without extension in <gloss>1)</gloss> substance? For everything that has come to be in a physical body is partitioned along with its underlying substrate. What then? Is there not also a physical point <note>original: "semeion" — a mathematical point</note>? But this falls short of "indivisible being." It is a point among physical things, but not a point in the absolute sense; the precise definition of a "point" will not strictly apply to such a thing. In general, just as the accounts of the intelligible <note>original: "noēton" — the highest realm of forms</note> will not apply to objects of discursive thought <note>original: "dianoētois" — mathematical-type reasoning</note>, so neither will the accounts of objects of science apply to sensible objects <note>things perceived by the senses</note>. For the intelligibles are the patterns for discursive thoughts, and discursive thoughts are the patterns for sensibles. For it is the Soul that adorned the great heaven and continues to adorn it along with the Father; so whenever we speak of "circles" in the heavens, and "contacts," "bisections," and "equalities," we speak accurately <gloss>2)</gloss> only if we are *not* speaking about sensibles; for <gloss>3)</gloss> in the case of all material things, such talk is nonsense.

If someone were to ask us: "What then? Is the 'truly equal' not a reason-principle <note>original: "logos"</note>, and is the 'true circle' not without extension?" for each is a universal, and the universal is an indivisible reason-principle and form; but the things in the heaven are divisible, not atomic, and exist within a substrate. Again <margin>D</margin> <unclear>here</unclear>, we say that neither circles nor equalities nor any other such thing exists among the sensibles, and thus we hold that their definitions do not agree with themselves. 

We say then, in brief, that Plato sometimes uses the term "science" <note>original: "epistēmē"</note> <gloss>4)</gloss> <unclear>for</unclear> providing causes alone; sometimes <gloss>5)</gloss> for having a <unclear>stable</unclear> substance in the underlying subjects completely alongside the provision of the demonstrations of the cause; and sometimes for when the principles are not mere hypotheses. And according to this <unclear>third</unclear> way, he defines a single science as that which ascends to the "true" <gloss>6)</gloss> principle; <unclear>for</unclear> this science sets the truly non-hypothetical principle at its head, making its accounts from the cause and the truly existing substrate. According to the second way, he also calls discursive knowledge "sciences." But according to the first way only, the name of "science" is applied even to natural philosophy <note>original: "physiologia" — the study of nature</note>. But now, seeing <gloss>7)</gloss> the <margin>E</margin> second form, he deems it right to call it "likely discourse" <note>original: "eikotologia" — a likely or probable account</note>. 

So much for the <unclear>word</unclear>ing. The entire phrase, which has some difficulty in its syntax <unclear>and</unclear> must be corrected by itself with a brief addition: "If, O Socrates, saying many things about many things," then <gloss>9)</gloss> he added "of many <unclear>strange</unclear> gods and the generation of the universe," and these are <unclear>many</unclear>. "If then," he says, "saying many things about many things—about the <unclear>generation</unclear> of both the universe and the gods within it—since both of these are many, we are unable to provide accounts that are perfectly accurate, do not be surprised." He said this because among necessary things...

# PROCLUS

242

...in the paradigm. The demiurgic <note>The "demiurgic" refers to the "Demiurge," or the divine craftsman who shapes the universe.</note> property pre-exists there; for there is the primary Zeus, and for this reason <gloss>1)</gloss> he made Phanes <note>original: "Phanēta" — In Orphic theology, Phanes is the first-born god and the "Paradigm" or model for the universe.</note> the demiurge. But the one within the creator is the paradigm. For Metis <note>Metis represents divine wisdom or counsel; in myth, Zeus swallowed Metis to internalize her wisdom.</note> was also swallowed within him; and for this reason <gloss>2)</gloss> he brought the paradigmatic cause into identity with the demiurgic cause. Enough has been said regarding these matters.

If Plato has called the cosmos an "image," one should not be surprised. For although it is the most beautiful of things, it is nonetheless an image of intelligible beauty <note>original: "noētou kallous" — the perfect beauty found in the realm of Forms</note>; and through this similarity, those things which oversee generation <gloss>3)</gloss> and receive the form of the paradigm as a whole are revealed. In this way, the philosopher also called the cosmos an "image" of the intelligible, as it resembles its own paradigm. Furthermore, the addition of the word "necessity" reveals that its likeness to the model is wondrous, unspoken, and truly ineffable <gloss>4)</gloss>. After this, he testifies to the demonstration as having <gloss>5)</gloss> an indisputable and fixed character. For it has proceeded from the very hypotheses themselves.

->**It is a very great thing to start every [discourse] from its natural beginning.** (Page 29)<-

<margin>103</margin> Some read this by placing a punctuation mark after "every" [matter]; for them, the phrasing indicates that the greatest thing of all is to establish the natural beginning as the start of one's arguments. Others, however, connect "of every" with what follows "a very great thing"; for them, the clause signifies that it is a very great thing to start from the natural beginning of the whole universe. Some say this was stated for the sake of what preceded, as those points were correctly concluded <gloss>6)</gloss> through necessary hypotheses. Others say it refers to what is about to be said, as it is necessary—if we are to establish the proper beginning—to first define what sort of accounts are appropriate for sensible things. Others say it refers to what will be handed down later regarding the final cause; for this is the greatest and most natural beginning, which must be especially contemplated, and starting from which it is fitting to provide the subsequent explanations. But before giving the account of this, let us state <gloss>7)</gloss> what the manner of these physical accounts will be. To me, however, it seems that this axiom is correctly stated regarding all things. For it is universal and applies both to what has been said <margin>B</margin> and what follows, and to what will be said hereafter—or rather, not only to these, but to the entire act of creation <note>original: "demiurgia"</note>. For just as one starting from the natural beginning as if <gloss>8)</gloss> from a root, he produces [accounts] that are in harmony with it...

On the previous page, Proclus discussed how the world is an "image" of the intelligible paradigm and how the likeness between the two is "ineffable" or "unspoken." This page transitions into a discussion on epistemology—how different types of beings (gods, humans, etc.) perceive the same truth differently.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II. 253

[Knowl]edges are characterized, nor that "what is not fixed is not fixed" <note>This refers to the idea that knowledge of unstable things is itself unstable.</note> as the philosopher Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist and student of Plotinus; he wrote a famous commentary on the Timaeus that Proclus frequently cites.</note> says (for he further proclaimed that "silence is better" <note>original: "arrhēton ameinon"</note>) but because the mode of knowledge changes according to the differences of those who know. For God knows the same thing in a unified way, [Mind] in a total way, Reason in a universal way, Imagination in a formative way, and [Sen]sation in a sensory way. It is not the case that because the object of knowledge is one, the knowledge of it is also one. Furthermore, if knowledge belongs to the gods by their very essence and is not something acquired, then as they *are*, so they also know. Since they are immaterial, eternal, and pure, they therefore know immaterially, eternally, and in a unified way.

Thus, they have pre-grasped the material in an immaterial way, the dispersed multitude in a unified form, that which changes in a stable and eternal manner, and everything unnatural <margin>C</margin> and impure in an undefiled way. Therefore, let us not think this point requires further explanation. We must, in turn, take three <note>A textual note suggests "three" (treis) might be a mistake for "clearly" (tranōs).</note> [images] from what has been said. For we require imagination, sensation, and many other [tools] for knowledge; but the gods, by their "One" and their [nature], have embraced these things as well. For regarding things under the moon <note>The "sublunary" realm: the physical world of change, decay, and the four elements.</note>, we are mostly content [with an account] that is unstable because of the underlying matter. Regarding celestial things, again, using sensation and instruments, we are filled with [probability] <note>original: "eikotos" — Plato argues that an account of the physical world can only ever be a "likely story" (eikōs mythos).</note>, and because of this, even among those things, what is "nearly" certain is to be welcomed by those of us dwelling at the bottom, as they say, of the universe.

This is also clear from those who have treated these matters and gathered data about them from different hypotheses: some [saving the appearances] through eccentric circles, some through [epicycles], and some through revolving lines <note>original: "anelittousōn" — likely referring to homocentric spheres or the "evolvents" used in Greek mathematical astronomy to explain planetary motion.</note>. What then? Shall we be content hearing from Plato as he discourses on nature regarding such things, and shall we be satisfied with the phrase "second to none"? <margin>D</margin> Or rather, is it most fitting to speak about them in this way to those who pursue the mean between irony and [boasting]? For "more than all" would be the mark of the latter, and [less than any] the mark of the former, but the mean is "second to none." Furthermore, "second to none" would refer to those who have already come before as observers of nature, but also...

***

<summary>Proclus explains that gods know physical and changing things in a divine, unified, and eternal way, unlike humans who rely on imperfect senses. He notes that human astronomy uses various mathematical hypotheses (like eccentrics and epicycles) to "save the appearances" of the stars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s Commentary on the Timaeus. On the previous page, Proclus discussed the different modes of knowledge—divine versus human—explaining that while gods know in a unified and eternal way, human knowledge is limited by our embodied and "partial" nature. This page moves into the famous justification for why the study of the physical world can only ever be a "likely story" (mythos) rather than an exact science.</meta>

# PROCLUS

since the things themselves are likely <note>original: "eikotōn"</note>, as if he were saying: if we ourselves provide likely accounts that are no less likely than the things themselves, and if we do not fall short of the nature of the things known, we should be content. The gods know these things in a more excellent way, but for us, it is enough if we even come close to them. For we are humans and have been stationed within a body; we are clothed in a partial form of life and are ourselves filled with much of "the likely." Consequently, we will naturally <note>The Greek word "eikotōs" means both "naturally" and "likely," playing on the theme that our likely stories match our likely nature.</note> speak likely accounts in the form of myths. For our own reason is filled with the great thickness and irrationality that the myth displays, and one must grant indulgence to human nature.

<margin>E</margin>
->***"Excellent,<sup>10)</sup> O Timaeus, and we must accept it entirely just as you command. | We have accepted the prelude from you wonderfully;***<-
->***now, proceed to finish the discourse<sup>11)</sup> for us in order."*** (Page 29 D.)<-

In the *Republic*, while Socrates was arranging the arguments, Timaeus remained in sil<unclear>ence</unclear>, not revealing his own judgments concerning what was being said. Here, however, Socrates accepts Timaeus in a marvelous way, since—in the case of the actual things of which these characters are images—while the secondary beings are active <unclear>—</unclear> the primary beings remain established in themselves and do not depart from their own state, nor do they lean toward lower things. Yet, when the more divine beings are moved, even the "hollower" <note>The Greek "koilotera" (hollower) is unusual here; a textual note suggests it might be "koinotera" (more common things).</note> things are raised toward a participation in them through a love <term>eros: a divine driving force or desire for the Good</term> of great wonder. Naturally, then, Socrates bestows every praise upon Timaeus in these matters; for through this wonder, he is joined to him in a greater way. Indeed, the word "excellent" points toward the perfection, the intellectual nature, and the scientific quality of Timaeus’s teaching; it also points toward his analogy to the Creator <term>demiurgos: the divine craftsman of the universe</term>.
<margin>F</margin>
For just as the Creator is the "best" of causes in his works, | so too is Timaeus the "best" in his words. And the phrase "we must accept it entirely just as you command" shows what sort of person he ought to be who is to rightly receive accounts concerning divine matters: namely, one who holds fast to the teacher with persistence, doing everything in his power that is commanded by him, and persuading himself that it is right to be persuaded by the things the teacher says. Furthermore, the "prelude" indicates the scope of the universal concepts contained within the hypotheses; for every...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on the famous passage in Plato's Timaeus (29B-C) regarding the relationship between the "model" (the eternal Paradigm) and the "copy" (the physical world), and how our language must adapt to each.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II. 245

...not in a single way. Nor is there a single kind of precision for all various kinds of accounts, whether they concern truly existing things <note>referring to the eternal, unchanging Forms</note> or those that subsist through <term>becoming</term> <note>original: "genesis" — the world of change and physical matter</note>. Rather, just as the things themselves are, so too are the accounts divided alongside the things. They possess precision and clarity according to the subjects underlying them, so that some accounts express the precision of doctrines, while others express that which is likely. For it is necessary for the account to be similar to the things it describes; otherwise, it could not explain their nature unless it were related to them. For what the thing is in a concentrated way, the account must be in an "unrolled" way <note>Proclus uses the metaphor of "unrolling" (aneiligmenōs) to describe how human discourse takes a single, unified truth and explains it step-by-step through time and logic.</note>, so that it may both reveal the thing and yet remain subordinate to its nature. For in this same way, the divine causes of discourse |

<margin>B</margin>

reveal the essences of the things that come before them and are naturally united with them. Among the gods, for instance, the messenger of Zeus—who is the Word <note>original: "logos"</note> in relation to the Intellect of the Father—announces his will to the secondary beings. Among essences, the Soul, being the "reason-principle" of the intelligibles, reveals the unified cause of all things within them, taking its starting point from them. And among the ranks of beings superior to us, the angelic order, having its subsistence from the gods, continually interprets and conveys the "unspoken" nature of the gods. It is likely, therefore, that here too the account of things is related to the things themselves. Let this be stated as a foundational principle before we discuss the specific divisions; what follows divides the different types of accounts according to the quality of the things they describe.

***"Of that which is permanent and stable, and manifest with intellect, it is fitting for the accounts to be permanent and unchangeable, and as far as possible irrefutable and invincible; and from this, nothing should be lacking."*** (Timaeus, Page 29 B.)

Previously, Plato called the Paradigm "that which always is," "existing according to the same," and "grasped by intellection." Now, however, he calls it "permanent and stable"—the first term instead of "always being and manifest with intellect," and the second instead of |

<margin>C</margin>

"grasped by intellection." He calls the accounts concerning it "permanent," so that through the identity of the name he might show their similarity to the things themselves; and "unchangeable," so that they might mirror the stability of the object; and "irrefutable," so that they might imitate that which is grasped by intellection and proceed in a scientific manner. For it is necessary, if the accounts are to be appropriate to the intelligibles, that they possess total precision.

<summary>Proclus explains Plato's "correspondence theory" of truth: discourse about eternal things must be stable and certain, while discourse about the physical world can only be "likely." He illustrates this through a hierarchy of "messengers" (Logos, Soul, Angels) who translate higher truths into lower forms.</summary>

<keywords>Proclus, Timaeus, logos, paradigm, becoming, intellect, soul, angels, precision, likelihood, correspondence theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, transitioning from a discussion of the world as an "image" of an eternal model to the ultimate purpose or "Final Cause" of the universe—the Good itself. It addresses page 256 of the Greek text.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...just as the Good is the cause of all beings, so indeed the generation of the cosmos proceeds from this most primary principle. For all things come from the Good. And although the <term>Demiurgic Intellect</term> <note>original: "demiourgikos nous" — the divine mind that crafts the physical world</note> is a cause, the Good is the cause of the things for which the Intellect is not—such as <term>matter</term> <note>original: "hylē"</note> and those things that do not have a primary <term>paradigm</term> <note>original: "paradeigma" — the eternal blueprint or Form</note> subsisting for them. Even these things stand by means of the Good. 

<margin>C</margin>

For "all things are for its sake, and it is the cause of all beautiful things," as is said in the *Letters* <note>original: "Epistolais" — referring to Plato’s Second Letter, 312e, a text highly influential on Neoplatonists</note>. For this reason, Timaeus refers the other causes back to this one single Cause. Having discovered the form of the cosmos through his initial proposals—both its exemplary cause <note>the Paradigm</note> and its creative cause <note>the Demiurge</note>—he now wishes to render the most authoritative and ancient of the causes: the <term>final cause</term> <note>original: "telikē aitia" — the purpose or goal for which something exists</note>, which he especially desires for the work of creation. 

For if even a man living according to intellect does everything for the sake of the Good, how much more does Intellect itself—even the Divine Intellect—create all things for the sake of the final cause? For even if a virtuous man often seems to act for the sake of the body or for lesser things in general, this is not his ultimate "end" <note>the Greek "telos" means both end, goal, and perfection</note>—that is, the good of the body or the good of the lesser thing. Rather, he does this too for the sake of a likeness to the Divine, and he makes that his most deliberate goal. 

<margin>D</margin>

How much more greatly, then, would the Creator of the universe create for the sake of the Good and the final cause? For he does not make his activity aimless or indefinite. 

For this reason, it seems to me that Plato does not even ask the starting question of whether there *is* a final cause for the composition of the cosmos, but rather, as this is something agreed upon by everyone, he seeks to find *what* that final cause is. For it is assumed that the Creator and God is an Intellect, and not "chance" <note>original: "automaton" — spontaneous or random action</note>, as some people claim <note>referring to Epicureans or atomists who argued the world formed by random collisions</note>. And if the universe is a product of Intellect, then surely there is a "that for the sake of which" <note>the purpose</note> in its creation. Just as a soul that is set right acts in accordance with intellect, so the creating Intellect establishes all things in accordance with God <note>here meaning the ultimate principle of the Good</note>. This is the same as saying it acts in accordance with the Good. 

Whether one must follow the Aristotelian method of inquiry—where after asking "what" the whole is and "what kind" of thing it is, one must necessarily ask "why" it is—for it has been said that it is created and is an image of Being, and one must further consider for what purpose it came to be; or whether one follows the Platonic causes, after finding the Creator and the Paradigm, it is proper to find the final cause of the world-making. 

<margin>E</margin>

For indeed, all other things are suspended from this: the divinity of the | paradigm, the goodness of the creator, and the perfection of the thing being made. Up to this point is the ascent for those who love to contemplate the truth. 

It is the custom to call these causes by specific names:
*   The **final cause** is "that for the sake of which" <note>original: "di' ho"</note>
*   The **paradigmatic cause** is "that toward which" <note>original: "pros ho"</note>
*   The **demiurgic cause** is "that by which" <note>original: "hyph' hou"</note>
*   The **instrumental cause** is "that through which" <note>original: "di' hou"</note>
*   The **form** is "that according to which" <note>original: "kath' ho"</note>
*   The **matter** is "that out of which" or "in which" <note>original: "ex hou" or "en hō"</note>

They take these names as appearing in Plato himself. For now, in seeking the final cause, he asks "for what reason" <note>original: "di' hēn aitian"</note>...

<summary>Proclus argues that the "Final Cause" (the Good) is the ultimate reason for the universe's existence, surpassing even the Creator's mind. He outlines the Neoplatonic system of "six causes" used to explain how the world is formed and sustained.</summary>

<keywords>Final Cause, The Good, Demiurge, Paradigm, Plato's Letters, Aristotelian inquiry, Neoplatonism, teleology, six causes</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus. On the previous page, we discussed the "Final Cause" (the Good) and how the Divine Intellect creates all things for the sake of a purpose. We now move into the specific definitions of "generation" and "the All" as they apply to the physical universe.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II.

...of the **paradigms**, while the **demiurgic** <note>original: "demiourgikon" — the creative or craftsman-like aspect of the divine</note> cause belongs to that which is **becoming** <note>original: "gignomenō" — refers to the realm of change and physical existence</note>, for it must necessarily arise from some cause. As we proceed, we shall mark the remaining points of **Plato**, except to say even now that these matters are proper to the science of philosophical distinction. But what is the "generation of the All"? 

Some, having heard the word <term>generation</term> <note>original: "genesis" — the process of coming-into-being</note> and thinking only of the sublunary region <note>The area below the moon, which ancient science believed was the only place where things truly changed, decayed, and were reborn</note>, [interpret] the "All" as the entire world. These people completely fail to understand Plato. 

<margin>F</margin>

For the **Demiurge** is not presented as molding only material things, but specifically the whole world. Moreover, **generation** itself is a | part of the **All**. If, however, one calls the "All" the **heaven** <note>original: "ouranon"</note>, because it is the greatest part of the world (for the rest is small), it is because it is the most divine and authoritative part, acting as the "head" of the entire world. For even the head is called the "all," as in the phrase "Teucer, dear head" <note>A quote from Homer’s Iliad, also used by Plato, where the "head" represents the whole person</note>, and even **Plato** says the rest of the body's bulk is wrapped around the head. Nevertheless, the philosopher is also accustomed to calling this "generation." 

Others have called <term>matter</term> <note>original: "hylē"</note> "generation," and the "All" that which has been ordered from matter. It is necessary to reject the views of these people based on | what Plato has written. 

<margin>109</margin>

For he says that everything that has **come into being** or is in **generation** is "sensible or tangible and visible." Furthermore, he contrasts **generation** with **matter**, as when he says these three things exist separately: **Being**, **Space**, and **Generation**, from which the **All** subsists.

Our **teacher** <note>Proclus is likely referring to Syrianus, his predecessor and mentor at the Neoplatonic Academy</note> says that the "making of the world" is conceived in two ways: one part is the **bodily** formation, and the other is the **fitting together** of those bodies into the completion of a single world. It is one thing to mold the bodies themselves through their geometric shapes, and another to harmonize them into the **All**. Thus, "generation" refers to the molding of the bodies, while the "All" refers to the wholeness and perfection of the entire universe. For that which is composed of parts must have the creation of those parts pre-conceived. 

Therefore, every [act of creation] involving both matter and the entire cosmic decoration, as well as the completion of the single world, should be attached to the "generation of the All," so that it may be a path toward the **Whole**, in which the parts are | contained. 

<margin>B</margin>

For this is the **All**: a **perfect** thing composed of **perfect** parts, established according to a single harmony of the whole. But since this is a **sensible** <note>perceivable by the senses</note> "all" and not the **intelligible** "all" (which was the **Paradigm**) nor the **intellectual** "all" (which was the **Demiurgic**), he added the word "**this**," indicating both its sensible nature and its particularity. For every bodily thing, even if it is a whole, is a "this" <note>meaning a specific, bounded thing in space</note>. But most properly, a "whole" is that which is **immaterial**, **dimensionless**, and truly that **Being** which is both intellectual and intelligible. 

So much for these matters. As for what the "**composition**" <note>original: "systasin"</note> is: perhaps it indicates that the world is a composite of many things, or perhaps it shows the **generation** of the world from dissimilar parts, and perhaps also the fact that he [the Creator] gave it unity and...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the *Timaeus*, specifically focusing on the character and motives of the Demiurge (the divine craftsman). # PROCLUS

...that stability proceeds from the whole of the creative process. For the preposition "with" indicates union and the "breathing together" <note>original: "sympnoias" — a Stoic and Neoplatonic term for the organic harmony of the universe</note> of all things into one, while "stability" indicates the firm and permanent nature of the thing created. Furthermore, to interweave the minds—both the present and the past—demonstrates the completeness of the creative act and its eternal nature. For the term "to establish" <gloss>1)</gloss> <note>original: "sunistan" — Proclus notes the present tense implies ongoing creation</note> indicates the continuous and 

<margin>C</margin> 

likewise | perfected production, while "he has established" indicates the wholeness that has obtained its being in full. Moreover, to signify the different times through the same names shows that divine creation proceeds through identity and similarity. For as the creative power is, so too is its activity; and as it exists, so does it create. This is because it acts according to its very being and its own essence.

->**"He was good, and in him who is good <gloss>4)</gloss> no envy ever**<-
->**arises <gloss>5)</gloss> concerning anything." (Timaeus, Page 29 E.)**<-

Those who have called the Demiurge "The Good" <note>original: "tagathon" — referring to the First Principle or "The One"</note> are altogether ridiculous. For "The Good Itself" and "a good being" are not the same thing. The former is "unparticipated" <term>unparticipated</term> <note>original: "amethekton" — a primary principle that remains pure and does not divide itself among the things it creates</note> and is the "itself" of all things, set apart from everything; but the latter is "good" by participating in that First Good. The first reigns over all the <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "noētōn" — the realm of pure ideas or forms that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</note>, whereas the Demiurge, if he is the same as the Paradigm <note>The "blueprints" of the universe</note>, is those very intelligibles and thus does not "reign" over them. But if he is secondary to the Paradigm, he is far inferior to the one who reigns over all the intelligibles. Generally, every god is "a certain good"—one is creative, 

<margin>D</margin> 

another is life-giving, | and another is perfecting—but "The Good" is not "a certain good," but simply "The Good." If you call him "creative," you diminish his simple nature. Having made these distinctions, let us now look at the opening of this passage and state first that, just as when Plato sought the cosmic form and asked whether the world was born or is unborn, he introduced the conclusion that "it was born" before the full proof; and just as when investigating the <term>paradigmatic cause</term> <note>The model used by the creator</note> he first assumed it was "clear to everyone" that it was modeled on the eternal; so too, having set out to find the <term>final cause</term> <note>The "purpose" or "end goal" (telos) for why something exists</note> for everything, he introduced the statement "He was good." Through this exclamation, he mimics the Intellect and its grasp of this very truth. For in this short phrase, the entire subject of inquiry is contained: this is the final cause, namely "Goodness"—both Goodness in its simple sense and creative Goodness. For just as the Paradigm is twofold—the one being "intelligible" and the other "intellectual"—the first exists before the Demiurge as primarily eternal and unified <gloss>12)</gloss> and...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's detailed commentary on the *Timaeus*, specifically examining the relationship between "The Good" (the ultimate principle) and the "Goodness" inherent in the Demiurge (the Creator). On the previous page, Proclus established that the Creator acts according to his essence; here, he explores how this goodness translates into the act of creation and addresses historical interpretations by other philosophers like Amelius.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.

<margin>E</margin> ...comprehensive of intelligible living beings, while that which is in the Creator of all things <note>original: "ton holon" — the critical apparatus suggests this reading over "ton onton"</note> contains the species in a unified way. In this same way, goodness is one thing simply—that which resides in the creative Intellect—and it is the fountain of all good things: the intelligible, the intellectual, and the supracosmic. Yet, another kind of goodness, while being a form of goodness, is the cause of some things while having been allotted a lower rank than others. For if we wish to examine what makes a thing intelligible, or intellectual, or heavenly, or worldly, it would be nothing other than the Good. For what makes each of the bodies animate, if not the power of the soul? And what makes the intellectual souls as they are, if not the radiance within them from the Universal Intellect? What then would deify both the Intellect and the intelligible essence, if not the participation <gloss>2)</gloss> in the First and the illumination proceeding from it? 

And what is the First? If it were less than the beautiful <note>original: "hetton en" — the text ponders if Beauty could be the highest principle</note>, we would say that the Intellect is a god by virtue of its beauty. But since that First is The Good, and the Intellect is a god by participating in goodness, this then is the existence of the gods—this is the very essence of the gods, if it is permissible to say so: Goodness. It is according to this that every god has his being as a god, and through this is <margin>F</margin> providential, or creative, or life-giving, or sustaining. For Intellect, insofar as it is intellect, is naturally suited only to think and to know <gloss>5)</gloss>, but to exercise providence is divine. 

Consequently, the creative Intellect has its being as "creative" through the goodness within it. For because of this goodness, the Intellect within it is a maker and not only a knower of being; and the Being that is the "Paradigm" <term>Paradigm</term> <note>The "Paradigm" is the eternal model or blueprint of the universe that the Creator gazes upon.</note> within it is active, creating by its very existence and not only perfecting the mind. Thus, the Intellect is empowered by both in its making: it is empowered by the Paradigm, because it creates in relation to it, and by goodness <margin>110</margin>, because it creates for the sake of it. The Paradigm, however, derives from the Monad <note>original: "henados" — the One or the principle of Unity</note>. 

You have, therefore, in order: Goodness, the Paradigm, and the Intellect. These exist in one way within the Creator, and in another way prior to the Creator. If you wish to speak of them this way: the first goodness is "The One," which is beyond even the intelligibles (for that is the unparticipated <note>original: "amethektos" — a principle that is not "shared out" or diminished by its products</note> goodness); the Paradigm is the "Intelligible," which contains the entire number of forms in a unified way; and the Maker is the "Intellectual" Mind, the sustainer of all things. 

It was in this manner that Amelius <note>Amelius Gentilianus, a 3rd-century Neoplatonist and student of Plotinus</note> spoke of the three creators. In seeing this triad, he spoke correctly. For he says one is the "handler" of things, the second acts by "command" only, and the third by "will" alone. The first is ranked like the manual craftsman, the second exists beforehand as the architect, and the third is established before both as the overseer <note>original: "epiplea" — a term for one who "fills" or oversees from above</note>. 

Therefore, insofar as the Creator is Intellect, he produces all things by his own thoughts; insofar as he is <margin>B</margin> intelligible, he produces by his existence alone; and insofar as he is a god, by his will alone. But if one should tear these three creators away from the One, we shall not follow them, for we follow Plato. For the same...

<summary>Proclus defines the essence of divinity as "Goodness" rather than "Intellect," arguing that while Intellect knows, only Goodness provides and creates. He harmonizes Amelius's theory of three creators into a single divine hierarchy of Will, Thought, and Being.</summary>
<keywords>Proclus, Timaeus commentary, Amelius, Demiurge, The Good, Paradigm, Intellect, Neoplatonic triad, Providence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's examination of the Timaeus 29e: "He [the Creator] was good, and in one who is good, no envy ever arises concerning anything." Proclus moves from defining the Creator's essence to a grammatical and ontological analysis of the word "was" (en) and the concept of "envoy" or "jealousy" (phthonos).</meta>

->### PROCLUS<-

...and he is good as a god, and through his goodness, by his will, he makes all things and is intelligible in an intellectual manner. <note>original: "noetos esti noeros" — an object of thought perceived by the intellect</note> For such is the creative being, and he is the world-crafting intellect. The statement "he was good" has the following explanation: in the word "was," the super-fullness, the absolute perfection, and the supra-eternal <term>supra-eternal: existing beyond even the realm of eternal forms</term> nature of the divine existence are indicated. For while the word "is" signifies eternal things, "was" signifies the supra-eternal unities <note>original: "henades" — the "Ones" or primary divine principles in Neoplatonism</note>, and "will be" signifies those things consist within time. For if "is" belongs to eternal beings, then "was" is appropriate for those prior to these, and "will be" for those after the eternal—specifically, those things requiring time. 

Since the <term>Demiurge: the divine Creator or Craftsman of the universe</term> is good, no envy ever arises in him concerning anything. Someone might ask: what is the significance of saying an intellect does not feel envy? For this quality belongs even to decent men. Let the word "never," then, be a sign of eternal perfection; <margin>C</margin> for while our souls are sometimes affected by passions and | at other times run back toward a state of passionless-ness, the phrase "concerning anything" signifies self-sufficiency. This is because we are often free from envy for the sake of some people, yet when we consider others to have less than us, we are seized by the passion.

What then is the meaning of the word "no one" <note>original: "oudeis" — used here to mean "no kind of envy"</note>? Did he add "no one" as if there were many kinds of envy, or is it said as an exaggeration, making a total denial of envy? And what kind of exaggeration is even possible to find in discourses concerning the gods? For all their names and words <note>original: "rhemata" — some manuscripts read "noemata" or "thoughts"</note> fall short of their true dignity. Perhaps, then, "envy" is the pain felt at the goods of others—a mixed passion produced in us from pleasure and pain, as Socrates showed in the *Philebus*. <note>Plato, Philebus 48b</note> But "envy" can also mean the ability to do good but refusing to do so, keeping the good for oneself; or indeed, "envy" may be the very lack of good things. It is this last meaning that the philosopher <note>Plato</note> seems to me to be especially adopting now, banishing it from the divine essence. For it is the nature of this essence alone to be exempt from lack, since it is substantialized according to goodness itself.

<margin>D</margin> For to be pained by the goods of others | belongs to all who are good by participation, but not to those who are primarily good. For the acquired good is one thing, the good held as a habit is another, and the primarily good is yet another. The first is mixed with its opposite, just as acquired beauty is fouled by ugliness; the second is entirely "good-form," yet it is such by participation; but the "Good-in-Itself" <note>original: "autoagathon"</note> is primarily good. For just as the "Intellect-in-Itself" is primarily intellect, and "Beauty-in-Itself" is primarily beauty, so the "Good-in-Itself" is primarily good. What, then, is this? It is the deity of each thing, according to which each of the truly real beings is a god. For nothing...

<summary>Proclus analyzes the grammar of Plato's description of the Creator, arguing that "was good" implies a state beyond time and eternity, and defines divine goodness as a total absence of "envy" or "lack." He distinguishes between the Good-in-Itself and things that are merely good by participating in that higher principle.</summary>

--- Page 306 ---
<meta>This page continues Proclus's detailed commentary on the nature of the Demiurge's goodness. Having established that the "was" in "He was good" refers to a supra-eternal state, Proclus now distinguishes between being good by nature (as God is) and being good by participation (as souls and intellects are), using this to prove that the Creator is entirely free from envy.</meta>

->### ON THE TIMAEUS II<-

...of goodness; but if any of the secondary beings is called either a god or good, it belongs to those who are deified or made good. Such a being is a god through participation, but not according to its own essence nor from itself. <note>original: "ex heautou" — from its own nature</note> <note>translator: The Latin notes indicate variations in early manuscripts (A and B) regarding whether this refers to "itself" in the masculine or feminine gender.</note> This kind of participation is what they are accustomed to call "need," <note>original: "endeian" — a lack or deficiency</note> just as in the *Symposium* <note>Plato's dialogue on the nature of Love</note> he [Plato] described Love <note>original: "Eros"</note> as being in need of the beautiful and the good. Therefore, the divine, insofar as it is divine, is of such a nature—it is good not by participation, so that it is not in need of the good. It is, therefore, | superior to all things. <margin>E</margin> For just as it is impossible for darkness to approach the sun, which is the generator of light—rather, darkness is shut away somewhere far off in the hollows of the earth—in the same way, it is impossible for envy to approach the divine. For what "need" can there be in such an abundance? What weakness in the all-powerful divinity? What participation <note>original: "metousia"</note> in the goods? Therefore, by the very fact of being good, the Creator <term>Creator: the Demiurge, the divine craftsman of the world</term> transcends all need and all participation that comes from another, being united with and never departing from the One. <note>original: "tou henos" — the ultimate Principle in Neoplatonism</note> For there is one kind of goodness that is intellectual, and another prior to the intellect, through which the generative divinity of the Creator and the goodness that holds all things together is joined to the One itself. For this [goodness] is not some power beneath the One, as some say, but is the measure of every power; nor is it a "will" in the sense of a choice, but the goodness itself is his will; nor is it a habit <note>original: "hexis" — a stable quality or state of being</note>—for a habit belongs to someone else, but this goodness is his very self. Nor is it at all a substantial reality <note>original: "ousiodes hypostasis"</note>, but it is the unifying force of substance, the containment of ineffable power, and the source of creative activities.

As | intellect is given substance according to its being as intellect, but that which is above intellect is participable by it; <margin>F</margin> and as every soul is given substance according to its being as soul, but intellect is participable by it; so too every god is given substance—or rather, "supra-substance" <note>original: "hyporousiotai" — existing beyond the category of Being</note>—in being a god, and nothing is participable by him, because the gods are the most ancient of all things. The creative intellect, then, insofar as he is a god, exists primarily in being a god and is not a god by participation; and this is the same as being "good." Just as if someone said that the intellect was in need, even the partial intellect <note>meaning individual human minds</note> would be superior to envy, and the soul even more so; for the soul is in need of intellect, because it is intellectual by nature through the participation in intellect. <margin>111</margin> Thus also regarding goodness: if envy is the "need" or "lack" of goods, and everything that is not primarily good is "in need," then soul and intellect are in need of goods because they are not primarily good. But the god, being good insofar as he is a god, is exempt from all envy and transcends every "need" that exists in any way, whether by deficiency or by turning away; for "need" is twofold: one kind is not evil, as has been said, [but the other is] evil.

***

<summary>Proclus argues that the Creator is "good" by his very essence rather than by participating in a higher goodness. Because he is the source of all and lacks nothing, he is ontologically incapable of feeling envy, which Proclus defines as a deficiency or "need" for goods one does not possess.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the metaphysical nature of the Creator to the methodological limitations of human language. Proclus is explaining Plato's famous "likely account" (eikos logos), arguing that because humans are embodied and limited, our descriptions of the physical world can only ever be "likely" approximations of the divine truth known perfectly by the gods.</meta>

-># PROCLUS<-

...since the things themselves are merely likely, <note>original: "eikotōn" — meaning probable, resembling the truth, or "like" the reality they describe</note> it is as if he were saying: If, therefore, we cannot provide likely accounts for all things, nor fall short of the nature of the things known, we must be content. The gods, to be sure, know these things in a superior way, but for us it is enough if we even strike near them. For we are humans; we have been stationed within a body and are clothed in a partial form of life, and we ourselves are filled with much of this "likelihood" <note>A textual variant in the manuscripts suggests the word "mud" (pēlou) instead of "likelihood" (pollou), implying that being in a physical body "muds" our perception.</note>—consequently, we shall tell stories that resemble "likely myths." For our discourse is filled with much of the density and the weakness that the myth itself exhibits, and one must be forgiving toward human nature.

***

<margin>E</margin>
->**"Excellent, Timaeus! We must altogether accept your proposal as you command. We have indeed admired your prelude wonderfully; now finish the discourse for us in order."**<- (Timaeus, page 29 D.)

***

In the *Republic*, while Socrates was setting forth the arguments, Timaeus remained in silence, not showing his own judgments regarding what was being said. But here, Socrates admires Timaeus in a marvelous way. This is because in actual reality—of which these characters are images—the primary beings remain established in themselves; they do not depart from their own nature nor do they incline toward the inferior. However, when the more divine beings are in motion, the lower beings <note>original: "koilotera" — literally the "hollower" things, referring to lower levels of existence</note> are raised up toward participation in them through a love <note>original: "eros" — the divine drive toward beauty and truth</note> that produces immense wonder. 

Reasonably, then, Socrates pours out every form of praise upon Timaeus in these lines; for through this wonder, he is more greatly joined to him. Furthermore, the term "excellent" <note>original: "ariston"</note> points to the perfection, the intellectuality, and the scientific nature of Timaeus’s teaching. It also indicates Timaeus's own analogy to the Creator. <term>Creator: the Demiurge, the divine craftsman of the universe</term> For just as the Creator is the "best" of causes in his works, so this man is "best" in his discourses. 

The phrase "must altogether be accepted as you command" demonstrates how a person who is to correctly receive teachings about the gods ought to behave: namely, by clinging persistently to the teacher, by doing everything commanded with all one's strength, and by convincing oneself that it is right to be persuaded by what the teacher says. Furthermore, the "prelude" indicates the way universal concepts are contained within the foundational hypotheses, [while the "discourse"...] <note>The text breaks off as the page ends.</note>

<summary>Proclus explains why human descriptions of the cosmos are "likely myths" rather than absolute truths, due to our embodied nature. He then analyzes Socrates' enthusiastic praise of Timaeus as a model for how a student should receive divine philosophy.</summary>

### ON THE TIMAEUS II.

<warning>Large dark stain/ink blot on the left side of the bottom critical apparatus, obscuring the beginning of several lines.</warning>

...the prefaces [contained] in it. Why there is a preface has been stated, **108** as well as the <term>form</term><note>The specific philosophical nature or category</note> of the object of inquiry, the types of hypotheses it depends on, which points were previously demonstrated, the style of the arguments, and the <term>goal</term><note>original: "skopos"—the central target or theme of a Neoplatonic commentary</note>. The term "law" <note>original: "nomos"—this word in Greek means both "law" and a specific type of musical "mode" or "melody"</note> is taken from the "laws" of cithara-playing. These were certain compositions: some were Athenian, others were "Areic" <note>related to Ares, the god of war</note>; some were <unclear>inspired</unclear>, while others were for the <unclear>cultivation</unclear> of character. Before these musical "laws," it was customary to place prefaces, which they called "preliminary touches" <note>original: "propselaphēmata"—literally, "testing the strings" or "fingering the instrument" before the main performance</note>. 

He has therefore taken the term from that practice. It contributes to the subject at hand because the entire visible world-order, being harmonic, remains eternally through the goodness of the **gods**; it also shows that the world proceeds from Intellect and according to Intellect, and that it possesses powers that are distinguished and arranged as is fitting for each. Indeed, they called these musical modes "laws" because they remained unchanging, and because they distributed what was appropriate to each.

->**"Let us now state for what cause the Creator composed the process of becoming and this universe."**<- (Page 29 D.) **B**

All the things mentioned previously were preparations for us regarding the entire "preparation-discourse" <note>original: "paraskeuasiologia"—a technical term for the introductory section setting the stage for the main argument</note>. Some of these showed the contemplation of the world through images and symbols, while the prefaces laid the foundation for the entire treatise. Of the demonstrations through images or symbols, some revealed the unity of worldly things, while others revealed their distinction. Of the prefaces, some were hypotheses, others were like "axioms" <note>original: "lemmata"—assumed premises</note> demonstrated through the hypotheses. 

Indeed, one might place the discussion about the "accounts" among the things demonstrated: for from the fact that the world has been proven to be generated, it follows that the treatise concerning the world is a "likely account" <note>original: "eikotologia"—the study or speaking of what is probable or like the truth</note>. Since these points have reached their proper end, Timaeus—beginning the craftsmanship of the universe—takes his start from the Good, believing this to be the finest starting point: the discovery of the <term>Final Cause</term><note>The "Final Cause" is the purpose or "that for the sake of which" something exists; for Proclus, this is the goodness of the Creator</note>. For as all...

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Proclus discussed the "preface" of Plato’s Timaeus, comparing it to the musical "preliminary touches" used before a performance. ### PROCLUS

->**[BOOK II]**<-

The Good is the cause of all things that exist, and so the generation of the cosmos also proceeds from
<margin>C</margin> this very first principle. For all things are from the Good, and even those things of which
the <term>demiurgic</term><note>The "Demiurge" is the divine craftsman or Creator-Intellect in Plato’s philosophy.</note> Intellect is not the [direct] cause, the Good is the cause—such as **matter**—and even those things for which the <term>Paradigm</term><note>The eternal blueprint or model the Creator looks at when making the world.</note> is not the constitutive basis, even these receive their existence from there [the Good]. For all things are for its sake, and it is the cause of all beautiful things, as it is said in the *Letters* <note>original: "Epistolais"—referring to Plato’s Second Letter, 312e, a key text for Neoplatonists.</note>. Therefore, Timaeus refers the other causes back to this single cause. For having discovered the form of the cosmos through the hypotheses, as well as the <term>paradigmatic cause</term> and the <term>efficient cause</term>, he now wishes to assign the most authoritative and
ancient of the causes, the **final cause**, which he especially desires in regard to the
creation. For if even a person living according to intellect performs
all actions for the sake of the good, how much more does Intellect itself and the Divine Intellect
create everything for the sake of the final cause? For even if the
virtuous man often seems to do something for the sake of the body or for the sake of inferior things in general, this is not
his [ultimate] goal—the good of the body or of the inferior thing—but rather he
does even this for the sake of likeness to the divine, and makes that his most
<margin>D</margin> targeted end. How much more | then would the Creator of the universe create for the
sake of the **Good** and the final cause? For he does not make his
activity aimless or indefinite. Therefore, it seems to me that Plato does not even ask the starting question of
*whether* there is a final cause for the constitution of the cosmos, but rather, as this is
agreed upon by everyone, he seeks *what* the final cause is. For a demiurgic
Intellect and God is presupposed, and not "spontaneity" <note>original: "automaton"—referring to the idea of a universe formed by chance or random atoms, as argued by Epicureans.</note>, as some say. If then Intellect [is the cause of] the
whole, there is surely a "for the sake of which" in the creation. For just as a soul that is set right
performs all things according to intellect, so the demiurgic Intellect brings all things into existence according to God;
and this is the same as acting according to the **Good**. Whether, then, one must follow the
Aristotelian problems—where after [asking] *what* the whole is and *what kind* it is, it is necessary to seek
*why* it is; for it has been said that it is "generated" and is an "image of Being," and one must
further consider for what sake it came to be—or whether, according to the Platonic causes, after
the efficient and the paradigm, it is fitting to find the final cause of the world-making.
<margin>E</margin> For, indeed, all other things are suspended from this: the | divinity of the
paradigm, the goodness of the maker, and the perfection of that which is produced;
and the ascent for those who love the vision [of truth] goes as far as this. They are accustomed to call
the **final cause** "that because of which" <note>original: "di' ho"</note>, the **paradigmatic** "that toward which" <note>original: "pros ho"</note>, the **demiurgic** "that by which" <note>original: "hyp' hou"</note>,
the **instrumental** "that through which" <note>original: "di' hou"</note>, the **form** "that according to which" <note>original: "kath' ho"</note>, and the **matter** "that out of which" <note>original: "ex hou"</note> or "that in which" <note>original: "en hō"</note>.
These terms are used because they also seemed [correct] to Plato himself. For
seeking the final cause now, he says "for what cause," while the paradigmatic [he calls] "toward which"...

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Proclus transitioned from discussing the "Final Cause" (the Good) to the specific phrasing of Plato’s text. He is now beginning a detailed analysis of the terms "generation" (becoming) and "the All" (the cosmos) as they appear in the Timaeus.</meta>

### ON THE TIMAEUS II.

**17**

<warning>Shadow on the bottom left corner slightly obscures the start of the apparatus criticus.</warning>

...[more authoritative] of the models, while the **demiurgic** <note>The "Demiurge" is the divine craftsman or Creator-Intellect in Plato’s philosophy.</note> cause relates to that which is becoming, for whatever becomes must of necessity become by some cause. As for the rest, as we proceed we shall note them ¹) in Plato's own words; however, let it be said even now that these matters are proper to the philosopher's science of discernment. But what is "becoming" <note>original: "genesis"</note> and what is "the All"? Some, hearing "becoming," take it to mean the sublunary ²) region <note>The "sublunary region" is the area below the moon, which in ancient cosmology was the realm of change, decay, and the four elements.</note>, and have called "the All" the whole world, but these people completely miss Plato’s meaning. For the Demiurge is not presented as molding material things separately and the whole world separately; moreover, "becoming" itself is a part of "the All." 

<margin>F</margin> If they say ³) "the All" is the Heaven, because it is the greatest part | of the world (for the rest is small) or because it is the most divine and authoritative part, like the head of the whole world (for the head is also called "the whole," as in "Teucer, dear head," ⁴) <note>A reference to Homer, Iliad 8.281, where the head represents the whole person.</note> and for the sake of this [head] ⁵) Plato says the rest of the body's mass has been placed around it), nevertheless, the philosopher is also accustomed to calling this "becoming." 

Others have called matter "becoming" and the world ordered out of matter "the All"; for these people, it is necessary to reject much of what Plato has written. 

<margin>109</margin> For he says ⁶) that everything generated | and all "becoming" is sensible, or tangible and visible. Furthermore, he distinguishes "becoming" from matter somewhere, as when he says ⁷) there are three distinct things: Being ⁸), Space, and Becoming, from which the All subsists. 

But our own teacher <note>Proclus refers here to his mentor, Syrianus.</note> says that the creation of the world is conceived in two ways. For one part of it is **body-making**, and the other is the joining of the bodies into the completion of a single world. For it is one thing to mold the bodies themselves through shapes, and another to harmonize the things molded into the All. Therefore, "becoming" refers to the molding of the bodies, being a creation directed toward the wholeness and perfection of the All. For that which is composed of parts has the creation of the parts pre-conceived; one must therefore call all ⁹) the intermediate stages between matter and the total arrangement and the single completion of the universe "becoming," so that there may be a path toward the whole in which the 

<margin>B</margin> parts are contained. For this is "the All," | a perfect thing composed of perfect things according to the single harmony of the whole. Since this "All" is also sensible, but not the "intelligible All" (for that was the model) nor the "intellectual All" (for that was the demiurgic cause), for this reason he added the word "this," indicating by this ¹⁰) "this" both the sensible and the particular. For everything bodily, even if it be a whole, is particular. But most properly, "whole" refers to the immaterial and non-extended, and truly that One which is both intellectual and intelligible. So much for these matters. And what shall we posit as the "constitution"? Perhaps it indicates both that the world is composed of many things and its generation from things unlike ¹¹) one another...
