# PROCLUS

...stability extends from the whole of creation. For the prefix "con-" <note>original: "sun-"</note> signifies the union and the breathing-together of all things into one, while "stasis" <note>original: "stasis", meaning standing or station</note> indicates the settled and permanent nature of the created work. Furthermore, the weaving together of the tenses—the present and the past—indicates both the completeness and the eternal nature of the creation. For "establishing" ¹) <note>original: "sunistan"</note> indicates the continuous production that is always being 
<margin>C</margin>

To signify both tenses through the ²) same words shows that the divine creation proceeds through identity and likeness. For just as the creative power is, so too is its activity; as it exists, so it creates. Therefore, it acts according to its very being and by ³) its own essence.

> He was good, and in the good ⁴) no envy ever arises concerning anything. (Page 29 E.)

Those who have called the Demiurge <note>The "Demiurge" is the Divine Craftsman who shapes the universe in Plato's philosophy.</note> "The Good" <note>original: "tagathon", referring to the absolute First Principle or the One</note> are completely ridiculous. For "The Good" is one thing, and "the good one" is another. The former is unparticipated, existing by itself and set apart from all things, whereas the latter is good by participating in that First Principle. Furthermore, The Good reigns over all intelligible beings <note>The "intelligible" realm refers to the world of pure ideas or forms, accessible only by the mind.</note>, but the Demiurge—if he is identical to the Model—is the intelligibles themselves but does not reign over them; if he is secondary to the Model, he is far inferior to the one who reigns over all intelligibles. In general, every god is "a good," whether 
<margin>D</margin>
demiurgic, | life-giving, or perfecting, but The Good is not merely "a good," but simply Goodness. If you call him "demiurgic," you diminish his simplicity. 

Having distinguished these points, let us now look at the beginning of the passage and say ⁷) first that, just as when Plato sought the cosmic form and asked whether the world was born or ungenerated, he introduced the conclusion "it was born" before the whole proof; and just as when investigating the model-cause he anticipated the conclusion—which is clear to everyone—by stating it was "modeled after the eternal" before the whole argument; so now, intending to find the "Final Cause" <note>The "Final Cause" is the purpose or "the why" for which something exists.</note> above all else, he introduced the phrase "He was good." In this exclamation, he mimics the Intellect and its sudden, total grasp of truth. For in this short phrase, the entire object of our search is contained: that the Final Cause is goodness—both Goodness in itself and demiurgic goodness. For just as the Model is twofold (one being intelligible and the other intellectual), the one exists before the Demiurge, being primarily eternal and unified ¹²) and all...

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 2

<margin>E</margin> [Just as the Model is] comprehensive of all intelligible living beings, so too the Creator <note>original: "dēmiourgos"</note> of the whole ¹) contains within himself the creative number of the Forms <note>The "Forms" or "Ideas" are the eternal blueprints of all things in Platonic thought.</note> in a unified way. In the same manner, "Goodness" is of two kinds: one is simply the Good itself, and the other exists within the creative Intellect. The former is the fountain of all good things—whether they be intelligible, intellectual, or supra-cosmic <note>Proclus uses these terms to describe different levels of reality: "Intelligible" (pure being), "Intellectual" (pure thought), and "Supra-cosmic" (beyond the physical universe).</note>—while the latter is a specific kind of goodness that acts as a cause and source for some things, while holding a subordinate rank for others. For if we wish to examine what makes a god "intelligible," "intellectual," "heavenly," or "worldly," we will find nothing other than the Good. What makes each body "ensouled," if not the image of the Soul? What makes intellectual souls what they are, if not the Intellect within them, which is an illumination from the Universal Intellect? What then would "deify" both the Intellect and intelligible essence, if not the participation ²) in the First Principle and the radiance that comes from it? What, then, is this First Principle? If it were "Lesser Beauty" ³), we would say ⁴) that the Intellect is a god through Beauty. But since that First Principle is The Good, the Intellect is a god by participating in Goodness. This, therefore, is the very existence of the gods—this is the "essence" of the gods, if it is permitted to speak so: Goodness. It is according to this Goodness that every god has his being as a god, and through | this he is providen- <margin>F</margin> tial, or creative, or life-giving, or connective. For while Intellect, insofar as it is Intellect, is naturally suited to think and know ⁵) existing things, the act of "providing" <note>original: "pronoein", literally "fore-thinking" or providence</note> is divine. Thus, even the creative Intellect possesses its creative nature through the Goodness within it. Because of this Goodness, the Intellect within him is a "maker" and not merely a "knower" of being; and the Being that serves as the Model within him becomes active, creating by its very existence and not merely perfecting the Intellect. And the Intellect, in its making, is empowered by both: by the Model, because it creates according to it, and by Good- <margin>110</margin> ness, because it creates for its sake. The Model, in turn, derives from the Monad <note>original: "henados", the state of being One or ultimate unity</note>. You have these things, then, in order: Goodness, the Model, and the Intellect. They exist one way within the Demiurge, and another way prior to the Demiurge. If you wish to speak of them: the First Goodness is "The One," which is beyond even intelligible things—for that is the "unparticipated" ⁶) Goodness; the Model ⁷) is the Intelligible, which contains the entire number of Forms in a unified way; and the Maker is the intellectual Intellect, the one who gives substance to the whole. Thus, if Amelius ⁸) spoke of "three creators" in this way, seeing this triad within the one, he spoke correctly. For he says that one creator "works with his hands" in the act of making, another by "command" alone, and another by "will" alone. One is ranked as the "self-working" craftsman, the second exists beforehand as the "architect," and the third is established before both as the "king." Therefore, ⁹) insofar as the Demiurge is Intellect, he produces all things by his own thoughts; insofar as he is | Intelligible, <margin>B</margin> he creates by his very being; and insofar as he is God, he creates by will alone. But if one were to tear these three creators apart from the One, we—following Plato—would not tolerate it. For he...

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 2

...and he is good as a god, and through his goodness, he creates all things by his will and is <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "noētos"; refers to things that can be grasped by the mind rather than the senses</note> in an <term>intellectual</term> <note>original: "noerōs"; refers to the active operation of the mind</note> manner. For such is the creative Being, and he is a world-crafting Intellect. The statement that "he **was** good" has the following explanation: the word "**was**" indicates the over-fullness, the absolute perfection, and the supra-eternal nature of the divine existence. For the word "**is**" is significant of eternal things, while "**was**" signifies the supra-eternal <term>Henads</term> <note>original: "henades"; the "Unities" or "Ones," the highest level of divinity in Proclus's system, existing above even Being itself</note>, and "**will be**" signifies those things that consist in time. For if "**is**" belongs to eternal beings, then "**was**" is appropriate for those prior to these, and "**will be**" for those after eternal things; and such are the things that require time. 

Because the Demiurge is good, no envy ever arises in him concerning anything. Someone might ask: "What is so special about this, if an Intellect does not feel envy? For this trait also belongs to even moderate men." Let the word "**never**" <note>original: "mēdepote"</note> then be a sign of eternal perfection; <margin>C</margin> since souls are sometimes affected by passion and at other times run back up to a state of <term>impassibility</term> <note>original: "apatheia"; a state of being undisturbed by emotions or external influences</note>. Let the phrase "**concerning nothing**" signify his self-sufficiency; since we ourselves are often free from envy for the sake of some things, but in cases where we believe ourselves to have less than others, we are gripped by this passion. 

But what logic does the word "**no**" <note>original: "oudeis," used as "no envy at all"</note> have? Did he add "no" as if there were many kinds of envy, or is it said as a superlative, making a complete denial of envy? And what kind of superlative can be found in discussions about the gods? For all their names and words are inferior to their true dignity. 

Perhaps, then, while "envy" is usually the pain felt over the goods of others—a mixed passion produced in us from pleasure and pain, as Socrates pointed out in the *Philebus*—there is another sense of "envy": the inability to do good, or rather, not doing good but keeping the good to oneself. Indeed, envy is also the very **deficiency** of goods, which it seems to me the Philosopher <note>Plato</note> especially adopts here, banishing it from the divine essence. For it is the nature of this essence alone to be exempt from deficiency, since it is substantialized according to goodness itself. 

<margin>D</margin> For to feel pain over the goods of others belongs to all those who are good by **participation**, but not to those who are **primarily** good. For an **acquired** good is one thing, a **habitual** good another, and the **primary** good yet another. The first is mixed with its opposite, just as acquired beauty is mingled with ugliness; the second is entirely "good-form," but is such by participation; the third is the **Good-itself**, which is primarily good. For just as the **Intellect-itself** is the primary Intellect, and the **Beauty-itself** is the primary Beauty, so the **Good-itself** is the primary Good. What, then, is this? It is the deity of each thing, according to which each of the truly existing beings is a god. For nothing...

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 2

...differs from Goodness itself. If any of the secondary beings are called either "god" or "good," they belong to the class of things that are <term>deified</term> <note>original: "ektheoumenōn"; things made divine by a higher power</note> and made good; they are a god through <term>participation</term> <note>original: "metochē"; the Platonic concept where a lower thing "shares in" the qualities of a higher Form</note>, but not through their own essence, nor from themselves ¹). This is the kind of participation that Plato is also accustomed to mention, just as in the *Symposium* ³) he described **Eros** as being in need of beautiful and good things. Therefore, the divine, insofar as it is divine, is such [goodness] and is not good by participation; consequently, it is not in need of good.

<margin>E</margin> It is, therefore, superior to all **envy**. For just as it is impossible for darkness to approach the sun, which is the source of light ⁴), but is instead shut away somewhere far off in the hollows of the earth, in the same way, it is impossible for envy to approach the divine. For what "need" could there be in such an abundance? What "weakness" in the all-powerful divinity? What "sharing" [of lack] in the fountain of all goods? By the very fact of being good, the **Demiurge** <note>original: "dēmiourgos"; the divine craftsman of the world</note> transcends all need and all participation that comes from another, being united to the **One** itself by his very being and never departing from the One. For there is one kind of union that is <term>intellectual</term> <note>original: "noera"; relating to the higher Mind or Intellect</note>, and another that is prior to the Intellect, according to which the <term>generative</term> ⁵) divinity of the Demiurge and the goodness that holds all things together is joined to the **One** itself. For this "good" is not a certain power, as some say, but the measure of every power; nor is it a "will," but rather the will comes from it; nor is it a "habit" <note>original: "hexis"; a stable disposition</note>, for a habit belongs to something else ⁶), but Goodness ⁷) belongs to itself. Nor is it in any way a substantial <term>subsistence</term> <note>original: "hypostasis"</note>, but it is both the unifier of essence and the ineffable bond of powers, and the source that brings forth creative activities. Therefore, just as every | **Intellect** is given essence according to its being an intellect, while that which is "above intellect" is participated in by it,

<margin>F</margin> and just as every **soul** is given essence according to its being a soul, while the light [of intellect] is participated in by it, so too every **god** is given essence in being a god—or rather, is "supra-substantial" <note>original: "hyperousiōtai"; existing beyond the level of Being or Essence</note>—and nothing is participated in by him. This is because the gods are the most ancient of all things. Thus, the **creative Intellect** (the Demiurge), insofar as he is a god, exists primarily in being a god and is not a god by participation; and this is the same as saying he is "good." Therefore, just as if someone were to say that the Intellect possessed envy, even a partial intellect would be superior to such envy, but the **soul** 

<margin>111</margin> itself would be even more superior; for the soul is in need of intellect, because it is by participation in intellect that its nature becomes intellectual. So too regarding goodness: if **envy** ⁹) is the lack of good things, and everything that is not "primarily good" is in need ¹⁰), then the soul and the intellect are in need of good things because they are not primarily good. But the God, insofar as he is a god and is good, is set apart from all envy and transcends every kind of need that might exist, whether in terms of existence or in terms of "turning away." For "need" is twofold: one kind is not an evil, but the other, as has been said ¹²), is an evil.

# PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 2

> And being free from this [envy], he desired that all things should become as like himself as possible. (Page 29e)

This was consistent with the previously mentioned axioms. For the first [axiom] showed the rank of the **Demiurge** <note>original: "dēmiourgos"; the divine craftsman of the world</note> and his existence—namely, that he is God. And as for God, one kind is <term>unparticipated</term> <note>original: "amethektos"; a primary principle that does not share itself with lower things</note>, while another is <term>participated</term> <note>original: "methektos"; a principle that can be shared in by lower beings</note>. He has shown through this very phrase that the Demiurge is participated; for he did not say that he was "The Good" ¹) <note>original: "tagathon"; the absolute first principle or the One</note> but that he was "good" <note>original: "agathos"; possessing the quality of goodness</note>.

Now, that which is "good" participates in **Goodness** itself. Goodness itself is primarily <margin>B</margin> good, while **Mind** <note>original: "nous"</note> or **Being** is good by participation. Secondly, it is shown that the Demiurge is preeminent among those beings that are <term>deified</term> <note>original: "ektheoumenōn"; beings elevated to divine status by a higher power</note>. For there is that which is entirely unparticipated, such as The Good ²); and there is that which is good by sharing in another, as is the case with everything that is deified. But the Demiurge is himself primarily good, yet he is also participated in and stands as a "middle" between both of the aforementioned extremes—just as all the intelligible and intellectual orders of the gods are described.

Thirdly, this very point contains the specific characteristic of the creator. For not only to be good himself, but because of his superabundance and extensiveness to proceed unto all things, is indicative of the demiurgic and productive cause. For this cause is always desiring itself and seeking to make all things good, so that all things might become as like him as possible, participating in something divine and ineffable symbols which reach them from the whole of creation. 

If, then, the Maker of the universe is free from all envy, he is set apart from all weakness, and this eternally—which the word "being" ⁵) signifies as eternal. And because he makes all things as good as possible, bestowing upon all the <margin>C</margin> measure of the good, beyond which it is not in the nature of each recipient to contain more, | this demonstrates the extensiveness of **Providence**. 

And if he wishes to grant the participation of the good to all, there is nothing in the universe that is purely evil, nor disordered, nor outside of providence, nor undefined. Instead, all things participate in order and arrangement insofar as they are naturally capable of receiving it. He therefore makes all things like himself insofar as he is a God who makes things good as they come into being. Yet, he also works according to other <term>paradigmatic reasons</term> <note>original: "logous paradeigmatikous"; the eternal blueprints or Forms</note>. 

For just as **Atticus** ⁸) <note>a 2nd-century Platonist</note> says, the carpenter makes everything in a "carpenter-like" way, but he makes one thing according to one plan (like a stool) and another according to another (like a bed). In the same way, God, insofar as he is good, makes all things like himself by making them good; but according to the **Forms** <note>original: "eide"</note> which divide the essences of each thing, he creates them in relation to their specific paradigmatic causes. 

**Porphyry** ⁹) <note>the 3rd-century Neoplatonist scholar</note>, while accepting these points, thinks it worthwhile to consider what exactly things brought into being ¹⁰) receive in order to be "good." He says they receive **harmony**, **symmetry**, and **order**; for these things are beautiful, and everything beautiful is good. <margin>D</margin> Plato shows, at least, that the good consists in these things where he says ¹¹) that | [he brought the world into order from disorder].

### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 2

...the disordered state [was organized] by God because of his will to communicate his goodness. From all these points, it is easy to conclude that the **Demiurge** <note>original: "dēmiourgos"; the divine craftsman</note> acts eternally, and that the world is eternal ¹) according to an eternity that extends through all time. It is always becoming ordered, and although as something indestructible it does not "exist" in a static eternal sense, it "becomes" ²) eternally, being made good—though it is not good of itself, like the Father ³) who begat it. For all things exist in him in a unified way ⁴), yet not truly in the same way they exist among eternal beings. 

For consider: if the universe is "generated" <note>original: "genēton"; having a beginning or being caused</note>, was its prior non-existence due to the Demiurge, or due to the underlying nature <note>matter</note> being disordered? If it were due to the Demiurge, would it be because he himself did not exist eternally? To say such a thing is not even lawful, and is otherwise futile; for ⁵) the same line of questioning would apply to him, and we would either have to make everything "generated," or there must be something primarily "ungenerated," and the latter is more likely. Should we then posit that the Demiurge was once not acting? If so, did he not create because he was unwilling, or because he was unable? 

If we say he was unwilling, we unwittingly <margin>E</margin> destroy his **Goodness**; but if we say he was unable, it is absurd for him to possess power ⁶) at one time and inability at another; for we would be stripping away his eternity. If, on the other hand, the delay was due to the underlying nature, was that nature then unsuitable or suitable? If it were suitable, then the delay was not because of the nature; for whatever the underlying matter ought ⁷) to have, it would have already possessed. But if it were unsuitable, how is it that after an infinite duration of being unsuitable, it has now changed ⁸)? Did it move itself? But matter is not self-moving. Rather, it was moved by the Demiurge. And why not sooner, if indeed ⁹) he was good even then and willed that all things should become ¹⁰) like him? 

Therefore, the extension of **Providence** <note>original: "pronoia"; divine foresight and care</note> is linked to the goodness of the Father; to this Providence is linked the everlasting activity of the Demiurge; and to this activity is linked the eternity of the universe throughout infinite time—an eternity that is "becoming" and not "static." The same logic that would take away this [eternal becoming] would also take away the goodness of the Creator. For if the Demiurge was good, he always wills good things for all. Just as the sun, for as long as it exists, illuminates ¹¹) all things, and as fire <margin>F</margin> warms—for this is their very essence; the one being illuminative and the fire being heat-giving—so also that which is eternally Good always wills good things. This is so that he does not suffer the condition ¹²) of the most base—willing but being unable; for even a virtuous man does not will anything other than what he is able ¹³) to do. 

If he is always able to do good, he always enacts good, so that his power is not incomplete ¹⁴). And if he always enacts good, he always creates good things. If he himself is always creating, then the world is always becoming ¹⁵). Therefore, the world is eternal ¹⁶); for [he is] always good—

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Proclus’s argument regarding the eternity of the world. He previously discussed why the Demiurge (the Creator) must be eternally active and good. He now moves to explain that the world’s order is the direct result of this eternal goodness, distinguishing between the "Final Cause" (the goal), the "Paradigmatic Cause" (the model), and the "Efficient Cause" (the maker).</meta>

**PROCLUS**

**112** […good] is the **Demiurge** <note>original: "dēmiourgos"; the divine craftsman who shapes the universe</note>. Therefore, the world is eternal—not by being a static entity, but by becoming ¹) a world eternally. Thus, as we have said ²), the eternity of the universe is bound up with the goodness of the One who makes it. For the internal arrangement of the universe is perfectly suited to reveal the power of the Creator. Indeed, because **Matter** <note>original: "hylē"</note> is formless and shapeless, it has seemed to some to be "godless," and they think its chaotic and disordered state is far removed from divine **Providence** <note>original: "pronoia"</note>. However, the universe as a whole, being well-ordered and distinguished by beauty, clearly demonstrates its divine making. This visible order, then, being the offspring of the creative cause, exists alongside the goodness of the Father.

-> This, then, as the most authoritative principle of generation and the world, one would most rightly accept, receiving it from wise men. (Plato, *Timaeus* 30a) <-

In assigning the **Final Cause** <note>original: "telikē aitia"; the ultimate "why" or goal of a thing’s existence</note> to the goodness of the Demiurge, Proclus notes that the Creator unites himself to the Primary Good. By imitating that Good ³), he
**B** gives birth to all things (for that Primary Good is what first brings all things forth). He calls this the "most authoritative principle" because it is what moves the other causes. For the creative power moves the thing being made, but is itself moved from that higher source; likewise, the **Paradigm** <note>original: "paradeigma"; the eternal blueprint</note> moves ⁴) the entire work of creation, but is itself moved by Goodness. This is because the Good exists even before the **Intelligible** beings <note>original: "noēta"; things that can be known by pure intellect, like the Forms</note>, whereas the Paradigm is Intelligible, and the Demiurge is **Intellective** <note>original: "noeros"; the divine mind that acts and thinks</note>. All Intelligible and Intellective things revolve around the Good, while the arrangement of Intellective things ⁵) revolves around the Intelligible. Thus, while the **Efficient Cause** (the maker) is authoritative, the **Paradigmatic Cause** (the model) is more authoritative ⁶), and the **Final Cause** (the goal) is the most authoritative. For this goal is that for the sake of which ⁷) all things exist, and upon which all others depend; it is the true end of creation. Therefore, the world is perfected by being given a soul and becoming a living thing ⁸), but it is most perfect insofar as ⁹) it participates in the Good and in the unity that has permeated ¹⁰) through the whole. Just as the Good leads all things, so too does the specific goodness within each thing hold the highest rank. For these reasons, he called the Final Cause the "most authoritative principle." The word "principle" includes even the
**C** **con-causes** <note>original: "synaitia"; auxiliary factors or tools that help a cause but aren't the primary source</note>, but the addition of "most authoritative" points to the true ¹¹) cause. For causes are "more authoritative" principles of things that come to be ¹²), while con-causes are "slaves" to others, existing within the results themselves. Regarding "generation" and the "world," as has been said before, these refer to the path between raw matter and the total arrangement, and to the perfection of the universe itself. And since ¹³) in the doctrines concerning these highest causes, there is a need for an intellectual [disposition] in the speaker...

# ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK 2

<unclear>H</unclear>aving a state <note>original: "hexis"; a stable disposition of mind</note> and a wise judgment of the listeners, especially in discourses concerning the **Good**. For **Intellect** <note>original: "nous"</note> is directed toward the Good, and the intellect within us is directed toward the Good within us. For this very reason, those who speak about the most authoritative Principle must be wise, and those who listen must receive the arguments most correctly. What then? Could not even an ordinary person say something ¹) about God and the **Final Cause** <note>original: "telikē aitia"</note>? And what of it? Is it not possible to hear many people saying every day, "God is good"? But the name "God" is empty without virtue, as **Plotinus** <note>A foundational Neoplatonist philosopher (3rd century AD) who emphasized the "One" as the source of all being</note> says; it is spoken by the masses not according to wisdom, but by chance. 

<margin>D</margin> What then? Do not even **daimons** <note>original: "daimones"; intermediary spirits between gods and humans</note> know the goodness of the Father—those who dance around him—and the **demiurgic angels** <note>divine messengers involved in the crafting of the universe</note> who lead the way for the Father’s poetic creation, and those who receive the creative powers from the single Cause? Yes, but **Gods** know it in a unified way, **Angels** know it intellectually, and **Daimons** know it immaculately, eternally, and in a manner akin to those beings who precede them. We, however, should be satisfied if we know it wisely <note>original: "emphronōs"; with practical wisdom or prudence</note>, being something in the middle between the more divine beings and the masses, between the intellectual and the senseless. 

For such is human **Wisdom** <note>original: "phronēsis"</note>: it proceeds from **Intellect** and **Intention**, but stands apart from the senseless life. Thus, when we speak of the most authoritative Principle, we must receive the words as coming from wise men ⁶). For wisdom is the middle ground between pure Intellect and mere opinion, so that a correct judgment will be in harmony with it. Therefore, one would add the word "most." For one must "most" especially accept this discourse from wise men. From those who are above humanity, one must seek a "superior" word, and from the masses, a "random" one.

# PROCLUS

After the single "will" of the Intellect <note>original: "nous"</note>, he introduced the divided "contemplation" of the same thing. From that point on, he unfolds the entire creative providence <note>original: "pronoia"</note> and all the parts of creation, proceeding into the full plurality and extension of thought. Indeed, there is a continuity: the third part follows the second, and the second follows the first.

<margin>F</margin> Since the first segment was "He was good," the second | section consequently began from "Goodness" and proceeded until it reached the "Will" <note>original: "boulēsis"</note> of the Father. Then the third section, starting from that "Will," transmits the entirety of Providence. For if He was good, He willed to make all things good; and if He willed it, He also acted and brought the whole universe into order. For Providence is suspended from the Will, and the Will is suspended from Goodness. Let this much be said regarding the order and continuity of the arguments. Now, let us look at what this "Will" itself actually is, 

<margin>113</margin> so that we may also understand how it is joined to Goodness. This | "supra-essential" <note>original: "hyperousios"; referring to a reality that exists beyond the level of Being or Essence</note> union, which is itself set apart from all existing things, is one, ineffable <note>too sacred or great to be expressed in words</note>, and unlimited. It possesses its uncircumscribed and incomprehensible nature by virtue of the "One" itself. If, however, we must contemplate within this union the "unified triad" based on what has been said, then **Goodness** takes the lead within it; second is **Will**; and third is **Providence**. 

**Goodness** produces that which is perfect, sufficient, and desirable. 
**Will** exhibits that which is overflowing, extended, and generative. 
**Providence** provides the active, perfecting, and untainted power. 

According to this ineffable and unified existence of the Triad, the "Intelligible" realm is also divided in a threefold way: by **Essence**, **Power**, and **Activity** <note>original: "ousia, dynamis, energeia"; the three standard stages of Neoplatonic procession</note>. Within this, Essence is stably fixed and self-complete; Power possesses an unfailing and infinite procession; and Activity has obtained perfection and essential production. Furthermore, the **Intellect** is divided in the same ratio into three: **Being**, **Life**, and **Intellectual** nature. For one provides the "to be," the second the "to live," and the third the "to know." 

<margin>B</margin> Following these is the **Soul**, divided into the | **Object of Knowledge**, **Knowledge**, and the **Knowing Faculty**. For one is the thing known, the other is the knowledge itself, and the third is that which fulfills them both. Since there are these four triads, they are analogous: as Goodness is to Will, so is Essence to Power, Being to Life, and the Object of Knowledge to Knowledge. And as Will is to Providence, so is Power to Activity, Life to Intellect, and Knowledge to the Knowing Faculty. For Essence, Being, and the Object of Knowledge hold the rank analogous to Goodness; for that which is cohesive, stable, and uni-

# ON TIMAEUS II.

<warning>The left edge of the main text block is slightly clipped, cutting off initial letters in the first few lines.</warning>

...[unified] and perfecting of goodness; to the **Will** belong power, life, and knowledge; for that which is self-begotten, and which encompasses and measures all things, belongs to the Will. To **Providence** <note>original: "pronoia"</note> belong activity, the intellect, and the faculty of knowledge; for that which is effective, which permeates through all things, and which has pre-grasps of the images of all things, belongs to divine providence. Since, therefore, the Demiurge <note>The "Architect" or Creator figure in Plato's philosophy</note> is both God and an "imparticipable" <note>existing independently and not shared by lower things</note> Intellect, insofar as he is God, he possesses goodness, will, and providence; insofar as he is an "intelligible" <note>an object of pure thought</note> being, he possesses essence, power, and activity; and insofar as he is Intellect, he exists and possesses life and knowledge of the whole. Furthermore, the "monad" <note>a state of oneness or unity</note> within him is the connective bond of the Triad, while the ineffable monad is the bond of the "Henad" <note>the ultimate unit or "One"</note>. 

<margin>C</margin> So much, then, regarding the Will. Following this, we must investigate how it is that he "wills all things to be good," and whether this is possible, and in what manner. For some say that if he truly willed this, the "progression" <note>term: <term>proodos</term>; the process by which higher divine realities flow down into lower forms of existence</note> of creation should have stopped at the gods and the "untainted" essences. If he did not create only these, but also wild beasts, reptiles, men, and everything material, then he did not actually will for all things to be good; for surely he does not "will" the better things while "creating" the worse. They argue that if he willed all to be good, he would have ended his poetic creation at the level of the gods. 

To this we shall reply: if the progression stopped at the gods, then "all things" would *not* be good. For those first beings, were they to occupy the very last rank of existence, would lose their characteristic goodness. Because they are able and willing to generate further life due to their own inherent goodness, if they were placed at the end of the line, they would become barren and unproductive—and thus, they would not be good. Those critics say: "If all things are good, the progression stops at the gods." But we say: "If the progression stops at the gods, then all things are not good." 

<margin>D</margin> For how can the divine be "good" if it is barren? And it will be barren if it is the last thing in existence. For everything that generates is superior to that which is generated; but where there is no "inferior" being, there is no place for a "superior" one. 

Therefore, let there be gods who hold the very first rank, and after the gods, let a progression be established even down to matter itself. Let us grant to all beings a progression from the first to the last, and let nothing be missing from the lowest levels, nor let there be any "void" in existence. For how could there be a void when there are: first, the things that exist "in themselves"; second, the things belonging to them; third, the things belonging to those and others; fourth, the things produced from another; and fifth, the things that hold the rank of "other" beings? <note>Proclus is describing a chain of being where each level is a slightly more distant reflection of the original Source.</note> Within all these, things are arranged as "dissimilarly similar" <note>things that are different in essence but similar in their underlying divine pattern</note> on both sides, and there is such great continuity among all things. What could possibly be missing when there are, first, the "unmoved" beings established in their place; second, the "self-moving" beings; and third, those moved by others?

He defines the hierarchy of the Demiurge's attributes and refutes the idea that a perfect Creator should only produce perfect things.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the discussion of the "progression" (proodos) of creation from the Divine Demiurge, moving from the higher, unified realities down to the lowest, most divided forms of existence, leading into a classic philosophical investigation of the nature and existence of evil.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...[of things] in motion, all of which are indeed the lowest of beings (for all beings are completed by the things mentioned); and generally, through many approaches, the production of things is shown to be continuous and, if you wish to say so, there is an analogy [extending] from on high down to the last things, according to the progression <note>term: <term>proodos</term>; the process of "flowing out" from a divine source into lower forms of existence</note> from the One of all things. 

<margin>E</margin> Let all these things, then, be agreed upon, and let the generation of beings be brought down as far as nothingness. But is there no evil <note>original: "kakon"</note> among these things, or shall we grant that so-called "wickedness" exists somehow in both bodies and in souls? Driven by this very puzzle, some have entirely done away with evil, while others have despaired of providence <note>original: "pronoia"</note>. The latter believe that if providence exists, then all things must be good. For if God willed evil to exist, how is He **good**? For it belongs to the Good to make everything good—since goodness is His very essence—just as it belongs to heat to make things warm, since heat is its essence. And it is not lawful for the Good to produce anything except the good. But if He does *not* will it, how does evil exist? For then something would have come into being against the will of the Father of all things. 

Such then is the puzzle. It must be addressed by those who grasp the teachings of Plato himself according to our teacher <note>Proclus refers here to his mentor, Syrianus</note>: namely, that there must be one kind of relationship between God and things, and another between us and things; and again, a different relationship of things toward the divine and toward us. 

<margin>F</margin> For the relationship of wholes to parts is not the same as that of parts to one another. To God, therefore, nothing is evil, not even among those things called "evils," for He makes use even of these. But for "partial" beings <note>individual things or people, as opposed to the Whole/Universe</note>, there is such a thing as evil, which they are naturally suited to suffer. And this same thing is an evil to the part, but to the Entirety and to the whole it is not evil, but rather good. 

For insofar as a thing exists and insofar as it participates in some kind of order, it is good. For if you were to suppose this so-called "evil" to be destitute of all good, you would place it even beyond "that which in no way exists" <note>Absolute non-existence</note>. 

<margin>114</margin> For just as the Good Itself <note>original: "autoagathon"</note> is prior to Being, so the **Evil Itself** <note>original: "autokakon"</note> would be after the nothingness of non-being. For evil is that which is furthest removed from the Good, and not that which in no way exists. If, therefore, that which in no way exists does not exist—nor does the "Evil Itself"—but the former is among the things impossible to exist, then this [absolute evil] is even more impossible. But if it is not entirely evil, but is intertwined with the good, you will grant it a place among beings, and this will make it "good" for other things. And how could it be otherwise, if it is a being? For that which is a "being" participates in Being; and that which participates in Being also participates in the One; and that which participates in the One participates in the Good. Therefore...

He concludes that absolute evil cannot exist because anything that has existence must participate in Being, Unity, and therefore Goodness.</summary>

# ON THE TIMAEUS II.

<warning>Stains on the bottom left corner of the page partially obscure the text of the footnotes.</warning>

...insofar as it exists, it participates in the good <note>original: "agathou metekhei"</note>. Therefore, it is not purely evil, nor entirely out of tune, nor indefinite. Who then makes it so? Who provides it with measure, order, and limit? Clearly, it is the Demiurge <note>term: <term>Demiurge</term>; the "Craftsman" or Divine Creator in Plato's philosophy</note>, who works to make all things similar to himself. For he fills both the wholes and the parts with good things. 

<margin>B</margin> If indeed he makes all things good and colors even evil itself with the good, then nothing is worthless according to the power of God and of those who receive it. For this power is twofold: one belongs to God, which makes even "much-cursed" <note>original: "polyaraton"</note> evil good; the other belongs to the recipients, who partake in the goodness of the Demiurge according to the measure of their own order. Thus, for the Demiurge who wills that nothing be evil, nothing is evil. 

But if some blame him because he established particular things—claiming he is the cause of evils—they do away with the making of the world, they overturn the fertile power of the whole, and they confuse the nature of the first things and the last things together. That we are stating things that agree with Plato's views is easy to see from his writings. 

In the *Statesman* <note>term: <term>Politicus</term>; Plato's dialogue on the art of ruling</note> he says explicitly: **"For from the one who fashioned it, the world has acquired all beautiful things; but from its previous condition, many unjust and difficult things happen in the heavens."** Because there is "generation" (coming into being) and "corruption" (passing away), that which is "contrary to nature" has a byproduct-existence <note>term: <term>parhypostasis</term>; a central Neoplatonic concept where evil is not a primary creation but a parasitic "side-effect" of good things</note>. 

<margin>C</margin> And because the cause found in matter fills the particular souls with shapelessness through their long association with it, for this reason the "irrational" also obtains a certain byproduct-existence. Nevertheless, all these things become beautiful through the goodness of the one who has made the whole. 

And in the *Republic*: **"Of good things no other cause must be blamed than God, but for evils one must seek other causes."** Through these words he has shown that evils do not come from elsewhere <note>note: i.e., they have no primary source or "First Principle" of Evil</note>. For he says it is not the nature of fire to chill, nor of snow to heat, nor of the All-Good to do evil; and he shows that we must set down particular causes for these things, and that these causes are indefinite. For just as with good things, where the "One" and the "Primary Good" precede the "Many," it is not so with evil things, due to the indefinite "pouring out" of wickedness. 

Therefore, the words "others" and "certain things" <note>original: "alla kai atta"</note> reveal the particular and indefinite nature of the causes of wickedness. For neither is the soul one of those things that naturally [flees from nature—yet soul and nature are distinct entities], nor is the body one of the irrational things. For even the virtuous have bodies, and they possess virtue along with the body. And in the *Theaetetus*: **"But it is not possible for evils to be destroyed, O Theodorus..."**

He cites Plato's Statesman, Republic, and Theaetetus to prove that God is the cause only of good, while evil arises from indefinite, secondary causes.</summary>

# PROCLUS

<warning>The right margin is partially lost or obscured by the binding (gutter), causing some words to be cut off at the end of lines.</warning>

<margin>D</margin> ...is not possible, nor can these things exist among the gods. However, mortal nature must, by necessity, haunt this [earthly] region. If, then, by necessity <insert>■</insert> evil is carried along within this mortal place, it would not be—at least according to Plato—something that does not exist at all, nor would it be entirely separated <note>original: "exērtēmenon"</note> from all other beings. Thus, according to him, evil both exists and arises from particular causes, and it is "made good" through the providence <note>original: "pronoian"</note> of the Demiurge. This is because nothing is entirely evil; rather, there is a way in which everything is fulfilled according to justice and the divine.

Let us distinguish the matter in this way: of all things in the universe, some are "wholes" and others are "parts." Among the parts, some preserve their own good eternally, such as the individual intellect and the individual spirits <note>term: <term>daimones</term>; intermediary spirits or guardian beings in Greek philosophy</note>. Others, however, are not always able to preserve their own specific good. Of these, some are moved by others <note>term: <term>heterokineton</term>; things that do not move themselves, like inanimate matter</note>, while others are self-moved <note>term: <term>autokineton</term>; entities with the power of choice, like souls</note>. Among the self-moved, some have their vice limited to their choices, while others let it result in outward actions.

The "wholes," then, are altogether good—not only for themselves, but also providing the good for the parts. Those that are "parts" but guard their own good possess <margin>E</margin> the good in a secondary and partial way. Those that are parts but are moved by others have their existence from another; they depend on the providence of those others and are changed according to what is necessary, just like bodies that are born and perish. 

For if there must be "becoming" <note>term: <term>genesis</term>; the process of coming-into-being</note>, there must also be "perishing." Becoming occurs through change, and is itself a kind of change. And if there is to be perishing, there must also be the "sneaking in" of that which is contrary to nature. Just as a thing that has perished is destroyed relative to itself, but is not lost to the Whole—for it becomes air or water or something else into which it changed—so also that which is "contrary to nature" is disordered relative to itself, but is ordered within the Whole. 

For if even a perished thing, stripped entirely of its own order, does not break the order of the Whole, how could that which is merely "contrary to nature"—which is itself nothing and deprived of all order—cause the entire arrangement of the world to vanish?

Furthermore, regarding things that are "parts" but are self-moved and act upon the world outside themselves: to themselves, the resulting evil is a wound, but in some way this too is good and according to the divine. For since impulses and actions follow from choices, the actions follow the choices according to justice <margin>F</margin> whenever | the one who chooses is worthy not only of the choice, but also of the action that follows it. In an absolute sense, the action might not be good, but for the one who chose it in this specific way and had such an impulse, it is brought about according to justice and is "good" in a certain way for this specific person and this specific kind of life. For among good things, some are good for everyone, some for those differing by species, and some even for individuals as individuals. For example, food is not good for everyone, nor is it good for all bodies, nor even for all sick bodies.

He classifies beings into "wholes" (always good) and "parts" (which may experience corruption or make poor choices), arguing that the Demiurge uses providence to ensure everything serves a purpose.</summary>

### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II

<margin>115</margin> ...but for the one who is ill in this way and from such an origin, [the treatment] is healthy. Whether each action be just or unjust, it is good for those performing it insofar as it is according to justice. However, it is not good for them in another sense; rather, it is the greatest evil. Insofar as it comes from themselves, it is evil; but insofar as it comes from the whole to them, it is not evil. Insofar as it pertains to them, having committed the act, they have worn away their life by becoming actively evil; but insofar as it comes from the whole, having suffered the penalty, they have paid the price for their choice <note>original: "hairesis"</note>. 

This is like the story they tell of the gods: when some people were deliberating about betraying a suppliant, God permitted it for no other reason <note>original: "dia ouden allo"</note> than that they might suffer the penalties for their intent. <note>Proclus refers here to a story from Herodotus (Book 1, Chapter 159) where the oracle of Branchidae tells the people of Cyme to hand over a suppliant, not because it is right, but to lead them to a punishment they already deserved for their wicked thoughts.</note>

But now we must consider the remaining points: how many things are partial and move themselves <note>term: <term>autokineton</term>; a being that has the internal power to initiate its own movement or choice</note>, and how far they allow their wickedness to extend until it reaches the point of choice. I will omit saying that even these pay a penalty for their mere thought <note>original: "ennoias"</note>. For indeed, there is a certain punishment for a bare imagination, an impulse, or a will, just as has been said. For the gods govern us from within, and just as they honor those choices that are toward the Good, so they also punish those that are the opposite. 

How, then, could even this choice be according to justice and the divine? <margin>B</margin> It is because it was necessary for such an essence to exist—a power that is ambiguous <note>original: "amphibolon"</note> and leaning toward different ways of life. If, then, the authority of the choice comes from God, then the choice itself comes from God; and if this is so, it is also good. For when the soul chooses, it moves toward matter and is shifted into a different rank. 

Every choice either leads the soul upward or drags it down. If the choice is seen as coming from the soul <note>specifically a soul acting in isolation or error</note>, it is evil; but if it restores the one who chose to their proper rank, it is according to justice and is good. For the choice itself brings justice upon the one who chooses; or rather, the choice becomes a punishment within the one who chooses by separating the soul from the Good. 

For just as a choice directed toward the Good is its own fruit, so a wicked choice is its own punishment. This is the unique characteristic of self-moving powers. Therefore, nothing is so evil that it is not also good in some way; instead, all things participate in providence. 

But if some wonder for what reason a "cause of evil" was produced in the first place—and if it is nothing in the "wholes" but only in the "parts"—it must be said to them that the progression of beings is continuous and no void has been left among things that exist. Whether, then, the self- <margin>C</margin>

### PROCLUS
272

...otherwise all life would have to be immobile <note>original: "akinēton"</note>; but in doing so, we would do away with many of the divine things as well. But should we say the wholes are self-moving <note>term: <term>autokineton</term>; a being that initiates its own motion or choice, a key characteristic of the soul in Neoplatonism</note>, while the parts are not? And how is it possible for there to be totalities deprived of their own parts? 

How would the continuity of beings be preserved if the wholes pre-exist as self-moving, while the parts are merely moved by others <note>original: "heterokinēta"</note>, and yet we were to remove the things in between—those which are not self-moving, yet are partial, becoming involved in relationships because of their partial form, yet being released from that relationship through their self-motion? It is necessary, therefore, that this life also exists as a middle point among beings and a bond between those things arranged as if in opposition <note>original: "ap’ enantias"</note> to one another. Evil is not natural to this life simply because it is essentially the mistress of choices <note>original: "haireseōn"</note>. 

For the body also has an essential tendency toward disease—for it was perishable by its very essence—but disease is not according to its nature. Therefore, disease itself is an evil for the specific part <margin>D</margin> to which this body happened to belong, but it is a good for the totality of bodies. For it was necessary for that which is composed of other things to change into something else. 

Just as it is a good for the nature within us to transform food <note>Proclus compares the "destruction" of food during digestion to the "destruction" of parts in the universe</note> if the living being is to be preserved, so too it is a good for nature as a whole that the part be destroyed, if it is to preserve the totalities always before the parts. For if the parts were produced from the wholes and remained permanently after being produced, the wholes would soon be exhausted once all the parts had been created. From a finite source, if continuous subtraction occurs, the whole must necessarily fail. 

If these things did not happen, either generation would stop, or the change for the partial things would have to come from somewhere else. But this was the original point: the wholes must be preserved. Thus, what is evil for the partial nature is good for the life of the whole. 

Furthermore, let us take up the question from the beginning in another way. For if someone were to ask us whether God willed evil to exist, or did not will it, we shall answer: in both ways. 

He willed it insofar as He provides being to all things—for everything <margin>E</margin> that exists in any way whatsoever in the universe proceeded from the Demiurgic <note>term: <term>Demiurgic</term>; relating to the divine 'Craftsman' who fashions the material world</note> cause. But He did not will it insofar as He makes all things good; for He concealed evil within the use of the good. 

And if you wish to approach this through natural principles: evil arises "of itself" <note>original: "kath’ hauto"</note> from the partial soul, but "by accident" <note>original: "kata symbēbēkos"</note> from God—insofar as it is evil, if someone were even to grant this, seeing as He established the soul. But insofar as it is good, it arises "of itself" from the divine cause, and "by accident" from the soul; for it possesses the good insofar as it occurs according to justice. Furthermore, the punishment itself... <margin>Regarding punishment, Plato in the *Laws*: manuscript A</margin>

<summary>Proclus argues that while evil is a failure of the "part" (the individual soul or body), it is integrated into the "whole" of the universe as a good, much like digestion or the recycling of matter. He concludes that God wills evil only "by accident" as a byproduct of creating self-moving beings, but "of itself" God only wills the good and the justice that rectifies evil.</summary>

### PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS II. 273

...as Plato defined in the *Laws* <note>original: "Nomois"; referring specifically to Book V, 728c</note> regarding its nature: that while it seems to wear down the one who suffers it, it actually resembles the opening of an ulcer. That which cannot be healed without such an action is summoned toward it, so that the soul, having been delivered from its labor pains <note>original: "ōdinos"; often used by Plato to describe the soul's intense internal struggle or creative tension</note> and the frantic terror <note>original: "ptoias"</note> regarding what is shameful, may enter into a state of repentance for its own evils and establish a beginning for its own purification. For shameful and unjust actions appear desirable to the foolish while they are merely anticipated, but once they have occurred, they fill those who committed them with regret; while they are being meditated upon, they make the soul ulcerous, but when they proceed into actualization, they expose their own 

<margin>F</margin> weakness and release the soul from its most shameful labor pains. Some people display this punishment throughout the whole of their lives, while others do so during specific activities. For everyone who does something irrational <note>original: "paralogon"</note> does so by choice, having been impelled toward that which they chose, and bringing into actualization that which previously existed only in the imagination. 

Let us say, then, in summary, that evil exists neither in the Intellectual <note>term: <term>noeros</term>; the realm of pure, divine intellect which is prior to the soul and physical matter</note> beings—for the entire Intellectual race is free from evil—nor in the universal souls, nor in the universal bodies. 

<margin>116</margin> For all "wholes" <note>term: <term>holos</term>; refers to the complete, cosmic entities like the World Soul or the planetary spheres</note> are free from evil, being eternal and always in accordance with their nature. It remains, therefore, that evil exists either in partial souls or in partial bodies. But even among these, it does not exist in their essences—for all their essences come from God—nor in their powers, for these are according to nature. 

It remains, then, that evil exists in their activities <note>original: "energeiais"</note>. And even in souls, it does not exist in the rational part—for all rational parts reach out for the Good—nor in the irrational parts, for these also act according to their nature; rather, it exists in the lack of symmetry <note>original: "asymmetria"</note> between them. Likewise, in bodies, it exists neither in the form—which wishes to master the matter—nor in the matter itself, which yearns to be ordered by the form; rather, it exists in the lack of symmetry between the form and the matter. 

From this, it is clear that all evil exists as a byproduct <note>term: <term>parupostasis</term>; a key Neoplatonic concept where evil has no independent existence but is a "parasitic" byproduct of good intentions or processes</note>. And yet even this byproduct subsists by being "colored" by the Good. Thus, all things are good because of the will of God, and nothing is entirely destitute of the Good in its potential, even if evil exists in whatever way it does. For it was not possible, given that "becoming" <note>original: "genesis"</note> exists, for this byproduct not to exist as well, as it is necessary for the perfection of the whole. 

<margin>B</margin> Regarding evils, then—how they subsist and what kind of providence they receive from the gods—these remarks are sufficient for the present. They have been discussed at greater length in other works <note>original: "en heterois"; likely referring to Proclus's treatise "On the Subsistence of Evil"</note>. However, this much is clear from what has been said: neither is the will of God in vain (for all things are good to God, and there is nothing among beings which is not mastered by the portion of the Good), nor is the phrase "according to its power" <note>original: "kata dynamin"</note> added to the text redundantly. For it does not signify a deficient power, but rather the power that masters all things and, through an abundance of goods, makes all things good.

<summary>Proclus argues that evil is not a primary force but a parasitic "byproduct" arising from the lack of symmetry in partial beings. He concludes that divine providence uses even these flaws to ensure the ultimate goodness and perfection of the entire cosmos.</summary>

### PROCLUS
### ON THE TIMAEUS II. 274

<note>Translator's Note: The right margin of this manuscript is partially lost, affecting the ends of several lines. The translation completes these thoughts based on the standard Greek text of Proclus's commentary.</note>

"Thus, taking over all that was visible—which was not at rest but moving discordantly and without order—he led it into order from disorder, judging that the former was in every way [better than the latter]."
(Plato, *Timaeus* Page 30 A.)

Those associated with Plutarch of Chaeronea <note>Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD), the famous biographer and Middle Platonist philosopher</note> and Atticus <note>Atticus (c. 175 AD), a Platonist who insisted on a literal reading of Plato’s creation story</note> stubbornly insist on these words as testimony that the world has a beginning in time. They even claim that unformed matter <note>original: "hyle"; the raw "stuff" of the universe</note> existed before the world was generated, <margin>C</margin> and that there was also a "maleficent soul" <note>original: "kakergatin psychēn"; a soul that produces disorder</note> which moved this matter. For from where else could movement come, if not from a soul? And if the movement was disordered, it must come from a disordered soul. Indeed, they say Plato stated in the *Laws* <note>original: "Nomois"; referring to Book X, 896d-897d</note> that while the good-natured soul leads all things rightly and with wisdom, the "maleficent" one moves things in a disordered way and leads whatever it manages into discord. They argue that when the "world-making" of the Divine Craftsman <note>term: <term>demiourgos</term>; the divine figure who fashions the physical universe using the Forms as a blueprint</note> occurred, the [material] composition was settled into the structure of the world, and the maleficent soul, becoming a participant in Intellect, was made wise and began to produce a regulated motion. Thus, order was brought to the material by the participation in Form, and order was brought to the soul by the presence of Intellect. 

However, those associated with Porphyry and Iamblichus <note>Porphyry and Iamblichus were later Neoplatonists who favored a symbolic, eternalist reading of Plato</note> reject this opinion as [impossible], because it places the disordered before the ordered and the incomplete before the complete. They argue that such a view assumes a lack of intellect at the foundation of the universe; further, it is not only a mistake regarding the world, but is actually impious toward the Divine Craftsman himself. It either denies his benevolent will entirely, or denies his generative power. For if both his will and power are <margin>D</margin> eternal, then the world must necessarily be created by him eternally. They say, instead, that Plato wished to demonstrate the providence that extends from the Divine Craftsman to the whole of reality. To show what the soul and the Intellect provide—and how many great goods they cause for the world—the account first looks at the entire "body-like" composition by itself, seeing it as discordant and disordered. This is done so that you, by seeing the world as it would be by itself, might be able to distinguish what kind of order comes from the soul and what kind of arrangement it received from the divine creation. While the world itself is [eternal], the philosophical account divides the product from its Maker, and presents in a temporal sequence things that actually exist together simultaneously, because the world is a composite and [conceptually] generated thing. To these correctly stated points, you might also add that...

<summary>Proclus debates whether Plato's account of the world's creation from "disorder" into "order" refers to a literal event in time (as Plutarch and Atticus held) or a conceptual analysis of an eternal universe (as Porphyry and Iamblichus held).</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the exploration of Plato’s creation narrative. On the previous page, Proclus discussed the views of Plutarch and Atticus regarding the literal "beginning" of the world. Here, he distinguishes between the "making of bodies" and the "ordering of the cosmos," debating whether matter itself is created by God or exists eternally alongside Him.</meta>

### ON THE TIMAEUS II. 275

<note>Translator's Note: The left margin of this manuscript is missing characters. The translation restores the sense of the text based on standard editions of Proclus.</note>

...[Since there are two types] of demiurgic <note>original: "demiurgikēs"; the work of the Divine Craftsman</note> making—one being the making of bodies <note>original: "sōmatourgikēs"</note> and the other being the work of ordering <note>original: "kosmētikēs"</note>—
Plato, beginning from this work of ordering, supposes that all that is bodily exists in every way and altogether, but is moving discordantly and without order. <margin>E</margin>
For it is such a thing by its own nature—an unordered motion—having not yet become mindful in itself,
nor yet having been ensouled by the intellectual soul. For when the Whole <note>the Universe</note> becomes such a thing,
it participates in supernatural powers. But if it is movable as something naturally movable,
and is moved neither by Intellect nor by a wise soul (from which order arises), it will produce a disordered
motion. A little later, he will also hand down to us the body-making aspect of the demi-
urgic providence. For the Creator <note>original: "dēmiourgos"</note> fashions for himself all that is bodily—which he now
says he "takes over"—being himself the maker, himself the decorator, himself the
[producer], himself the craftsman. If, therefore, he also produces the primary bodies, it is clear
that their generation is also a part of the craftsmanship, the visible world having received
the "precursory traces" of the forms before their full articulation; once that articulation occurs, each thing
is perfectly ordered and holds its proper place and rank in the universe. And
concerning that which moves discordantly and without order, there is not much more to say; he
himself will expressly state <note>original: "erē"; referring to *Timaeus* 52d</note> that God builds all that is bodily within the soul.
Furthermore, it is clear that in the case of the soul, it was not as if one part was a pre-existing substrate while he produced only <margin>F</margin>
the ordering. For he established the essence itself first—both the Same
and the Other—from which the soul is composed as if from elements. If, then, he produced the elements
of the soul and the mixture <note>original: "krama"</note> arising from them, he produced the soul in its entirety, and did not
"take over" one part while adding the other himself. While this is true regarding the incorporeal soul,
regarding the body, we accept that God is the cause of the primary forms; but concerning matter itself, one might
ask whether it is ungenerated <note>original: "agenētos"; without a beginning or cause</note> from a cause (as those around Plutarch and
Atticus say), or whether it is <margin>117</margin> generated, and from what cause. For Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), Plato’s student, who argued for an eternal universe</note>
demonstrated in another way that matter is ungenerated, as it is not composite nor subsisting from other matter,
nor again being dissolved into anything else. But the present discourse maintains that it is eternal,
yet it seeks to know if it is "ungenerated from a cause," and if these two are the primary principles <note>term: "archai"; the ultimate "starting points" or "first causes" of reality</note>
of the whole according to Plato—Matter and God—with God not producing Matter
nor Matter producing God, so that Matter is entirely eternal and "without God," while God
is entirely [pure] and simple. This very subject is among those most heavily debated,
and we have spoken of it elsewhere; but for now, it is enough to examine these men's views to see
what Plato’s intention truly is. For it is clear from what he will say further on that the
Demiurge is not the first to establish matter, for these three things [existed before the world]...

<summary>Proclus examines the role of the Divine Craftsman in ordering pre-existing "discordant" matter, debating whether matter is an independent eternal principle or something caused by God. He contrasts the literalist views of Plutarch and Atticus with a more nuanced Neoplatonic understanding of eternal generation.</summary>

--- Page 329 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page follows the discussion of whether the world had a temporal beginning. Proclus is now moving into a deeper metaphysical analysis of the origins of matter (hyle), arguing that Plato views matter not as an independent eternal substance, but as something derived from higher divine principles—specifically the principle of "Infinity."</meta>

### PROCLUS

...to precede the generation of the cosmos, which he calls both "place" and "generation," <note>original: "chōran kai genesin"</note> calling generation the "offspring" and place the "mother." Through these terms, he appears to distinguish <margin>B</margin> **matter** from the **Demiurge** <note>The Divine Craftsman or Creator</note> according to the specific traits of "maternal" and "paternal" roles, while suggesting that "generation" is produced by both the Demiurge and matter together. Perhaps, then, he establishes matter from another rank of existence ordered before the Demiurge. Indeed, in the *Philebus*, Plato writes explicitly: "We say that God revealed the **Limit** <term>peras; the principle of boundary and definition</term> of all beings, and also the **Infinite** <term>apeiron; the principle of multiplicity and potentiality</term>, from which both bodies and all things have their composition."

If, therefore, bodies are composed of Limit and Infinity, what is the "Limit" within them, and what is the "Infinity"? It is clear that we should call **matter** "Infinity" and **form** "Limit." If, as we have said, God establishes all Infinity, then He also establishes matter, which is the "ultimate" or "lowest" form of Infinity. This is the primary and ineffable cause of matter. 

Now, since Plato establishes that everything in the sensible world exists in analogy to its intelligible causes—for example, "equality" here <margin>C</margin> comes from "Equality Itself," and "likeness" and all animals and plants here come from their divine counterparts—it is clear that he derives the **Infinity** found here in the physical world from the **Primary Infinity**, just as he derives the **Limit** here from the **Primary Limit**. It has been shown elsewhere that he establishes this Primary Infinity (the one existing before "mixed" beings) at the very summit of the Intelligible realm. From there, its radiance extends all the way to the lowest things. Thus, according to Plato, matter proceeds from both **the One** and **Being**; or, if you prefer, it proceeds from the **One-Being** <note>The first stage of reality after the Absolute One</note> insofar as it is "potential being."

For this reason, matter is in a sense "good" and "infinite," yet also most obscure and formless, existing as it does before the arrival of forms and their manifestation. Orpheus <note>Proclus frequently cites the mythical poet Orpheus as the "Theologian" who provided the mysteries Plato later turned into philosophy</note> hands down these same doctrines. Just as Plato produced two causes from the One—Limit and Infinity—so too does the Theologian <note>Orpheus</note> establish **Aether** and **Chaos** as arising from **Time** <note>Chronos, the first principle in Orphic cosmogony</note>. He makes Aether the cause of all Limit and Chaos the cause of all Infinity. 

From these two principles, he generates the divine orders of the world, both hidden and manifest. From the "higher" principle <note>Aether/Limit</note> comes everything that is stable, identical, measuring, and containing. From the "remaining" principle <note>Chaos/Infinity</note> <margin>D</margin> comes all that is mobile, changing, and an inexhaustible progression; this includes the nature that is defined by others and held together by others, and finally, the **Ultimate Infinity**, by which matter is encompassed. For this reason, matter is "dissimilarly likened" <note>original: "anomoiōs hōmoiōtai"; it resembles its divine source only in a paradoxical, distant way</note> to its source. It is a "receptacle" <note>original: "chōrisma"</note>, acting as the "place" and "room" for forms, yet it is neither a limit nor a solid foundation...

<summary>Proclus argues that matter is not an independent accident but is divinely created, deriving from the principle of "Infinity" found in both Plato's Philebus and Orphic theology (as Chaos).</summary>
<keywords>Matter, Hyle, Limit, Infinity, Peras, Apeiron, Philebus, Orpheus, Aether, Chaos, Demiurge, Intelligible Causes</keywords>

--- Page 330 ---
<meta>Continuity: Proclus continues his examination of Plato’s *Timaeus*, specifically focusing on the relationship between the Creator (the Demiurge) and the pre-cosmic state of matter. He is transitioning from a discussion on the "Infinite" as a divine principle to the practical "ordering" of the physical world.</meta>

### ON THE TIMAEUS, BOOK II.

...creation being of two kinds: one that produces the body <note>original: *sōmatourgikēs*</note>, and the other that provides the arrangement <note>original: *kosmētikēs*</note>. Beginning with the arrangement, Plato establishes <margin>E</margin> that all physical substance exists in every way and altogether, but that it moves in a discordant and disordered fashion. He sees it as possessing such motion in itself, not yet having become mindful <note>original: *ennoun*</note> as far as its own nature allowed, before it was inhabited by the intellectual soul. For when the "Whole" <term>the Totality of the universe</term> becomes such a thing, it participates in innate powers. But if it is movable because it is naturally prone to motion, yet not directed by a wise soul—from which order arises—it will produce disorder. 

A little later, Plato will also hand down to us the "body-making" aspect of the divine craftsmanship. For the Creator molds for himself the entirety of the physical, which Plato now calls "Him" <note>referring to the Demiurge</note>, identifying Him as the Maker, the Orderer, and the Craftsman <term>cheirourgon; literally "one who works with his hands"</term>. If, therefore, He also brings forth the primary bodies, it is clear that their generation also belongs to His craftsmanship; the visible realm receives the preliminary traces of their articulation, and once this is complete, each thing perfectly possesses both its position in the universe and its fitting order. 

There is no need for a long discourse regarding that which moves "discordantly and disordered." For Plato himself will say <margin>F</margin> that God builds the entire physical world within the Soul. It is clear that the Soul was not just a pre-existing substrate to which He merely added something; rather, he says He established the very essence of the soul first, as well as the "Other" <note>referring to the "Same" and "Other," the metaphysical components of the Platonic Soul</note>, from which it is composed as if from elements. If, then, He brought forth both the elements and the mixture <note>original: *krama*</note> made from them, He brought forth the whole, and did not simply add one part to another. 

While this is true for the Soul, which is incorporeal, one might ask a different question regarding the Body and the primary forms: it has been shown in a way that God is the cause of these, but what of **Matter** itself? Is it "ungenerated" <note>original: *agennētos*</note> without a cause, as the followers of Plutarch <margin>117</margin> and Atticus <note>Platonist philosophers who believed matter was an eternal, chaotic principle independent of God</note> claim, or is it generated, and from what cause? 

Aristotle, for his part, demonstrated that matter is "ungenerated" in the sense that it is not a composite, nor does it arise from some other underlying matter, nor is it dissolved into anything else. However, the present argument says that matter is "eternal" <note>original: *aidion*</note>, but asks whether it is "ungenerated" in the sense of having no cause. Should we follow Plato in setting down these two as the principles of the whole—Matter and God—with neither God producing Matter, nor Matter producing God? This would mean Matter is entirely eternal and "godless" <term>atheos; in the sense of existing without divine origin</term>, while God is eternal and simple. This specific problem is among the most highly debated, and we have discussed it elsewhere; for now, it is enough to demonstrate to these men what Plato's true intention is. That the Creator does **not** bring matter into existence is clearly seen from what he will say further on, namely these three things...
